Psalm 110:1 — “The Lord says to my Lord: Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool” — is the most-quoted Old Testament text in the New Testament. The early church was obsessed with it because it explained everything: Christ reigns now, at the Father’s right hand, over all things, for his church (Ephesians 1:20–23). He is not waiting to begin his kingdom; his kingdom is already here, hidden but real, advancing through the witness of the Spirit-filled church. Every prayer prayed in his name, every sermon preached, every soul converted is an act of the reigning Christ extending his dominion.
1.examples:
Then: The disciples in Jerusalem, staring at the sky, confused about timing and kingdom, learning that faithfulness in the interval between the ascension and the return looks like prayer and witness. They had no map, no strategy document, no budget — only a promise and an upper room.

Now: We live in the same interval — between the first coming and the second, between the already and the not-yet. The temptation is still to stand looking into heaven, obsessing over the date of the return, while the mission sits unfinished at our feet. The command is unchanged: wait in prayer, go in the Spirit, witness to the ends of the earth. He is coming. In the meantime, there is work.

2.title: The Spirit Poured Out

And the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved.
2.overview:
Everything changes on the day of Pentecost. The sound of a rushing wind fills the house — not a gentle breeze but a roar, a theophany, the breath of God filling the room as he once breathed life into Adam’s nostrils. Tongues of fire rest on each one of them — not one tongue over Peter, not one flame above the leaders, but one for each. The Spirit is poured out, as Joel said, on all flesh. This is not an upgrade of the old covenant. This is the new creation beginning.

Peter stands up. This is the same Peter who three times denied knowing Jesus by a charcoal fire. Now he stands before thousands and opens his mouth and the Scripture pours out — Joel, David, the resurrection, the exaltation, the gift of the Spirit. The sermon does not argue for the resurrection; it announces it. And the announcement lands with the force of a hammer: “they were cut to the heart.” Three thousand baptized in one day. The church is born not by strategy but by proclamation.

And then the four marks of the early church appear, simple and complete: the apostles’ teaching, the fellowship, the breaking of bread, and the prayers. Everything the church needs to be the church was given on that day and has never been taken back.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Coming of the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Fifty days after a Friday execution, in a house in Jerusalem, the sound of a gale fills a room where the air is not moving. Fire appears and does not burn. A hundred and twenty Galileans walk out into a festival crowd and begin speaking the languages of Parthia and Egypt and Rome, and the men who own those languages stand in the street and hear their own mother tongue coming out of the mouths of provincials who have never left home. That is the morning. Luke reports it with three careful comparisons — a sound like wind, tongues as of fire, other tongues — because he is a precise writer describing something for which the vocabulary had not yet been invented.

What it means is Babel run backwards. At Babel the human race, united in ambition and building upward, was scattered by having its speech confused, and from that day the map of the world has also been a map of misunderstanding. At Pentecost God does not abolish the languages. He fills them. He does not gather the nations into one tongue; he says the same thing in all of them at once. The curse is not repealed so much as conquered — every language that was a wall is now a road, and the church has been building roads out of them ever since.

Then the crowd divides, as crowds do. Some ask the honest question — What does this mean? — which is the question the rest of the book is written to answer. Others reach for the cheapest explanation available and say the men are drunk, at nine in the morning, on wine that will not be pressed for another three months. The open question and the closed dismissal stand side by side in verses 12 and 13, and they have stood side by side at every proclamation of the gospel since. Peter preaches to both of them without distinguishing between them, and three thousand people are baptised before the day is out.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit and the Age He Opens

The Old Testament had promised a day when God would put his Spirit not on a handful of officeholders but on his whole people — Joel 2, Ezekiel 36–37 and Jeremiah 31 all say it, and Moses had wished for it out loud a thousand years earlier (Numbers 11:29). Pentecost is that day arriving. This governs how the event should be read. The Spirit's coming is not a private enrichment handed to a hundred and twenty people who happened to pray hard enough; it is a public, datable, once-for-all act in the history of salvation, standing alongside the birth, the cross and the empty tomb. Christ was born once, died once, rose once, and poured out his Spirit once. What is repeated afterwards is not the outpouring but the filling — and Luke will use that second word again of these same people (4:8, 4:31, 13:9), which is a mercy, because it means what happened to them is not sealed inside one morning in the first century.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Parthians, Medes, Elamites, residents of Mesopotamia — the first four names on Luke's list are exile addresses. Assyria deported the northern tribes to Halah, and on the Habor, the river of Gozan, and to the cities of the Medes (2 Kings 17:6), and seven centuries later the descendants of the deported are standing in a Jerusalem street hearing the mighty works of God in the language of the country their forefathers were carried off to. Now: The same thing happens every time the Bible is put into a language that has never had it. The God who gave the church its first sermon in fifteen languages at once has never shown the slightest interest in making anyone learn a holy one first.

verseByVerse.quote: When the day of Pentecost arrived, they were all together in one place. And suddenly there came from heaven a sound like a mighty rushing wind, and it filled the entire house where they were sitting.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke does not say the day of Pentecost came. He says it was fulfilled — the verb is the one used of a term running out, of a measure filling up to the brim. Fifty days had been counted off since the sabbath of Passover week, exactly as Leviticus 23 prescribes, by every observant household in the empire; and on the morning the count reached its end, the thing the counting had been counting toward walked into the room. That calendar had been pregnant for fifteen centuries.

Consider what the feast was for. At Passover a farmer brought the first sheaf of barley and waved it before the LORD. Fifty days later, at Weeks, he brought two loaves of ordinary bread baked from the new wheat — and, alone among Israel's offerings, baked with leaven (Leviticus 23:17). It is the one loaf on the altar made the way bread is made at home. The whole feast was firstfruits: a handful brought in early as the guarantee that the fields were coming. That is the morning God chose. Before the day is out, three thousand people will be brought in as the firstfruits of a harvest that is still coming.

Then the sound. Luke, who is careful with words, does not write that a wind came. He writes that there came a sound like a mighty rushing wind, and he marks the comparison as a comparison. Nothing was blowing. Nothing in that room moved. What filled the house was the noise a gale makes without the gale — which is stranger than a storm and considerably harder to explain away. The word he chooses, pnoe, is the word the Greek Old Testament uses in Genesis 2:7 for the breath God breathed into a figure of dust until it sat up and became a living man. The same breath is in this room, and what is about to sit up is the church.

Notice also the order. It filled the house, and then, in the next verse, the people. God takes the building before he takes the men in it.

The last thing to see is what the hundred and twenty were doing when it happened. They were sitting. Ten days earlier they had been told to stay in the city and wait (1:4), and they had done that and nothing else — no campaign, no technique, no working up of atmosphere. Whatever else Pentecost is, it is not something anybody in that room produced. That is worth holding onto by any Christian who has been told that the Spirit's work in a life or a congregation can be triggered by sufficient intensity, and who has tried it, and has come away concluding that the failure must be his. It cannot be triggered. It can only be waited for, in the place obedience has put you, on a morning God has already circled on a calendar you have not been shown.

verseByVerse.quote: And divided tongues as of fire appeared to them and rested on each one of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fire in Scripture is where God is and where God may not be touched — the bush that burned and was not eaten (Exodus 3:2), the pillar that went before Israel by night, the fire that fell on Carmel, the coal carried off the altar to Isaiah's mouth. Every one of them is a fire kept at a distance, or a fire that would have killed a man who came nearer. Here it comes down and settles on people's heads, and nobody dies. The whole gospel is in that picture: the fire that could not be approached has come to rest on the very thing it should have consumed.

Two details in the sentence carry a great deal. The first is divided. Fire is the one thing that can be shared without being lessened; light a hundred candles from a single flame and the flame you started with is no smaller. The Spirit is not being rationed out in portions, a larger share for the apostles and a thinner one for everybody else. The second is each one of them. In the old covenant the Spirit came on the man with the office — on Moses, on Bezalel to design the tabernacle, on Gideon, on Samson, on Saul, on David. Never on everybody. Now the flame settles on a fisherman, on Mary, on the brothers who had once thought Jesus was out of his mind (John 7:5), on a great many people whose names Luke does not trouble to record. Moses had said out loud that he wished it were so (Numbers 11:29). It took a thousand years, and it happened on a Sunday morning in a borrowed room.

They began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance. The Greek word for tongues is the same word Luke has just used for the tongues of fire; the sign was shaped like the gift it announced. And the gift itself is unambiguous in this chapter — real, existing, human languages, because the crowd outside identifies them and says so three times (vv. 6, 8, 11). Nobody here is in a trance. They are speaking Coptic and Latin and Parthian.

Which raises the question every reader of this chapter eventually asks: is this the gift Paul discusses at Corinth? The two are not obviously identical. What happens here is understood instantly by native speakers; what happens at Corinth needs an interpreter and is unintelligible to the hearer without one (1 Corinthians 14:2). Some conclude they are two gifts sharing a name. Others, more probably, take them as one gift in two settings — a genuine language is a sign to the man who owns it and undecipherable noise to everyone else, and there were no Parthians in the Corinthian assembly. The text does not settle it, and a reader is allowed to leave it unsettled.

What should not be left unsettled is the pastoral use this verse is put to. It is regularly held over believers as the test of whether the Spirit is truly in them. Scripture will not carry that. Paul asks the Corinthians, in a run of rhetorical questions built so that the answer to every one of them is no, Do all speak with tongues? (1 Corinthians 12:30). The apostle who wrote more about the gift than anyone else expects the answer to be no, and says so to a church that prized it above everything. A Christian who has never spoken a syllable of another language is not standing outside anything. And the traffic runs both ways: the same chapter forbids the contempt that says I have no need of you, so a believer who is quietly certain the whole business is nonsense should notice that Paul did not say that either.

Luke, for his part, tells us plainly what the fire was for, and it is not an experience. As the Spirit gave them utterance — the first recorded act of the Spirit in the church is to make ordinary people talk about God to strangers, out loud, in the street, in words the strangers can understand.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men from every nation under heaven. And at this sound the multitude came together, and they were bewildered, because each one was hearing them speak in his own language.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word Luke uses of these men — dwelling in Jerusalem — does not mean visiting. He has a separate word for visitors and uses it five verses later of the Romans. These are residents: Jews born in Parthia or Egypt or Cappadocia who had come back and settled. Some had come for the schools. A great many had come home to die. It was the deep desire of Diaspora Jews to be buried in the land, and near the temple if it could be arranged, and the hills around Jerusalem were quarried with the tombs of men who had crossed an empire in old age so that their bones would lie in the right country. On this particular morning some of those men, who had organised the whole last chapter of their lives around a grave, stood in a street and heard, in the language they had learned as children, that a man had been raised from the dead.

Devout is Luke's word for a certain kind of serious Israelite. He uses it of old Simeon waiting in the temple for the consolation of Israel (Luke 2:25), and later of the men brave enough to bury Stephen (8:2). These are not sightseers at a festival. They are the people who had been waiting.

Then the sound draws a crowd, and the crowd is bewildered. The Greek verb repays stopping over. It is the verb the Greek Old Testament uses at Babel: the LORD confused the language of all the earth (Genesis 11:9). Luke has reached for Babel's own word and turned it inside out. At Babel men were thrown into confusion because they suddenly could not understand one another. Here they are thrown into confusion because they suddenly can. The same bewilderment, running the other way.

And it is a specific bewilderment. They are not staggered by volume or spectacle. They are staggered by intelligibility: each man is hearing his own language. Where exactly the miracle sits is worth naming, because it is sometimes suggested that it happened in the ears rather than the mouths. Verse 4 has already settled it — the disciples began to speak in other tongues. God did not adjust fifteen nationalities of hearing. He gave a hundred and twenty Galileans fifteen nationalities of speech.

Consider what that decision discloses about him. He could have done this in Hebrew, the language of the covenant, and required every nation to come and learn it, which is what every other religion in that world required of anyone who wanted to approach. He did the exact opposite. The first sermon of the Christian era was delivered in the languages people count money in, swear in when they drop something, and sing over their children at night. From the first morning of the church, God has been the one who crosses the room.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were amazed and astonished, saying, "Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? And how is it that we hear, each of us in his own native language?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd's objection is an accent. Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? — and everyone in that street knew what a Galilean sounded like. The northern pronunciation was a standing joke in Judea; Galileans were said to swallow their gutturals so badly that a hearer could not tell which word was meant, and for that reason a Galilean was not always allowed to read the Scriptures aloud in a synagogue. It was the accent of the provinces — fishing villages, small farms, no rabbinic schools within a day's walk.

Which makes the identity of the man about to do the talking almost unbearable. Fifty-three days before this, in a high priest's courtyard, a servant girl looked at Peter and said, Certainly you too are one of them, for your accent betrays you — and he swore he had never met the man. The accent that exposed him as a coward is the accent now filling a public square with the resurrection. God did not give Peter a new voice. He gave him a new message and sent him back out with the same voice that had denied it, into the same city, to be identified by the same sound.

Anyone who has kept quiet about Christ because of how they sound should sit with that for a moment. The disqualification this crowd cannot get past is a regional accent. The disqualification most believers privately hold against themselves is of precisely that order — not enough education, the wrong background, a stammer, a criminal record, a voice that goes thin exactly when it matters. The council will lodge the same complaint against these men in chapter 4, where it is answered at length.

What must not be drawn out of it is the sneer's mirror image — that learning is a hindrance and ignorance a qualification. Luke writes some of the most polished Greek in the New Testament. The man who will do more preaching than anyone else in this book was trained under Gamaliel. The point is not that God prefers the untaught; it is that he is not confined by the paperwork, and that on this morning a set of credentials which mattered enormously in that street abruptly stopped mattering at all.

Luke stacks two verbs on the crowd: they were amazed and they marvelled. The first means, literally, to be put out of one's place — the same verb used of Jairus and his wife when their dead daughter sat up and asked for something to eat (Luke 8:56). That is where the chapter stands by verse 8: several thousand religious, sober, widely travelled men in a street at nine in the morning with no category left to put the thing in. It is exactly the right condition in which to hear a sermon, and Peter is about to stand up and preach one.

verseByVerse.quote: Parthians and Medes and Elamites and residents of Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya belonging to Cyrene, and visitors from Rome,
verseByVerse.commentary:
A reader's eye slides over a list of place names. Luke put it in on purpose, and it repays being read as a map rather than as a catalogue.

He begins in the far east, outside the empire altogether. Parthia was the one great power Rome never managed to conquer; for a man standing in Jerusalem the Euphrates was the edge of the known world, and Luke opens his list on the wrong side of it. Then Media and Elam and Mesopotamia — and those names are exile addresses. When Assyria carried the northern tribes away it settled them in Halah, and on the Habor, the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes (2 Kings 17:6). Seven hundred years later the descendants of the deported are standing in a Jerusalem street. No king ever brought them home in triumph. They had trickled back, family by family, over centuries — and on this morning God gathers a scattering that history never repaired, and preaches to it.

From there the list sweeps north and west through Asia Minor — Cappadocia, Pontus, Asia, Phrygia, Pamphylia — which is very nearly the route Paul will spend the second half of this book walking. Then south to Egypt, whose Jewish community at Alexandria was large enough to have produced its own translation of the Scriptures, and along the coast to Cyrene, whose Jews turn up again in this book both as opponents (6:9) and as the men who first preached to Greeks at Antioch (11:20), and one of whom had carried a cross up a hill outside this city seven weeks earlier. And the list ends at Rome, which is where Luke's own second volume ends (28:16). He names his destination on page two.

One oddity deserves an honest word. Judea sits in the middle of the list, between Mesopotamia and Cappadocia, which is strange in a roll-call of foreign parts and stranger still as geography. Ancient copyists were bothered enough to try substituting other names. The simplest explanation is that Luke is tracing the arc of the Fertile Crescent from east to north-west and Judea lies on the arc, named as territory rather than as a foreign country. It is exactly the sort of small roughness a fabricated list would not have; a forger tidies.

Underneath the geography a promise is being kept in the wrong order. Jesus had said the witness would go from Jerusalem to Judea and Samaria and to the end of the earth (1:8). On the first morning, the end of the earth has come to Jerusalem. Before a single missionary has packed a bag, the gospel is being heard by men who will carry it home to Parthia and Egypt and Rome — which is why, when Paul finally writes to the Roman church years later, he is writing to a congregation he did not plant and had never visited. Somebody in this street was listening.

verseByVerse.quote: both Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabians — we hear them telling in our own tongues the mighty works of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list ends with two words that widen it past nationality altogether. Proselytes were Gentiles who had gone the whole distance into Judaism, and the distance was considerable. A man born in Rome or Cyrene who wanted in did not merely change his opinions. He renounced the gods his family had honoured for generations, which in that world meant walking out of his own household's religion and frequently out of his standing in the city. He was circumcised as an adult, without anaesthetic. He was immersed. He brought an offering. And having paid all of it he remained, in many eyes, a second-tier member of the covenant, admitted no further into the temple than the outer court. Such men are in this crowd, hearing the wonders of God in their own language — and within twenty years the church will meet in this same city to decide whether Gentiles need any of that machinery at all (15:1–11). The door they crawled through is about to be taken off its hinges.

Then Cretans and Arabians, the far islands and the desert, added as if to say the list could go on. And then the sentence that tells us what all these languages were being used to say.

We hear them telling in our own tongues the mighty works of God. The phrase Luke uses is Old Testament vocabulary; in the Greek Bible it is the language for the great things God did in bringing Israel out of Egypt — the plagues, the sea, the pillar of fire (Deuteronomy 11:2). The first Christian speech in history was not a body of moral instruction and it was not a report of religious feelings. It was a recital of things God had done, in the same register Israel used for the exodus, now attached to a tomb outside a city wall.

That order has never changed, and it is worth testing yourself against. Christianity is first news and only afterwards advice. Subtract the announcement — suppose God has not in fact done anything, suppose nothing happened in Jerusalem that spring — and what is left is a philosophy of life, and there are cheaper ones on the market. This is not to say a believer's own story does not matter; Paul tells his three times in this book. But notice what actually filled the street on the first morning. Not a hundred and twenty people describing what had happened to them. A hundred and twenty people describing what God had done.

And it is worth saying plainly what a strange and glorious way that is for God to introduce himself to the nations. He does not open with a demand. He opens by reciting his own acts of rescue, in fifteen languages at once, to men who had crossed an empire in order to worship him at a distance and had no idea he had come out into the street to meet them.

verseByVerse.quote: And all were amazed and perplexed, saying to one another, "What does this mean?" But others mocking said, "They are filled with new wine."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two sentences, and every crowd that has ever heard the gospel is inside them.

The first is a real question. What does this mean? — in Greek, more nearly, what does this want to be? These men have no explanation and they say so, and by saying so they hold a door open. The whole of the rest of the book is an answer to that sentence. It is also, in miniature, the difference between the two halves of this crowd: one group has run out of explanations and admits it, the other has run out of explanations and invents one.

Because the second sentence is not an argument. They are filled with new wine. Notice how poor an explanation it is. The word is gleukos, the sweet juice of a fresh pressing — and Pentecost falls in late spring with the vintage a good three months away. Nor was there any drinking to be had at that hour on a feast morning, when observant men did not eat or drink before the morning prayer, which is precisely the point Peter makes in his first breath. The mockers were not weighing evidence. They grabbed the nearest available insult and did not stop to check whether it fitted the season.

That is generally how the closed dismissal works. It does not need to be true. It only needs to arrive fast enough to spare a man from standing there with no explanation, which is an uncomfortable place to stand. Anyone who has tried to speak about Christ at work has met the sentence that comes too quickly to be a real reply — that's fine for you, people believe what they need to believe — and has felt how efficiently it closes a conversation that had not yet begun.

There is one thing the sneer concedes without meaning to. Drunkenness was the closest thing these men could find to what they were watching. Whatever was happening in that street, it did not look like a ceremony being performed correctly. It looked like people who had stopped guarding themselves. Paul later plays the comparison back the other way and tells the Ephesians not to get drunk with wine but to be filled with the Spirit, as though the two sit on the same shelf and only one of them delivers what it advertises.

And here is what should stop any believer writing off the scoffer at the back. Peter preaches to both halves of this crowd without distinguishing between them, and by evening three thousand of them have been baptised. The arithmetic guarantees that some of the men shouting about new wine at nine in the morning were in the water before dark. Nobody in that street was beyond the reach of the next twenty minutes. It is a poor idea to conclude from one dismissive sentence that a person is finished; the gospel has a long history of being sneered at by people who go on to preach it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–36 — Peter's Sermon: The Risen Christ Proclaimed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
This is the first Christian sermon, and the most striking thing about it is who is preaching. Seven weeks earlier this man could not hold his claim to know Jesus in front of a servant girl warming herself at a fire. He is now standing in the middle of Jerusalem, in the city that killed his master, in front of several thousand people, some of whom had shouted for the execution, saying out loud that they crucified the Lord and that God raised him. Nothing in Peter's temperament accounts for that. Something happened at nine o'clock that morning.

The sermon runs in three movements, each anchored in a text. First, an explanation of what the crowd is looking at, out of Joel 2 (vv. 14–21): this is not drunkenness, it is the promised outpouring, and the age it opens is one in which anyone at all may call on the name of the Lord and be saved. Second, the announcement of Jesus — publicly accredited, crucified by wicked hands and by God's settled plan, raised — with Psalm 16 brought in to show that David was writing about a grave that stayed clean, which his own emphatically did not (vv. 22–32). Third, the exaltation, out of Psalm 110: the noise the crowd can hear is the receipt for a coronation they cannot see, and the man they condemned has been installed as Lord and Christ (vv. 33–36).

Notice what Peter never does. He does not argue for the resurrection from probability. He asserts it, produces eleven eyewitnesses standing at his shoulder, points at a tomb in their own city that still has David in it, and then shows them a hundred and twenty people speaking languages they never learned and asks the crowd to account for it. And he issues no appeal at all. The call to repent does not come until verse 38, and only after the crowd has interrupted to ask for it. He preaches Christ, and lets the Spirit do the wounding.
verseByVerse.theology:
How Peter Reads the Psalms

Peter's argument from Psalm 16 is not proof-texting; it is a method, and he shows his working. David wrote you will not let your Holy One see corruption. David died, was buried, and his tomb was a landmark a short walk from where Peter was standing. Therefore the words say more than David's own life could pay, and they are prophecy — and the man they fit is the one whose tomb is empty. He does the same with Psalm 110: David did not ascend into the heavens, so the psalm in which David hears the LORD speak to my Lord must be about somebody else. This is the way the risen Christ himself had taught them to read on the road to Emmaus, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets (Luke 24:27, 44). The Reformed tradition has taken this sermon as the pattern for reading the whole Old Testament — not squeezing Christ out of texts that will not hold him, but recognising that the Scriptures were written by a Spirit who knew where the story was going and left the shape of it in the words.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter preached to people who were personally implicated — this Jesus whom you crucified — and he said it to their faces in the seventh week after they had done it. He did not soften the charge in order to get a hearing, and three thousand of them were baptised before dark. Now: A gospel that never implicates the hearer never has anything to forgive him for. The reason this crowd asked what shall we do is that Peter had left them with something that needed doing. Preaching which manages to be about sin in general, committed by people in general, will produce interest, and will not produce that question.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter, standing with the eleven, lifted up his voice and addressed them: "Men of Judea and all who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and give ear to my words. For these people are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is only the third hour of the day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three details before the sermon starts carry more than they look. Standing with the eleven — Peter is not a solo act, and Luke has counted: eleven beside him makes twelve, the number restored eight verses earlier when the lot fell on Matthias (1:26). The apostolic band is complete and standing together on its first working day. What follows is testimony, not personality.

Lifted up his voice is a phrase straight out of the Greek Old Testament, the formula for a solemn public declaration. It is also, quite literally, what he had to do. There was no amplification of any kind. Preaching to thousands in the open air meant shouting until the throat tore and the men at the back strained to catch it. The church was born out of one man's raw throat.

Then the defence, which is almost dry. These people are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is only the third hour of the day. Nine in the morning — and the point is sharper than a modern reader hears, because on a feast day observant Jews took nothing at all before the morning sacrifice and prayer. Peter is not merely saying it is early. He is saying that what the mockers have alleged would have been an act of impiety on a holy day in a city full of people who would have noticed. He disposes of the charge in a sentence and never returns to it. It is not what he came to talk about; it is only the door the mockers accidentally held open for him.

But stay with the man a moment longer. This is the same voice. Fifty-three days ago, in this city, under pressure from a girl with no authority over anybody, it said I do not know the man — three times, the last time with oaths. It is now saying, at the top of its range, to the assembled population of the city and within earshot of the authorities who arranged the execution, that the man they killed is alive and is Lord. Between those two mornings Peter attended no course. Nor did he simply resolve to do better; he had already tried that, had promised out loud that he would die first, and had folded inside a few hours. What came between was Pentecost.

That is worth pressing, because the standard advice to a frightened Christian is to try harder, and Peter's own history is the standing refutation of it. His problem was never a shortage of determination. He had determination in quantity, and at the point of testing it was worth nothing. What he lacked was the Spirit; and when the Spirit came, the courage came with him — not as a technique to be mastered but as a Person to be received. The church's boldness has the same source this morning that it had at nine o'clock on that one, which is an enormous relief to anybody who has already found out what his own resolve is worth.

And note whom he addresses: men of Judea and all who dwell in Jerusalem — the settled residents of verse 5, the Diaspora that had come home. He is speaking to the people who had spent their lives waiting, and he opens by telling them the waiting is over.

verseByVerse.quote: "But this is what was uttered through the prophet Joel:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
These few words are the hinge of the sermon: this is what was uttered through the prophet Joel. Peter's first move is not to explain the phenomenon, or defend it, or invite anyone to admire it. It is to say that this was on the schedule. Nothing new has happened. Something promised has happened.

It is worth knowing which book he has reached into, because Joel is not the obvious place to go on a morning of glory. Joel is about locusts. A real swarm had come through a real country and stripped it — what the cutting locust left, the swarming locust has eaten, four waves of them, the vine withered, the fig tree dried up, the grain offering cut off from the house of the LORD, the priests in mourning and the cattle wandering because there was no pasture. It is one of the bleakest chapters in the prophets, and it is not a figure of speech for something else; the farmers were ruined. Out of that ruin God makes the promise everybody knows: I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten (Joel 2:25). And immediately after the promise of the restored years comes the promise of the Spirit.

That is what Peter reaches for. The outpouring this crowd is watching is the sequel to a promise made to people who had lost everything, and it is the sign that God means to put the years back. Anyone reading this who has lost years — to an illness, to a marriage that came apart, to a decade of his own stupidity, to nursing someone who died anyway — is reading a promise addressed to exactly that condition. The Spirit is not given first to the flourishing. He is promised to a field that has been eaten bare, as the down payment on a harvest that is coming back.

One honest qualification is needed here, because Peter is about to quote a paragraph containing blood and fire and a blackened sun, none of which happened that morning. This is that does not mean the prophecy was used up before breakfast. It means the age Joel described has begun. Scripture habitually speaks of the last days as a single stretch running from the coming of Christ to his return, and Peter is standing at the front of it, quoting the whole span because the era has opened, not because it has closed. The next two verses raise the difficulty head-on, and it is faced there.

What should not be lost in the mechanics is the sheer confidence of the move. A fisherman stands up in front of scholars and tells them what their own Scriptures are about, and he is not guessing. Somebody had taught him to read like this, on a road out of this city seven weeks earlier, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets (Luke 24:27).

verseByVerse.quote: "'And in the last days it shall be, God declares, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams; even on my male servants and female servants in those days I will pour out my Spirit, and they shall prophesy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take the promise slowly, because the shock of it is entirely in the list. Who had the Spirit of God under the old covenant? A very short roll, and nearly every name on it holds an office: Moses and the seventy elders, Bezalel to design the tabernacle, Othniel and Gideon and Samson, Saul and David, the prophets. Perhaps a hundred named individuals across a thousand years, almost all of them men, almost all of them leaders — and the Spirit came upon them for the work and could depart again, which is precisely what David is terrified of when he begs God not to take his Holy Spirit from him (Psalm 51:11). Now read Joel's list against that. Sons and daughters. Young men and old men. And then, so that the direction of travel cannot be mistaken, male servants and female servants — the word means slaves. The lowest person in the household, with no property, no standing, no vote in the synagogue and in most cases no name recorded anywhere on earth, is written into a promise about the Spirit of God.

Note one phrase you may misread: 'in the last days.' Peter takes Joel's 'afterward' and declares 'the last days' to have arrived — at Pentecost. So in the Bible's reckoning the 'last days' are not only a short future window before the end; they are the whole gospel age, from Christ's first coming to his return ('in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son,' Heb. 1:2; 'it is the last hour,' 1 John 2:18). We have been living in the last days for two thousand years. (Scripture does also speak of these days intensifying as the end nears, 2 Tim. 3:1 — a note our dispensational friends rightly stress — but the era as a whole is already underway.) The effect is urgency, not date-setting: we live in the final act of God's story, awaiting only the King's return.

That change is the largest of three, and the other two run the same way. Where Joel says simply that God will pour out his Spirit, Peter inserts God declares, so that the sentence is signed. And where Joel's line about the male and female servants ends without further comment, Peter adds four words — and they shall prophesy. This is not carelessness with a text. It is a man saying what the text turned out to mean, now that he can watch it happening in front of him, and refusing to let the slaves be quietly dropped from the promise on the way past.

Which raises a fair question: what does it mean that the daughters prophesy, and does it still happen? Luke does not leave it hanging. He shows us four of them — the unmarried daughters of Philip the evangelist, prophesying at Caesarea (21:9) — and a prophet named Agabus arriving at the same house. Whatever prophecy is in Acts, it plainly includes women. It should also be said, because this verse is sometimes produced as though it settled every question about women and church office in a single move, that by itself it does not settle that question; the New Testament argues the matter of teaching and eldership from other passages, and believers who read this verse in exactly the same way end up in different places on those. What this verse does establish, and establishes past argument, is that the gift of the Spirit is distributed with no regard whatever to sex, age or social rank. Whatever else is debated, that is not.

And this is the thing to stand still in front of. Under the old covenant the Spirit came down on one man and Israel gathered round him to hear what God had said. Under the new, God has moved into the whole house — the daughters, the old men who assumed their useful years were behind them, the slave girl in the kitchen. He did not spread himself thin in order to manage it. Each of them has the same Spirit, entire and undivided. There is no seniority in the gift and there was never going to be, because the God who gives it is not the kind who runs short.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I will show wonders in the heavens above and signs on the earth below, blood, and fire, and vapor of smoke; the sun shall be turned to darkness and the moon to blood, before the day of the Lord comes, the great and magnificent day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the difficulty every honest reader of this chapter runs into, and this is the place to face it. Peter has just said this is that. He then quotes a paragraph about blood and fire and columns of smoke, a sun turned to darkness and a moon turned to blood — and none of it had happened in Jerusalem that morning. The sun was up. The crowd could see one another's faces. If the prophecy was fulfilled at nine o'clock, a third of it was visibly not.

Three things go a long way toward resolving that, and they are worth having.

The first is that this is simply how the prophets speak of the fall of a power. When Isaiah announces the end of Babylon he says the stars will not give their light and the sun will be dark at its rising (Isaiah 13:10). When he announces the end of Edom the sky rolls up like a scroll (Isaiah 34:4). When Ezekiel announces the end of Egypt, God covers the sun with a cloud and the moon does not give its light (Ezekiel 32:7). Babylon fell. Edom fell. Egypt was humbled. The sun came up through the whole of it. This is not failed prediction, and it is not a code to be broken; it is the settled idiom of Scripture for saying that a world is ending — which, for the people living inside it, is what the fall of a nation actually is. Jesus used the same language of the destruction of Jerusalem, which arrived inside the lifetime of some of the men standing in that street.

The second is that a piece of it had happened, and they had watched it. Fifty-three days earlier, in this city, at midday, the sun went dark for three hours while a man died on a hill outside the wall (Luke 23:44–45). Peter is not describing something his hearers have never seen. He is quoting a prophecy about a darkened sun to people who had stood under one, gone home unsettled, and never been given a satisfactory account of it. Part of the reason this sermon lands as hard as it does may be that the crowd is being handed the meaning of something they had already survived.

The third is the shape of the whole promise. The last days are not a fortnight at the end; they are the entire stretch between the coming of Christ and his return, and Peter is standing at the front of it. He quotes Joel to the end of the paragraph because he is opening an era, not closing one. The signs belong to the era. So does the outpouring. So, above all, does the sentence he is driving toward, which is the next verse and the reason he quoted any of it.

What the passage will not bear is the industry that has grown up on top of it — the charts, the calculated dates, the eclipse tables, the recurring announcements that some particular sequence of blood moons has started a countdown. Every generation of the church has produced men who were certain, and every one of them has been wrong, and the wreckage is not confined to their own embarrassment: people sell houses, and their children lose their faith when the date goes past. The purpose Joel's paragraph actually serves is stated in the line immediately after it. The signs are not a timetable to be decoded. They are a reason to call on the name of the Lord while there is still time to call.

And there is a mercy hidden inside the terrible phrase itself. The day of the Lord was a phrase Israel rather liked, until Amos told them what was in it: Why would you have the day of the LORD? It is darkness, and not light (Amos 5:18). Peter takes the darkest phrase in the prophetic vocabulary, quotes it in full without softening a word, and then uses it as an invitation.

verseByVerse.quote: "And it shall come to pass that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the sentence the whole citation has been climbing toward, and Peter stops here. Joel goes on; Peter does not. He wanted this line.

Take the three parts in turn. Everyone — with no qualifier of nation, class, sex, age or record. Who calls upon the name of the Lord — the single condition, and it is not a work, an achievement or a standard of behaviour; it is the noise a man makes when he has run out. Shall be saved — not may be, not stands a better chance. Peter is quoting a promise, not proposing a scheme.

But there is something here that ought to stop a reader in his tracks, and English hides it. In Joel the word behind the Lord is the covenant name of God, the name Israel would not say aloud and read as Adonai instead. Everyone who calls on the name of YHWH shall be saved — that is what Joel wrote. Peter quotes it; and fifteen verses later he tells the same crowd who the Lord is: God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified. A verse about calling on the unutterable name of the God of Israel has just been applied to a Galilean tradesman who was executed outside the city seven weeks ago.

Nor is it a slip in the excitement of a first sermon. Once you have seen the move it is everywhere in this book. Peter will say there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved (4:12). Saul rides to Damascus with warrants against all who call on your name, which by then is simply the ordinary description of a Christian (9:14), and at his own baptism is told to be washed, calling on his name (22:16). Paul, writing to Rome, quotes this very line of Joel and applies it to Jesus without pausing to justify himself (Romans 10:13). And Stephen dies praying Lord Jesus, receive my spirit — a Jewish monotheist, being executed for blasphemy, praying to Jesus with his last breath (7:59).

Notice, then, how the deity of Christ actually entered the church. There was no committee, no vote, no slow inflation of a human teacher into a god across three centuries, which is the story usually told. What happened is that Jewish monotheists — men who would sooner have died than pray to a creature, and some of whom did die — began praying to Jesus, and reached for the Old Testament's YHWH texts to explain why, within weeks of the resurrection. The doctrine was not invented at a council. It was already sitting in the way a fisherman quoted Joel on the morning the church was born.

And then there is what calling on the name looks like in practice, which is where a reader most needs help, because the phrase sounds like something one would have to know how to do. It is not a formula and it is not a technique. It is what the tax collector did at the back of the temple when he could not lift his eyes, and beat his chest, and said, God, be merciful to me, a sinner. Seven words. No preparation, no cleaning himself up first, no promise of improvement — and he went home justified (Luke 18:13–14). A man who believes he must repair himself before he is entitled to call has the order exactly backwards; calling is what the unrepaired do. The word is everyone, and it was spoken over a crowd who had between them killed the Son of God.

verseByVerse.quote: "Men of Israel, hear these words: Jesus of Nazareth, a man attested to you by God with mighty works and wonders and signs that God did through him in your midst, as you yourselves know — this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the sermon turns from explaining the morning to announcing the man, and Peter begins where his hearers already are: as you yourselves know. He is not introducing a stranger. Jesus of Nazareth had worked in public, in their own country, within the last three years, and the whole city had an opinion about him. The word rendered attested means publicly displayed, accredited — as a document is authenticated, or a man's credentials are produced in court. God had put his signature on this man in front of witnesses. And Peter appeals to the memory of a hostile crowd for confirmation, which is a dangerous way to preach unless it is true. Seven weeks after the events, in the city where they happened, a man tells several thousand people what they saw with their own eyes, and nobody laughs.

Then comes one of the most compressed sentences in the Bible. This Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and you crucified and killed him by the hands of lawless men. Two claims about one event, welded together, with no attempt to soften either.

The first phrase is worth its weight. Definite plan translates a term built on the verb for marking out a boundary — the word behind our horizon. The cross was not a contingency God accommodated after the fact; it lay inside a line drawn before the world was made. And foreknowledge here is not God peering ahead and noticing what people would decide. When Scripture says God foreknows, he is not a spectator with unusually good eyesight; the word carries his settled purpose, not merely his advance information.

The second claim is left every bit as sharp. You crucified him — not events, not circumstances, not the system: you. And by the hands of lawless men, the men without the law being the Romans, so that Peter distributes the guilt without diluting it. The Jerusalem crowd wanted it done; the empire's soldiers did it; nobody in the transaction is a mere instrument and nobody's hands are clean.

Hold the two together, because the moment they come apart something is lost. Take away the plan and the cross becomes a tragedy God salvaged — a rescue improvised after the worst had already happened, which is comfort of a very thin sort. Take away the guilt and the cross becomes theatre in which nobody is responsible, and there is nothing left for it to forgive. Scripture has kept them in one sentence since Isaiah, who watched God send Assyria as the rod of his anger against his own people — but he does not so intend, and his heart does not so think — and then announced that God would punish the king of Assyria for the arrogance of his heart (Isaiah 10:5–12). The Assyrian was doing God's work and his own wickedness in the same act, and was judged for the second.

Two guards are needed here, and both matter. This verse does not make God the author of sin: Peter charges his hearers with murder in the same breath in which he says it was planned, and no preacher could do that if the real agent of the crime were God. Nor is this a sentence to be handed to a suffering person as an explanation of what has happened to him — it was meant — because Peter is not explaining a tragedy at all. He is announcing that the worst thing the human race has ever done is the thing God used to save it.

Which is where the comfort actually lies. If the murder of the Son of God did not fall outside the plan, nothing does. Whatever a reader has done that he believes has put him permanently beyond reach, and whatever has been done to him that looks like the end of every good purpose, is smaller than this and stands inside the same sovereignty. The cross was not plan B. There has never been a plan B.

verseByVerse.quote: "God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two things are said about the resurrection in this one line, and the second changes everything.

The first is the picture. Loosing the pangs of death — the word is the word for labour pains. The Greek Old Testament uses it where David describes being caught in the cords of Sheol, and Peter takes it up and lets it do its work: death is in labour, and it cannot keep what it is carrying. Something is coming out. The language of birth is not a later flourish of the church's; Paul calls the risen Christ the firstborn from the dead and John calls him the firstborn of the dead, and the word was chosen because on one particular Sunday a tomb behaved like a womb, and tombs have been unreliable ever since.

The second is the sentence to slow down over: it was not possible for him to be held by it. Not unlikely. Not difficult. Not possible. The New Testament gives three reasons why not.

One is who he is. The men standing at Peter's shoulder will say a few chapters later that Jerusalem killed the Author of life (3:15), and life does not stay dead any more than fire stays cold. What happened in that tomb was less a rescue mounted from outside than a contradiction resolving itself.

Another is what he had not done. Death in Scripture is not a natural process; it is a wage, and wages are paid to those who have earned them (Romans 6:23). Jesus had earned nothing. Death is a bailiff who arrives holding a warrant, and when the warrant was read out in that tomb it had somebody else's name on it. He had gone in voluntarily, carrying other men's debts; the moment those were discharged there was no ground in law on which he could be detained another hour. The stone was not rolled back to let him out. It was rolled back to let the world in to look.

The third is that God had sworn it. That is the argument of the next eight verses: the promise had been in writing for a thousand years, in a psalm the crowd had sung, that God's Holy One would not see corruption — and heaven and earth would go first.

One guard is needed, because the sentence can be misread in a way that empties the cross. Not possible to be held is not not possible to die. He really died. The blood ran out, the body went cold, friends made the arrangements, and on the Saturday evening women went and bought spices for a job that genuinely needed doing. Anything less than a real death would leave the human race precisely where it was.

And then the comfort that is the reason this belongs in a sermon rather than a lecture. What death could not do to him it will not finally manage against those who are in him. A believer standing at a graveside is not looking at a permanent arrangement. He is looking at a room that death has already been made to give up once, by a man who walked out of it and took the keys with him.

verseByVerse.quote: "For David says concerning him, 'I saw the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand that I may not be shaken; therefore my heart was glad, and my tongue rejoiced; my flesh also will dwell in hope."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter now does something a first-century audience found perfectly natural and a modern reader often finds baffling: he settles a question about a man who died seven weeks ago by quoting a poem written a thousand years earlier. It is worth watching how he does it, because the method is the one the whole New Testament uses.

Psalm 16 is a psalm of trust, headed simply as David's, and it is genuinely his. He is not a ventriloquist's dummy with an inspired hand working his jaw; the psalm reads like a man's own settled confidence in God, and he meant every word of it about himself. That is the ordinary way prophecy works in the Psalms. The words fit the writer — and then they overflow him. David could say my flesh will dwell in hope and mean that he expected God to bring him through the present trouble alive. What he could not do was make the sentence come true in the sense the words will actually bear, and Peter is about to point at the man's grave to prove it.

Look at the two lines quoted here. I saw the Lord always before me — a deliberate act of keeping God in view, not a feeling that he is near; the psalm's own wording in Hebrew is I have set the LORD always before me, which is something a man does whether or not he can feel anything. And then he is at my right hand that I may not be shaken. A soldier's shield hung on his left arm, so his right side was the exposed one, and what a man in a battle line wanted above everything was somebody he trusted standing at his right, covering the side he could not cover himself. That is where the psalm puts God.

Then the consequence, and notice its order: therefore my heart was glad, and my tongue rejoiced; my flesh also will dwell in hope. Heart, tongue, body — the gladness works outward until even the flesh is included, the part of a man that knows perfectly well it is going to die. This is not stoicism, which teaches a man to expect nothing and so not be disappointed. It is a man expecting his own body to have a future.

And these are the words Peter puts into the mouth of Christ. Which means we are being told what held the Son of God steady on the road to the cross: not the absence of dread, but the Father in view. He kept looking. That is also what is asked of anyone walking into something he cannot get out of — a diagnosis, a court date, a conversation he has been dreading for a month — and it is one of the very few instructions in Scripture that costs nothing to obey and changes everything about the walk.

A small technical note, since a reader with two Bibles open may notice it. Peter quotes the Greek Old Testament, the version his Diaspora hearers used, and in one clause it renders the Hebrew a shade differently. Nothing in the argument depends on that clause. The decisive word is the one about corruption in the next verse, and it stands in Hebrew and Greek alike.

verseByVerse.quote: "For you will not abandon my soul to Hades, or let your Holy One see corruption. You have made known to me the paths of life; you will make me full of gladness with your presence.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the hinge of Peter's argument, and it contains a phrase that has troubled ordinary readers for centuries. Both deserve attention.

First the argument. You will not abandon my soul to Hades, or let your Holy One see corruption. To see something, in Hebrew idiom, is to experience it — to see corruption is to undergo it. And what is being denied is not death but decay. Peter's hearers knew exactly what the sentence described, because burial in that country was a two-stage business: the body was laid on a shelf in a rock tomb and left for a year while it decomposed, after which the bones were gathered into a box and stacked. Everyone in that crowd had done it for a parent. The women who went out on the Sunday morning went carrying spices for exactly that reason — they were not expecting a resurrection, they were expecting the smell. And when the tomb was opened, nothing had begun.

Now the phrase. Hades is not hell. It is the Greek word for the realm of the dead, standing in for the Hebrew Sheol — the place where the dead simply are. And this verse, with one other, is where the line in the Apostles' Creed comes from that has made congregations uneasy for a very long time: he descended into hell. Since it is recited by millions who are given no explanation of it, it should have one here. Nobody in the mainstream of the church has ever taught that Jesus went somewhere to be punished further after the cross; the punishment was finished there, and he said so with his last breath. Some read the creed's phrase as meaning simply that he was truly dead and went where the dead go — no swoon, no shortcut, the full distance travelled. Others, in the Reformed tradition especially, have taken it to describe the anguish of the cross itself, the God-forsakenness of those three hours. Either reading is honest to the words. And notice that the psalm itself claims something more modest than what people fear: it does not say he would not go there. It says he would not be abandoned there.

Then the two clauses that close the quotation, which are pure light after all of that. You have made known to me the paths of life — the word is plural, roads, a whole country to walk in and not a bare survival. And you will make me full of gladness with your presence, which in the Greek is literally with your face.

That last phrase is worth a test any reader can run on himself. Suppose the resurrection delivered everything except that one thing — a body that never failed again, a world with no funerals in it, the people you have buried handed back to you — and God himself somewhere else, benevolent and absent. Would that be enough? Most of us would take it gladly, and then find out in a century or so what was missing. The psalm does not describe the joy of the risen Christ as a location or a condition. It describes it as a face. Whatever else the life to come is, it is the end of God being somewhere else; and that, rather than the absence of trouble, is what the church has always sung about.

verseByVerse.quote: "Brothers, I may say to you with confidence about the patriarch David that he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. Being therefore a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him that he would set one of his descendants on his throne,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter now does the boldest thing in the sermon, and it is easy to walk past because it looks like a piece of local history. He appeals to a landmark. The patriarch David... died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. That tomb was a real building on the southern ridge of the city, known to everybody in that street and a fixed point in Jerusalem's geography for centuries; Josephus reports that a king had once broken into it looking for treasure. Peter could have raised his arm and pointed at it while he was speaking. And nobody in the crowd said: no it is not.

Consider what he has therefore done. He has staked the argument on two graves in one city, both within an easy walk of where he is standing, and made both of them checkable that same afternoon. David's tomb is occupied — go and see. The tomb of Jesus is empty — go and see that too, and ask the guard on your way past. This is not how legends are put together. A story that needs distance and time to survive has just been nailed to two addresses in the town where the events happened, seven weeks after they happened, in front of the people best placed to demolish it.

The logic is plain enough. David wrote that God's Holy One would not see corruption. David saw corruption, and the proof is a sealed door on the ridge. Therefore the psalm is not autobiography. It is prophecy, and it has been waiting for somebody.

But Peter adds a step, and the step matters: being therefore a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him. David is not merely a poet who happened to write past himself without noticing. He knew, at least in part, what he was doing, because he had been given a promise on oath — that God would set one of his own descendants on his throne, and that the throne would have no end (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Psalm 132:11). David wrote Psalm 16 as a man who had been told his family would produce a king whose reign would never stop, which is a promise that cannot be kept unless somebody in that family stops dying.

And then look at what God had to steer in order to keep it. The royal line ran through adultery and murder in its very first generation; through a son who split the kingdom; through kings who burned their own children as offerings; through exile, when the throne stood empty for centuries and the family ended up as village carpenters. At one point the whole line came down to a single infant. A usurping queen had every royal child she could reach put to death, and one baby was carried out of the killing by his aunt and hidden in a room off the temple for six years, while the woman who wanted him dead ruled the country (2 Kings 11:1–3). The oath God swore to David hung, for six years, on whether a hidden child would cry at the wrong moment.

Anybody waiting on a promise of God that looks by now to be past saving should sit with that a while. The promise did not fail while the nation was in exile, or while the throne stood empty, or while the last heir was a toddler behind a curtain. God keeps his word across a thousand years and through a family history that would have finished any human undertaking — and the promise is kept, in the end, by a man from Nazareth whom this crowd had watched die.

verseByVerse.quote: "he foresaw and spoke about the resurrection of the Christ, that he was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption. This Jesus God raised up, and of that we all are witnesses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He foresaw and spoke. Peter will not let the psalm be an accident that happens to fit — a set of old words that turned out to be usable. David saw something coming and said so, which means the resurrection was not the salvage of a wrecked plan. It was announced in Israel's hymn book a thousand years before there was a tomb for it to empty.

Then Peter puts the psalm down and does something quite different: This Jesus God raised up, and of that we all are witnesses.

Notice the shift. He has argued from Scripture for eight verses; now he argues from the eleven men standing beside him. We all — not I, and not a report that reached him. The qualification for the vacancy back in chapter 1 was set at exactly this point: a man who had been with them the whole time and had seen the risen Lord (1:21–22). These are not people passing on a rumour from another province. They are named men, in their own city, seven weeks after the event, telling several thousand of their neighbours that they saw it — and inviting cross-examination from a crowd that included the friends and families of the men who had arranged the execution.

It is worth being careful with the argument usually built on this, because in its common form it is weaker than it sounds. People say that nobody dies for a lie. In fact people die for lies constantly; the world is full of sincere martyrs for things that are not true, and always has been. The real point is narrower and much harder to get round. These particular men were in a position to know whether it was a lie. A man may well die for a doctrine he was taught and cannot check. He does not ordinarily die for a body he moved himself. And what happened to these witnesses across the next thirty years — floggings, prisons, and for most of them execution — is not the record of men who had the option of quietly correcting themselves at any point.

The word itself carries the story. Witnesses is martyres, and the only reason it became our word for a person killed for the faith is that so many of the first ones were. The job description was to say what they had seen. What the job cost was settled afterwards, by other people.

Which leaves the church with an inheritance and a limit, and both should be stated plainly. The inheritance: Christian faith is not a philosophy that would survive the disproof of its own history, and it has never claimed to be — it rests on something that either happened outside a wall in Jerusalem or did not, and Peter is content for it to be tested. The limit: nobody today is a witness in the sense Peter means it here. What the church holds is the testimony of the men who were, written down while people who could have contradicted them were still alive. That is a great deal, and it is enough to build a life on; but the honest name for it is testimony received rather than experience possessed, and no believer should feel awkward saying so.

verseByVerse.quote: "Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you yourselves are seeing and hearing. For David did not ascend into the heavens, but he himself says, 'The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter has reached the point where the sermon turns back on the crowd, and the move he makes is one of the neatest arguments in the New Testament. He has told them Jesus was raised and produced eleven witnesses. But a witness can be doubted, and nobody at all saw the exaltation. So Peter does not ask the crowd to take it on trust. He points at the noise.

He has poured out this that you yourselves are seeing and hearing. The thing that dragged several thousand people into the street at nine in the morning is itself the evidence. You cannot see a throne in heaven; you can hear a hundred and twenty Galileans speaking Parthian. The argument runs from an audible effect back to an invisible cause. The crowd came out looking for an explanation of a noise, and Peter tells them the noise is the sound of a coronation that has already taken place somewhere they cannot look.

Three persons are named in this single sentence, doing three different things. Jesus is exalted at the right hand of God. He receives the promise of the Holy Spirit from the Father. He pours out the Spirit. Anyone who wants to read the New Testament as though Father, Son and Spirit were three costumes worn in turn by one person has to get past this verse, in which all three are active at once and the traffic between them runs in a definite direction. The question is taken up again at verses 37 and 38 and worked out there at length.

And notice what the risen Christ does first with his authority. An accession in the ancient world was marked by largesse — the treasury opened, gifts scattered, debts remitted, prisoners released, because that is how a new reign announced itself to a city. The first recorded act of Jesus after his enthronement is to give something away, and what he gives is not a benefit but a Person. The Spirit in the church is not an impersonal force on loan. He is the coronation gift of a King who had nothing left to prove and gave anyway.

Which puts a Christian's own experience in a light he may not have considered. Every time a believer understands a verse that was closed to him a year ago, or finds he wants to pray when he does not feel like praying, or discovers that a sin which used to own him has quietly loosened its grip, he is holding a piece of evidence about where Jesus is. That is Peter's argument, and it did not stop working when the languages did. The Spirit's presence in an ordinary life is a receipt, and the transaction it records took place at the right hand of God.

Then Peter reaches for his second psalm and introduces it with exactly the logic he used on the first: David did not ascend into the heavens. David's body is on the ridge. David did not go up. So whatever the psalm is about, it is not about him — it is about the one he calls his Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: until I make your enemies your footstool.' Let all the house of Israel therefore know for certain that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Psalm 110 is the most quoted passage in the New Testament, and the reason is in its first line. The Lord said to my Lord. Two different words stand behind those two Lords in the Hebrew: the first is the covenant name of God, the second is the word for a master, a superior, one to whom a man owes allegiance. So David — the king, with nobody above him in Israel — overhears a conversation and finds God addressing somebody David himself has to call his master. Jesus had put that puzzle to the scholars in this very city a few weeks earlier and none of them could answer it: if the Christ is David's son, how does David call him Lord? Fathers do not address their descendants that way. The son of David turns out to be the master of David, and the riddle had been sitting in the temple songbook the whole time.

Until I make your enemies your footstool. The picture is literal and it is not gentle. Ancient kings had footstools with their conquered enemies worked into them; one was found in an Egyptian royal tomb with bound captives carved across the surface, so that the king put his feet on the nations every time he sat down. That is the image — not a negotiated settlement with the powers that oppose God, but their subjugation, placed under the feet of a man who is sitting still.

And the sitting matters. The priests in the temple a few hundred yards from where Peter was preaching never sat down. There were no chairs in the holy place, because the work there was never finished. This King sits. Nor does until mean that the reign expires when the job is done; it means the reign is what does the job. He is not waiting for reinforcements. He is waiting for the last of it to be brought in.

Then the sermon's final sentence, and the hardest thing in the chapter. God has made him both Lord and Christ.

Read carelessly it sounds as though there was a time when Jesus was not Lord, and the resurrection promoted him — that a good man was handed a divine job at Easter. That is not a modern anxiety. It is exactly what the adoptionists taught in the second century, and it is what is meant today when people say the church made Jesus God; this verse is regularly quoted in support. It will not carry the weight, and three things show why.

The first is the verb. Made, in a sentence of this kind, is appointment language, and Greek uses it that way constantly. The Greek Old Testament says the LORD made Moses and Aaron, which every English Bible renders appointed, since nobody imagines God manufactured two grown men on the spot. The Gospels say Jesus made twelve, meaning he appointed them. To be made Lord in this sense is to be installed in an office, not brought into existence.

The second is the man writing it down. Luke has already told us, in the first volume of this same work, what an angel said over a newborn at Bethlehem: unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord. Both titles, spoken over an infant, some thirty years before this sermon, by the same author who now records verse 36. Whatever Luke meant here, he cannot have meant that Jesus acquired those two titles in the spring of that year, because he had already used both of them of a baby in a feeding trough.

The third is what the resurrection is actually said to have done. Paul puts it precisely: Jesus was declared to be the Son of God in power by the resurrection from the dead — and the verb he chooses is built on the same root as the definite plan back in verse 23 of this chapter, the word for marking out and appointing. What is new at Easter is not the nature but the office, publicly entered. A king's son is royal from birth and is crowned at thirty; nobody at the coronation supposes the crown created the man. The hall fills, the trumpet sounds, and the herald announces what has been true since the day he was born.

Which leaves the sentence saying what Peter actually meant by it, and that is a good deal more alarming than the doctrinal difficulty. This is not a statement about promotion. It is the closing move of a prosecution. This Jesus whom you crucified. A court in this city examined a man, found against him, and had him put to death. Heaven has reviewed the case. The verdict is overturned, and the prisoner has been seated on the bench. Every person in that street stood in some relation to a legal decision that had just been publicly reversed, and the judge under the new arrangement is the defendant from the old one.

And now stand still and watch what he does with it. He has been given the name above every name. His enemies are being gathered under his feet. And the first exercise of that power is not a reckoning. The crowd, hearing what they have done, cries out to know whether anything at all can be done about it — and the answer that comes back is that they may repent, and be forgiven, and receive the very Spirit whose arrival they had been jeering at an hour before. The man they murdered is Lord of heaven and earth, and the first thing he does as Lord is offer them himself. There is nothing else like it in the history of the world.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The sermon ends and the crowd interrupts it. That is worth noticing, because Peter had made no appeal at all. He preached Christ, and the cutting was done by somebody else — they were cut to the heart, a violent word, the sort used of a blow that goes right through. Three thousand people are baptised before the day is out, and the church exists.

What Peter tells them to do repays reading twice, because the last of it is easily lost. Repent. Be baptised. And then, in verse 40, a summary of the exhorting he went on doing for however long the rest of that sermon lasted: Save yourselves from this crooked generation. In Greek that is not a command to perform a rescue. It is passive — be saved, let yourselves be got out — and the phrase behind crooked generation is lifted from the Song of Moses, where it describes Israel. Peter is telling his own nation that what they most need saving from is the way of being they were born into, and that they cannot do it themselves.

Then Luke shows what came out the other side, and he does it in a tense that means kept on — they kept devoting themselves, kept selling, kept meeting. This is not a photograph of one extraordinary week; it is the description of a habit. Four devotions: the apostles' teaching, the fellowship, the breaking of bread, the prayers. And two settings, held together in verse 46 and easy to skip past: the temple courts, the largest sacred enclosure in the ancient world, and somebody's kitchen. The church has needed both ever since, and has generally been strong in one and thin in the other.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Four Marks of the Apostolic Church

Verse 42 gives the church four practices, and in Greek each carries the definite article: the apostles' teaching, the fellowship, the breaking of bread, the prayers. These are not four vague virtues but four definite things a visitor to Jerusalem that summer could have been taken to and shown. Reformed ecclesiology has read them as the permanent shape of church life. The apostles' teaching — which is now the New Testament — norms everything else, so that no experience, however vivid, is permitted to correct it. The fellowship is not sociability but a shared life the Spirit creates, and in this chapter it costs people money within three verses. The breaking of bread is the Supper in which his death is proclaimed until he comes. And the prayers are the church's dependence made audible. A congregation strong in all four will be healthy in almost any circumstances; a congregation that quietly lets one go will be impoverished in ways it may take a generation to notice.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Where do you baptise three thousand people in a city with no river? Jerusalem was already equipped. The southern approach to the temple mount was honeycombed with stepped immersion pools cut into the bedrock, so that pilgrims could purify themselves before going up; dozens have been excavated and can still be walked into. The infrastructure of the old covenant was standing ready on the morning the new one needed it.
