Then the covenant text itself: in your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed. It matters enormously where that sentence comes from. It is spoken on a mountain in Genesis 22, after the knife is stopped and the ram is found caught by its horns in a thicket — the promise that the whole world would be blessed through Abraham's line is given at the exact moment God provides a substitute for a beloved son. Peter quotes it in a sermon about a beloved Son for whom no substitute was provided, and no ram was found, and the knife was not stopped. Abraham got his boy back down the mountain. God did not spare his own.

And then the last sentence, which is where the whole chapter has been going. God, having raised up his servant, sent him to you first, to bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness.

Take the two halves in turn. To you first — in the city that killed him, to the crowd that asked for a murderer instead, the offer arrives before it goes anywhere else in the world. That is the pattern of the whole book, to the Jew first, city after city, long after the doors start closing. And it is a window onto the character of God, who deals with the people who have wronged him worst by putting them at the front of the queue.

Then the definition. To bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness. Peter states outright what the blessing consists of, and it is not what most people mean by the word. Ask a room of ordinary people what a blessing is and the answers will be about health, safety, provision, children doing well, a scan that came back clear. Ask a congregation and the answers will be much the same with a religious accent laid over them. Here is an apostle, at the climax of a sermon, defining the blessing promised to Abraham for the entire world — and it is being turned away from your own wickedness.

That deserves a test. Suppose a man were given a long life and an easy one, comfortable, well provided for, with every person he loves kept safe — and suppose he arrived at the end of it exactly as he began, still governed by the temper, the appetite, the coldness or the dishonesty he has had since he was twenty. Was he blessed? By the definition in this verse he was never touched. And suppose another man loses most of what he owned and half of what he hoped for, and is prised loose over thirty years from the thing that was quietly destroying him. Peter says God blessed the second one.

Which is the note this chapter ends on, and it is worth hearing for what it says about God. He does not send his Servant to a crowd of murderers with a bribe, an amnesty, or a fresh start on the same old terms. He sends him to change them — to take hold of the people who killed him and turn them round, one at a time, every one of you. The man at the gate asked for a coin and was given his legs. Israel asked for a Messiah who would deal with the Romans and was offered something far more expensive and worth incalculably more: to be turned, personally, out of their own wickedness, by the one they had nailed to a cross.

3.theology: The Name of Jesus. “His name — by faith in his name — has made this man strong” (v. 16). This verse is not about a formula but about a person. The name in the ancient world carried the authority and presence of the one who bore it. When Peter speaks the name of Jesus, he is not invoking magic; he is acting in the delegated authority of the reigning Christ. The healing is an act of the risen Lord performed through his servant. Faith is the hand that reaches for what the name offers. And what the name offers is the full power of the one who conquered death — resurrection life, flowing through a living faith, into a broken body and a guilty conscience alike.
3.examples:
Then: A man lame from birth, set daily at the gate of the temple he could not enter, excluded by his condition from the presence he longed for. His whole life had been one long reaching-out of an empty hand. And then, in the name of Jesus, he entered the temple walking.

Now: The church still carries what the world cannot give. No program, no therapy, no government initiative can do what the name of Jesus does — not because those things are worthless, but because they cannot raise the dead. The church’s temptation in every generation is to be embarrassed by its true wealth and to offer silver and gold instead. The world has plenty of silver and gold. It has only one name by which it can be saved.

4.title: Boldness Before the Council
4.text: <sup>1</sup>And as they were speaking to the people, the priests and the captain of the temple and the Sadducees came upon them, <sup>2</sup>greatly annoyed because they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection from the dead. <sup>3</sup>And they arrested them and put them in custody until the next day, for it was already evening. <sup>4</sup>But many of those who had heard the word believed, and the number of the men came to about five thousand. <sup>5</sup>On the next day their rulers and elders and scribes gathered together in Jerusalem, <sup>6</sup>with Annas the high priest and Caiaphas and John and Alexander, and all who were of the high-priestly family. <sup>7</sup>And when they had set them in the midst, they inquired, “By what power or by what name did you do this?” <sup>8</sup>Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, “Rulers of the people and elders, <sup>9</sup>if we are being examined today concerning a good deed done to a crippled man, by what means this man has been healed, <sup>10</sup>let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead—by him this man is standing before you well. <sup>11</sup>This Jesus is the stone that was rejected by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone. <sup>12</sup>And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.” <sup>13</sup>Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were uneducated, common men, they were astonished. And they recognized that they had been with Jesus. <sup>14</sup>But seeing the man who was healed standing beside them, they had nothing to say in opposition. <sup>15</sup>But when they had commanded them to leave the council, they conferred with one another, <sup>16</sup>saying, “What shall we do with these men? For that a notable sign has been performed through them is evident to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and we cannot deny it. <sup>17</sup>But in order that it may spread no further among the people, let us warn them to speak no more to anyone in this name.” <sup>18</sup>So they called them and charged them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus. <sup>19</sup>But Peter and John answered them, “Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you judge, <sup>20</sup>for we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard.” <sup>21</sup>And when they had further threatened them, they let them go, finding no way to punish them, because of the people, for all were glorifying God for what had happened. <sup>22</sup>For the man on whom this sign of healing was performed was more than forty years old. <sup>23</sup>When they were released, they went to their friends and reported what the chief priests and the elders had said to them. <sup>24</sup>And when they heard it, they lifted their voices together to God and said, “Sovereign Lord, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them, <sup>25</sup>who through the mouth of our father David, your servant, said by the Holy Spirit, ‘Why did the Gentiles rage, and the peoples plot in vain? <sup>26</sup>The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers were gathered together, against the Lord and against his Anointed’— <sup>27</sup>for truly in this city there were gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, <sup>28</sup>to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place. <sup>29</sup>And now, Lord, look upon their threats and grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness, <sup>30</sup>while you stretch out your hand to heal, and signs and wonders are performed through the name of your holy servant Jesus.” <sup>31</sup>And when they had prayed, the place in which they were gathered together was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and continued to speak the word of God with boldness. <sup>32</sup>Now the full number of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one said that any of the things that belonged to him was his own, but they had everything in common. <sup>33</sup>And with great power the apostles were giving their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all. <sup>34</sup>There was not a needy person among them, for as many as were owners of lands or houses sold them and brought the proceeds of what was sold <sup>35</sup>and laid it at the apostles’ feet, and it was distributed to each as any had need. <sup>36</sup>Thus Joseph, who was also called by the apostles Barnabas (which means son of encouragement), a Levite, a native of Cyprus, <sup>37</sup>sold a field that belonged to him and brought the money and laid it at the apostles’ feet.
4.overview:
The Sadducees are annoyed. They have tolerated a great deal, but the resurrection — they cannot have the resurrection preached in the temple courts. For the Sadducees, resurrection is not just wrong theology; it is a direct challenge to their authority. So they arrest Peter and John. But it is too late: five thousand have believed. The arrest comes after the harvest. This is the pattern in Acts: the Word goes out, the kingdom grows, the opposition rises — and the opposition never wins.

The next morning Peter stands before the same council that tried Jesus. He is not the same Peter. Filled with the Holy Spirit, he does not hedge, does not soften, does not negotiate. He gives them the name: Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead. And then the sentence that has stopped every comfortable ecumenism in its tracks: “there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.” The council marvels. They cannot deny the miracle — the healed man is standing right there. They can only warn. And Peter and John go back to the church and they pray.

The prayer is worth lingering over. They do not pray for safety. They do not pray for the opposition to relent. They pray for boldness. And the place is shaken.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The first opposition the church ever meets does not come from Rome or from the pagans. It comes from the temple — from priests, the officer commanding the temple police, and the Sadducees, who arrest Peter mid-sentence and hold the two apostles overnight. And the arrest achieves precisely nothing, because the sermon was already out: many of those who had heard the word believed, and the number of the men came to about five thousand. They took the preachers into custody and left the message at large.

Next morning the supreme court of the nation assembles — the same body that had condemned Jesus, with the whole high-priestly family in the room — and puts two Galilean fishermen in the middle of the semicircle and asks the question the entire book turns on: by what power or by what name did you do this? Peter's answer is not a defence. He names the name they least want to hear, quotes at them the psalm Jesus had quoted at them in this same building, and tells them there is salvation in nobody else. The council notes that these are men without credentials, and then supplies the real explanation without meaning to: they had been with Jesus.

Then comes the private session, and Luke records what was said in it. We cannot deny it. A hostile court of inquiry, with every motive to find a hole, examines the case and concludes that a notable sign has been done and everybody in Jerusalem knows it — and then resolves to suppress it anyway. That is the shape of unbelief at its most naked: not a shortage of evidence but an unwillingness to be moved by it. They forbid the name, and Peter and John reply with the sentence the church has been repeating ever since — not a boast, but a plain statement of incapacity: we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard.

And they walk out free, because the council can find no way to punish them without a riot. Luke's last note is a legal one: the man was over forty years old. The record of the nation's own supreme court now contains the fact of the miracle, the age of the man, and the reason no charge could be brought.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Exclusivity of Christ

Peter's declaration in v. 12 — there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved — is among the clearest statements of Christ's exclusive lordship in salvation anywhere in Scripture, and it is worth noticing that it is spoken under oath, in a courtroom, to men who could imprison him for it. Reformed theology has always held this exclusivity to follow from the incarnation itself: if God became flesh in one particular person, in one particular place, at one particular hour of history, then salvation is tied to that person and cannot be detached from him. A plurality of saviours would require a plurality of incarnations, which is not a thing the gospel can be stretched to accommodate. And the same logic that makes the claim exclusive makes it universal: the name is given among men, offered, held out — the door is single and it is not shut.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter and John were laymen without rabbinic training, standing in the middle of the supreme court of Israel, and their boldness astonished the men trying them — parresia, a word that in Greek public life meant the free speech of a citizen in the assembly, the very thing a slave did not have. Now: The same Spirit who supplied it is given to every believer, and the church prays for more of it in this very chapter (v. 29). Boldness in the New Testament is not a temperament. It is a gift, asked for and granted, and it is perfectly compatible with being frightened.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were speaking to the people, the priests and the captain of the temple and the Sadducees came upon them, greatly annoyed because they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection from the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Note the timing: as they were speaking. They do not wait for the sermon to finish. Whatever else this is, it is not a considered response to a case that has been heard out.

Three groups come down on them, and it is worth knowing who they were. The priests were the men on duty. The captain of the temple was the officer commanding the Levitical guard, the second most powerful man in the temple hierarchy after the high priest himself; this is not a verger, it is the head of a police force with the power of arrest. And the Sadducees were the aristocratic party who controlled the priesthood, worked with Rome, held the written law of Moses above everything else, and — as Luke tells us plainly later on — denied that there is any resurrection, or angel, or spirit (23:8). Their whole position, religious and financial and political, rested on the temple continuing to operate as it was.

Luke says they were greatly annoyed, and the verb is stronger than it sounds in English: it means worked up, exasperated, thoroughly put out. And he tells us exactly what put them out, in two parts.

The first is that the apostles were teaching the people. Two laymen with no standing whatever were instructing a crowd, in the temple, on the priests' own premises, without anybody's permission. That alone was an affront to a body whose authority rested on being the only legitimate interpreters of these things.

The second is the content: proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection from the dead. This is the doctrine the Sadducees had built a career on denying, and the apostles are not arguing it in the abstract. They are pointing to a specific instance and naming the man. Consider how that landed. Seven weeks earlier these same officials had believed the matter closed — a stone, a seal, a guard, and a body that would trouble nobody again. Now the claim is back, in their own courtyard, at the hour of prayer, with a healed cripple standing next to it and several thousand people listening.

There is a third irritant that Luke does not need to state, because the previous chapter has already supplied it: the apostles were telling the population of Jerusalem that its rulers had handed the Messiah to Pilate and killed him. Men do not usually take that well.

It is tempting to draw from this the tidy conclusion that opposition to the gospel is never really intellectual and always about protecting an interest, and that conclusion should be resisted, because it is not always true and it is a lazy way to avoid an argument. Some people object to the Christian faith because they have thought about it and find it incredible, and they deserve to be answered rather than psychoanalysed. But it is worth noticing what actually triggered the first arrest in Christian history. Not a doctrine as such. A doctrine that, if true, cost a group of powerful men everything they had.

verseByVerse.quote: And they arrested them and put them in custody until the next day, for it was already evening. But many of those who had heard the word believed, and the number of the men came to about five thousand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two sentences sitting side by side, and Luke has put them together on purpose. In the first, the authorities do the only thing they can think of. In the second, it turns out to have been beside the point.

They arrested them and put them in custody until the next day, for it was already evening. That last clause is a legal detail: Jewish practice held that a case of this kind was not to be tried after dark, so the two men spend the night in a cell under the temple precincts. It is the first Christian imprisonment. By the end of this book it will be so routine that Luke barely stops to comment on it, and one of the two men in that cell will die under Herod's sword within a few years while the other goes on to be jailed twice more. Everything that would happen to the church for the next three centuries began on an ordinary evening with a locked door and two tired men who had been to a prayer meeting.

But many of those who had heard the word believed. The sentence is built to defeat the one before it. They can stop the speaker; they cannot retrieve what has already been said. The word was out of the building before the guards arrived, working in several thousand people they could not arrest and did not know how to find. They took the preachers into custody and left the sermon at large.

Then the number, and it should be read carefully. The number of the men came to about five thousand — and the word is the one for adult males, as distinct from women and children. So five thousand is not the size of the church; it is the size of one column in the register. Add wives and households and the community in Jerusalem may already be well past ten thousand people, in a city whose ordinary resident population was a fraction of what it swelled to at the feasts. Within a matter of weeks the followers of a crucified Galilean had become one of the largest identifiable groups in the capital. No wonder the temple authorities were alarmed. From where they were sitting this was not a fringe irritation; it was a movement that had taken a visible share of the city while they were deciding what to do about it.

One guard, because this passage is often preached as though it were a promise. Luke does record a pattern in Acts in which pressure and growth run together, and it is real. But it is a pattern, not a law, and Scripture nowhere guarantees that opposition will produce numbers. There have been faithful churches that were persecuted and shrank, and faithful men who preached for forty years to a nation that never turned. What this passage promises is not that the church will grow under pressure. It is that the word, once spoken, is no longer under the control of the people who object to it.

verseByVerse.quote: On the next day their rulers and elders and scribes gathered together in Jerusalem, with Annas the high priest and Caiaphas and John and Alexander, and all who were of the high-priestly family.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The full apparatus assembles. Rulers and elders and scribes is Luke's shorthand for the Sanhedrin: seventy-one men, the supreme council of the nation, with authority over religious law, over the temple, and — within the limits Rome allowed — over life and death. This is the body that had condemned Jesus a few months earlier. The room, the procedure, and most of the faces are the same. Only the defendants have changed.

Then Luke names names, and one of them raises a question a careful reader is entitled to ask. He writes Annas the high priest and Caiaphas — but Caiaphas was high priest. He held the office from about AD 18 to 36, and the events of this chapter fall squarely inside that. Luke appears to have given the title to the wrong man, and this has been produced more than once as evidence that he did not know the Jerusalem he was writing about.

The explanation is not a strain, and it tells you something about the city. Annas had been high priest from AD 6 to 15, until a Roman prefect removed him. But by the law of Moses the high priesthood was for life; a pagan governor deposing the high priest of Israel was, in the eyes of most Jews, an act with no authority behind it whatever. So the office passed on paper and the man did not. Five of his sons held the high priesthood after him, and so did his son-in-law — who was Caiaphas. It was a family firm, and Annas ran it the way a patriarch runs a business through his children: out of the chair, and in charge. Which is why, when Jesus was arrested, he was taken to Annas first, before being sent on to the man who actually held the title (John 18:13). Luke, who elsewhere dates the ministry of John the Baptist to the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas together, is not confused. He is doing what a good historian does: naming the office-holder and the power, and not pretending they are the same person.

John and Alexander are otherwise unknown, and that is itself worth a moment. A writer inventing a scene does not clutter it with two names that do nothing and lead nowhere. Luke includes them because they were in the room and somebody who was there remembered.

Stand back and look at the arithmetic of the morning. On one side: the high-priestly dynasty, the aristocracy of the nation, the men who controlled the temple, its treasury, its police and its courts, seated in the chamber where they had sentenced a man to death. On the other: two fishermen from a lake a hundred miles north, who had spent the night in a cell, with no lawyer, no credentials and no allies in the building. The odds are not close. And by the end of the session it will be the seventy-one who cannot think what to do.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had set them in the midst, they inquired, "By what power or by what name did you do this?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had set them in the midst — the phrase is describing the furniture. The Sanhedrin sat in a semicircle so that every member could see every other, with the accused placed in the open space at the centre. There is nowhere to look that is not a face, and every face belongs to somebody who can ruin you. It is a room designed to make a man feel the weight of the institution before a word is spoken.

Then the question: by what power or by what name did you do this?

It sounds neutral and it is not. Asking a man to name the power and the name behind a wonder is the language of the world of magic and exorcism, where results were obtained by invoking a particular being and everything depended on which one you had used. The council is not enquiring into a healing; it is inviting Peter to identify his source, and there is a trap under the invitation. Israel's law prescribed death for a man who worked a sign or a wonder and used it to draw the people after another god (Deuteronomy 13:1–5). Give the wrong answer here and the charge is not disorderly preaching. It is capital.

They had used the same move on his master. When Jesus cast out demons, the accusation was not that nothing had happened — it was that he did it by the prince of demons. It is a durable tactic, because it concedes the event and poisons the source, and it does not require the accuser to explain anything.

Notice also the small contempt in the wording. Not by what power did you heal this man. By what power did you do this — an unnamed this, a thing, an incident. The court has forty years of a man's life in front of it and refers to the whole business as this. Peter is about to make them say what it was.

And it should be admitted that the council has, without meaning to, asked exactly the right question. By what power and by what name — that is the question the entire book of Acts exists to answer, and it has one answer, and it is about to be given to the men least willing to hear it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, "Rulers of the people and elders, if we are being examined today concerning a good deed done to a crippled man, by what means this man has been healed,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Filled with the Holy Spirit. This is the second time Luke has said it of Peter, and it will be the third before the chapter is out (2:4; here; 4:31). The point is not that Pentecost has worn off and needed topping up. It is that Luke's filling language describes a repeated equipping for particular moments, and this is one of them: a man who is about to speak for his life is given what he needs at the hour he needs it and not before.

Which is exactly what had been promised. When they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities, do not be anxious about how you should defend yourself or what you should say, for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say (Luke 12:11–12). Peter is standing in the sentence. He had heard it perhaps three years earlier from a man on a hillside, and he is now in a room with rulers and authorities finding out that it was not a figure of speech.

A guard is needed on that promise, because it gets misapplied. It is not a general licence to go into the pulpit unprepared and call it faith; the setting Jesus specified is the dock, not the desk, and the same New Testament tells a preacher to do the work of study. What is promised is that when a believer is put on the spot for Christ — in a courtroom, a hostile family, an interview — he will not be left to improvise alone.

Then watch what Peter does with his first sentence. He is courteous: rulers of the people and elders, the proper address, no sneering. Boldness in this chapter never once shades into rudeness, and that is worth registering by anyone who has met the sort of Christian who mistakes being obnoxious for being faithful.

And then he takes the vague this of the council's question and gives it a name. If we are being examined today concerning a good deed done to a crippled man. The word for examined is the technical term for a judicial hearing, so he is granting the proceedings their full formality — and then reading the charge sheet aloud in language nobody in that chamber would want in the minutes. We are on trial for making a cripple walk. He has not raised his voice, and he has already made the court's position sound absurd, which is what it was.

One word in that sentence is the hinge of the whole speech, and English hides it. By what means this man has been healed — the verb Peter uses for healed is the ordinary Greek word for saved. He uses it here of a man's ankles. Three verses later he will use it of the whole world's only hope. The council asked him about a body, and he is going to answer about a soul, and he does it by keeping one word running through both.

verseByVerse.quote: "let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead — by him this man is standing before you well. This Jesus is the stone that was rejected by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He answers the question exactly and without a syllable of diplomacy. They asked for a name; they get the name, with the address attached and the crucifixion attached and the resurrection attached, in one clause: Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead. Two verbs, two subjects, side by side — what you did, and what God did about it. And he is saying it to the men who did the first one, in the room where they voted for it.

By him this man is standing before you well. Peter can point while he says it, because the healed man is in the chamber — verse 14 tells us so. The court's exhibit walked in on his own feet and is standing there for the duration of the hearing. Forty years he could not get through the door of the temple; this morning he is inside the supreme court of Israel.

Then Peter quotes Scripture at them, and the choice of text is not casual. The stone that was rejected by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone is Psalm 118:22 — and every man in that room could have finished the psalm from memory, because it is the last of the psalms sung at Passover, and because a crowd had shouted its next lines at a man riding into this city on a donkey a few months before.

But there is a sharper reason it lands the way it does. Jesus had quoted this identical verse to these identical men, in this building, at the end of the parable about tenants who killed the owner's son — and Luke records that they understood he had told it against them and tried to arrest him on the spot (Luke 20:17–19). Peter is not producing a clever proof-text. He is finishing his master's sentence, in front of the same audience, and they know precisely which conversation he is resuming.

He also adjusts the psalm in two small ways, and both are deliberate. He puts in by you, which the psalm does not have, so that the builders have faces. And he swaps the psalm's verb for a blunter one meaning to treat as worthless, to count for nothing. That is the charge: not that they made a technical error, but that they looked at him and assessed him as being of no value.

The image itself deserves a moment, because it is a working man's picture and it is savage. Builders handle stone all day; judging which block goes where is the whole of their competence. These are men whose entire standing rests on being able to tell what is load-bearing and what is rubble. They examined this stone with the best professional judgement in the nation and threw it on the spoil heap. And God took it off the heap and set it at the corner, where every line in the building is measured from.

There is something in that worth carrying about. The judgement of the most qualified people in the world, delivered unanimously, in the proper forum, after due process, was wrong about the most important thing that has ever happened — and God overturned it without consulting them. It is a caution against being impressed by consensus, and it is a comfort to anybody who has been weighed by people with every right to weigh him and found to be of no value.

verseByVerse.quote: "And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the sentence the chapter is famous for, and the first thing to see is that it is an answer to a question about a pair of ankles.

The council asked how a crippled man came to be walking. Peter used the ordinary Greek word for saved to describe the healing in verse 9, and he now runs that same word straight on into its largest possible meaning: there is salvation in no one else. He has taken the small case in front of the court and enlarged it until it covers everything. You want to know how one man got his legs back. I will tell you how anybody gets anything back.

Every clause tightens it. Salvation is in no one else. There is no other name under heaven — which is to say, nowhere in the world, not merely nowhere in Israel. The name is given, a gift handed down rather than a prize achieved. And the last phrase carries a quiet necessity: by which we must be saved — not may be, not can be. Peter includes himself in that we, which is worth noticing. He is not standing over the council as a man who found the way; he is standing beside them as a man who needed it.

This is also one of the great apologetic verses, for the world calls it narrow and arrogant: how can Jesus be the only way? Three things help. First, it is not a boast about Christians but a confession about Christ: if God himself became man and died and rose to save sinners, then salvation simply is found in him and nowhere else — not because we are better, but because there is only one Saviour who did this. Second, the one narrow door opens to all: narrow in the way (one Saviour), infinitely wide in the welcome ('whoever calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved,' Rom. 10:13). Third, sincerity cannot save — a man can be sincerely wrong, as one who sincerely drinks poison thinking it medicine; salvation rests on the truth of who Christ is, not the earnestness of the seeker.

As for those who never hear, Scripture's answer is honest and sobering: all are accountable for the light they have (Rom. 1:20), none seek God on their own (Rom. 3:11), the Judge of all the earth will do right (Gen. 18:25) — and therefore we must go and tell ('how are they to hear without someone preaching?' Rom. 10:14), leaving the secret things to God (Deut. 29:29). (Others soften the exclusivity — pluralism says all religions are valid paths; inclusivism says some may be saved through Christ without conscious faith in him. The historic and Reformed position is that salvation is through Christ alone, received by conscious faith in him, normally through the gospel preached.) Far from cruel, this is the most loving truth there is: if Jesus really is the only Saviour, then telling people is the kindest thing we could ever do.

Finally, remember where he is standing when he says it. This is not a lecture hall. He is under arrest, in front of a court that could flog him and had recently arranged an execution, answering a question designed to trap him into a capital charge. A man in that position has every incentive to find a broader formula — to say that Jesus is one road among several and that the council need not feel implicated. Peter tells them instead that the man they threw away is the only name there is, and that they too must be saved by it. The narrowness people object to in this verse was spoken by a prisoner who gained nothing by it, to the men holding the keys, and it included an invitation to them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were uneducated, common men, they were astonished. And they recognized that they had been with Jesus. But seeing the man who was healed standing beside them, they had nothing to say in opposition.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word Luke uses for what the council saw is parresia, and it carried a specific weight in the Greek world. It meant the right to say everything — the free speech of a citizen standing up in the public assembly, the liberty of a free man. A slave did not have it. A foreigner did not have it. It was one of the things that made a citizen a citizen.

So the Sanhedrin is watching two men with no standing whatever in that room exercise the freedom of men who own the place. They are prisoners, fetched up from a cell, addressing the court that holds them, and they are talking like free men. Luke uses this word all through his book — the church prays for it in this chapter (v. 29) and receives it (v. 31), and the very last line of Acts leaves Paul in Rome under house arrest, preaching the kingdom of God with all boldness. It is a fair candidate for the theme word of the whole book, and it always belongs to somebody who has no business being that free.

The council's own description is worth getting right, since it is often misheard. Uneducated does not mean illiterate; the word means without formal training in the rabbinic schools — no letters after the name. And common men renders a word for laymen, private persons, amateurs as opposed to professionals. The Sanhedrin is not saying that Peter and John cannot read. It is saying they have no credentials: they have not sat at the feet of a Gamaliel, as the young Saul of Tarsus had.

This is not an argument against learning — Luke writes careful Greek, Paul was thoroughly trained, and the church has needed both kinds of men ever since. It is a note about where the power was not coming from. The council looked for a qualification that would explain what they were seeing, found none on paper, and then named the real one without meaning to: they had been with Jesus.

Then the sentence that has outlived everything else in this chapter. They recognised that they had been with Jesus. The verb is the one Luke used two chapters earlier of the crowd recognising the beggar at the gate — not a guess but an identification. Something in the bearing of these two men made a hostile court think of a prisoner it had condemned.

How much of that is memory of a face and how much is recognition of a manner, Luke does not say, and both are possible; some of these men had seen Peter in the courtyard on the night of the trial. But the sentence as it stands is not really about faces. It is about the fact that time spent with Jesus leaves a residue which outlasts any argument, and that the people who dislike him are very often the first to spot it.

Which yields a test, and it is uncomfortable precisely because it does not run on self-assessment. Not: do I consider that I am walking closely with Christ? But: if somebody who wanted to find fault with me had to account for me, what would they reach for? The council reached for the only explanation available to it, and it was not education, temperament, social position or nerve. It was company.

And then verse 14 supplies the last piece: seeing the man who was healed standing beside them, they had nothing to say in opposition. He came. Nobody made him. A man with forty years' experience of staying out of trouble walked into the highest court in the land of his own accord and stood next to the accused, and by doing it he ended the prosecution. Luke gives him not one line of dialogue. He did not need one. He stood where everybody could see him, which is very largely what the church has been asked to do ever since.

verseByVerse.quote: But when they had commanded them to leave the council, they conferred with one another, saying, "What shall we do with these men? For that a notable sign has been performed through them is evident to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and we cannot deny it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke now takes us into a session held behind closed doors, which raises a fair question: how does he know what was said in it?

There is no mystery. This council was not sealed. Nicodemus was a member and had come to Jesus by night; Joseph of Arimathea was a member and had not consented to their decision. Luke will tell us within two chapters that a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith (6:7) — men who had sat in meetings like this one and later sat in Christian ones. Paul himself had moved in exactly these circles. By the time this account came to be written, the private deliberations of the Sanhedrin were not private any more, because some of the men in the room had changed sides.

And what they said is one of the most extraordinary sentences in the New Testament. We cannot deny it.

Consider who is speaking. This is not a sympathetic witness. It is a hostile court in closed session, with no audience to perform for, every motive in the world to find a flaw, and the investigative resources of the nation at its disposal. They have the man. They have the history. They have forty years of testimony from every worshipper who ever stepped round him at the gate. They examine the case with the settled intention of destroying it — and their finding, entered into their own minutes, is that a notable sign has been performed, that it is evident to everybody in Jerusalem, and that denial is not available to them.

And then, in the next breath, they resolve to shut it down.

This is the passage to put in front of anyone who assumes that unbelief is fundamentally an information problem — that if only the case were laid out clearly enough, people would believe. Here is a case laid out with total clarity and conceded in writing by qualified and hostile investigators, followed immediately by a decision to suppress it. The obstacle was never the evidence.

Which does not make evidence worthless, and the opposite error does just as much damage. Peter's entire speech is an appeal to evidence. The healed man is standing in the room precisely because he is evidence. Luke wrote two volumes so that his reader might have certainty about the things he had been taught. Christians are not asked to believe without grounds, and they are not asked to argue without facts. What this passage shows is that facts are necessary and not sufficient — that a man may be persuaded in his understanding and remain unwilling in his will, and that the second is where the real business is transacted.

The proof of it lies in a comparison Luke almost certainly intends. At Pentecost a crowd that had just been told they crucified the Messiah cried out, Brothers, what shall we do? Here a council that has just been told the same thing asks, What shall we do with these men? Nearly the same words. One is asking to be changed; the other is asking how to make the problem go away. Everything turns on two syllables.

verseByVerse.quote: "But in order that it may spread no further among the people, let us warn them to speak no more to anyone in this name." So they called them and charged them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The plan they settle on tells you they had run out of arguments. There is no attempt to explain the healing, no rival account of what happened, no enquiry into fraud. They go straight to containment: in order that it may spread no further among the people. The verb carries the sense of something being distributed, handed round — they are treating the message as stock in circulation that has to be withdrawn. It is an administrative answer to a theological problem, which is what institutions reach for when they have lost the argument and kept the power.

There is an irony in it that Luke, of all people, will not have missed. The measure taken to stop the name travelling is recorded in a book that carried the name to Rome, and out of Rome to everywhere else.

Now look at what they actually prohibit. Not healing. Not gathering. Not charity, or prayer, or religious activity of any kind. They ban a name: not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus. They had grasped the essential point rather better than some of the church's friends have since. Everything in this movement is carried in a person; make the person unmentionable and the remainder is harmless.

There is a small tell in their own words as well. They say this name. They will not say it. In a private session, among themselves, with nobody listening, seventy-one men discuss the problem of Jesus of Nazareth without once pronouncing it.

The modern shape of this is recognisable enough to be worth naming, and worth naming carefully. Christian activity of most kinds is welcome nearly everywhere: the food bank, the night shelter, the hospice, the school. It is the speech that draws the objection — the naming of the name, the claim that this particular man is Lord and that what anyone does about him matters. Institutions perfectly happy to fund the soup will often ask, in so many words, that the sentence not be said. That is the council's exact position, and the church's answer to it has been on the record since the next verse.

But it should be said plainly, and by comfortable Western Christians most of all, that there is an enormous distance between being thought awkward at work and a night in a cell under the temple, and a further distance again between either of those and what believers in a good many countries will face this week. Peter and John are flogged for this in the next chapter. A man who finds a conversation uncomfortable and calls it persecution has not read the passage he is quoting.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter and John answered them, "Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge, for we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The most quoted sentence in the chapter, and what is usually missed about it is the form. Peter does not make a declaration. He asks the court a question and leaves it with them.

Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge. He could have said: we will not obey you. Instead he puts the case to the men trying him and invites them to deliver the verdict — and they cannot deliver it, because there is only one answer and it dismantles their own order. A body whose entire authority rests on claiming to represent God has just been asked, on the record, whether God ought to be obeyed. It is the most respectful thing Peter could have said, and the most devastating.

Then the second half, and the wording repays attention: we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard. Not we will not stop. We are not able. It is a statement of incapacity rather than defiance — the position of a man who has seen something and cannot arrange to un-see it. You may forbid him to mention it; you cannot make him not know it. A witness can be silenced and cannot be un-witnessed, and that is the whole of Peter's case.

Notice too how modest the claim is. He does not say they cannot stop because they are courageous, or called, or full of conviction. He says they cannot stop reporting what they have seen and heard. The apostles are not claiming a temperament. They are claiming an experience — that a man they watched die was afterwards alive in front of them, and that they had eaten with him. Everything the church has ever said rests on that being either true or false.

The larger question of when a Christian may refuse a lawful command — how it squares with the New Testament's instruction to be subject to the governing authorities, where exactly the line falls, and what it costs the man who draws it — is worked out fully at 5:29, where these same two men give the same answer to the same court and are flogged on the way out. What belongs here is the ordinary version, because very few readers will ever stand in a Sanhedrin.

Most Christians meet this verse in a much smaller room. A conversation turns, and there is a sentence that would be honest and a silence that would be easier, and both are available in the same second. Nobody is threatening anything. The cost is a slight chill, a reputation for being that sort of person, a subject quietly avoided at the next lunch. It is worth being honest that this is not heroism and never feels like it. But the mechanism Peter names is the same one. A believer is not being asked to be impressive. He is being asked not to pretend he has not seen what he has seen.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had further threatened them, they let them go, finding no way to punish them, because of the people, for all were praising God for what had happened. For the man on whom this sign of healing was performed was more than forty years old.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The court gives up, and Luke is careful to record why. Not because it was persuaded, and not because it had scruples. Finding no way to punish them, because of the people.

The restraint is a calculation about public opinion. All Jerusalem was praising God for what had happened, and men whose position depends on popular acquiescence cannot afford to flog the heroes of the hour. So the apostles walk out — not acquitted, not vindicated, simply released by an institution that could not work out how to hurt them without cost to itself.

And it is worth remembering who this protective crowd is. A few months earlier, in this same city, a crowd had stood in front of a Roman governor and asked for a murderer instead of Jesus. Public opinion killed the Master and is now shielding the servants — and it will swing again before long: by chapter 7 a crowd is stoning Stephen, and by chapter 8 a persecution has emptied the city of Christians. A church that reads its safety off the public mood is watching a gauge that moves.

There is a warning in that for any period in which the faith is broadly respectable, and a comfort in it for any period in which it is not. Neither condition measures anything except the weather.

One detail in the crowd's reaction is easy to skip and should not be. They were praising God. Not the apostles. Peter had spent the whole of the previous chapter pushing the attention off himself and onto a name, and here is Luke's quiet note that it worked.

Then the closing line, which Luke has deliberately held back: the man on whom this sign of healing was performed was more than forty years old. He could have told us in chapter 3 and chose not to. He gives it here because here it functions as evidence — it is the kind of fact a court establishes and enters in a record. Forty years puts the case beyond any question of a passing complaint, a nervous condition, or a good day. It is a lifetime of fixed and public disability, ended in an afternoon.

And so the session closes. The supreme council of the nation, with the high-priestly dynasty in attendance, the temple police at the door and the power of life and death within its gift, has examined the case of two fishermen and a healed cripple and has succeeded in establishing exactly two things: that it happened, and that nothing can be done about it. They threaten, and they let them go. It is the first recorded attempt by human authority to stop the gospel, and the result is on file.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–37 — Prayer, Power, and the Community of Grace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Released with a threat ringing in their ears, Peter and John go home — Luke says they went to their own — and the church does the one thing it knows how to do. It prays. And the prayer is not what a modern congregation would produce in the circumstances.

It does not begin with the problem. Four verses go by before the threat is even mentioned. They start with God as maker of the heaven and the earth and the sea, move to Psalm 2 and the nations raging to no purpose, and then read their own week into the psalm — Herod and Pilate and the Gentiles and Israel gathered against God's anointed, doing exactly what his hand had already determined. Only then, with the doctrine laid down under them like a floor, do they raise the matter in hand. And they do not ask for what anyone would expect. Not for the threats to stop, not for protection, not for the council to be dealt with. They ask for boldness to go on saying the thing that got them arrested, and for God to keep stretching out his hand.

The answer comes at once. The building shakes, they are all filled with the Spirit again, and they carry on speaking. Notice that what arrives is precisely what was asked for and nothing else: no judgement falls on the Sanhedrin, no obstacle is removed, nothing is made easier. They asked for nerve and were given nerve.

Then Luke turns and shows what that Spirit produces in a community, which is not what people expect either. One heart and soul; nobody saying that what belonged to him was his own; land and houses sold as needs arose; the apostles preaching the resurrection with great power in the middle of it; and not a needy person among them — the sentence Israel's own law had held out as a possibility and Israel had never once achieved. And then a name, because Luke likes to put a face on a pattern: a Levite from Cyprus called Joseph, whom the apostles had nicknamed Son of Encouragement, who sold a field and laid the money down without making a speech about it. The reader is meant to remember him. He is about to become the counter-example to a man named Ananias, and only a chapter division stands between them.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sovereignty of God and Human Responsibility

Verses 27 and 28 are among the most explicit statements of divine sovereignty in the New Testament: Herod, Pontius Pilate, the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel gathered against Jesus to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place. What is striking is the setting. This is not a chapter of argument. It is a prayer, offered by frightened people the morning after a night in custody. The doctrine is not being defended here; it is being leaned on. Reformed theology has always insisted that the two truths — real human guilt and a real divine purpose — must be held together rather than traded against each other, and this chapter shows what holding them together is actually for. If the murder of the Son of God fell inside the plan, then a threat delivered yesterday morning falls inside it too. Which is why the prayer runs straight on from verse 28 to verse 29 without a pause. The sovereignty is not the conclusion of the prayer. It is the ground they are standing on in order to ask for courage.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Luke reports the result of the church's generosity in a sentence lifted out of the law of Moses: there was not a needy person among them. Deuteronomy had held exactly that out as a possibility, attached a condition Israel never met, and admitted in the same chapter that the poor would never cease out of the land. What fifteen centuries of covenant history had not produced, the Spirit produced in Jerusalem inside a year. Now: The particular form belonged to a moment; the open hand does not. And Luke's arrangement is worth attention — he sets the giving immediately beside the preaching, in the same paragraph, so that the community's life and the apostles' message are not two subjects but one.

verseByVerse.quote: When they were released, they went to their friends and reported what the chief priests and the elders had said to them. And when they heard it, they lifted their voices together to God and said, "Sovereign Lord, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two details before the prayer begins, and both are worth having.

They went to their friends — the Greek is warmer and more particular than that. They went to their own. Released from custody with a formal charge hanging over them, the first place these two men go is to the people they belong to. Nobody scatters. Nobody suggests that association with them has become dangerous, which by any sensible reckoning it now had.

They lifted their voices together to God. The word for together is a favourite of Luke's for the early church — with one accord, of one mind, all facing the same way; he uses it of the hundred and twenty waiting in the upper room and of the daily meetings in the temple. Whether the whole company spoke the words in unison or one man led and the rest carried it, Luke does not say and it does not much matter. What he is describing is a room in which nobody is a spectator.

Then the address, and it is not the usual one. They call God Sovereign Lord — the word is the one for an absolute master, the owner of a household with total authority over everyone in it, and it is not the ordinary word for Lord that appears on every other page of the New Testament. Luke has used it of God once before, in his first volume, in the mouth of an old man in the temple who had waited his whole life and was now handing it back: Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace. It is the vocabulary of somebody who has stopped owning himself.

And then, before a single word about the council, four clauses about creation: who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them. It is a line out of the Ten Commandments and out of the Psalms, and it is the largest sentence available to them.

Here is the thing to see, and it is the most instructive feature of the entire prayer. They have a real emergency. Two of their leaders have spent the night in a cell, the supreme court has issued a formal prohibition, and everyone in the room understands that arrests of this kind escalate. And they spend the opening of the prayer on doctrine — not because they are avoiding the subject, but because they are getting the subject into proportion. The Sanhedrin controls the temple, the treasury and the police. It did not make the sea.

A reader can run that against his own practice without much difficulty, and most of us will not enjoy the result. Prayer under pressure tends to begin at the pressure and stay there — the diagnosis, the letter, the money, the person, round and round. There is nothing wicked in that; God invites us to bring exactly those things and never once complains about it. But this church begins somewhere else, and by the time the threat is finally raised in verse 29 it has been set inside a universe that has a Maker in it, and it has come down to something like its actual size.

One guard. This is not a technique for getting prayers answered, and treating it as one would turn a good instinct into a superstition. They did not begin with creation in order to unlock anything. They began there because it was true, and because frightened people need to hear themselves say what is true.

verseByVerse.quote: "who through the mouth of our father David, your servant, said by the Holy Spirit, 'Why did the Gentiles rage, and the peoples plot in vain? The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers were gathered together, against the Lord and against his Anointed' —"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the quotation there is a sentence about how Scripture came to exist, and it is dropped in without any fuss at all: God spoke through the mouth of our father David, your servant... by the Holy Spirit.

Count the agents. God is the speaker. The Holy Spirit is the speaker. David's mouth is the instrument. Three clauses, one act, and not the faintest sense that these are competing explanations. The people praying this had no difficulty holding together the conviction that David composed a poem out of his own head and heart, and that God said it. And it is worth noticing that the clearest statement about inspiration anywhere in Acts occurs not in an argument about the Bible but in the middle of a prayer, where nobody was trying to prove anything to anyone.

Then Psalm 2 itself. It is a coronation psalm, written for the day a son of David was crowned, when the vassal states looked at a new and untested king and began calculating their odds. Why did the Gentiles rage? — the verb is a vivid one, used of a horse snorting and tossing its head and going nowhere. And the peoples plot in vain — the word means empty, hollow, to no purpose. The psalm is not describing feeble opposition. It is describing furious, well-resourced, entirely serious opposition, and calling it empty.

What the church does with it is the important thing. They are not hunting for a verse that suits their mood. They are reading their own week and finding it already written down — the kings, the rulers, the gathering together, the conspiracy against the Lord and against his Anointed. The Sanhedrin met yesterday morning, and Psalm 2 has the minutes.

And they stop the quotation just before the best part, which tells you they knew perfectly well where it goes. The next line of that psalm is that the One enthroned in heaven laughs. They do not quote it and they do not need to; nobody recites the punchline of something every person in the room has known since childhood. But it is lying underneath the prayer, and it accounts for the extraordinary confidence of what they are about to ask for.

There is a use for that in ordinary Christian life, and it is not the cheap one. The point is not that opposition to God is comic and can be laughed off by his people — the men praying this had been in prison overnight, and one of them would be executed by Herod's sword within a few years. The point is that from the only vantage that finally matters, the raging is futile: not harmless, not painless, but futile. The kings of the earth have been setting themselves against the Lord's Anointed for three thousand years, and that psalm has never once needed rewriting.

verseByVerse.quote: "for truly in this city there were gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the church does something with the psalm that is worth watching closely. They take it apart and put names into it.

Psalm 2 lists four parties: the nations, the peoples, the kings of the earth, and the rulers. The prayer supplies the roster. The kings — Herod. The rulers — Pontius Pilate. The nations — the Gentiles. The peoples — the peoples of Israel. Four slots, four names, and the sum of them is one Friday morning in this city.

The mention of Herod is a small mark of authenticity, because the meeting between Herod and Pilate over Jesus is recorded by nobody except Luke, who also notes that the two men, who had been enemies, became friends that day. The prayer of a Jerusalem congregation and the research of a Greek physician are describing the same afternoon.

Then the sentence: they did whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place. The double agency of the cross has already been set out in this book, with all the guards that belong to it, at Peter's first sermon. What is different here is not the doctrine but the setting — and the setting is the entire point.

This is not an argument. Nobody in the room is defending predestination against an objection, or drawing careful distinctions, or fielding the question about whether God is then the author of sin. These are frightened people the morning after a night in prison, and they are using the doctrine — putting their weight on it to see whether it holds. It holds.

And the logic they draw out of it is exact. If the crucifixion of the Son of God — the worst single act in the history of the world, carried out by a coalition of everybody, freely, wickedly, with full culpability — was nevertheless inside the hand and plan of God, then what happened in a council chamber yesterday morning is inside it too. Which is why the prayer does not pause here. Verse 28 runs straight on into verse 29 without so much as a breath. The sovereignty is not the conclusion they are working toward. It is the floor they are standing on in order to ask for something.

It is worth saying what the doctrine is not being used for. Not to make the threat harmless — the threat was real and the flogging came in the next chapter. Not to excuse the men who made it; this same prayer calls what they did a gathering against God's holy servant. And not as an anaesthetic: nobody here is saying the situation does not matter. They are saying it is not out of hand.

Most people meet predestination as a controversy — something to be argued about, usually with somebody who has already decided. Here is its native habitat: a small, frightened, illegal congregation in an occupied city, using it as a place to stand.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, Lord, look upon their threats and grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness, while you stretch out your hand to heal, and signs and wonders are performed through the name of your holy servant Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now, at last, the problem: Lord, look upon their threats. They ask God to look at it. And then, having drawn his attention to it, they ask him for something else entirely.

Set out what is not in this prayer, because the omissions are the most striking thing about it. They do not ask for the threats to be withdrawn. They do not ask for the council to be judged, or humbled, or replaced. They do not ask for protection, or for the arrests to stop, or for Peter and John to be spared a second night in a cell. They do not even ask for wisdom about proceeding more discreetly. Every one of those would be a perfectly reasonable Christian prayer, and not one of them is here.

What they ask for is boldness to continue to speak your word — which is to say, more of the exact behaviour that got two of them arrested the previous afternoon. And they ask God to go on stretching out his hand to heal, with signs and wonders through the name of Jesus — which is to say, more of the exact thing that started the trouble. Put plainly: the council forbade the name, and the church's response is to ask God to make the name more conspicuous.

Two words locate them precisely. At verse 24 they addressed God as Sovereign Lord, the absolute master of a household. Here they call themselves your servants, and the word is the ordinary one for slaves. Master and slaves. It is not an anxious relationship and it is not a negotiation. A slave does not ask his master to arrange easier work; he asks for what he needs to do the work he has been given.

And the word they choose for boldness is the very word the council had noticed in them at verse 13. They already had it, in a courtroom, without asking for it. They ask anyway. Whatever they were given yesterday, they treat as spent, and they come back for more this morning.

Here a guard is essential, because a passage like this is very easily turned into a rebuke. It would be a serious mistake to conclude that praying for safety is unspiritual. Paul asks the Roman church to pray that he may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea. The church in chapter 12 of this same book prays Peter out of a prison cell and God sends an angel to open the door. Jesus himself taught his disciples to pray to be delivered from evil. Nobody reading this passage should come away feeling that asking God to protect his children is a second-class prayer, and a parent praying for a sick child does not need to be told that his praying is insufficiently missionary.

What the passage does show is what these particular people wanted most when they were badly frightened, and that is a different question and a more searching one. A prayer reveals what is actually being protected. It is worth asking, quietly and without theatre, what the last genuinely hard week produced in one's own praying — and whether any of it would still have been wanted if the whole business had simply been made to go away.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had prayed, the place in which they were gathered together was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and continued to speak the word of God with boldness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The answer arrives before they have got up off the floor.

The place in which they were gathered together was shaken. God does not reply in words. He moves the building. In Scripture a shaking of this kind is what happens when God arrives somewhere — the mountain trembling at Sinai, the doorposts shifting on their foundations when Isaiah saw the Lord in the temple. Here it comes in answer to a prayer that had opened by naming him as the maker of heaven and earth and sea. They had reminded themselves whom they were addressing, and he replied by moving the walls a few inches, which is a very short way of saying: correct.

Then they were all filled with the Holy Spirit. All of them, not the apostles only. And filled once again — the same word used of these same people seven weeks earlier at Pentecost, and of Peter twenty-three verses ago. This is not a second Pentecost, and Luke does not treat it as one; the Spirit does not arrive, because he has never left. What this language describes is fresh supply for fresh demand, which is a mercy, since it means the church is not living off a reserve laid down once and steadily running down.

And then the answer proper: and continued to speak the word of God with boldness. Not felt bold. Spoke. The verb is continuous — they kept on doing it, which is the only form courage takes that can actually be measured.

Two things about this answer deserve attention. The first is that it is exactly what was asked for and not one item more. The council was not struck down. The prohibition was not lifted. The danger did not decrease — by the next chapter these men are arrested again and flogged. God supplied precisely what was requested, which was nerve, and left every circumstance standing. That is one of the ways God answers, and it is worth knowing in advance: not by removing the situation but by re-equipping the person who is inside it.

The second is a caution. The shaking is reported once in Acts and never becomes a pattern. Nobody in the New Testament goes looking for it, and no writer anywhere suggests that a prayer without a physical sign has gone unheard. The point of this verse is not the tremor; it is the clause after it. Luke's evidence that God had answered is not that the walls moved. It is that a roomful of intimidated people went straight back out and said the thing they had been forbidden to say.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the full number of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one said that any of the things that belonged to him was his own, but they had everything in common. And with great power the apostles were giving their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke describes the church here with language his Greek readers would have recognised at once, and it is worth knowing why it would have stopped them.

Of one heart and soul. In the Greek world there was a well-worn saying that a friend is a single soul living in two bodies, and an older proverb still that friends hold all things in common. These were the classical ideals of friendship — much quoted, much admired, and universally understood to be out of reach except perhaps between two rare individuals over a lifetime. Luke uses both of them in consecutive clauses and applies them not to a pair of philosophers but to a congregation of several thousand people in an occupied city, most of whom had met one another within the previous three months.

Then a sentence that is nearly always paraphrased and should not be, because the precision is the whole of it. No one said that any of the things that belonged to him was his own. Read it slowly. It does not say that nobody owned anything. It says that things still belonged to people — Luke uses the language of possession — and that nobody was saying so. Ownership survived. The claim was dropped. The property register was unchanged and the vocabulary had altered completely.

That distinction does more work than a page of argument. This is not the abolition of private property, and Peter will say as much to Ananias within a few verses. It is something harder and more interior: people who still held the deeds and had stopped speaking as though the deeds settled anything. Anybody can be talked into a scheme. What Luke reports is a change in what people assumed when they were not thinking about it.

And then, dropped straight into the middle of all that, verse 33: with great power the apostles were giving their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus.

The placing is deliberate and it is easily missed, because chapter headings and sermon habits tend to file these two subjects separately — the church's inner life over here, evangelism over there. Luke puts the preaching inside the paragraph about the money. The community that had stopped saying mine is the community in which the resurrection was announced with power, and Luke plainly did not consider those to be two different topics.

The last clause can be read two ways and probably means both. Great grace was upon them all — the favour of God resting on the whole company, and equally the goodwill of a watching city, which is how Luke used the same word two chapters earlier. Both were true for a season, and the sentence does not need to be made to choose.

verseByVerse.quote: There was not a needy person among them, for as many as were owners of lands or houses sold them and brought the proceeds of what was sold and laid it at the apostles' feet, and it was distributed to each as any had need.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was not a needy person among them. Luke is quoting, and any hearer who knew the law would have caught it.

In Deuteronomy, God speaks to Israel about the seventh year, when debts were released, and adds a promise: there will be no poor among you. It comes with a condition — if only you will strictly obey the voice of the LORD your God — and seven verses later the same chapter states, flatly and without apology, there will never cease to be poor in the land (Deuteronomy 15:4, 11). The law held out a possibility and in the same breath admitted that Israel would not reach it. And Israel did not. Fifteen centuries of covenant history, with prophets thundering about the neglected widow and the pledged cloak and the corner of the field left unreaped, produced a great deal of legislation and never once produced that sentence.

And then Luke, writing about a group of people in Jerusalem perhaps a year after Pentecost, uses it as a plain statement of fact.

Notice how it came about, because the method is not the one anybody would have designed. Nothing was collected. Nobody was assessed. As needs arose, people who owned land or houses sold them — the tense suggests this went on over time rather than in one grand liquidation — and the proceeds were laid at the apostles' feet.

That gesture repays a pause. Not handed to the apostles: laid at their feet, which is the posture of submission and also of anonymity. You put the money down and you walk away. There is no transaction between the giver and the person who receives it, no thanks owed, nobody beholden. The widow eating that week does not know whose field paid for it, and the man who sold the field does not know which widow he fed. The arrangement makes patronage impossible, and patronage is the disease that has attended religious giving in every century since.

A word here, since this is sometimes called 'Christian communism' and pressed into political service: it was nothing of the kind. It was wholly voluntary — Peter tells Ananias, 'while it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal?' (5:4) — so private property was kept and giving was free, never compelled. It was love-driven and Spirit-prompted, flowing from hearts made 'one,' not enforced by any state. And it was needs-based generosity ('as any had need'), not mechanical equalising. This is the very opposite of coercive collectivism: it is the free, glad open-handedness of people whom the Spirit had loosed from the grip of money. The abiding call is that same generosity and care for the needy among us; the particular form was one Spirit-filled moment's response.

Which suggests a test, and a sharper one than the usual question of whether a person would give if he were asked. Would you be willing for the gift to be untraceable? Not merely for your name to be left off a list, but for the person helped never to discover that it was you, never to be grateful to you, never to know that they owe you anything whatever. That is the arrangement Luke is describing. The money went on the floor at the apostles' feet, and after that it was nobody's.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus Joseph, who was also called by the apostles Barnabas (which means son of encouragement), a Levite, a native of Cyprus, sold a field that belonged to him and brought the money and laid it at the apostles' feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke has been describing a pattern. Now he gives it a face, and the face turns out to matter enormously to the rest of the book.

The man's name is Joseph. Almost nobody remembers that, because the apostles gave him a nickname and it stuck so completely that the New Testament uses it more than twenty times while the real name effectively disappears. They called him Barnabas, which Luke glosses as son of encouragement — and the word behind encouragement is the noun from which the Spirit's own title, the Helper called alongside, is built. The apostles looked at this man and named him after something the Holy Spirit does.

He was a Levite from Cyprus, and because the tribe of Levi received no territory when the land was divided, some readers have assumed an irregularity in his owning a field. There is probably none. The restriction concerned tribal allotment within Israel; Levites held houses and pasture land; a priest bought a field as far back as Jeremiah; and Luke does not tell us where this one was. It is a detail to read carefully rather than to press.

What matters is what Luke chose to record about him first, and it is a cheque. Before anything else in his biography, before a single word he ever said, the first fact on file about Barnabas is that he sold a field, put the money down, and made no speech about it.

Keep him in view, because he is about to do the three things that hold the New Testament together. When Saul of Tarsus came to Jerusalem after his conversion and every Christian in the city was too frightened to go near a man who had been arresting them, one person took him by the arm, brought him to the apostles and vouched for him (9:26–27). When the gospel unexpectedly broke out among Greeks at Antioch, Barnabas was sent to look into it, approved it, and then travelled to Tarsus to find Saul and bring him into the work — which is how the apostle to the Gentiles was started (11:22–26). And when Paul refused to take young John Mark on a second journey because the boy had deserted them, Barnabas took him anyway and lost his partnership with Paul over it (15:37–39). Years later Paul writes from a prison cell asking for Mark, for he is very useful to me for ministry. Barnabas had been right, and Paul lived long enough to say so.

That is the man Luke introduces here with a field and a payment. It is worth noticing that the encouraging of other people, which is what he became famous for, began as a habit of open-handedness in a matter of money; and that the whole Gentile mission of the church runs through a man whose first recorded act was to give something away.

One last thing, and the chapter break conceals it. The next sentence in Luke's narrative begins But a man named Ananias... There is no gap. Barnabas and Ananias are two halves of one paragraph — the real thing and the imitation, set side by side, both bringing money and both laying it at the apostles' feet, and one of them dead within the week.
