As if the Son of Man rose to his feet to receive his first martyr home. They stop their ears and rush at him. He dies praying his Lord’s own prayer for his killers. And at the edge of the scene, holding the coats, is a young man named Saul.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–50 — Stephen's Defense: Israel's History and God's Patience
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
This is the longest speech in Acts, and it is the one readers skip. It looks like a history lesson delivered by a man who has misunderstood the question. It is nothing of the kind. Stephen is on trial on two charges — that he has spoken against the holy place, and against the customs Moses delivered — and every paragraph of what follows is aimed at one or the other of them.

Against the temple charge he assembles a case out of their own Scriptures. The God of glory appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia, seven hundred miles away, before there was a promised land to stand in. He was with Joseph in an Egyptian prison. He called a patch of Midianite scrub holy ground and told Moses to take his sandals off on it. The sanctuary he designed himself was a tent with poles, built to be carried; and when David finally offered to build something permanent, God's reply was that he had never asked for one. Isaiah put the matter beyond argument: heaven is his throne, and what sort of house did you have in mind?

Against the charge about Moses, Stephen does something cleverer. He does not defend himself; he changes who is in the dock. Israel rejected Moses the first time at forty, and thrust him aside again at Sinai while he was up the mountain collecting the law on their behalf. They made a calf and rejoiced in the works of their hands, and carried a pagan shrine through the desert alongside the tabernacle. A man accused of dishonouring Moses spends twenty verses showing that he honours him more than his accusers ever have.

Underneath both runs a single rhythm which is the real argument of the speech: the deliverer is rejected, and God sends him anyway. Joseph is sold by his brothers and becomes their rescuer. Moses is refused by his own people and is sent back as their ruler. Stephen never once mentions Jesus by name in the whole recital. He does not have to. By the time he reaches verse 51 the pattern has been laid down so thoroughly that his hearers can finish the sentence themselves — which is exactly what they do.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Temple and the Transcendence of God

Stephen's climax — the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands (v. 48) — is not an outsider's attack on the temple. It is the temple's own prophetic self-criticism, read back to the men who ran it. Solomon said it himself on the day he dedicated the building: the heaven of heavens cannot contain God, how much less this house (1 Kings 8:27). Isaiah said it within sight of the same building. God had said it to David before a stone was laid, pointing out that in four hundred years he had never once asked anybody for a house of cedar. The problem was never the temple; it was the reduction of God to a location — the belief that having the building in Jerusalem meant having God in a form that could be managed and defended. Reformed theology has read Stephen's argument as the permanent warning against every arrangement in which the sign is kept and the reality quietly replaced by it. And the warning has teeth precisely because Stephen is not against the sign: God designed the tent, God filled the temple, and God was the one who said he would not be confined to either.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Every institution Stephen's accusers trusted came after the God who made it. Abraham had the covenant and no land; the patriarchs had the promise and a grave; Moses had holy ground in a foreign desert; Israel had a sanctuary that could be packed up in a day. Now: The question the speech puts to a congregation is not whether it values its building, its tradition or its structures — Stephen valued the tabernacle and said God designed it. It is whether it could lose them and still know where to find God.

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest said, "Are these things so?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four words in Greek, and they hand Stephen the longest speech in the book. The high priest is following procedure: the charges have been read, and the accused is invited to answer them. Are these things so?

What follows is the passage most readers of Acts quietly skip. It reads, on a first pass, like a man who has been asked a direct question and has responded with a summary of the Old Testament. Fifty verses on Abraham, Joseph, Moses, the tabernacle and Solomon, and not one word of denial, not one appeal for acquittal, and no mention of Jesus by name until the very end. It is worth knowing before starting that this is not evasion and it is not rambling. It is the most carefully aimed speech in Acts.

Remember the two charges from the previous chapter. He is accused of speaking against this holy place, and of saying that Jesus would change the customs that Moses delivered to us. Hold those two in mind and the speech stops looking like a history lesson and starts looking like a brief.

The temple charge gets answered by geography. God appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia. God was with Joseph in Egypt. God called a bush in a Midianite desert holy ground. God designed his own sanctuary as a tent with carrying poles. God told David he had never asked for a building. Isaiah asked what kind of house anyone imagined they could put him in. Stephen does not argue that the temple is bad. He walks his accusers through their own Scriptures and lets them notice that God has spent the entire story refusing to be located.

The Moses charge gets answered by turning the accusation round. Stephen honours Moses extravagantly — sent by God, ruler and redeemer, receiver of living oracles, worker of signs and wonders for forty years. And in the middle of the tribute he points out that Israel rejected him twice, and made a golden calf while he was up the mountain fetching the law. By verse 53 the man accused of despising the law is telling the court that they received it from angels and did not keep it.

And it should be said what Stephen never does with the floor he has been given. He never asks to be let off. He does not produce character witnesses, does not clarify what he actually said, does not seek to establish that the testimony against him was perjured — which it was, and which he could presumably have proved. He has one hour and the undivided attention of the supreme council of his nation, and he spends the whole of it preaching to them.

Which is worth sitting with before reading further. A man is given the last opportunity of his life to save it, and uses it instead on the people who are going to take it.

verseByVerse.quote: And Stephen said: "Brothers and fathers, hear me. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran, and said to him, 'Go out from your land and from your kindred and go into the land that I will show you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers and fathers. He opens by calling the court that is going to kill him his family, and using the respectful address a younger man owes his elders. There is no defiance in the first sentence and there will be none until verse 51. It is the same opening Paul uses years later when he is standing in front of a mob in this same city (22:1), and both men are doing the same thing: establishing, before anything else, that this is an argument inside the house and not an attack from outside it.

Then the first clause of the speech, which is the whole thesis. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran.

Every word in that sentence is doing work. The God of glory — and glory is the temple word. It is what filled the tabernacle when it was finished and the house when Solomon dedicated it, until the priests could not stand up to do their work. If there is one thing these men believe belongs to their building, it is the glory. Stephen takes the title and attaches it to an event that happened before Israel existed, in what is now southern Iraq, roughly seven hundred miles from the room they are sitting in.

And he is careful about the timing: before he lived in Haran. Genesis 12 has the call coming at Haran; Stephen follows the older summons in Ur, which Scripture itself records — I am the LORD who brought you out from Ur of the Chaldeans (Genesis 15:7). So the very first appearance of God to the founder of the covenant people happened in a pagan city, in a family that served other gods, to a man who had never heard of Canaan and did not know the name of the God speaking to him.

Then the command, and it is worth measuring what it asked. Go out from your land and from your kindred. In that world those two things were not sentiment; they were survival. Your kindred were the people who fed you in a bad harvest, avenged you if you were wronged, buried you, and remembered your name. Your land held the graves of your fathers and the shrines of the gods who were thought to look after that particular patch of ground. To leave both was not an adventure. It was to make yourself a man with no protection, no insurance and no standing, in a world that had no other kind.

And he is not told where he is going. The land that I will show you — future tense, no name, no map, no coordinates. God gives him the leaving in full detail and the arriving not at all.

There is a great deal in that for anyone who has been asked to obey without being shown the destination — the move, the resignation, the relationship ended, the thing put down that cannot be picked up again. Abraham's instructions consisted entirely of what to leave, plus a promise that there would be somewhere to go. It is the ordinary shape of obedience, and Scripture holds up the man who managed it as the father of everybody who has since.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he went out from the land of the Chaldeans and lived in Haran. And after his father died, God removed him from there into this land in which you are now living. Yet he gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot's length, but promised to give it to him as a possession and to his offspring after him, though he had no child.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two facts sit side by side here and Stephen wants the collision. God brought Abraham into this land in which you are now living — and gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot's length.

Take the measurement seriously, because the measurement is the argument. Not a farm; not a field; not the width of a foot. The man to whom the entire country was promised died holding legal title to exactly one thing in it — a cave with his wife buried in it, bought from a Hittite at a price he did not trouble to haggle over. He lived his whole adult life in tents, in a land that was his by promise and nobody else's by law, and he never once slept in a house standing on ground he owned.

Stephen is saying this to men whose entire case rests on a plot of land and a building on it. He is pointing out that the founder of their nation had neither, and that the lack of them did not make him less the friend of God. It made him the pattern.

There is a difficulty buried in the clause Stephen uses to get there, and a reader with Genesis open will find it. He says Abraham moved on after his father died. But Genesis appears to say otherwise: Terah was seventy when he fathered Abram (Gen. 11:26), Terah died at two hundred and five (11:32), and Abram left Haran at seventy-five (12:4). That leaves Terah alive for another sixty years. It looks as though Stephen, or Luke, has slipped.

He has not, and the answer is in how Genesis writes these lines. Terah lived seventy years and fathered Abram, Nahor and Haran does not mean that all three arrived in his seventieth year; it means that is when he began having sons. Genesis uses the identical formula of Noah — five hundred years old, and fathered Shem, Ham and Japheth — and nobody imagines triplets there either. In both places the sons are listed by prominence rather than birth order, which is why Abram heads a list he may well have come last in. Put Abram's birth in Terah's hundred and thirtieth year and every number falls into line: Terah dies at two hundred and five, Abram is seventy-five, and he leaves for Canaan exactly as Stephen says. The arithmetic that looked like an error turns out to be the arithmetic that fixes it.

It is worth adding that ancient readers noticed this too — the Samaritan copies of the Pentateuch give Terah's age at death as a hundred and forty-five, which smooths the difficulty by another road. And it is worth remembering who is speaking. This is a man with the Scriptures at his fingertips, about to be killed for what he is drawing out of them. He is not being careless with Genesis; he knows it better than the men who are about to stone him for it.

verseByVerse.quote: And God spoke to this effect — that his offspring would be sojourners in a land belonging to others, who would enslave and afflict them four hundred years. 'But I will judge the nation that they serve,' said God, 'and after that they shall come out and worship me in this place.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The promise as God actually gave it contained something people rarely notice when they quote it: four centuries of slavery, announced in advance.

God did not tell Abraham the land would come quickly or that the road would be short. He told him his descendants would be strangers in another people's country, that they would be enslaved and mistreated, that it would go on for four hundred years — and that only then would they come out. Abraham was being informed that his great-grandchildren's great-grandchildren would be born in chains, and that this was not a failure of the plan but the plan.

That is a hard thing to sit with, and Stephen includes it because his hearers need to see how God's promises actually run. There is a gap between the word and the fulfilment, and God fills it with things nobody would have chosen. The four hundred years are not an interruption in this story. They are the story. Anyone who concludes from four months of silence that God has changed his mind should look carefully at the arithmetic Abraham was handed and still believed.

And then the clause Stephen is steering toward: they shall come out and worship me in this place. Which place? Not the temple. God says these words to Moses at the burning bush, and this place means the mountain in the desert where he is standing (Exodus 3:12). The first act of national worship God ever promised his rescued people was to take place at a rock in Sinai, several hundred miles from the building these men are prosecuting Stephen in order to protect.

On the four hundred years, a small note for the reader who checks. Stephen is quoting God's word to Abraham (Gen. 15:13), which says four hundred; Exodus gives the sojourn as four hundred and thirty (Ex. 12:40), and Paul uses that longer figure too (Gal. 3:17). There is no conflict. Four hundred is the round number for the affliction, spoken to Abraham in the shape a promise takes rather than a ledger; four hundred and thirty is the precise span, counted from a slightly different starting point. Scripture is quite capable of giving a figure to the year in one place and rounding it in another, exactly as we do, and Stephen quotes the text he is actually citing.

verseByVerse.quote: And he gave him the covenant of circumcision. And so Abraham became the father of Isaac, and circumcised him on the eighth day, and Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Notice where the covenant sign is given. Abraham has no land, no city, and at this point no child — and God hands him a sign to be cut into his own body.

That is a striking arrangement and Stephen has set it up carefully over the previous verses. The mark of belonging to God is put on the flesh, not on a plot of ground. It travels. Abraham carried it into Egypt and out again; Jacob's sons carried it down into slavery; every Israelite in Babylon carried it through seventy years with no temple to go to. Of all the ways God might have marked out a people, he chose the one thing they could not be separated from and could not leave behind when they were deported.

Then the list: Isaac, Jacob, the twelve patriarchs. Three generations in a single sentence, and a nation exists by the end of it. Stephen is moving fast, but he is establishing something no man in that room can dispute — that everything essential to being the people of God was in place and working generations before there was a land to live in or a house to worship in.

Why call it 'the covenant of circumcision'? The phrase names the covenant by its sign. The covenant itself was God's promise to Abraham — a people, a land, and blessing for all nations (Gen. 12; 15; 17) — and when God formalised it he gave Abraham circumcision as its token in the flesh: 'This is my covenant... every male among you shall be circumcised... it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you' (Gen. 17:10–11). Sign and covenant became so bound together that the whole covenant could be called simply 'the covenant of circumcision' — the covenant whose seal was circumcision, much as we might name an agreement by its signature. Two things are worth holding here. First, the sign sealed a promise already received by faith: Abraham was counted righteous through faith (Gen. 15:6) before he was ever circumcised (Gen. 17), so circumcision was 'a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith' (Rom. 4:11) — the mark never earned the promise; it pointed to it. Second, the eighth-day circumcision of Isaac, then of Jacob's line down to the twelve patriarchs, shows the covenant people being marked out generation by generation — the family through whom, in the end, the blessing to all nations would come in Christ (cf. Gal. 3:8, 16).

verseByVerse.quote: "And the patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt; but God was with him and rescued him out of all his afflictions and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who made him ruler over Egypt and over all his household."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt.

Consider whom Stephen is saying that to. In front of him sits the high priest, and on the high priest's chest, when he is robed, is a breastplate set with twelve stones, and engraved on those stones are twelve names — Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah and the rest (Exodus 28:21). The founding fathers of the nation, worn over the heart of the man presiding at this trial. Stephen has just described them, accurately and without a word of softening, as men who sold their brother into slavery because they could not stand him.

He does not linger, because he is laying down a pattern rather than scoring a point. But the pattern is now visible for the first time in the speech and it will run through everything that follows: the man his brothers got rid of turns out to be the man they cannot live without. Joseph goes down into Egypt in a slave train and comes up as the only source of food in the world, and the brothers who sold him arrive at his door to beg.

Then the clause that carries the other half of Stephen's case. But God was with him.

Where, exactly? Not in the promised land. Not at a shrine, an altar, a festival or a sanctuary. God was with Joseph in a slave caravan, in an Egyptian official's household, and in a prison cell on a false accusation, for something like thirteen years between the pit and the palace. There is no record in Genesis of Joseph in all that time having a priest, a place of worship, a copy of any Scripture, or a single one of the things his descendants would one day kill a man for defending. And the text says God was with him.

Note precisely what that presence did and did not do. It did not keep him out of prison. Stephen's phrase is that God rescued him out of all his afflictions — out of them, which means he was in them first, all of them, one after another. The rescue ran through the trouble rather than around it, and at no point during those thirteen years could Joseph have told you that it was working.

That is the part to take personally, and it needs handling honestly rather than cheerfully. There is a version of this story preached as a guarantee: hold on, because your Egypt is preparing you for a throne. Scripture does not promise that. Joseph received a visible return inside his own lifetime; a great many faithful people do not, and the letter to the Hebrews says plainly of a long list of them that they died still waiting. What this passage does establish is the thing Stephen actually needs, and it is enough to build a life on: there is no place a believer can be taken — sold, imprisoned, deported, forgotten, or simply stuck — where God is not already there ahead of him, and no institution whose absence can put him out of reach.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now there came a famine throughout all Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction, and our fathers could find no food. But when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent out our fathers on their first visit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A famine in the ancient world was not a disruption to the food supply. There were no reserves worth the name, no imports, and nobody to appeal to. A household ate its stores, then its breeding animals, then the seed corn it needed for the following year — and once the seed was gone, next year had been decided as well. After that it moved, or it died.

And notice where this one strikes. Throughout all Egypt and Canaan. The chosen family, standing in the land of promise, holding the covenant, descended directly from Abraham, could find no food. The country God had sworn to give them could not feed them, and the grain was in the pagan empire down the road.

Stephen is still quietly dismantling the same equation. His accusers hold that God's favour and God's land belong together, so that possessing the one proves the other. He observes that the covenant family's first great crisis was solved by leaving.

Then look at the machinery of it. When Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent out our fathers. That is the entire mechanism. A rumour reaches an old man in Hebron that there is wheat for sale in the south, and he sends his sons down to buy some. There is no vision, no angel and no word from God recorded anywhere in the transaction. A man hears a piece of market news and acts on it sensibly — and in doing so sets in motion the descent into Egypt, the four hundred years, the exodus, Sinai and the whole national existence of Israel.

That is how providence usually works, and it is worth noticing, because a great deal of Christian anxiety is spent looking for the other sort. Very little of what God does in a life arrives labelled. It arrives as the price of wheat, a conversation that ran longer than expected, a job that fell through, a piece of news somebody happened to mention in passing. Jacob was not being spiritual when he sent his sons to Egypt. He was being practical. He was also, without the faintest suspicion of it, delivering his household into the hands of the son he had spent twenty years mourning.

One guard, because this can slide into fatalism. That God governs the ordinary does not mean the ordinary decisions are unimportant or need not be weighed. Jacob still had to assess the risk and send the boys, and if he had not, they would have starved. What it means is that a man doing the sensible next thing in front of him, with no sense of destiny about it whatever, may be doing something that is still being discussed three thousand years later.

verseByVerse.quote: "And on the second visit Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and Joseph's family became known to Pharaoh. And Joseph sent and summoned Jacob his father and all his kindred, seventy-five persons in all."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two visits, and everything turns on the second. Joseph made himself known to his brothers — and Stephen says nothing whatever about what that cost. Genesis gives the scene three chapters and a room emptied of Egyptians and a man weeping so loudly that the household heard it through the wall. Stephen gives it seven words.

He is not being careless; he needs the shape rather than the detail. The brother they sold is the one they end up standing in front of, and the moment he tells them who he is, is the moment their lives are saved. They had assumed for twenty years that they had got away with it. The man they had wronged had in the meantime been put in charge of the only food in the world, and could have done anything he liked with them.

Then the descent. Joseph sent and summoned Jacob his father and all his kindred — the whole covenant family, counted, packed, and moved out of the land of promise into the land of the Nile. On the face of it, it is the end of the story: the people God had called out of Mesopotamia and settled in Canaan have now left Canaan for Egypt, and will be there for centuries. It is in fact the mechanism of the next act. A household goes down, and a nation comes up.

One clause in the middle is easy to skim and it decides everything that follows: Joseph's family became known to Pharaoh. A household of shepherds out of the Judean hills was presented at the Egyptian court, and Genesis records the king assigning them the best of the land in Goshen. Israel did not arrive in Egypt as refugees sleeping rough. They came in by royal invitation, with a grant of territory, under the protection of the second man in the kingdom. Which is exactly why the change of dynasty at verse 18 is such a catastrophe — everything they had rested on one man's standing at court, and courts forget — and why, four hundred years later, they were still there.

A sharp-eyed reader will notice Stephen says 'seventy-five' persons, while Genesis puts the number at 'seventy' (Gen. 46:27; Ex. 1:5). Stephen is following the Septuagint — the Greek translation of the Old Testament that Greek-speaking Jews used everywhere in his day — which reads seventy-five, counting several more of Joseph's descendants born in Egypt. The New Testament often quotes this Greek version; the difference is a matter of counting in two text-traditions, not a mistake. Either way Stephen's point holds: a family went down to Egypt, and a nation came up.

verseByVerse.quote: "And Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, he and our fathers, and they were carried back to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor in Shechem."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, he and our fathers. Six words for the death of an entire generation, and Stephen keeps moving.

But he stops for one thing, and it is the burial. These men died outside the land — every one of them, patriarchs of a people who had been promised a country — and their bodies were carried back across the desert so that they could lie in ground they had never owned. Joseph made his brothers swear to it on his deathbed, and four hundred years later a nation walking out of Egypt in a hurry took a coffin with them.

Consider that as a piece of evidence. The only real estate any of the patriarchs held in the promised land was a grave. They believed the promise so completely that they arranged their own funerals around it, and they believed it so patiently that not one of them expected to see it kept in his lifetime. Stephen's accusers hold the land, the city and the temple, and are about to kill a man over a building. The founding fathers held a tomb, and held on to God.

A careful reader with an open Bible will stop here, and should. Stephen says the fathers were carried to Shechem and laid in a tomb that Abraham bought from the sons of Hamor. Genesis records two separate transactions: Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah at Hebron from Ephron the Hittite (Gen. 23), and Jacob bought the plot at Shechem from the sons of Hamor (Gen. 33:19). Jacob himself was buried at Machpelah (Gen. 50:13); Joseph's bones were laid at Shechem in Jacob's plot (Josh. 24:32). Stephen has folded two purchases and two burial grounds into a single clause.

The natural explanation is compression. He is racing through two thousand years of history in one speech, on trial for his life, and he telescopes the patriarchal burials into a summary phrase; he is not filing a title deed. His hearers were the Sanhedrin — men who knew the Torah better than we do — and they do not challenge a syllable of his history. They rage at his conclusion, not his facts. (A few have suggested Abraham made a further, unrecorded purchase at Shechem, where he built his first altar in the land, Gen. 12:6-7; possible, but speculative.) And if anyone still judges it a slip, notice carefully what Scripture is doing here: Luke's task is to report the sermon faithfully, and he has. The Bible records accurately what people said — including Job's friends, who were wrong, and Gamaliel, whose history was loose (Acts 5:36-37). Inspiration guarantees a true record of Stephen's speech, not that a man on trial was infallible in a passing aside. Nothing hangs on it. What Stephen came to say — that God was never confined to this land or that building, that he met Abraham in Mesopotamia and Joseph in Egypt and Moses in a desert — stands untouched. That is the thing that got him killed.

verseByVerse.quote: "But as the time of the promise drew near, which God had granted to Abraham, the people increased and multiplied in Egypt until there arose over Egypt another king who did not know Joseph."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But as the time of the promise drew near. Stephen has been counting. Four hundred years were named to Abraham back in verse 6, and the clock has been running ever since. It is now nearly up — and what happens as it runs out is not a softening of Israel's circumstances but a hardening of them.

Put the two halves of the sentence together, because Stephen has welded them deliberately. The people increased and multiplied in Egypt — the promise working. Until there arose over Egypt another king who did not know Joseph — the terror beginning. Blessing and persecution arrive in the same clause, and the second is a direct consequence of the first: a rapidly growing foreign population in the delta is precisely what alarms a new dynasty.

Stop a moment on that phrase, did not know Joseph. A man had once saved the entire country from starvation, reorganised its agriculture and been made second in the kingdom — and within a few generations the palace has no idea who he was. It is a small, cold observation about the memory of nations and the shelf life of gratitude. Whatever a man does for a country, the country forgets him faster than he would believe, and his descendants are assessed on their usefulness this year.

But the harder thing in this passage is what the wider story makes plain, and it should be said carefully. Israel in Egypt before this king was doing well. They had land in Goshen, they were multiplying, they had standing because of Joseph, and they were four centuries into a country that was not theirs with no recorded sign of wanting to leave it. The promise required them to go. The thing that finally made them willing to go was the whip.

That has to be handled with care, because it stands one step away from a cruelty. It does not follow that every hardship is God prising somebody loose from a comfort, and it is never a thing to say to a person in the middle of one — a friend who explains your suffering to you has stopped being a friend. What can be said is only what the text says: this particular affliction fell inside a promise made four hundred years before, and the people groaning under it could not see that, were not told it, and found out afterwards. Most people do.

There is also a plainer application, and it cuts closer to home for readers in comfortable countries. It is entirely possible to be a member of the covenant people, prospering quietly, in a place you were never meant to settle, for a very long time, with no intention whatever of moving.

verseByVerse.quote: "He dealt shrewdly with our race and forced our fathers to expose their infants, so that they would not be kept alive. At this time Moses was born; and he was beautiful in God's sight. And he was brought up for three months in his father's house,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The verb for what Pharaoh did is unusual and exact. It means to outwit, to deal cleverly with — literally, to out-think somebody. The persecution was not a spasm of temper. It was policy: drafted, revised when it failed, and escalated by stages. First the forced labour to break them; then a quiet instruction to the midwives; then, when the midwives would not do it, the open decree that every son be thrown into the Nile. It is the coldest thing in the chapter, and it was arrived at in meetings.

Stephen then phrases the result in a way that puts the horror exactly where it belongs. Pharaoh forced our fathers to expose their infants. Not soldiers — the fathers. The policy was designed so that Hebrew parents would carry it out themselves, which is more efficient and far more destructive, and which is why a programme of that kind takes something out of a people that a massacre does not.

And against all of that — at this time Moses was born.

That is God's answer to the machinery of a superpower, and it is worth pausing over how small it is. No plague, not yet. No army, no uprising, nothing from the sky. A baby, born to slaves, in the middle of the programme designed to kill precisely him, and hidden three months in a house where one cry at the wrong moment would have finished the whole family. Three months of a household not breathing.

He was beautiful in God's sight, which is a Greek way of rendering a Hebrew superlative — beautiful indeed. The letter to the Hebrews picks up the same detail and says his parents hid him because they saw the child was beautiful and were not afraid of the king's edict. It is worth registering that the first act of faith in the deliverance of Israel was performed by a mother and a father with a basket, and that Scripture names their fear and reports that the faith went past it.

And now the thing that has to be said, because a passage about God's rescue of a nation is being read by people who know that rescues are not universal. The other babies died. Stephen does not mention them and Exodus does not name them, but they were there — the households who did what they were forced to do, whose sons were not hidden or were found, and for whom the deliverer being born down the street was, at the time, no help at all. Scripture neither explains them nor pretends they were not there. Any reading of this passage that leaves the impression that God protects the children of the faithful as a general rule is a reading which must be kept well away from anyone who has buried one.

What the passage does say is that a state which had decided to end a people could not manage to kill one particular child, and ended up paying for his upbringing. That is not an explanation of the others. It is a statement about who was actually in charge of the outcome, made to a court that was under the impression it was.

verseByVerse.quote: "and when he was exposed, Pharaoh's daughter adopted him and brought him up as her own son. And Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and he was mighty in his words and deeds."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rescue is arranged by the daughter of the man who signed the death warrant, and the child is brought up in the palace of the regime that wanted him dead. Stephen does not comment on the irony. He does not need to.

But look at what it cost. He was brought up as her own son, which means he was taken out of a Hebrew house and raised as an Egyptian prince. He grew up eating at the table of the people who had enslaved his family, speaking their language, wearing their clothes, learning their gods and their arithmetic, and being addressed by a name that was not the one his mother used. Whatever else that childhood was, it was not simple, and he spent forty years inside a court that belonged to his own people's enemy.

Which is precisely Stephen's point in this stretch of the speech, and it is aimed at the temple charge again. God's man is formed entirely outside the covenant community — in a pagan palace, by a pagan education, at the expense of the pagan state. And Luke's description of the result, mighty in his words and deeds, is the phrase he had used in his first volume of Jesus of Nazareth (Luke 24:19).

What was 'the wisdom of the Egyptians'? Egypt was the great seat of learning in the ancient world — its name a byword for advanced knowledge (even of Solomon it is said his wisdom 'surpassed... all the wisdom of Egypt,' 1 Kings 4:30). It embraced mathematics and geometry (the skill behind the pyramids and the re-surveying of fields after each Nile flood), astronomy and the calendar, a famed medicine, architecture and engineering, the scribal art of writing, statecraft and administration, and a large body of moral 'instruction' literature — together with the lore of the priestly class. As Pharaoh's daughter's adopted son, raised in the royal court, Moses would have received the elite education of an Egyptian prince — the finest schooling the age could give, which left him 'mighty in words and deeds.' (The detail that he was trained in 'all' this wisdom is not stated in Exodus itself; it is the natural inference from his upbringing, preserved also in Jewish tradition — Philo and Josephus describe his education at length.) Stephen's deeper point soon follows: for all his Egyptian learning and natural greatness, Moses' first attempt to deliver Israel in his own strength failed (vv. 23–29), and he had to wait forty years in the desert for God's call. The world's finest wisdom equipped him, but it did not make him the deliverer — God did.

verseByVerse.quote: "When he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the children of Israel. And seeing one of them being wronged, he defended the oppressed man and avenged him by striking down the Egyptian."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers. The Greek is more physical than that: it came up upon his heart. Something rose in him.

What rose was a decision about who he was. He had been raised as an Egyptian, and a man in that position has eventually to settle which of the two peoples inside him is going to win. The letter to the Hebrews describes the moment as a refusal — he refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, and chose to be mistreated along with the people of God rather than enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin. So this is not a young man's impulse. It is a renunciation, and it cost him a kingdom.

And then he kills a man.

Stephen reports it without a word of condemnation, which is worth noticing, and without a word of approval either. He gives the facts: an Israelite was being wronged, Moses defended him, and he avenged him by striking the Egyptian down. Exodus supplies two details Stephen leaves out, and they settle the moral question well enough — Moses looked this way and that, and seeing no one, and afterwards hid him in the sand. Those are not the movements of a man who believes he is executing justice. They are the movements of a man who knows exactly what he has done.

So the honest account is this. The loyalty was right and the hands were his own. God had not sent him; nobody had appointed him; there is no word from God anywhere in these two verses. The deliverer who eventually stands in front of Pharaoh will do it with a staff and a message and no violence of his own at all. Moses was correct about the cause, correct about which side he belonged on, and entirely wrong about the method — and the method cost him forty years.

That is a pattern worth recognising, because it is extremely common and it does not look like sin from the inside. A man is genuinely called to something. He is right about the need, right about the injustice, right that somebody ought to do something. And then he does it in his own strength and by his own means — forces the issue, manages the meeting, applies the pressure, says the thing that will certainly work — and the result is a body in the sand and a career in the desert. The wrongness is not in the caring. It is in the assumption that being right about the cause authorises whatever gets it done.

And then the mercy, which should not be hurried. God did not discard him. The man who buried an Egyptian at forty was standing in front of a burning bush at eighty, and the intervening decades turned out to be preparation rather than punishment. But they were real decades. He lost forty years, a nation waited forty years longer in its slavery, and being forgiven was never the same thing as being spared the consequences.

verseByVerse.quote: "He supposed that his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation by his hand, but they did not understand. And on the following day he appeared to them as they were quarreling and tried to reconcile them, saying, 'Men, you are brothers. Why do you wrong each other?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Verse 25 is not in Exodus. Stephen is telling us what Moses was thinking, and the book of Exodus does not record it — this is a preacher interpreting, as preachers do, and the interpretation is the key that unlocks the whole speech.

He supposed that his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation by his hand, but they did not understand.

Read that twice, because everything Stephen says afterwards is built on it. God was giving Israel salvation by Moses's hand; that is stated as fact, not as Moses's opinion of himself. What was Moses's opinion was that they would grasp it. They did not. The deliverer arrived, God was genuinely at work in him, and the people he had come to rescue looked straight at it and saw a court-raised Egyptian who had killed a man.

The failure is not in the sending. It is in the seeing. And the word Stephen chooses for it — they did not understand — hangs over everything that follows. Twenty-seven verses later he will tell these men that they have betrayed and murdered the Righteous One. He does not have to draw the line between the two statements. He has already shown them what happened the last time God sent Israel a deliverer and Israel did not recognise him: another forty years went by, and a great deal more suffering, before the rescue actually arrived.

Then the following day, and the second scene is harder than the first. Moses finds two Israelites fighting each other and tried to reconcile them. His first recorded words in Scripture are a peacemaker's: Men, you are brothers. Why do you wrong each other?

Notice the progression. Yesterday he stepped between an Egyptian and a Hebrew, which is the easy kind of intervention — there is an oppressor and a victim and everybody knows which is which. Today he steps between two Hebrews, where there is no obvious villain, both men have a grievance, and neither of them wants him there. Anyone who has tried to make peace inside a family or a congregation knows which of those two days is the harder, and knows what tends to happen next: the two parties, who agree about nothing else in the world, unite instantly against the man who came to help.

It is a small scene and it contains a great deal. The sentence Moses says here — you are brothers — is true, and is the only reason he had any business being there, and is precisely the thing that neither of them wished to hear. He came to his own, and his own would not have him; and that sentence has been true of somebody else since.

verseByVerse.quote: "But the man who was wronging his neighbor thrust him aside, saying, 'Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who made you a ruler and a judge over us?

Stephen has included that sentence for a reason, and the reason arrives eight verses later. At verse 35 he says: this Moses, whom they rejected, saying, Who made you a ruler and a judge? — this man God sent as both ruler and redeemer. The question of verse 27 receives its answer in the question's own words. Israel demanded to know who had made him a ruler. The answer, which took forty years to become visible, was God.

That is the spine of the whole Moses section, and it is worth watching for, because Stephen leaves the third instance of it unspoken. The men in front of him had put the identical question in the temple courts not long before — tell us by what authority you do these things (Luke 20:2) — and had received an answer they did not care for from a man they subsequently killed.

Now the second half of the taunt, which is the sting. Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday? Moses had looked around and seen nobody. Somebody had seen. And the man who tells him so is one of the two he has just tried to reconcile — which is to say, the secret is out, and it is out through the people he was trying to help.

Two things are worth saying about this rejection, and the second is the fairer.

The first is that it establishes the pattern Stephen is building: the rescuer refused by the rescued, and refused specifically on the question of his standing. Nobody in this scene disputes that the Egyptian was in the wrong. They dispute Moses's right to do anything about it.

The second is that Israel had some reason. Consider how it looked from the labour camp. A man who has spent forty years in the palace, who eats Egyptian food and speaks with an Egyptian accent and has never in his life carried a brick, turns up, kills a foreman, and expects to be recognised as the nation's deliverer. It is not obvious that this is good news. It is at least as likely to be a catastrophe, and the reprisals would fall on them and not on him. Their failure was genuine and Stephen names it as a failure. But it was not stupidity. It was the ordinary difficulty of recognising a deliverer who does not look like one — which is exactly the difficulty the men listening to this speech had lately failed to overcome, with a carpenter from Nazareth.

verseByVerse.quote: "At this retort Moses fled and became an exile in the land of Midian, where he became the father of two sons."
verseByVerse.commentary:
One sentence, and forty years disappear into it.

Stephen's arithmetic of Moses's life is worth laying out, because this speech is the only place in Scripture where it is spelled out. Forty years in Egypt (v. 23). Forty in Midian (v. 30). Forty in the wilderness with Israel (v. 36) — which brings him to the hundred and twenty at which Deuteronomy says he died. Two-thirds of that life was over before God said anything to him at all.

Consider what the middle forty actually contained. He married a Midianite priest's daughter and kept another man's sheep in another man's country. He named his first son Gershom, which Exodus explains as meaning I have been a sojourner in a foreign land — and a man who names his child after his own homelessness is telling you something about how the years were going. He had been a Hebrew in Egypt and an outsider; he was now an Egyptian in Midian and an outsider again. Nothing in the record suggests he expected to go back.

The contrast between the two men at either end of the gap is the point. At forty he was a prince with an education, a position and a plan, convinced that God was going to save Israel by his hand and that everyone would see it. At eighty he was a shepherd who stood in front of a burning bush producing five separate excuses as to why God ought to send somebody else. God waited for the second man.

This is where the passage is worth handing to a reader in a long fallow stretch — the years after the thing that was supposed to happen did not, the decade of ordinary work with no visible point to it, the ministry that closed, the plan that came to nothing and was never replaced. Scripture does show this shape repeatedly and it is real: David between the anointing and the throne, Paul in Arabia and then back in Tarsus for years until Barnabas came looking for him.

But a guard is needed, because the pattern is easily turned into a promise it does not make. Not every fallow decade is preparation for something visible, and telling somebody in year twelve that God is getting them ready is a guess dressed up as a word from the Lord. Moses did not know. There is nothing in Exodus to suggest he spent those years in expectant training; as far as the record goes he was a man who had failed, had run, and was keeping sheep. What can be said is that the desert was not wasted and that God had not finished — and that nobody in Midian could have told you either of those things at the time.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when forty years had passed, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush. When Moses saw it, he was amazed at the sight, and as he drew near to look, there came the voice of the Lord:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when forty years had passed. Stephen puts the silence in first. Whatever else the burning bush is, it is the end of four decades in which God said nothing whatever to the man he intended to use.

Then the fire — and what stopped Moses was not the fire.

Picture the setting honestly. He is in the Sinai with a flock: bare rock, thorn scrub, the sort of dry bush that catches in a moment and is a handful of ash a minute later. A burning bush in that country is not a marvel. It is a commonplace and a nuisance. Exodus tells us exactly what arrested him — I will turn aside and see this great sight, why the bush is not burned. It was the duration. He looked, and it was still there; and it was still there; and at some point he understood that he was watching something which was not obeying the rules.

And Exodus records what came next in an order that repays attention: When the LORD saw that he turned aside to see, God called to him out of the bush. The voice came after the turning aside. God did not speak to a man walking past. He spoke to a man who had stopped.

It would be a mistake to convert that into a technique, as though a sufficiently attentive person could generate revelations by noticing things harder; God was in that bush whether Moses looked or not. But it is worth registering how much of what God does is available to anybody prepared to stop and look at it twice, and how much of a life can be spent walking briskly past. Moses was eighty, in the middle of an ordinary working morning, minding animals that were not his, and the entire remainder of the Bible turns on his deciding to go over and have a proper look at something odd.

One further detail, and it is Stephen's real interest. Where does this happen? In the wilderness of Mount Sinai. Not in Egypt, where God's people were. Not in Canaan, which God had promised them. In a stretch of desert belonging to nobody, on the wrong side of a border, with one man and a flock of sheep for a congregation. Stephen is on trial for saying that God is not confined to a building, and he is walking the court step by step through the places their own Scriptures record him turning up.

verseByVerse.quote: "'I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob.' And Moses trembled and did not dare to look. Then the Lord said to him, 'Take off the sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob.

Four hundred years of silence, and the first thing God says is that he is the same. There is no explanation of the delay and no account of where he has been. He identifies himself by the names of three men who had been dead for centuries, and in doing so tells Moses that nothing has been dropped: the promise made in Mesopotamia to a childless man is the promise being kept this morning in a desert.

And Moses trembled and did not dare to look. Set that beside the man of verse 24. At forty he was ready to take on Egypt single-handed; at eighty he cannot raise his eyes to a bush. Whatever the desert did to him, it did not leave his nerve where it found it — and this is the man God has decided to send.

Then the sentence Stephen has been building toward since he opened his mouth. Take off the sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.

This is the first time in the Bible that any ground is called holy, and it is worth being exact about where it is. A patch of dirt in a foreign desert with a thorn bush on it. There is no altar. No priest. No ark, no tabernacle, no temple, no city — no Israel, which does not yet exist as a free people and will not for another year. There is no ceremony and no sacrifice, and nothing whatever that could be photographed and put on a coin. And when God had finished speaking and Moses walked back to his sheep, it was scrub again.

What made it holy was that God was there. Nothing else did, and nothing else ever has.

The sandals matter too, and the instruction is more homely than it sounds. In that world a man took his shoes off at the door of a house, because you do not carry the street into somebody's home; and the priests would later serve barefoot in the tabernacle for the same reason. God is telling Moses that this hillside is his house. The command is domestic. It assumes he lives there.

Now hold that against the charge sheet. Stephen is on trial for saying that God does not dwell in houses made by hands. He has just shown the court, out of the Torah they revere, that the first ground God ever called holy was unmarked desert in the territory of Midian, and that it was holy for exactly as long as he was standing on it. Not one man in that room can dispute a word of it, because Moses wrote it down.

verseByVerse.quote: "'I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and have heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them. And now come, I will send you to Egypt.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three verbs, and they arrive in an order worth following. I have surely seen... and have heard their groaning... and I have come down.

The first is emphatic in the Hebrew underneath it — the verb is doubled, seeing I have seen. Not glanced at, not been aware of. Looked at, steadily, the whole way through. Four hundred years of it.

The second is the one to sit with. God says he has heard their groaning — and Exodus, describing the same moment, does not say that Israel prayed. It says they groaned because of their slavery and cried out, and their cry came up to God, and God heard their groaning and remembered his covenant. There is no record of a national repentance, no prayer meeting, no petition properly addressed and correctly worded. There is a noise made by people at the end of their strength; it goes up; and God treats it as a communication.

That is worth knowing by anybody who has been unable to pray properly — who has sat with something so heavy that the words would not assemble, and concluded that whatever was happening did not count. Scripture is explicit that God hears groaning. Paul goes further and says that when we do not know what to pray for as we ought, the Spirit himself intercedes with groanings too deep for words. Whatever it is that reaches God, it is not the wording.

And then the third verb, which is the strangest. I have come down to deliver them.

Notice what God does not do here. He does not explain. Four hundred years have passed exactly as he told Abraham they would, and he offers Moses no account of them whatever — no reason for the timing, no theology of the delay, no answer to the question every Hebrew slave for four generations must have asked in the dark. He says that he has seen, that he has heard, and that he has come down. Israel received a rescue and never received an explanation.

That is not a comfortable thing to write, and it may be the most useful sentence in the chapter. An enormous amount of Christian energy goes into demanding from God the reason for a silence — and Scripture's most sustained example of a long silence ends without one being given. What was given instead was God himself, in motion, on the way.

Then the last clause turns the whole thing over. And now come, I will send you to Egypt. God says he has come down to deliver them, and then sends a man. The coming down and the sending are one act. It is how he has always worked — and the men listening to this speech had recently watched him do it in a form so complete that they killed the messenger, and are about to kill the next one.

verseByVerse.quote: "This Moses, whom they rejected, saying, 'Who made you a ruler and a judge?' — this man God sent as both ruler and redeemer by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush. This man led them out, performing wonders and signs in Egypt and at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Something changes in the rhythm here, and it is audible in the Greek. Stephen begins hammering a demonstrative pronoun at the head of each sentence: this Moses, this man, this man, this is the Moses, this is the one — five times in four verses. He has stopped narrating. He is pointing.

And what he points at is a contradiction his hearers have never resolved. This Moses, whom they rejected, saying, Who made you a ruler and a judge? — this man God sent as both ruler and redeemer.

The answer comes in the question's own words. Israel demanded to know who had made him a ruler and a judge. God made him a ruler and a redeemer. The very office they refused him is the office he was given, and the men who asked the question spent the next forty years being led by the man they had asked it about.

The second title is rare and worth a moment: redeemer, a word that occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. It belongs to the world of the kinsman who buys a relative out of slavery or debt — the man with both the right and the resources to pay what you cannot pay yourself. Stephen is describing Moses, and he has chosen a word that his hearers will not be able to keep at a comfortable distance.

Then verse 36 spreads the vindication over forty years: wonders and signs in Egypt and at the Red Sea and in the wilderness. It is worth noticing that this is the phrase Luke has been using in this book of the apostles, and used two chapters ago of Stephen himself. Moses, the Twelve and the man currently on trial are being quietly set in a single line — all sent, all attested, and all disbelieved by the same institution.

The pattern is now fully drawn, though Stephen still refuses to name it. Joseph, sold by his brothers, became the man who fed them. Moses, thrust aside by his people, became the man who brought them out. Twice God sent Israel a deliverer; twice Israel refused him at first sight; and twice God sent him anyway, and the refusal cost the refusers years they did not have to spare.

Which leaves one question hanging in that chamber. Every man on the council can hear it. Stephen has not asked it yet.

verseByVerse.quote: "This is the Moses who said to the Israelites, 'God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers.' This is the one who was in the congregation in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him at Mount Sinai, and with our fathers. He received living oracles to give to us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stephen now plays what looks like his strongest card, and does something unexpected with it.

This is the Moses who said to the Israelites, God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers. That promise is the text Peter preached from in the temple courts a few chapters back, and the full weight of it — where it came from, who it fits, and why it will not fit anybody else — belongs there and is worked out at 3:22.

What Stephen does with it here is different, and it goes straight at the second charge against him. He is on trial for saying that Jesus would change the customs Moses delivered. His answer is that Moses himself told Israel to expect somebody else and to listen to him when he came. The man they accuse Stephen of dishonouring is the man who pointed away from himself.

Then the description in verse 38, and it is extravagant. Moses was in the congregation in the wilderness — the Greek word is the Old Testament's term for the assembly of Israel, and it is also the word the New Testament uses for the church. He was with the angel who spoke on Mount Sinai. He was with the fathers. And he received living oracles to give to us.

Weigh that phrase. Living oracles — not a dead code, not a rulebook, not an antique. Words with life still in them, still speaking. It is one of the highest things anybody in the New Testament says about the law of Moses, and it is said by the man on trial for despising it.

And note the last two words. Stephen does not say Moses received the law to give to you. He says to us. He puts himself among the people the law was given to and claims it as his own inheritance, in the middle of a hearing convened on the charge that he has thrown it away.

There is something to learn from that, because the instinct under a false accusation is to deny — I never said that — and denial is very nearly useless. It is the weakest move available and it always sounds like a man on the back foot. Stephen denies nothing. He states what he actually believes, at length and in terms so high that the accusation collapses under its own implausibility. The best answer to being misrepresented is usually not a correction but a demonstration.

One detail in passing, because it returns at the end of the speech. The angel who spoke to him at Mount Sinai — Stephen says the law came through angelic mediation, as the New Testament says elsewhere. He is not diminishing the law by saying so. He is about to use it, at verse 53, as the aggravating factor in the charge he brings against them.

verseByVerse.quote: "Our fathers refused to obey him, but thrust him aside, and in their hearts they turned to Egypt, saying to Aaron, 'Make for us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses who led us out from the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two verses, and the second half of Stephen's case lands.

First the verb. Our fathers refused to obey him, but thrust him aside — and thrust aside is the identical word he used at verse 27, where the quarrelling Israelite shoved Moses away in the labour camp. He has used it twice deliberately. Israel pushed Moses aside at the beginning, before the exodus, and pushed him aside again at the summit, after the sea had opened. The rescue made no difference at all to the reflex.

Then the sentence that does the most work in the entire chapter. In their hearts they turned to Egypt.

They had been out of Egypt a matter of weeks. They had walked through a sea on dry ground and watched an army drown behind them. And they wanted to go back — not because anybody had persuaded them that slavery was preferable, but because Egypt was familiar and the food arrived. Numbers records what they actually missed, and the list is worth reading aloud: the fish, the cucumbers, the melons, the leeks, the onions and the garlic. They remembered the menu and forgot the whips. A nation that had groaned under forced labour until God heard the groaning had, within a month or two, retained the garlic and mislaid the graves.

This is the verse a Christian reader should find hardest to walk past, because it is not about somebody else. It is the standard experience of the redeemed life. A man is genuinely delivered — the thing that owned him has been broken, he knows it, and he would not go back if you asked him outright. And there is nevertheless a homesickness in him for the country he was rescued from. Not for the misery of it: for the familiarity, the predictability, the not having to trust anybody for tomorrow. Egypt fed you every single day and asked nothing of you except your life.

Then the request they put to Aaron, and its timing. Make for us gods who will go before us — spoken while Moses was up the mountain collecting the law on their behalf. They gave him about forty days before replacing him. And the phrasing of the complaint is a small masterpiece of contempt: as for this Moses who led us out from the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him. Not our leader; not the man God sent. This Moses.

One guard, because this passage is easily turned into a lash. The people who did this had seen the sea open. They had eaten manna that morning. Whatever else the golden calf demonstrates, it demonstrates that witnessing miracles does not make anybody faithful — and a Christian who assumes he would have done better is precisely the sort of person Stephen has in front of him. Every man on that council would have agreed warmly that their ancestors were a disgrace. That is the trap he is walking them into, and it closes in twelve verses.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they made a calf in those days, and offered a sacrifice to the idol and were rejoicing in the works of their hands. But God turned away and gave them over to worship the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: "'Did you bring to me slain beasts and sacrifices, during the forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two things in these verses, and the second half of verse 42 has been missing from this commentary until now — a whole clause of Stephen's argument that was in neither this entry nor the next.

The first is a phrase that explains why Stephen dies. They were rejoicing in the works of their hands. Hold that expression, because its twin arrives at verse 48, where the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands. They are the same idea, and the word at verse 48 is not neutral. In the Greek Old Testament, made by hands is very largely a word for idols; it is how the translators render the contemptuous Hebrew term for the things people carve and then bow down to (Leviticus 26:1; Isaiah 2:18; 46:6).

So when Stephen applies it to the temple, a Jewish ear does not hear a remark about architecture. It hears the temple put into the same category as the golden calf. That is the offence. Not that he disparaged a building, but that he used the vocabulary of idolatry about the house of God — having spent the previous verse establishing that Israel has a very long history of rejoicing in things it made itself.

Then the judgment, and it is the most frightening kind there is. God turned away and gave them over to worship the host of heaven. He did not strike them. He let them have it. The word is the one Paul uses three times in the first chapter of Romans — God gave them up, God gave them over — and it describes a judgment which, from the inside, feels like nothing happening at all. A man insists on his idol and God stops arguing with him. There is no thunder. The worst thing God does to people determined on a substitute is to withdraw his objection.

And now the clause that carries the rest of Stephen's case, quoted out of the prophet Amos: Did you bring to me slain beasts and sacrifices, during the forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel?

It is a rhetorical question expecting the answer no, which is an extraordinary thing to ask, because of course they did. The wilderness generation sacrificed constantly; the book of Leviticus is the paperwork for it. Amos is not denying that the ritual happened. He is denying that it arrived. Forty years of offerings, and God asks whether one of them was ever actually brought to him.

Notice who is hearing this. Stephen is standing in front of the men who run the sacrificial system, on trial for allegedly attacking the temple, and he quotes a prophet asking whether Israel's sacrifices were ever for God at all. He is not merely arguing that the building cannot contain God. He is putting the offerings themselves in question, which is a far more dangerous thing to do in that room.

And it puts a question to anybody who does religious things. Not whether the activity is happening — it plainly was, for four decades, in enormous quantity, exactly as prescribed. The question is whether it is being brought to God or merely performed in his vicinity. The test is not the volume of it, nor the correctness of it, nor how sincere it felt at the time. Amos's question has only one honest way of being answered, and it is never answered on the day of the offering.

verseByVerse.quote: "'You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan, the images that you made to worship; and I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The quotation runs on, and it names what Israel was carrying alongside the tabernacle.

That is the force of it, and it should be stated plainly before the names are examined. Israel in the wilderness had two tents. One was the tent of witness, built to the pattern God showed Moses on the mountain, with the ark inside it and the cloud over it. The other was the tent of Moloch, carried through the same camp, on the same march, by the same people. Stephen's accusers have built their whole case on the sanctity of the sanctuary. He is telling them that from the very first generation the sanctuary had a rival travelling beside it in the baggage — and that the golden calf was not a single lapse but the visible part of something the nation never put down.

Then the sanction: I will send you into exile beyond Babylon. Amos wrote beyond Damascus. Stephen extends it to the exile that actually came, which is not carelessness but the ordinary freedom of a preacher pressing a prophecy to the event it reached. The judgment threatened by the prophet is the judgment their ancestors received — and Stephen is placing the court he is standing in inside the same sentence.

Who were these two? Moloch (Molech) was a pagan deity, named as 'the abomination of the Ammonites' (1 Kings 11:7) and notorious across the region for child sacrifice — children 'passed through the fire' to him (Lev. 18:21; 2 Kings 23:10; Jer. 32:35). The name is tied to the Hebrew melek, 'king' — 'the King'-god (Hebrew scribes seem to have pointed it with the vowels of bosheth, 'shame,' a deliberate jab). The 'tent of Moloch' is a portable idol-shrine carried in procession — a grim parody of the tabernacle, God's own tent. Rephan (also spelled Remphan/Rompha) is 'the star of your god' — an astral deity, almost certainly the planet Saturn worshipped as a god; this is star-worship, the bowing to 'the host of heaven' that Scripture repeatedly condemns (Deut. 4:19; 2 Kings 21:3–5).

An honest word on the names: Stephen is quoting the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) of Amos 5:25–27, and its wording differs from the Hebrew, which at this point is genuinely obscure. Where the Hebrew has 'Sikkuth' and 'Kiyyun' (Chiun) — themselves probably names of Mesopotamian astral gods (Saturn again) — the Greek rendered them 'Moloch' and 'Rephan.' So the exact identifications are the best scholarly reconstruction, not certainty; but the sense is plain and that is Stephen's point: even in the wilderness — the very generation that carried God's tabernacle — Israel was also carrying the shrines of pagan star-gods. The idolatry his temple-proud accusers would rather forget ran right through their history from the start.

verseByVerse.quote: "Our fathers had the tent of witness in the wilderness, just as he who spoke to Moses directed him to make it, according to the pattern that he had seen. Our fathers in turn brought it in with Joshua when they dispossessed the nations that God drove out before our fathers. So it was until the days of David,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stephen now turns to the sanctuary itself, and the first thing to notice is that he defends it. Our fathers had the tent of witness in the wilderness, just as he who spoke to Moses directed him to make it. God ordered it. God specified it. There is not a syllable of criticism in the sentence, and any reading of this speech which makes Stephen an opponent of Israel's worship has to get past it first.

But look at what he calls it, and what he says about it, because both are doing work.

He calls it a tent. Not a house, not a sanctuary, not a temple — a tent, with pegs and ropes and curtains and poles, and a book of instructions in Numbers specifying which family carried which section on the march. It had no foundation. It could be struck in a morning and standing again by evening. The one building God ever designed for himself was designed to be portable, and every piece of its furniture was fitted with rings so that poles could be run through and men could pick it up and walk.

And he adds that it was made according to the pattern that he had seen. So even the tent was a copy. Moses was shown something on the mountain and told to build a model of it, which means the tabernacle was never the real thing either. It was a scale drawing of a reality located somewhere else.

Then the history. Our fathers in turn brought it in with Joshua — and it kept moving: into Canaan with the conquest, and then around the country for centuries, to Gilgal and Shiloh and Nob and Gibeon. For something like four hundred years after Israel entered the land of promise, the place where God met his people had an address that changed.

So it was until the days of David. That is the hinge, and everything after it concerns what happened when somebody decided the arrangement ought to be permanent.

There is a question in this for any congregation, and it is not the obvious one about whether buildings matter. Stephen thought the tabernacle mattered enormously; God designed it. The question is whether a church could move. Whether the thing it actually runs on is the sort of thing that can be picked up and carried — or whether, over a few quiet generations, it has become the sort of thing that has foundations, and cannot.

verseByVerse.quote: "who found favor in the sight of God and asked to find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. But it was Solomon who built a house for him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
David comes off well here and Stephen means him to. He found favour in the sight of God, and what he wanted was to build God a house. It was a generous impulse in a man who had noticed that he was living in a palace of cedar while the ark of God sat under canvas, and Scripture never once suggests the motive was wrong.

But it was Solomon who built a house for him.

That but is carrying a great deal, and to feel it you have to know what God said when David proposed the idea. The answer came through the prophet Nathan and it is one of the most remarkable speeches in the Old Testament. Would you build me a house to dwell in? I have not lived in a house since the day I brought up the people of Israel from Egypt to this day, but I have been moving about in a tent for my dwelling. And then a question that should be read slowly: Did I speak a word with any of the judges of Israel... saying, Why have you not built me a house of cedar?

God says, in as many words, that in four hundred years he had never asked anybody for a building and had never once complained about not having one.

Stephen is saying this to a court that is about to execute a man for allegedly threatening the temple. He has just reminded them, out of their own Scriptures, that the temple was a human suggestion which God had not requested — and that when it was offered, God's reply was to turn it round. You will not build me a house; I will build you a house. The play on the word is the point of the whole passage: David offered God a building and God gave David a dynasty. And the dynasty is the one these men had lately helped to nail up outside the city wall.

None of which makes the temple illegitimate. God permitted it, filled it with his glory on the day it opened, and Jesus called it his Father's house. And the man who built it said at the dedication, in front of the whole nation, that the heaven of heavens could not contain God, so how much less this house that he had built. Even the builder knew.

What the passage does expose is a very ordinary religious mistake, and it is worth naming because sincere people make it almost invariably. David's desire was good. The impulse to do something substantial for God is good. But there is a step from I want to honour God with this to God requires this, and must be honoured here — and the step is short, and it is very nearly invisible. Four hundred years after Solomon, a man is on trial for his life because a building God never asked for had become the thing his people could not imagine him without.

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands, as the prophet says, 'Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the sentence they kill him for.

Yet the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands. Two things in it detonate, and both are deliberate.

The first is the phrase made by hands. As at verse 41, this is idol vocabulary — the standard term in the Greek Old Testament for the manufactured objects the prophets pour contempt on. Stephen has already used its twin of the golden calf, where Israel rejoiced in the works of their hands, and now he fastens it onto the temple. To the men in that chamber this is not an architectural observation. It is a charge of idolatry, levelled at the sanctuary, by a man on trial for blasphemy against it.

The second is the title he chooses. The Most High is the name for the God of Israel that outsiders use — the name on the lips of Melchizedek, of Nebuchadnezzar, of a demoniac in the Gospels, of a fortune-telling slave girl later in this same book. It is the God of Israel described from beyond the boundary, and it is exactly the right title for a speech about a God who declines to be kept inside one.

Then, so that nobody can accuse him of inventing the idea, he quotes Isaiah. Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest?

Look at the picture rather than skimming it. God is seated with the sky beneath him for a chair and the planet under his feet for a stool. Now, says the prophet, describe the building. Give the dimensions. Say where the resting place is to go. It is God asking a contractor for a specification, and the question answers itself the moment anybody tries.

But the most devastating thing about the quotation is what Stephen leaves out — and his hearers knew the passage well enough to supply it for themselves. Isaiah's very next sentence answers the question. Having asked what house anyone imagines they could build him, God says: But this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word.

So Isaiah does say where God dwells. Not in a structure — in a certain sort of person. Humble. Contrite. Trembling at what God says.

Stephen stops one line short of that, and the line he stops short of is a description of precisely what the men in front of him are not.
