They are proud of their building, unmoved by their guilt, and about to demonstrate what they think of the word of God by killing the man reciting it. He does not need to quote the sentence. Every man in the room can hear it, which is worse.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Did not my hand make all these things?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Did not my hand make all these things? Five words, and they close the argument.

Follow the logic to the end of it. The temple was built by human hands. Human hands were made by God. The stone came out of ground he made, quarried with tools of metal he put in the earth, cut by men whose lungs he was keeping full while they worked. There is nothing in that building which did not come from him, and therefore nothing in it capable of containing him. A man cannot house his maker in materials his maker supplied.

And notice that Stephen ends this whole section with a question rather than a statement. He has been quoting Isaiah for three verses, and the last thing the council hears before he turns and faces them is God's own voice asking whether they had ever stopped to consider who made the quarry.

There is a sweet turn here. If God never truly dwelt in the building, where is his dwelling now? The New Testament answers: in Christ first of all (Jesus called his own body 'this temple,' John 2:19–21, 'in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily,' Col. 2:9), and then, through him, in his people — 'you are God's temple and God's Spirit dwells in you' (1 Cor. 3:16; 6:19; Eph. 2:21–22). The God too great for any house made of stone has chosen to make his home in the hearts of ordinary believers. Stephen's point is not that buildings are wrong, but that we must never trap the living God in a place or a thing while missing him where he truly dwells.

Which leaves a question worth putting to oneself rather than to an institution, because the error Stephen is exposing is not confined to men who own a temple. It is entirely possible to know perfectly well that God is not contained in a building, and to have quietly relocated him somewhere just as manageable — a style of service, a set of convictions, an hour of the week, a way of feeling when the music is right. The test is not what a man says about where God lives. It is what he would have left if the thing were taken away from him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The speech has run for fifty verses and Stephen has said our fathers nine times. At verse 51 he says your fathers, and the trial changes direction. Everything before that pronoun was a defence conducted by a man inside the family. Everything after it is a prosecution.

You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. He calls circumcised men uncircumcised, using Moses' own vocabulary to do it, and then states the charge: which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? They killed the men who announced the Righteous One, and you have betrayed and murdered him. You received the law by the hand of angels and did not keep it. He never denies what he is accused of. He simply changes who is being examined.

What follows is not a verdict. It is a lynching carried out by a court. They grind their teeth; Stephen looks up and says he can see heaven open and the Son of Man standing at God's right hand; and at that they put their fingers in their ears — the physical performance of the deafness he has just named — and rush him. He is dragged outside the wall and stoned, and the witnesses whose testimony was bought throw the first stones, because the law required the witnesses to throw first.

Then two things Luke will not let the reader hurry past. Stephen dies praying twice — for himself, in a psalm addressed to God which he addresses to Jesus, and then, at the top of his voice and with the last breath he has, for the men killing him. And the coats of the executioners are being minded by a young man from Cilicia named Saul. Luke gives him no introduction whatsoever. The man who would write more of the New Testament than anybody else walks into it as a cloakroom attendant at a murder — and the first Christian prayer he is recorded as hearing is a dying man asking that this not be held against him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Stephen and the Pattern of Martyrdom

The Greek word for a witness is martys, and it did not come to mean somebody killed for the faith until enough witnesses had been. Stephen is where the shift begins, and the shape of his death is the shape the church has recognised ever since: the truth told without softening, Christ seen at the moment of dying, the killers prayed for. Reformed theology has been careful about what this is and is not. It is not heroism and it is not an achievement that earns anything — Luke states plainly that Stephen was full of the Holy Spirit at the moment he looked up, which is to say that the courage and the vision and the forgiveness were all supplied to him. What this passage exhibits is not a strong man but a sustained one. And it should be added, because the church has periodically forgotten it, that martyrdom is nowhere in the New Testament something to be sought. Stephen did not go looking for this. He was preaching, and it was done to him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Stephen's last recorded words asked that God not hold this sin against the men throwing the stones. A few feet away, minding their coats and approving of the execution, stood the man who never, to the end of his life, stopped mentioning that he had been there (22:20; 26:10). Now: Nobody watching that morning could have identified what was actually happening. The church lost its most gifted man and gained nothing visible; the persecution that followed emptied Jerusalem of Christians; and between them those two disasters put the gospel into Samaria, into Antioch and eventually into Rome. It is worth remembering on a day when a loss looks total.

verseByVerse.quote: "You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. As your fathers did, so do you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The turn is abrupt, and it is locatable to a single pronoun.

Nine times in this speech Stephen has said our fathers. Our father Abraham. Our fathers could find no food. Our fathers had the tent of witness. He has been standing inside the family the whole way, arguing as a member of the household about the household's own history. Then in this verse he says your fathers, and says it again in the next. That is the moment the defence becomes a prosecution, and every man in that chamber will have felt the floor shift.

Then three charges, and every one of them is a quotation.

Stiff-necked is a farming word. It describes an ox that sets its neck against the driver's hand and will not be turned — not an animal that bolts, but one that simply refuses to go the way the plough needs to go and cannot be made to. It is the word God himself used of Israel at Sinai, in the aftermath of the golden calf, when he told Moses he would not go up among them lest he consume them on the way.

Then uncircumcised in heart and ears, which to that audience is the deepest insult the language holds. He is calling circumcised men uncircumcised — telling the covenant people, in the covenant's own vocabulary, that the mark cut into their bodies never reached the place it was pointing at. And it is not his coinage. Moses said it in Deuteronomy, Leviticus said it, and Jeremiah said it twice. Stephen is doing here exactly what he has done for fifty verses: quoting their Scriptures at them and letting the Scriptures do the accusing.

You always resist the Holy Spirit. The verb means to fall against, to fight, to shove back at something coming toward you. And always is the sting — not sometimes, not in the bad generations, but as a continuous national habit running from the wilderness into this room. The recital of the last fifty verses turns out not to have been a history lesson. It was the evidence for this sentence.

A word of care is needed, because sentences like this one have been lifted out and used as a weapon against Jewish people for the better part of two thousand years. Notice the speaker and the setting. This is a Jew, in the Jewish council, quoting Moses and the prophets, saying to the leadership of his own nation what Isaiah and Jeremiah had said to the leadership of theirs. It is prophetic speech inside a family, which is the oldest and most Jewish form of address in the Bible. The full guard belongs at 3:14, where it is set out at length. What belongs here is the plain observation that a man does not get to borrow Stephen's sentence unless he is standing where Stephen was standing, and almost nobody who has quoted it ever has been.

There is a use of it that is entirely legitimate, and it is the one closest to home. The resistance Stephen names is not an ancient national peculiarity. It is the ordinary daily possibility of hearing something true from God and setting the neck against it — knowing precisely what ought to be done and declining to be turned. The council did it at the top of their voices. Most of it is done quietly, by people who would be very surprised to find themselves described in this verse.

verseByVerse.quote: "Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, whom you have now betrayed and murdered, you who received the law as delivered by angels and did not keep it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three sentences, and the case closes.

Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? It is a question with no available answer, which is precisely why he puts it as a question. Israel's history of prophets is a history of men who were ignored, mocked, imprisoned, dropped into a cistern, and by tradition sawn in two — and it was not the pagans who did it. The men who suffered most at Israel's hands were the men God sent to Israel.

Then the charge, and Stephen chooses his title for Jesus with care: the Righteous One. Not Messiah, not Son of God, not the Nazarene. It is the title Peter used in the temple courts (3:14), and the one Paul will hear applied to Jesus at his own conversion (22:14) — three times in this book and nowhere else. And it is the exact word for the thing a court exists to protect. The supreme judicial body of the nation is being informed that it convicted the one genuinely innocent man in its history.

Whom you have now betrayed and murdered. The Greek does not say they committed betrayal and murder. It calls them betrayers and murderers. He has turned the verbs into nouns and hung them round their necks as titles.

And then the last line, which is the answer to the charge that began all this. You who received the law as delivered by angels and did not keep it.

Sit with that. Stephen has been on trial on the accusation that he speaks against the law of Moses. His closing sentence on the subject is that the law came to them by the hand of angels — an honour he described in glowing terms at verse 38 — and that they broke it. He never denies the charge. He never explains what he actually said. He does something better and far more dangerous: he changes who is being examined. The question in that room is no longer whether Stephen kept the law. It is whether they did.

Notice as well what he does not say. He does not say the law is finished, or mistaken, or superseded, or that it never mattered. Every word he has spoken about the law in this speech has been high. What he says is that they had it and did not do it — which is the most conservative accusation available and the hardest of all to answer.

That is worth carrying away from a chapter of this length. The final word of the first Christian to die for the faith was not an attack on Israel's Scriptures. It was a charge that Israel's leaders had not obeyed them, brought by a man who had just spent fifty verses demonstrating that he knew them better than the court did.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they heard these things they were enraged, and they ground their teeth at him. But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two reactions in one sentence, and they could not stand further apart.

The council is enraged — and Luke's word is a physical one, that they were sawn through, cut clean across. It is the same verb he used at 5:33 of this identical body hearing Peter. And they ground their teeth at him, which is not a figure of speech. It is what a room of men do when fury has gone past the point where words are available: seventy-one of the most dignified figures in the nation, in session, in robes, making a noise with their jaws.

And Stephen looks up. Luke's verb is the fixed, deliberate gaze again — the very word he used at the end of chapter 6, when this council stared at Stephen and saw a face like an angel's. Now the staring runs the other way, and what he is looking at is not in the room.

What does Luke mean by 'full of the Holy Spirit' here? It is a phrase he loves (he has already used it of Stephen at 6:3, 5, 8 — on how such fullness is recognised, see there), and it means a person so wholly yielded to and possessed by the Spirit that the Spirit's presence and power are manifest in and through him. But notice what it introduces at this moment. First, spiritual sight: filled with the Spirit, Stephen 'gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.' The Spirit gives him eyes for the unseen reality — 'the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God' and reveals what no eye could otherwise see (1 Cor. 2:9–10). Second, strength for the supreme test: this filling comes at the hour of his death, and it makes him able to die like his Lord — committing his spirit to Jesus (v. 59, as Jesus did to the Father) and forgiving his killers (v. 60, as Jesus did from the cross). This is exactly what Jesus had promised his witnesses — when dragged before councils, 'the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say' (Luke 12:11–12).

So this is not a sudden, first reception of the Spirit (Stephen was already 'full,' 6:5) but a fresh, heightened filling for a decisive moment — the same pattern as Peter 'filled with the Holy Spirit' just before he answered the council (4:8). The Spirit who abides in every believer also fills afresh for the crises of witness and suffering. And mark the point worth carrying away: being 'full of the Spirit' is not first about ecstatic feelings; its truest evidence is a man who sees Christ clearly and dies like Christ graciously. The Spirit did not spare Stephen the stones — he filled him to face them, fixing his eyes on the glory of God and on Jesus risen to receive him.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.

Two things about that sentence are extraordinary, and the first concerns a title.

Son of Man is how Jesus habitually spoke of himself — some eighty times in the Gospels. What is striking is how nearly nobody else ever uses it. In all four Gospels it appears on another speaker's lips exactly once, when a puzzled crowd throws his own phrase back at him and asks who this Son of Man is meant to be. Outside the Gospels no speaker in the New Testament uses it of Jesus at all, except here. Stephen is the one man in Scripture who calls Jesus what Jesus called himself — and he does it in the very chamber where Jesus had used it of himself under examination, and been condemned for it.

The second is a posture. Every other reference in the New Testament to Christ at the Father's right hand has him seated. Psalm 110 says sit. Peter preached him seated at Pentecost. The letter to the Hebrews builds an entire argument on the fact that this priest sat down, because his work was finished and there was nothing left to stand about. This is the one exception in the whole Bible. Stephen sees him standing.

Why? The setting supplies the answer, and once it is seen it is difficult to forget. Two courts are sitting that morning. In the lower one a man is being tried on the evidence of witnesses who were paid to lie, and the outcome was settled before he opened his mouth. In the higher one, at the moment the accused is about to be condemned, his advocate rises to his feet.

Jesus had promised exactly this, in Luke's own first volume: everyone who acknowledges me before men, the Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God. Stephen is acknowledging him before men, in the most expensive circumstances imaginable, and Luke shows the promise being kept while it is still being paid for.

There is comfort in that which reaches a long way past this chapter. Most Christians will never stand before a council, and will nevertheless be judged — by an employer, a family, a professional body, a country, or simply by their own conscience convening a court at three in the morning with the evidence stacked and no defence prepared. This verse says there is another court, that it is in session, and that the one thing it never does is let the testimony go unanswered.

And notice what the sentence does to the room. Stephen has just told the Sanhedrin that he can see the man they executed alive, in glory, at the right hand of God. That is precisely the claim Jesus made before this same council, and precisely what they condemned him for. They have now heard it twice, from two different men, in the same chamber. The second time, they do not wait for a verdict.

verseByVerse.quote: But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and rushed together at him. Then they cast him out of the city and stoned him. And the witnesses laid down their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears.

Read that as a picture. Seventy-one of the most dignified men in the nation, the supreme council of Israel in session, with their fingers in their ears, shouting so as not to hear what is being said to them. It is the behaviour of children, and Luke reports it without a syllable of comment. It is also the exact fulfilment of the charge Stephen laid against them six verses earlier: he said they were uncircumcised in the ears, and they proceeded to stop them with their hands.

What happens next is not an execution. It is a lynching carried out by a court. No verdict is recorded, no sentence pronounced, no vote taken. They simply rushed together at him. Whether the council even possessed the legal power to execute is doubtful — the Gospels record them telling Pilate that it was not lawful for them to put anyone to death — and this may have fallen into a gap between Roman governors when nobody was watching closely. Luke does not say, and the silence is itself informative. He is describing a proceeding that had stopped being a proceeding.

And yet the form is kept wherever it suits them. They cast him out of the city, because the law required a stoning to take place outside the camp. They keep the geography of Leviticus and abandon everything else in it. It is worth adding that the letter to the Hebrews makes a point of that same location: Jesus also suffered outside the gate.

Then a detail that ought to stop a reader cold. Luke says the witnesses laid down their garments — and he says it because the law of Moses required that in a stoning the witnesses throw first, so that any man who had sworn a life away had to be the one to take it. These are the witnesses of chapter 6: the men who were suborned, planted and briefed. The men who lied about Stephen are the men who killed him with their own hands, and they took their coats off in order to do it properly.

And then, in eleven words, the New Testament introduces the most important man in its second half. The witnesses laid down their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul.

No introduction. No description. Not a hint from Luke that this name will matter. He is minding the coats — doing the respectable part, the part that gets no blood on it, the part a man can afterwards tell himself was not really participation. Luke says plainly in the next verse that he approved. And Paul himself never let it go: he raises it in his own defence years later, standing in this same city, describing how he stood there approving and holding the garments; and elsewhere he admits he did rather more than watch, and that he cast his vote against them.

It is worth pausing on the arrangement. Every man in that field who threw a stone is anonymous. The one whose name Luke troubles to record is the one holding the coats — and the coats are the detail he would still be talking about thirty years later.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were stoning Stephen, he called out, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." And falling to his knees he cried out with a loud voice, "Lord, do not hold this sin against them." And when he had said this, he fell asleep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two prayers, and the order of them is the last thing Luke wants the reader to notice.

The first is for himself: Lord Jesus, receive my spirit. It is a quotation. Psalm 31 says into your hand I commit my spirit, and it is addressed to God; Jesus prayed it from the cross, addressed to the Father. Stephen prays it to Jesus.

Consider what that is. A Jewish man, being executed for blasphemy by the highest religious authority in Israel, spends the last moments of his life praying a psalm addressed to the God of Israel — and addresses it to Jesus of Nazareth. He is not constructing an argument for the deity of Christ. He is doing something far more telling: he is dying on the assumption of it. Nobody commends his soul to a creature.

Then falling to his knees, which is a decision. A man under a hail of stones does not kneel by accident. Standing, he might have lasted longer; turned away, he might at least have covered his head. He knelt because he was going to pray, and he wanted his whole body to say so.

And the second prayer is not for himself. Lord, do not hold this sin against them — and Luke notes that he cried this one out with a loud voice. The request for his own soul was spoken. The request for his murderers was shouted. He spent the last breath he had on the men who were taking it, and he made certain they heard him do it.

The parallel with the cross is exact and deliberate, and the order is reversed. Jesus prayed first for his killers and then committed his spirit. Stephen commits his spirit and then, with whatever he has left, prays for his killers. The first Christian death is shaped like the death of Christ, and the disciple takes the sequence the other way round because he was running out of time and would not go without saying it.

A guard belongs here, because this verse has been used to lay a burden on people that Scripture does not lay. It is not a rule that a Christian must feel forgiving at the moment of injury, or that failure to produce this prayer at the graveside of a murdered child is a failure of faith. Luke has already told us where it came from: Stephen was full of the Holy Spirit. The forgiveness in this verse is not an achievement being modelled for imitation. It is a gift being reported. What is asked of ordinary Christians is that they should want to get there, and be willing to be taken there slowly, which for most people is the work of years and not of minutes.

Then Luke's last word, which is the gentlest verb in the language attached to the most violent death in the book. He fell asleep. A man has just been beaten to death with rocks in a field outside the wall, and Luke writes it as though somebody had nodded off in a chair. That is not a euphemism and it is not sentiment. It is a statement about what death now is for people who belong to Christ, made by a writer who had every reason to reach for a harsher word and did not.

And one thing more, which Luke leaves the reader to assemble for himself. Stephen asked that this sin not be held against them. A few feet away, holding the coats and approving, stood a young man who would be struck down on a road to Damascus, would spend the next thirty years telling anyone who would listen that he was the foremost of sinners, and would write more of the New Testament than any other man. The prayer was answered — and it was answered first in the person who, that morning, would have been the very last to expect it.

7.theology: The Pattern of Rejection and Vindication. Stephen’s survey of Israel’s history reveals God’s way in the world: the one God sends is always rejected first. Joseph, Moses, the prophets, the Righteous One himself. And in each case, God vindicates the rejected one and uses that rejection as the means of redemption. This is not historical accident; it is divine pattern — the pattern of the cross. The grain of wheat must fall into the ground and die (John 12:24). The stone the builders reject becomes the cornerstone. And the martyr who follows the rejected-and-vindicated Lord shares the same arc: killed by men, received by God, his prayer answered in the conversion of his chief persecutor. Saul of Tarsus is Stephen’s greatest vindication.
7.examples:
Then: Stephen stands before the Sanhedrin in Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets, and preaches them their own history. He is the first Christian martyr, and he dies as he lived — full of the Holy Spirit, full of faith, his face like an angel’s. His death scatters the seed further than his life could have planted it.

Now: The church in every hostile culture faces Stephen’s question: what do you do when you cannot be silenced by argument and so are silenced by violence? Stephen shows us: you look up, you see the glory of God, you commend your spirit to Christ, and you pray for those who kill you. This is not heroism; it is the overflow of a life lived so close to Christ that even death cannot separate you from him — and cannot stop the gospel.

8.title: The Scattered Gospel
8.text: <sup>1</sup>And Saul approved of his execution. And there arose on that day a great persecution against the church in Jerusalem, and they were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles. <sup>2</sup>Devout men buried Stephen and made great lamentation over him. <sup>3</sup>But Saul was ravaging the church, and entering house after house, he dragged off men and women and committed them to prison. <sup>4</sup>Now those who were scattered went about preaching the word. <sup>5</sup>Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed to them the Christ. <sup>6</sup>And the crowds with one accord paid attention to what was being said by Philip, when they heard him and saw the signs that he did. <sup>7</sup>For unclean spirits, crying out with a loud voice, came out of many who had them, and many who were paralyzed or lame were healed. <sup>8</sup>So there was much joy in that city. <sup>9</sup>But there was a man named Simon, who had previously practiced magic in the city and amazed the people of Samaria, saying that he himself was somebody great. <sup>10</sup>They all paid attention to him, from the least to the greatest, saying, “This man is the power of God that is called Great.” <sup>11</sup>And they paid attention to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic. <sup>12</sup>But when they believed Philip as he preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women. <sup>13</sup>Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptized he continued with Philip. And seeing signs and great miracles performed, he was amazed. <sup>14</sup>Now when the apostles at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent to them Peter and John, <sup>15</sup>who came down and prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit, <sup>16</sup>for he had not yet fallen on any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. <sup>17</sup>Then they laid their hands on them and they received the Holy Spirit. <sup>18</sup>Now when Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money, <sup>19</sup>saying, “Give me this power also, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit.” <sup>20</sup>But Peter said to him, “May your money perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! <sup>21</sup>You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God. <sup>22</sup>Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you. <sup>23</sup>For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity.” <sup>24</sup>And Simon answered, “Pray for me to the Lord, that nothing of what you have said may come upon me.” <sup>25</sup>Now when they had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans. <sup>26</sup>Now an angel of the Lord said to Philip, “Rise and go toward the south to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.” This is a desert place. <sup>27</sup>And he rose and went. And there was an Ethiopian, a eunuch, a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasure and had come to Jerusalem to worship <sup>28</sup>and was returning, seated in his chariot, and he was reading the prophet Isaiah. <sup>29</sup>And the Spirit said to Philip, “Go over and join this chariot.” <sup>30</sup>So Philip ran to him and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet and asked, “Do you understand what you are reading?” <sup>31</sup>And he said, “How can I, unless someone guides me?” And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him. <sup>32</sup>Now the passage of the Scripture that he was reading was this: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opens not his mouth. <sup>33</sup>In his humiliation justice was denied him. Who can describe his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth.” <sup>34</sup>And the eunuch said to Philip, “About whom, I ask you, does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else?” <sup>35</sup>Then Philip opened his mouth, and beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus. <sup>36</sup>And as they were going along the road they came to some water, and the eunuch said, “See, here is water! What prevents me from being baptized?” <sup>38</sup>And he commanded the chariot to stop, and they both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him. <sup>39</sup>And when they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, and went on his way rejoicing. <sup>40</sup>But Philip found himself at Azotus, and as he passed through he preached the gospel to all the towns until he came to Caesarea.
8.overview:
Persecution was meant to silence the gospel. Instead it scattered it. The death of Stephen, the ravaging of the church by Saul, the flight of believers from Jerusalem — all of this was intended to put out the fire. But you do not put out a fire by scattering the embers. You only spread it further. Those who were scattered went about preaching the Word. Not the apostles, who remained — the ordinary believers, the unnamed men and women who had heard Peter preach and Stephen argue, and who could not stop telling the story wherever their flight took them.

Philip goes to Samaria — enemy territory by centuries of Jewish reckoning — and the crowds pay attention, and there is much joy in that city. Then the Spirit pulls him away from the revival to a desert road, to one man in a chariot reading Isaiah 53. The divine calculus is instructive: the sovereign God who fills a city with the gospel also directs one evangelist to one seeker on one road. Every soul matters to him.

The Ethiopian eunuch was an outsider twice over: a foreigner, and a eunuch, barred from the assembly of Israel (Deuteronomy 23:1). He had come to Jerusalem to worship the God of Israel and had found, in a sense, no entry. Now, on a desert road, he encounters the one who tears down every dividing wall — and he goes on his way rejoicing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — Persecution, Scattering, and the Gospel in Samaria
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The stoning of Stephen does not silence the gospel. It scatters it. There arose on that day a great persecution against the church in Jerusalem, and they were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria — and the next thing Luke records is that those who were scattered went about preaching the word. Note who that is. Verse 1 has just told us that everybody left except the apostles. So the men and women carrying the gospel out of Jerusalem are the ones with no office, no training and no commission. The professionals stayed. The gospel travelled in the luggage of refugees.

Philip goes to Samaria, which is not a natural destination but a five-hundred-year-old feud with a demolished temple in the middle of it, and a whole city believes. Then the apostles hear, and send down Peter and John — and John is the man who had once wanted to call fire down on a Samaritan village. He comes back to lay hands on them and pray that they would receive the Spirit.

Half of this section, though, is about a man the summaries usually leave out. Simon had been the religious power in that city for years, and when Philip arrives Simon believes and is baptised like everybody else. Then he watches the Spirit given through the apostles' hands, and offers money for the ability to do it. Peter's reply is the most severe sentence he ever speaks. It is worth reading the whole exchange, because Luke has placed a genuine revival and a counterfeit conversion in the same paragraph and refuses to tell us how the second one ended.

And Luke's last note on the section is quietly lovely. Peter and John came down to look into Samaria, and went home preaching the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans. They arrived as inspectors and left as evangelists. The visit changed the visitors.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Scattering as Mission Strategy

Reformed theology has read Acts 8 as the clearest narrative demonstration that God's purposes are not merely undamaged by human wickedness but advanced through it. Jesus had said the witness would go from Jerusalem to Judea and Samaria and to the end of the earth (1:8), and for perhaps two years nothing had moved; the church was large, joyful, generous and entirely stationary. It took a murder and a persecution to get it out of the city. The point is not that God needed the persecution, nor that the suffering was anything other than real — Luke records men weeping loudly over a grave in the same breath. It is that the machinery of opposition turned out to be the machinery of expansion, and that the man superintending the destruction was, without the faintest idea of it, dispersing the gospel across two provinces. The kingdom advanced that year in the shape of a defeat.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jews had no dealings with Samaritans, and the quarrel was not a misunderstanding — it had a ruined temple on Mount Gerizim in it, pulled down by a Jewish army. The gospel crossed that line before anybody had written a word of argument about whether it should. Now: The barrier a congregation is least likely to cross is never the one it debates. It is the one it has stopped noticing, because everyone it knows is on the same side of it.

verseByVerse.quote: And Saul approved of his execution. And there arose on that day a great persecution against the church in Jerusalem, and they were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles. Devout men buried Stephen and made great lamentation over him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter division cuts a sentence in half. And Saul approved of his execution belongs with the stoning at the end of chapter 7, and Luke wrote it as the last word on that scene: the young man holding the coats was not a bystander who happened to be present. He approved. The word means he thought well of it, and Paul spends the rest of his life saying so.

Then: there arose on that day a great persecution. On that day. Stephen's death was not merely the first casualty; it was the starting gun. Something had been held back until somebody was killed and nothing happened to the killers, and once that line was crossed the whole thing came down at once.

And then a detail that has puzzled readers for a long time: they were all scattered except the apostles. The twelve men most obviously identified with the movement, the ones who had already been arrested twice and flogged once, stayed in the city everybody else was fleeing. Whatever else that was, it was not caution. It is possible they judged that the shepherds should not be the first out of the field, or that Jerusalem had to keep a centre; Luke does not explain. What he does make clear three verses later is the consequence — the people who took the gospel to Samaria were not the apostles. They were the ordinary members who ran.

Then the burial, and it is braver than it looks. Devout men buried Stephen and made great lamentation over him. Jewish practice held that public mourning rites were not observed for a man executed by the court; part of the punishment was that his family grieved in silence and he went into the ground without honour. These men did the opposite, loudly, in a city where a persecution had begun that morning and where being associated with Stephen was now demonstrably dangerous. They gave a convicted blasphemer a funeral and made sure it was heard.

The word Luke uses of them is the one he used of old Simeon waiting in the temple, and of the Diaspora Jews at Pentecost. It may well be that these were not Christians at all, but devout Jews who had heard the speech, or had known the man, and were not prepared to let him be shovelled away. Luke does not say. Either way, somebody with something to lose stood at that grave and wept out loud on purpose.

And that is worth taking, because Christians are frequently given the impression that grief is a lapse — that a believer with a firm grasp of the resurrection should be able to bury somebody without much noise. The first Christian response to the first Christian martyrdom was a great lamentation. Paul's instruction to a grieving church is not that they should not grieve but that they should not grieve as those who have no hope, which assumes the grief and adjusts the quality of it. Stephen had seen heaven opened an hour before he died, and they still stood over the body and howled, and Luke records it without a syllable of correction.

verseByVerse.quote: But Saul was ravaging the church, and entering house after house, he dragged off men and women and committed them to prison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke picks a violent word and he picks it deliberately. Ravaging renders a verb used in the Greek Old Testament of a wild boar getting into a vineyard and wrecking it — an animal in an orchard, tearing at roots, ruining in an afternoon what took years to grow. Luke had a perfectly good word available for official persecution. He used this one instead.

Entering house after house. There were no church buildings; the church met in people's homes, ate in them, broke bread in them. So persecuting the church meant going through front doors. Someone had to compile the list of addresses, and somebody in the neighbourhood had to supply it. The scene is domestic and it is squalid: men coming into a kitchen where a family has been praying, and taking people out of it.

Men and women. Luke says it, and Paul confirms it twice in his own words later in this book — that he persecuted this Way to the death, binding and delivering to prison both men and women, and that he shut up many of the saints in prison and cast his vote against them when they were put to death. He does not soften it in the retelling. In one of his letters he calls himself, without qualification, a blasphemer, a persecutor and an insolent opponent.

The verb for dragged off is the one used for hauling a body along the ground. It is the same word Luke will use of Paul himself being dragged out of a city and left for dead, which is a small piece of authorial irony that he leaves for the reader to find.

And here is the thing about this verse that ought to arrest anybody: it is written about the man who wrote that love is patient and kind, that it does not insist on its own way, that it bears all things. There is no way to read the New Testament without holding these two facts together. The most tender pastoral writing in the Bible came out of a man who had gone door to door arresting mothers.

He never got over it, and that is the point rather than the biographical curiosity. Thirty years on he is still telling people he is the foremost of sinners, in the present tense, and still saying he is unworthy to be called an apostle because he persecuted the church of God. Grace did not give him amnesia. It gave him a permanent, accurate, unbearable memory that he carried without despair, which is a far more remarkable thing than forgetting.

One guard, because this passage is often preached as though it were a promise. It is not a guarantee that the persecutor in your life will be converted. Most of the men who arrested Christians in the first century died as they had lived, and the same is true in every century since. What it is, is a demonstration that nobody is disqualified by the record — which is a different and better thing to know, and which is what Paul himself says it was given for.

verseByVerse.quote: Now those who were scattered went about preaching the word. Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed to them the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The most important word in verse 4 is the one carried over from verse 1. Those who were scattered — and we have just been told that everybody was scattered except the apostles. So the people now preaching across two provinces are precisely the ones with no office, no ordination, no training and no commission to do it. The twelve stayed in Jerusalem. The gospel went to Samaria carried by refugees.

And the verb Luke chooses is not the formal one for public proclamation. It is the ordinary word for announcing good news — telling people something. What these men and women did was not preach in the sense of standing up in front of a congregation. They arrived in strange towns with whatever they could carry, and when people asked why they had left Jerusalem, they said.

That is worth registering by anyone who has quietly concluded that the spread of Christianity is a job for people with the relevant qualifications. The first missionary expansion in the history of the church was carried out entirely by amateurs, under duress, with no strategy, because they had been driven out of their homes and could not stop talking about the reason.

Then Philip — and note who he is. One of the seven appointed two chapters ago to make sure the widows got fed. Stephen, another of the seven, has just preached the longest sermon in the book and been killed for it. Whatever the table-servants were supposed to be doing, it is the table-servants who are breaking the boundaries in this book while the apostles hold the centre.

And the boundary he breaks is not a small one. Samaria was not simply an unevangelised region; it was the object of a feud five centuries old. After Assyria deported the northern tribes it resettled the territory with foreign populations, and the mixed people who resulted claimed the God of Israel, kept their own version of the law of Moses, and built a rival temple on Mount Gerizim. About a hundred and thirty years before this, a Jewish army marched north and pulled that temple down. The wound was still open in Jesus's day, which is why John's Gospel has to stop and explain to its readers that Jews have no dealings with Samaritans, and why the crowd in Jerusalem thought calling a man a Samaritan was a serious insult.

Philip walks into that and proclaimed to them the Christ. He does not open with an argument about the temple, or about which mountain was the right one, or about whose version of the Pentateuch was correct — all of which were live and available. He preaches a person. The quarrel that five hundred years of argument had not settled was left where it was, and something was announced that made it irrelevant.

verseByVerse.quote: And the crowds with one accord paid attention to what was being said by Philip, when they heard him and saw the signs that he did. For unclean spirits, crying out with a loud voice, came out of many who had them, and many who were paralyzed or lame were healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With one accord. It is Luke's word for the Jerusalem church — the hundred and twenty waiting in the upper room, the believers meeting daily in the temple, the congregation lifting its voice together after the arrest. He now uses it of a crowd of Samaritans, which for a first-century Jewish reader is a small shock, deliberately administered.

And what he says they did with one accord is worth noticing, because it is not what people usually remember about this passage. They paid attention to what was being said. The signs are in the sentence and they are in second place — they listened, when they heard him and saw the signs that he did. The miracles got him the room. What the crowd gave its attention to was the talking.

Then the signs themselves, and Luke lists them in a way that ties Samaria to Jerusalem on purpose: unclean spirits crying out and coming out, and the paralysed and the lame healed. That is precisely the list from the earlier chapters — in a despised half-Jewish city, through a man who had been appointed to hand out bread. There is no reduced edition of the kingdom for people on the wrong side of a border.

And notice which conditions he names. Paralysis and lameness are not ailments a man recovers from quietly and privately. They are chronic, visible and permanent, and in a town of that size everybody knew exactly who was carried where. Luke has already shown, at the Beautiful Gate and then in front of the council, what happens when God heals the one person whose condition the whole neighbourhood can verify: it becomes an argument nobody can answer. He is quietly making the same point about Samaria.

One small honesty is worth preserving in the wording, because it belongs to anybody reading this who has prayed a long time and not been healed. Luke writes that unclean spirits came out of many who had them, and that many who were paralysed or lame were healed. Not all. Even in a chapter of undisputed power, at the height of an outpouring, with an apostolic messenger in the town, Luke reaches for a word that leaves somebody still on the mat. He does not explain it and he does not hide it.

On what 'unclean spirits' actually are — real, personal, evil spirit-beings, the same the Gospels call 'demons,' and what Scripture does and does not tell us about them — see the fuller note on 5:15–16. Here the point is simply this: the same authority over them that marked the kingdom's arrival in Jerusalem now appears in Samaria. At the preaching of Christ they cry out and come out; the gospel advances and the unclean flee.

verseByVerse.quote: So there was much joy in that city. But there was a man named Simon, who had previously practiced magic in the city and amazed the people of Samaria, saying that he himself was somebody great.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So there was much joy in that city. It is one of Luke's markers, and he uses it carefully. Joy in a city, not merely in individuals; something had changed in the public atmosphere of the place. He will use the same note at the end of this chapter of a single man on a desert road, and the two are the same fact at different scales.

And then, without a paragraph break, Luke introduces the man who is going to spend the rest of the section demonstrating what the gospel is not.

It is worth being clear about what magic meant in that world, because the modern word has gone soft. This was not entertainment and nobody thought it was conjuring. A practitioner claimed genuine access to powers, and people paid him for results — a curse laid on a rival, a charm against illness, a name that could be invoked to make something happen. Written spells have survived from the period, and they are long lists of divine names collected from every religion available, on the principle that one of them might work. The man who could operate that machinery was feared, consulted, and rich, and he was the nearest thing that city had to a public authority.

Luke's summary of Simon's message is four words long and it is devastating: saying that he himself was somebody great. That is the entire content. Not a doctrine, not a God, not a promise — a claim about the speaker. Everything Simon offered was ultimately about Simon, which is why Luke puts the sentence where he does.

Because the collision Luke is setting up is not between power and no power. Philip has just been casting out unclean spirits and healing paralytics; there is plenty of power in the previous two verses. The difference is what the power is pointing at. Simon amazed people and they concluded that Simon was great. Philip did signs and the crowds paid attention to what was being said — they ended up listening to a message about somebody else entirely.

That is a serviceable test and it survives translation into any century. It is not whether remarkable things happen around a person; remarkable things happened around both of these men. It is what the people who watch end up attached to. If a ministry produces crowds who are knowledgeable about the minister, something has gone wrong that no amount of orthodoxy in the statement of faith will correct.

verseByVerse.quote: They all paid attention to him, from the least to the greatest, saying, "This man is the power of God that is called Great." And they paid attention to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They all paid attention to him, from the least to the greatest. Luke means the whole social range — the labourer and the magistrate, the woman at the well and the man who owned the well. Simon's hold on that city was not confined to the credulous poor, which is the comforting assumption people make about this kind of thing. It reached the top.

And they had a formula for him: This man is the power of God that is called Great. It is an odd, half-technical phrase, and it tells you that Simon had not merely impressed people, he had supplied them with a theology. There was a doctrine about him in circulation, with a title in it. He was not a street performer with a following. He was an established religious institution with a creed.

Then Luke gives the mechanism, and it is the most useful sentence in the paragraph: they paid attention to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic.

Two ingredients, and neither is truth. Amazement — the experience of watching something you cannot account for. And a long time — the sheer weight of years, during which nobody produced a better explanation and everybody grew up with this one. Put those together and you have the anatomy of most religious authority that is not from God. It does not require anybody to be persuaded of anything. It only requires that nobody can explain what is happening, and that this state of affairs goes on long enough to become normal.

Which raises the question a reader is entitled to ask at this point, since Philip's ministry in the previous verses looks, from outside, remarkably similar. Crowds, signs, amazement. How is anybody in that city supposed to tell the difference?

Luke answers it in the next verse, and the answer is not about the phenomena. When they believed Philip as he preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ. Simon offered an experience and a claim about himself; Philip offered a message about a king, and what people did with it was believe it. The signs got him a hearing. The content held them, and the content was somebody else's name.

A guard on the other side is needed too, because it is very easy to leave this passage as a cynic. The lesson is not that anything remarkable is suspect and the safest ministry is the one where nothing ever happens. Luke has just spent two verses describing genuine healings and genuine deliverances with evident approval, and the joy in that city was real. The test is not whether power is present. It is whose name is left standing at the end of the meeting.

verseByVerse.quote: But when they believed Philip as he preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women. Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptized he continued with Philip. And seeing signs and great miracles performed, he was amazed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Watch what displaces Simon, because it is not a stronger performance. They believed Philip as he preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ. A city held for years by amazement is released by a message.

Both men and women. Luke keeps saying this — it is the phrase he used of the Jerusalem church and, grimly, of Saul's arrests three verses earlier — and it is not filler. In a world where a woman's religious standing generally travelled through her husband, Luke records the women being baptised on their own account, in their own names, on their own faith.

And then Simon. Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptised he continued with Philip. Luke states it without qualification: he believed, he was baptised, he attached himself to the preacher. Nothing in that sentence is flagged as false, and a reading which has Simon play-acting from the start is reading something Luke has not written.

But the last clause is doing careful work. And seeing signs and great miracles performed, he was amazed. Amazement is the word that has followed Simon through this whole passage — he amazed the Samaritans, they were amazed by him, and now he is the one amazed. He has changed places in the sentence without changing his interest. What held him before is what holds him now: something remarkable is happening and he cannot account for it. Five verses later he will try to buy it.

What is it to 'preach the kingdom of God'? The kingdom is God's saving reign — his kingly rule breaking in through Jesus the Messiah to rescue and to rule. Notice Philip preached 'the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ' in one breath: you cannot proclaim the kingdom without the King. To preach it is to announce that God's long-promised reign has arrived in Christ, who died, rose, and reigns, and to call people to repent, believe, and bow to him as Lord — entering his kingdom now and forever (so Paul too, 'proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ,' Acts 28:31; on its 'already / not yet,' see on Col. 4:11).

Why is 'the kingdom of God' on nearly every page of Matthew, Mark, and Luke, yet rare in John and the letters? Not because the truth fades, but because the vantage point and vocabulary shift. The first three Gospels record Jesus' own preaching to Jewish audiences, and 'the kingdom of God' was his characteristic summary ('repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand,' Matt. 4:17), steeped in Israel's hope (Dan. 7:13–14) — they preserve his very idiom. John, later and more reflective, names the kingdom only twice (John 3:3, 5) but says the same thing with a different word: 'eternal life' — in Mark 10, 'inherit eternal life,' 'enter the kingdom,' and 'be saved' are interchangeable; for John, to enter the kingdom simply is to have life.

The Epistles, written after the resurrection and enthronement to mostly Gentile churches, put the focus on the King himself. Because Jesus has died, risen, and been seated at God's right hand, the apostles' shorthand becomes 'Jesus is Lord' (Rom. 10:9; Phil. 2:11), 'in Christ,' and 'Christ must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet' (1 Cor. 15:25) — kingdom-preaching centred on the reigning King. So the term grows rarer while the reality saturates everything (and Paul still uses it plainly — Rom. 14:17; 1 Cor. 6:9–10; Col. 1:13; 1 Thess. 2:12). A likely added reason: announcing 'another king' sounded seditious in the Roman world (Acts 17:7), so 'Lord' and 'Christ' were safer words. Same kingdom throughout — announced by Jesus in Israel's language, rendered by John as 'life,' proclaimed by the apostles through the lordship of the risen King.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the apostles at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent to them Peter and John, who came down and prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
News travels, and the sentence Luke writes is remarkable for what is not in it. When the apostles at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God — and there is no debate recorded, no committee, no objection, no summons for Philip to explain himself. A city of Samaritans has believed, and the response is to send two men down to pray for them.

That deserves a moment, because the apostles had every reason to be uneasy. Nobody had authorised this. Philip was not an apostle and had been appointed to a food distribution. The people involved were Samaritans, on the far side of a quarrel with five centuries and a demolished temple in it. Any institution presented with an unauthorised expansion into disputed territory has a standard set of reflexes available, and Luke records none of them.

Then the names, which are the best thing in the verse. They sent to them Peter and John.

John. Luke's own first volume records that when a Samaritan village refused Jesus hospitality, it was James and John who turned to him and asked whether they should call down fire from heaven and burn the place — and were rebuked for it. Now the same man walks down the same road into the same territory, and the errand is to put his hands on Samaritans and ask God to give them the Holy Spirit.

Nobody in the narrative comments on it. Luke simply puts the name in, having written the other story himself, and leaves it for anyone paying attention. What the Spirit had done to John in the intervening years is described nowhere. It is visible only in the fact that he made the journey.

That is worth holding onto by anybody who carries a settled contempt they have privately given up hope of losing — the group, the sort of person, the family, the whole category about whom the reflex is instant and ugly and has been there since childhood. James and John's instinct about Samaritans was to incinerate them. The instinct was not argued away. It was replaced, slowly enough that nobody recorded the process, and the only evidence that it had happened is a man on a road with his hands out.

And note what they came to do. Not to inspect, not to regularise, not to take charge of somebody else's work: they prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit. The two senior apostles arrive at a revival they had no part in starting, and their first act is to ask God to give those people more.

verseByVerse.quote: for he had not yet fallen on any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Then they laid their hands on them and they received the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke states the anomaly flatly and does not soften it. These people had believed. They had been baptised. And the Spirit had not come.

He knows how strange that is, which is why he stops the narrative to say so, in a phrase he uses nowhere else: he had not yet fallen on any of them. Everywhere else in this book the order runs the other way, or all at once. At Pentecost the Spirit falls and the preaching and the baptisms follow. In chapter 10 the Spirit interrupts Peter in the middle of a sentence, before anybody has been baptised at all, and the water comes after the wind. Here alone there is a gap — people who genuinely believed in the Lord Jesus and were genuinely baptised went about their business for some days without what every other believer in this book receives at once.

So the question cannot be dodged, and it has been argued over for centuries: what was the gap for, and does it mean anything for an ordinary believer now? The answer that best fits Luke's own narrative is that this was a hinge in the history of salvation rather than a pattern for individuals — the Spirit's coming held back until the apostles arrived, so that the long-estranged Samaritans would be visibly joined into the one apostolic church instead of starting a second and rival Christianity. Five hundred years of schism were repaired in public, by two Jewish hands on Samaritan heads. But godly Christians read the passage in more than one way, and the alternatives deserve a fair hearing.

This delay — genuine believers, baptized, on whom the Spirit had 'not yet fallen' until the apostles came — is one of the most discussed passages on receiving the Spirit, and godly Christians read it in different ways. Pentecostal and charismatic brothers often see here a distinct 'baptism in the Spirit' subsequent to conversion, a normative second stage (and read Acts 19 likewise). The sacramental traditions (Roman Catholic, Anglican) find here the root of confirmation, the Spirit given through the laying on of hands after baptism. The Reformed reading — taken above — sees this as a unique, transitional hinge in redemptive history rather than a pattern for every believer: just as the gospel crossed each great barrier (Jews at Pentecost, ch. 2; Samaritans here; Gentiles in ch. 10), God marked each crossing with a visible outpouring of the Spirit, so that the long-estranged Samaritans would be openly joined into the one apostolic church, not begin a rival Christianity.

On this view the regular doctrine of how we receive the Spirit is taught in the letters, not drawn from these one-time narratives — and there the answer is plain: the Spirit is given to all who believe, at conversion ('anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him,' Rom. 8:9; 'when you believed, you were sealed,' Eph. 1:13; Gal. 3:2). So you need not fear you are a half-Christian awaiting a second gift: if you belong to Christ, you already have the Spirit. The point is said with respect for brothers who differ.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles' hands, he offered them money, saying, "Give me this power also, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Simon saw that the Spirit was given. Saw. Whatever happened when Peter and John laid hands on those Samaritans was visible from across the room, and Luke declines to say what it was — a restraint worth noticing in a writer normally happy to describe wind and fire and buildings shaking.

Then the offer, which is the first attempt in Christian history to purchase a spiritual gift.

Look carefully at what he asks for, because it is not what people generally assume. He does not ask to receive the Spirit; he had been baptised already and does not raise the subject. He asks for this authority — the power to lay his own hands on somebody else and have the Spirit come. He is not applying for a blessing. He is applying for a franchise.

And here is what makes the scene so exact. By the standards of Simon's old profession the request is entirely reasonable and even courteous. That is precisely how the trade worked: names, formulas and techniques were commodities, bought from a practitioner at the going rate and then used on paying customers. A man who wanted a new capability approached the man who had it and made an offer, and everybody understood the arrangement. Simon is not being outrageous by his own lights. He is doing business the only way he has ever known, with a product he has just watched being demonstrated.

What he has entirely failed to notice is that he has changed worlds. In the one he has walked into there is no going rate, because the thing on offer was never for sale and the men holding it did not buy it either.

His name has been attached to the sin ever since. Simony — the buying and selling of church office and spiritual privilege — became one of the great scandals of the medieval church, with bishoprics going to the highest bidder and cathedrals financed by selling assurances about the next life. It took a Reformation to prise it loose, and it has never been a peculiarly Catholic disease; every tradition has since found its own way of putting a price on something God gives away.

The modern shapes are quieter and harder to see, and the general form is this: treating a relationship as a transaction. The giving that expects a return in blessing. The service undertaken with an eye on what it buys with God, or with the congregation. The prayer offered as a lever. In each case the assumption underneath is Simon's — that there is a rate, and that a man who pays it is entitled to the result. It is not a stupid assumption. It is how nearly everything else in life works. It is simply not how this works, and Peter's next sentence explains why not.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said to him, "May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
May your silver perish with you.

It is the harshest thing Peter says to anybody in the New Testament, and it is worth being clear what kind of sentence it is. He is not laying a curse on the man. The Greek is nearer to a statement of direction than a wish: your money is going to destruction, and on present course you are going with it. Peter describes the trajectory precisely because he wants it changed, which is what he tells him to do two verses later.

Then the reason, and it is the theology of the whole passage in one clause: because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money.

The word is gift. It is the same word Peter used at Pentecost — repent and be baptised, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. And a gift is not a cheap sort of purchase; it is a different kind of thing altogether. The moment a price is paid, whatever changes hands has stopped being a gift, and the man who insisted on paying has not acquired it at a discount. He has destroyed it, and gone home with something else in his pocket.

Which is why the answer is so severe. Simon has not merely made a procedural mistake. He has proposed an arrangement under which grace would cease to be grace — and if it were available on those terms, nobody in that room would have had any, Peter included.

You have neither part nor lot in this matter. The phrase comes straight out of the law of Moses, where it describes the Levite who has no portion and no inheritance when the land is divided. Peter is telling him that when the ground is measured out, his name is on none of it.

And then the diagnosis: your heart is not right before God. The word means straight, and it is a builder's word. Something in him does not run true.

Now the question this passage actually raises for an ordinary reader, and it should be answered plainly rather than left hanging in the air. Verse 13 said Simon believed and was baptised. Verse 21 says he has no share in this at all. What is that supposed to do to anybody's assurance?

Scripture is not embarrassed by the category. It says elsewhere that the demons believe, and shudder. It records a crowd in Jerusalem who believed when they saw the signs, and notes that Jesus did not entrust himself to them, because he knew what was in man. And John, writing to a church that had watched people walk out, says they went out from us because they were not of us. There is a kind of believing which is real as far as it goes and never goes as far as Christ. Simon is its portrait: genuinely gripped, genuinely impressed, genuinely attached to the preacher, and interested from first to last in what he could get.

But the pastoral point is the one that matters most here. The reader who finds this passage frightening — who has read verse 13 and thought, that could be me — is displaying the one symptom Simon never displays anywhere in this story. Simon is not worried about his heart. He is worried, as the next verses show, about what might happen to him. A man who is anxious about whether he truly loves Christ is asking a question that never once entered Simon's head, and the anxiety is itself evidence of an interest Simon did not have.

verseByVerse.quote: "Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything about these verses depends on noticing that Peter, having said the severest thing he ever says to anybody, immediately tells the man what to do about it.

Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord. The door is not shut. The diagnosis was brutal and the prescription follows in the same breath, which is what distinguishes a rebuke from a dismissal. The shape is worth learning, because most people manage one half or the other. Some will say the hard thing and leave the man standing in it. Others will not say the hard thing at all and will call the omission kindness. Peter does both inside two sentences, and the second is the reason for the first.

Then the phrase that troubles readers: that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you.

Read carelessly it sounds as though Peter were unsure whether God would forgive a sin of this size — as though there were a limit somewhere and Simon might have found it. That is not what the sentence is doing, and the distinction matters enormously to anyone carrying something he is afraid is too large. The uncertainty does not attach to God's willingness. It attaches to Simon. Peter has no way of knowing whether this man will actually turn, and he is honest about it rather than issuing a guarantee he is in no position to give. It is the difference between God may not forgive you and you may not repent, and every difficulty in the verse dissolves the moment that is seen.

Notice as well what Peter tells him to do: pray to the Lord. Not ask me to pray. The man who has just tried to buy access through an intermediary is told to go directly and ask for himself. In one sentence Peter refuses both the money and the role of broker.

The diagnosis in verse 23 is built out of two Old Testament phrases, and both are physical. The gall of bitterness reaches back to Moses warning Israel about a root among them bearing poisonous and bitter fruit — a thing growing underground and out of sight, which is exactly right for a man whose problem nobody could see until money was mentioned. The bond of iniquity is the language of chains, and it turns up in Isaiah in a passage about the fast God actually wants: to loose the bonds of wickedness and let the oppressed go free. Peter's picture is of a man who is not merely doing wrong but tied up by it — and what he prescribes is not effort but repentance and prayer, because a man in chains cannot untie himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And Simon answered, "Pray for me to the Lord, that nothing of what you have said may come upon me." Now when they had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon answers, and the answer is a small masterpiece of missing the point.

Pray for me to the Lord, that nothing of what you have said may come upon me.

Two things are wrong with it and both are quiet. The first is what he asks about. Peter had named a heart that was not straight, a bitterness growing underground, a bond of iniquity. Simon asks about the consequences — that nothing of what you have said may come upon me. He is not asking to be changed. He is asking not to be hit. That is the difference between a man who is sorry and a man who is frightened, and the two make very similar noises.

The second is whom he asks. Peter had told him, in as many words, to pray to the Lord himself. Simon's reply is: you pray for me. He is still in his old trade, still assuming that the power belongs to the practitioner and that a layman's best move is to hire the man who has it. He has been rebuked for treating the Spirit as a commodity, and his instinctive next move is to treat Peter as one.

And then Luke stops. We are told nothing more. Simon does not repent and does not refuse to repent. He simply leaves the narrative on an unfinished sentence.

The later church could not bear it and filled the gap enthusiastically; there is a considerable body of legend about Simon Magus, most of it lurid and none of it in Scripture. Luke had presumably heard some of it and declined to write it down. He leaves the man exactly where he found him: a serious warning delivered, a door held open, and no answer recorded.

It is worth asking why. Partly because Luke is honest and did not know. But partly, one suspects, because a resolved ending would let the reader off. If Simon repents, the passage becomes a story about the long reach of grace and the reader relaxes. If Simon is damned, it becomes a story about a bad man and the reader relaxes in the other direction. Left where it is, the question stays open — and it was never really a question about Simon.

Then verse 25, which is the loveliest note in the chapter. Peter and John finish their business and go home, preaching the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans. They had come down to see what was happening in one city. They went back seeding a whole region, on foot, village by village, having evidently decided that since they were walking that way in any case they might as well. The two men sent to look into a Samaritan revival went home having become part of it. That is what the errand did to them — and one of the two had once wanted the place burned to the ground.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–40 — Philip and the Ethiopian Eunuch
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Spirit calls Philip out of the most fruitful work of his life and sends him to stand on a road. Luke adds, in four words, that the place is a desert — no town, no crowd, no synagogue. Philip rises and goes without asking what for.

What comes down the road is a man whose identity Luke assembles with great care, and every item matters. He is Ethiopian, which in the geography of the day meant the far edge of the world. He is a court official in charge of a queen's entire treasury, so he is powerful and rich. He has travelled the length of the known world to worship in Jerusalem, so he is serious. And he is a eunuch, which means that when he arrived the law shut him out at the door. He has spent a fortune and a season of his life on a pilgrimage to a temple that would not fully have him.

He is reading Isaiah aloud in his carriage, from a scroll that cost more than most men earned in a year, and he has reached the passage about a man led like a sheep to the slaughter, denied justice, cut off from the land of the living, whose descendants nobody could number. Philip runs alongside and asks whether he understands it, and receives the most teachable answer in the book: how can I, unless someone guides me? Beginning from that Scripture, Philip tells him the good news about Jesus.

Then water, and a question — what prevents me from being baptised? — asked by a man who has known the answer since he was a boy, and who is really asking whether it still holds. It does not. He goes down into the water and comes up, and Philip is taken away, and the Ethiopian goes on his way rejoicing with no church, no minister, no Bible in his own language and a thousand miles to travel. Philip finds himself at Azotus and preaches his way up the coast to Caesarea — where, twenty years later, the man writing this book will stay in his house.
verseByVerse.theology:
Isaiah 53 and the Death of the Servant

Philip began from this Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus, and the Scripture was the last of Isaiah's Servant Songs. It is the passage in the Old Testament that comes nearest to explaining what a cross is for: the Servant is pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, the chastisement that brought us peace was upon him, and with his wounds we are healed. Notice the grammar, because the Reformed tradition has always insisted that everything turns on it: the transgressions are ours, the wounds are his, and the exchange is the entire point. He is not merely an instance of innocent suffering, of which the world has always had an ample supply. He is a substitute — the guiltless one bearing what the guilty had coming, so that the guilty go free. That is what Philip preached from. And it is worth noticing that he did not have to argue his way to Christ across a long distance. He started at Isaiah 53 and the road was short.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: A man barred from the assembly by Deuteronomy 23:1 was reading a scroll which, three chapters past where he had it open, promised eunuchs a name in God's house better than sons and daughters. He was reading his own exclusion, and without knowing it his own invitation. Now: The people most certain the door is shut to them are usually the ones who know the rules best. It was not a careless man who needed telling that nothing prevented him. It was the man who had read the regulation and accepted it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now an angel of the Lord said to Philip, "Rise and go toward the south to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza." This is a desert place. And he rose and went. And there was an Ethiopian, a eunuch, a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasure. He had come to Jerusalem to worship
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consider the timing of this instruction. Philip is in the middle of the most fruitful work of his life — a whole city believing, joy in the streets, the two senior apostles arriving from Jerusalem to see it — and an angel tells him to leave and go and stand on a road.

Luke then adds a note a modern reader hurries past: this is a desert place. The Gaza road ran south-west out of Jerusalem through open country, and Philip is sent to a stretch of it with nothing on it. No town, no crowd, no synagogue, and no indication of how long he is to wait. He is not being sent to a mission field. He is being sent to a road.

And he rose and went. Four words, and there is not a question in them. He does not ask what for, or for how long, or whether the Samaritan work will survive without him — and it is worth registering, before the famous part of the story begins, that everything which follows depended on a man being willing to leave something that was going extremely well.

'An angel of the Lord said to Philip' — and many a believer quietly wishes God would guide him so directly. Why was this common then but not now?
