First, a correction: angelic appearances were never everyday, even in Scripture. Across two thousand years they cluster at a few pivotal moments — the patriarchs, the Exodus, the prophets here and there, the birth of Christ, the empty tomb, the launch of the church. Most godly saints never saw or heard an angel; they fill the narrative because Scripture records the turning points, not the ordinary years.

And Acts is exactly such a turning point: the once-for-all launch of the gospel from Jerusalem to Samaria, to this Ethiopian, to Cornelius (ch. 10), to the ends of the earth. For that foundational breakout God used extraordinary steering — angels, visions, the Spirit speaking by name (10:3; 13:2; 16:9) — driving the apostles into territory they would never have entered on their own. Like the authenticating signs (see on 5:12), this belonged to the laying of the foundation (Eph. 2:20), which by nature is laid once.

Today God guides by settled and sufficient means — and we are not less supplied but more. We hold what the early church was still receiving: the completed Scripture, 'a lamp to my feet' (Ps. 119:105), able to make us 'complete, equipped for every good work' (2 Tim. 3:16–17); the indwelling Spirit who illumines it; and prayer, wisdom, godly counsel, and providence. Scripture even warns against craving angelic encounters — against the 'worship of angels' by those who do not hold fast to Christ the Head (Col. 2:18), noting that Satan 'disguises himself as an angel of light' (2 Cor. 11:14), and that even 'if an angel from heaven' preached another gospel he is to be rejected (Gal. 1:8). Deepest of all, God 'has in these last days spoken to us by his Son' (Heb. 1:1–2), far superior to angels (Heb. 1:4); to ask for an angel when we hold the word of the Son is to ask for something lesser. We 'walk by faith, not by sight' (2 Cor. 5:7), and 'blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed' (John 20:29).

Two honest qualifications. Angels are not idle — they remain 'ministering spirits sent out to serve those who are to inherit salvation' (Heb. 1:14), often unseen; God has not lost his freedom to use them. And no verse says outright that angels stopped speaking after the apostles; that they no longer do so as our normal guidance is a fair inference from the foundational character of the Acts era, the sufficiency of Scripture, and the Bible's own warnings. The settled point: do not hanker after an angel — you have the finished Word of God, the Spirit of God, and the Son of God himself. That is more, not less, than a voice from the desert road.

What was a 'eunuch'? Plainly, a man who had been castrated. In ancient royal courts such men were deliberately employed — above all to guard the king's or queen's household and women, since a man who could neither father children nor pose a dynastic threat was reckoned uniquely safe. Far from lowly, eunuchs often rose to the highest posts of trust — chamberlains, treasurers — like this man, 'in charge of all the treasure' of Candace. (The word could also be a looser title for a high official whatever his state — Potiphar is called a 'eunuch' though married, Gen. 39:1; and Jesus names three kinds, Matt. 19:12. Here, given his office and the exclusion below, he is most likely a literal eunuch.)

And here is the poignancy. Under the law, 'no one whose... male organ is cut off shall enter the assembly of the LORD' (Deut. 23:1) — a eunuch was, by his very body, barred from full membership in Israel's worship, however earnestly he sought God. So here is a man who has travelled the length of the known world to worship in Jerusalem, only to remain an outsider, shut out at the door. Yet he is reading Isaiah — the very book where God promised the day when the eunuch who holds fast his covenant would receive 'a name better than sons and daughters... an everlasting name that shall not be cut off' (Isa. 56:3–5). The gospel Philip is about to preach is that promise fulfilled: in Christ the excluded outsider is brought all the way in.

verseByVerse.quote: and was returning, seated in his chariot, and he was reading the prophet Isaiah. And the Spirit said to Philip, "Go over and join this chariot."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two details in verse 28 tell you a great deal about this man before he has said a word.

The first is that he was reading, and Philip could hear him doing it from the roadside. Reading in the ancient world was almost always aloud; silent reading was unusual enough that people remarked on it when they saw it. So the picture is of a senior official rolling south through open country, reading a Hebrew prophet out loud to himself in a moving carriage.

The second is the scroll. A hand-copied scroll of Isaiah was not a thing anybody owned casually. Every letter was written out by a trained scribe onto prepared skins over a matter of weeks, and a complete major prophet represented a serious capital purchase — the sort of item that would be listed in a will. This man is the treasurer of a kingdom, and he has spent real money on the sacred book of a religion that will not fully admit him, in a language that is not his own. Nobody made him do it. He is going home from a pilgrimage that ended at a barrier, and he has bought the book anyway and is reading it in the desert.

Then: the Spirit said to Philip, Go over and join this chariot. The verb is stronger than join suggests. It means to be glued to something, to attach oneself and stay attached; it is the word used of a man cleaving to his wife, and of Saul later in this book trying to attach himself to disciples who were frightened of him. Philip is not told to strike up a conversation. He is told to fasten on.

Notice the division of labour, because it is the pattern of every genuine piece of evangelism in Scripture and it takes an enormous weight off the messenger. The Spirit arranged the road, the timing, the scroll and the passage. He had a man reading Isaiah 53 aloud at the exact mile where Philip happened to be standing. What was left for Philip to do was walk over.

Most Christians will never receive an audible sentence, and it should be said plainly that this is not the ordinary form. But it is also worth noticing how much of Philip's obedience here consisted of doing something small and mildly awkward with a situation that was already in front of him. There was a chariot on the road. He went over to it. A great deal of what looks in retrospect like guidance turns out, at the time, to have been a nudge toward a conversation that was already available.

verseByVerse.quote: So Philip ran to him and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet and asked, "Do you understand what you are reading?" And he said, "How can I, unless someone guides me?" And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Philip ran to him. A grown man jogging along a desert road beside a moving carriage, out of breath, trying to keep pace with a state official's driver. Luke includes it, and it is not a dignified picture. Philip is not strolling across when it suits him.

Then the opening line, which is one of the best-judged sentences in the book: Do you understand what you are reading?

In Greek it is a pun — the verb for understanding and the verb for reading are the same root, so that it comes out as something like do you know what you are re-knowing? It is light, and it is precisely calibrated. Not a challenge, not a sermon, not a change of subject. Philip begins with the thing the man is already doing and asks a question about it.

That is worth taking seriously by anyone who dreads these conversations, because the dread is nearly always about having to introduce a topic out of nothing. Philip introduces nothing. He notices what is in the man's hands and asks how he is getting on with it. The entire encounter turns on a question whose whole content is: I see what you are doing, and I wondered.

And the answer is the most teachable sentence anybody speaks in the book of Acts. How can I, unless someone guides me?

Consider who says it. A man of rank, in his own carriage, with an escort, replying to a stranger who has just run up out of the desert on foot. He does not bluff. He does not say that he has his own view of the passage, or that he was only reading it out of interest, or that he has people at court who advise him on these matters. He admits at once, to an obvious inferior, that he is out of his depth — and then invites the man to sit down beside him.

Two errors are ruled out by this verse and they lie on opposite sides. The first is the assumption that Scripture is so plain that nobody ought to need help with it, and that asking is a confession of weakness. The Ethiopian is intelligent, serious and reading the right book, and he cannot get through Isaiah 53 without somebody to explain it; the God who inspired the text also gave the church teachers, and it is not a defect in the text or in the reader that the two were meant to go together. The second is the opposite error — that Scripture is so difficult ordinary people had better leave it to the qualified. Nobody suggests the eunuch should stop reading. He is reading, and the answer to his difficulty is not less Bible. It is a man in the carriage.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the passage of the Scripture that he was reading was this: "Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opens not his mouth. In his humiliation justice was denied him. Who can describe his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scroll is open at Isaiah 53, and it is worth being exact about which lines he was reading when Philip arrived, because they are the reason he had stopped.

First the picture. Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opens not his mouth. Anybody who has watched shearing knows the detail Isaiah is reaching for: the animal is turned over and held, and it stops struggling — it goes completely still, in a way that can look almost like consent. That is the image, and it is laid beside the other one, the sheep going quietly up the ramp. Silence in both. The prophet is describing a man who did not resist — and Luke's own first volume records exactly that: before Herod, questioned at length, he answered nothing.

Then in his humiliation justice was denied him, which is a legal sentence. Not that he suffered, but that the courts failed. And his life is taken away from the earth, which Isaiah puts elsewhere in the same paragraph as being cut off out of the land of the living.

And between them sits the line nobody can translate comfortably: Who can describe his generation? The Hebrew is genuinely difficult, and readers have taken it two ways — either that nobody could describe the wickedness of the men among whom he lived, or, more probably, that nobody could number his descendants. The second fits the paragraph, because a few lines later Isaiah says of this same Servant that he shall see his offspring — an extraordinary thing to say about a man who has just been described as cut off and buried.

Now put that in front of the man in the carriage.

He is a eunuch. He will have no children, no descendants, no name carried forward — and in the ancient world that was not a private sorrow but the erasure of a man from the future. The law that shut him out of the assembly had shut him out on precisely that ground. And he is reading, aloud, alone, on a desert road, about a man cut off from the land of the living, whose generation nobody could describe, and who would somehow see his offspring after all.

It is not difficult to see why he stopped. Whether or not he could have put it into words, he was reading his own biography and could not work out whose it was. The question he asks in the next verse is not academic curiosity. It is a man asking who this is, because whoever it is, is standing exactly where he is standing.

verseByVerse.quote: And the eunuch said to Philip, "About whom, I ask you, does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else?" Then Philip opened his mouth, and beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
About whom, I ask you, does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else?

It is the right question, and it was not a naive one. The identity of Isaiah's Servant was genuinely disputed and had been for centuries; readers proposed the prophet himself, or Hezekiah, or Israel as a nation, or a faithful remnant inside the nation, or a Messiah still to come. The eunuch has read the passage carefully enough to see that it is about a person, and honestly enough to admit that he cannot tell which.

Then Philip's answer, and the method is as instructive as the content. Beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus.

Beginning with this Scripture. He does not change the subject. He does not say that Isaiah is a difficult book and here is a simpler way of putting things. He produces no outline, no diagram, no sequence of steps. The man had a question about a text; Philip answers the question about the text, and keeps going until he arrives at Jesus. It is the same move the risen Christ made on a road out of Jerusalem, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets and interpreting to two men the things concerning himself.

That is worth learning, because the instinct in these conversations is nearly always to steer — to get off whatever the other person actually asked and onto ground where we know the material. Philip does the opposite. He starts where the man already is, in the passage the man had already chosen, with the question the man had already formed, and walks from there.

And the phrasing of what he preached is precise. He told him the good news about Jesus — literally, he gospelled Jesus to him. Jesus is not a topic within the message. He is the message. Whatever Philip said in that carriage, and Luke does not record one word of it, the content was a person.

One further thing follows, and it settles an old anxiety. If Isaiah 53 is about Jesus, it is not because the church later found it convenient. The eunuch is reading it and asking who it is about before Philip arrives. The text raised the question by itself, in the mind of a foreigner with no Christian instruction, on a road in the desert. Christ is not being imported into Isaiah. He is being identified in it.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were going along the road they came to some water, and the eunuch said, "See, here is water! What prevents me from being baptized?" And Philip said, "If you believe with all your heart, you may." And he answered and said, "I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
See, here is water! What prevents me from being baptised?

He asks it; Philip does not suggest it. Whatever was said in that carriage had evidently included the fact that people who believe this get baptised, and the Ethiopian has connected it to the water they are passing and raised it himself.

And the question he chooses is the one word he has carried his whole life. What prevents me? He knows the answer. He has known it since he was a boy, and he had it confirmed at the end of a journey of several thousand miles: his own body prevented him, the law said so in as many words, and the temple he had crossed the world to reach would not let him past the outer court. He puts the question to a man who has just spent an hour telling him about Jesus, and what he is actually asking is whether the barrier is still there.

What makes this scene so charged is where the eunuch has been reading. He has a scroll of Isaiah open to chapter 53 when Philip arrives — the Servant's vicarious suffering and death. But just three chapters later, Isaiah 56:3–5 makes the eunuch a figure of prophetic promise: let not the eunuch say, I am a dry tree; for thus says the LORD, to the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant, I will give in my house and within my walls a monument and a name better than sons and daughters. The very book the eunuch is reading contains the prophecy that he — the excluded one — will be gathered. He is not merely reading Isaiah 53; he is inhabiting Isaiah 56. Luke wants his readers to feel the precision of Providence: the Spirit does not just send Philip to the right road but to the right man reading the right book at the right passage.

One thing about verse 37 needs saying plainly, because your Bible may not have it. Many modern translations print verse 36 and then jump straight to verse 38, with the exchange about believing with all your heart pushed down into a footnote — which makes for a puzzling gap in the numbering if nobody explains it. The reason is that the words are missing from the earliest and best copies of Acts. They are old: Irenaeus is quoting them before the end of the second century. But they read exactly like the question and answer the early church used at the water's edge, and a scribe who knew that liturgy by heart would very naturally have supplied what looked to him like a missing line.

Nothing is lost if it goes. The eunuch plainly did believe — he asks for baptism himself, and he goes on his way rejoicing — and every word the verse contains is taught openly elsewhere in the same book: repent and be baptised (2:38), they believed and were baptised (8:12), believe in the Lord Jesus and you will be saved, and he was baptised at once (16:31-33). So no doctrine rests on it, and no doctrine is damaged by it. What the sentence preserves, even if the hand that wrote it was not Luke's, is an accurate photograph of what the church asked a man before it took him down into the water. The words may be a later copyist's. The practice they describe is apostolic.

verseByVerse.quote: And he commanded the chariot to stop, and they both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him. And when they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, and went on his way rejoicing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He commanded the chariot to stop. In this whole passage the powerful man gives exactly one order, and it is to halt his own carriage in the middle of a desert so that a stranger can baptise him in whatever water they have just come to. He does not ask whether it might wait until Ethiopia, or whether there is a more suitable place, or whether he ought to be further instructed first.

They both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptised him. Luke's wording — down into, and in the next verse up out of — is why this verse turns up in every discussion of how baptism should be administered. It is honest to say that it leans one way without settling the matter, since Greek prepositions will carry a man to the water's edge as readily as under it. It is not the point Luke is making, and Christians who love one another have differed about it for a very long time without either side being able to claim this verse outright.

What Luke does make a point of is what happens next. The Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more. The verb means snatched — it is the word Paul uses of a man caught up to the third heaven, and the word for the church being caught up at the last day. Luke reports it in half a sentence and does not pause over it at all.

Now stand where the Ethiopian is standing. He has been a Christian for perhaps ten minutes. He is wet, on a desert road, and the man who explained everything to him has gone — not travelled on, not said goodbye: gone. Ahead of him is a journey of a thousand miles and more, back to a court where there is not another believer on the continent. He has no church. He has no minister. He has no Bible in his own language, and the scroll he does have is in Hebrew and stops at Malachi. Nobody has taught him to pray or told him what to do on the first Sunday, and there is no one within a month's travelling to ask.

And Luke says he went on his way rejoicing.

Whatever he had received in that carriage did not depend on Philip's continued presence, and he appears to have understood that immediately. He had Christ. The joy in that sentence is not bravery under adverse conditions; it is the ordinary result of the gospel, and it is the same word Luke used of an entire city twenty verses earlier.

One guard, because this is occasionally used to argue that a Christian does not really need the church. Luke has spent seven chapters describing a community that ate together, prayed together, sold property for one another and buried its dead with great lamentation, and he is not now quietly withdrawing all of it. The eunuch's isolation is a circumstance, not a recommendation. What the verse establishes is narrower and more comforting: that a believer who has nothing but Christ has enough to be going on with — which is worth knowing by anyone reading this in a hospital, or a prison, or a country where the nearest congregation is a very long way off.

Later tradition holds that this man carried the gospel home and that the Ethiopian church traces itself to him. Luke does not say so and it cannot be established. What can be said is that a man went south that afternoon with the good news about Jesus, in the direction of the end of the earth, exactly as had been promised in the first chapter of this book.

verseByVerse.quote: But Philip found himself at Azotus, and as he passed through he preached the gospel to all the towns until he came to Caesarea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Philip found himself at Azotus. The phrasing is odd in Greek as well — he was found at Azotus, as though even Luke is not entirely sure how to put it. Azotus is Ashdod, one of the five old Philistine cities, some twenty miles up the coast. The gospel arrives in Goliath's country by way of a man who did not choose the destination.

And then, without pausing, he does what he has been doing all chapter: as he passed through he preached the gospel to all the towns until he came to Caesarea. Not one great mission and then a rest — a coastline of towns, one after another, across perhaps sixty miles, all the way to the Roman provincial capital.

Then Luke closes the chapter and Philip disappears out of the narrative altogether.

He reappears once, twenty years later and thirteen chapters on, in a single verse: we entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him (21:8). Two things in that sentence are worth noticing. The first is the word we. The man writing this book was in that house. Luke stayed several days under Philip's roof at Caesarea, and it is very hard to avoid the conclusion that the material in chapters 6 and 8 — the appointment of the seven, the Samaritan mission, the desert road, the Ethiopian's question, the water — came across a table from the man it happened to. This chapter has a named eyewitness, and he is in the book.

The second is what Philip had been doing in the meantime. He is still called the evangelist two decades on, which is evidently what people in Caesarea called him. And he has four unmarried daughters who prophesy — which quietly pays off the promise Peter had quoted from Joel on the first morning of the church, that sons and daughters would prophesy. He settled in a port city, raised a family, and went on being the man who tells people about Jesus.

Which is the note this chapter deserves to end on. Philip's famous day was the desert road, and it lasted an afternoon. What he actually did with his life was live in Caesarea for twenty years, keep the door open, bring up four daughters in the fear of God, and go on telling people town by town until a doctor from Antioch came to stay and wrote it all down. Most of a Christian life is the twenty years and not the afternoon. The afternoon is what gets recorded. The twenty years are what made the record possible.

8.theology: The Gospel Breaks Every Barrier. Acts 8 is the chapter in which the gospel crosses its first major boundary — from Jews to Samaritans, and then from Israel to Africa. This is not accidental; it is the working out of Acts 1:8: Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, ends of the earth. The Ethiopian eunuch is the first representative of the “ends of the earth” in the book — geographically distant, ethnically foreign, ritually excluded. And the gospel reaches him on a desert road through a text he happened to be reading. This is the Reformed doctrine of effectual calling in action: the Spirit directs the preacher, opens the Scriptures, and draws the seeker. Nothing is left to chance. The God who elects a people from every tongue and tribe and nation uses the ordinary means — a man, a chariot, a scroll — to accomplish his extraordinary purposes.
8.examples:
Then: Scattered believers, fleeing for their lives, who could not stop preaching. A deacon pulled off a city-wide revival and then redirected to one man on a road. An African official who came to Jerusalem seeking God and left having found him in the most unexpected way. The gospel in chapter 8 is gloriously uncontrollable.

Now: The church tends to think of mission in terms of programs and strategies. Acts 8 shows God doing his best work through disruption — persecution that scatters, divine direction that redirects, a Scripture passage that raises exactly the right question. The lesson is not that we should abandon planning, but that we must hold our plans loosely enough that we can hear “go over and join this chariot” when the Spirit speaks it.

9.title: The Road to Damascus
9.text: <sup>1</sup>But Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest <sup>2</sup>and asked him for letters to the synagogues at Damascus, so that if he found any belonging to the Way, men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem. <sup>3</sup>Now as he went on his way, he approached Damascus, and suddenly a light from heaven shone around him. <sup>4</sup>And falling to the ground, he heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” <sup>5</sup>And he said, “Who are you, Lord?” And he said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. <sup>6</sup>But rise and enter the city, and you will be told what you are to do.” <sup>7</sup>The men who were traveling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one. <sup>8</sup>Saul rose from the ground, and although his eyes were opened, he saw nothing. So they led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus. <sup>9</sup>And for three days he was without sight, and neither ate nor drank. <sup>10</sup>Now there was a disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, “Ananias.” And he said, “Here I am, Lord.” <sup>11</sup>And the Lord said to him, “Rise and go to the street called Straight, and at the house of Judas look for a man of Tarsus named Saul, for behold, he is praying, <sup>12</sup>and he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hands on him so that he might regain his sight.” <sup>13</sup>But Ananias answered, “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem. <sup>14</sup>And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name.” <sup>15</sup>But the Lord said to him, “Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel. <sup>16</sup>For I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name.” <sup>17</sup>So Ananias departed and entered the house. And laying his hands on him he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus who appeared to you on the road by which you came has sent me so that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” <sup>18</sup>And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he regained his sight. Then he rose and was baptized; <sup>19</sup>and taking food, he was strengthened. For some days he was with the disciples at Damascus. <sup>20</sup>And immediately he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues, saying, “He is the Son of God.” <sup>21</sup>And all who heard him were amazed and said, “Is not this the man who made havoc in Jerusalem of those who called upon this name? And has he not come here for this purpose, to bring them bound before the chief priests?” <sup>22</sup>But Saul increased all the more in strength, and confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus by proving that Jesus was the Christ. <sup>23</sup>When many days had passed, the Jews plotted to kill him, <sup>24</sup>but their plot became known to Saul. They were watching the gates day and night in order to kill him, <sup>25</sup>but his disciples took him by night and let him down through an opening in the wall, lowering him in a basket. <sup>26</sup>And when he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join the disciples. And they were all afraid of him, for they did not believe that he was a disciple. <sup>27</sup>But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles and declared to them how on the road he had seen the Lord, who spoke to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus. <sup>28</sup>So he went in and out among them at Jerusalem, preaching boldly in the name of the Lord. <sup>29</sup>And he spoke and disputed against the Hellenists. But they were seeking to kill him. <sup>30</sup>And when the brothers learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus. <sup>31</sup>So the church throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace and was being built up. And walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it multiplied. <sup>32</sup>Now as Peter went here and there among them all, he came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda. <sup>33</sup>There he found a man named Aeneas, bedridden for eight years, who was paralyzed. <sup>34</sup>And Peter said to him, “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; rise and make your bed.” And immediately he rose. <sup>35</sup>And all the residents of Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord. <sup>36</sup>Now there was in Joppa a disciple named Tabitha, which, translated, means Dorcas. She was full of good works and acts of charity. <sup>37</sup>In those days she became ill and died, and when they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room. <sup>38</sup>Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, urging him, “Please come to us without delay.” <sup>39</sup>So Peter rose and went with them. And when he arrived, they took him to the upper room. All the widows stood beside him weeping and showing tunics and other garments that Dorcas made while she was with them. <sup>40</sup>But Peter put them all outside, and knelt down and prayed; and turning to the body he said, “Tabitha, arise.” And she opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up. <sup>41</sup>And he gave her his hand and raised her up. Then, calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive. <sup>42</sup>And it became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. <sup>43</sup>And he stayed in Joppa for many days with one Simon, a tanner.
9.overview:
No conversion in history has been more dramatic, more sovereign, or more consequential. Saul of Tarsus is not seeking God. He is hunting God’s people — breathing threats and murder, armed with letters of arrest, heading to Damascus to drag more believers to prison. And the risen Christ stops him on the road. A light from heaven. A voice. “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” Not them — me. To touch the church is to touch Christ. The head and the body are one.

What happens to Saul on the Damascus road is not the result of prior openness, spiritual preparation, or moral readiness. It is pure, sovereign, unilateral grace — the kind that stops a man in the middle of his worst act and makes him a new creature. Saul does not choose Christ; Christ chooses Saul. “He is a chosen instrument of mine.” The word is skeuos eklogēs — vessel of election — and it is the language of sovereign divine appointment. The most violent persecutor of the church becomes its most prolific apostle. Only God could write that story.

And then there is Ananias — a small man in a small house on a street called Straight, who hears the Lord say “go to Saul of Tarsus” and who goes, against every instinct of self-preservation, and calls the man who had come to arrest him “Brother Saul.” Two words that cost everything and mean everything. Grace in the mouth of a frightened disciple.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Outside the resurrection itself there is no reversal in the New Testament like this one. The man who approved Stephen's execution and went through Jerusalem house after house dragging believers out of their kitchens is stopped on a road by the risen Christ, blinded, and led into Damascus by the hand like a child. Luke tells the story three times in this book — here, before a Jerusalem crowd in chapter 22, and before King Agrippa in chapter 26 — because everything in the second half of Acts runs out of it.

The exchange on the road is four sentences long and it rearranges the universe. Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? Saul had never met Jesus of Nazareth and had never laid a finger on him; he had arrested people in Jerusalem. And the voice says me. Then the answer to the only question he can think of: I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting — which means the man he was certain was dead is alive, and everything he had built his life on is now standing on its head.

The section does not stop at the road, and the second half is often forgotten. Saul is baptised by an ordinary disciple who had every reason to refuse and who opened his mouth with the word brother. He preaches in the Damascus synagogues he had come to raid. He is hunted, and leaves the city over a wall in a basket. He arrives in Jerusalem and the church will not have him — every Christian in the city is frightened of him and nobody believes he is a disciple — until Barnabas takes him by the arm and walks him in. Then a plot, and the brothers put him on a boat home to Tarsus, where he disappears from the narrative for the best part of a decade.

And Luke closes with a sentence that belongs to the whole passage: the church throughout Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace and was built up and multiplied. The man whose arrival had scattered it is gone, and the persecution goes with him.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sovereignty of Grace in Conversion

Saul's conversion is the purest demonstration in the New Testament of grace that does not wait to be wanted. He was not seeking Christ; he was hunting Christians. He was not wavering, not quietly troubled, not secretly drawn — he was riding to Damascus with an arrest warrant in his bag. Nothing in the account suggests any prior movement toward faith, and Paul himself, looking back, never once describes his conversion as a search that ended. He describes it as being laid hold of. Reformed theology has read it as the pattern rather than the exception: everybody who comes to Christ was, in one degree or another, going the other way when God stopped them, and the difference between Saul and a quieter case is a matter of speed and lighting rather than of mechanism. It is also the passage that makes despair about anybody unreasonable. The church's most violent enemy was three days from writing a third of its Scriptures, and not one person in Jerusalem could have guessed it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Ananias was told to go to the man who had done much evil to the saints in Jerusalem and who was carrying a warrant that covered Ananias himself. He said what he thought about it, out loud, to God — and then he went, and the first word out of his mouth was brother. Now: The church's most persuasive argument has always been the existence of people in it who ought, by every reasonable calculation, to be enemies. That is not an argument anybody constructs. It is one a congregation either exhibits or does not.

verseByVerse.quote: But Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest and asked him for letters to the synagogues at Damascus, so that if he found any belonging to the Way, men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Still breathing threats and murder. Luke's participle makes it a condition rather than an episode — it is what Saul respires, in and out, the atmosphere he lives in. And the second noun is not rhetorical. Murder means murder, and Paul confirms it in his own words years later: when believers were put to death, he says, he cast his vote against them. Stephen was not the only one.

Then the machinery, and it repays attention because it tells you what kind of man this was. He does not gather a mob. He went to the high priest and asked him for letters. Damascus lies about a hundred and thirty-five miles from Jerusalem, six days on foot, and it is outside Judea altogether — a different province under a different administration. The high priest's authority reached synagogues in the Diaspora by long-standing arrangement, and Rome had historically granted the Jewish authorities powers of extradition over their own people. So what Saul is carrying is not a licence to riot. It is paperwork, obtained through proper channels, enforceable in a foreign city.

That is worth sitting with, because it is easy to picture the persecutor as a man out of control. He was nothing of the sort. He was organised, credentialled, funded and legal, and he believed with his whole heart that he was doing God's work — which he says himself, later, without excusing it: he was zealous for God, and he was wrong.

Why Damascus? Because there was a large and ancient Jewish community there, and because the believers scattered by the persecution of chapter 8 had gone somewhere. Saul is not opening a new front. He is pursuing refugees he had himself created, a week's journey from home, to bring them back in chains.

Any belonging to the Way. This is the earliest name the Christians had for themselves — Luke uses it half a dozen times in this book — and it is worth pausing on. They did not call themselves a school, a party, a sect or a synagogue. They called themselves a road. Whether the name came from the Lord's own I am the way, or from the prophet's cry to prepare the way of the LORD, or from both, the effect is the same: it is a word about travelling, and it describes a manner of life rather than a set of opinions. It is also, as it happens, precisely the wrong kind of thing to try to stamp out. You can shut a building. A road runs.

And once more Luke writes men or women. It is the third time he has said it about Saul in two chapters, and he will not let the reader make this abstract. Whatever else was in those letters, they authorised the arrest of somebody's mother.

That is the last sentence of the paragraph. There is a comma after it in the Greek and then the road, and God interrupts a man in the middle of a journey he had every intention of completing.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as he went on his way, he approached Damascus, and suddenly a light from heaven flashed around him. And falling to the ground, he heard a voice saying to him, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Suddenly a light from heaven flashed around him. The verb is built on the word for lightning: it did not glow, it flashed, and it enveloped him. When Paul describes it to King Agrippa he adds two details that fix the scene — it happened at midday, and the light was brighter than the sun. This is a Syrian noon, the harshest light in the year, and something outshone it.

Since Luke tells this story three times in one book, it is worth laying the three accounts beside each other here, because the differences are the sort that get produced as evidence of invention and they repay an honest look.

The first is in this verse. Here the men with him stood speechless (v. 7); before Agrippa, Paul says we had all fallen to the ground (26:14). Standing in one, prone in the other. The resolution is not clever and does not need to be: everyone went down, and then the escort got up while Saul stayed where he was. Luke's summary at verse 7 picks them up after they had risen — men on their feet, staring, unable to speak, waiting for the man they were escorting to move. Anybody who has described the same accident twice will recognise the phenomenon.

The second is larger. In this chapter Saul is told simply to go into the city, where he will be told what to do — and the commission arrives later through Ananias. Before Agrippa, the commission is spoken by Christ on the road itself, at length, with the Gentiles named. But notice where Paul is standing when he tells it that way. He is in the dock in front of a king, with limited time and a Roman governor listening, and a Jewish disciple's testimonial from a back street in Damascus is worth nothing to that audience and would only lengthen the story. He compresses, folding what he was told into the encounter that authorised it — which is what any man does when summarising to a king. And in the middle account, before a Jerusalem crowd, Ananias is not merely present but is the point: Paul takes trouble there to describe him as a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews living in Damascus, which is exactly the credential that mattered to that audience and worthless to Agrippa.

The three tellings are the same event addressed to three rooms. That is not a mark of fabrication. It is how a truthful man talks.

Then the voice, and the first word is the man's name, said twice. Scripture does that sparingly and always at a hinge: Abraham with the knife raised, Moses at the bush, Samuel in the dark, Martha at the door, Simon on the last night. It is the address of somebody who knows the person and is about to change his life. And Paul notes, when he tells it later, that it came in the Hebrew language — so the risen and glorified Christ speaks to him in his mother tongue and uses his Hebrew name, not the Greek one the world would come to know him by.

And then the question, which is one of the most consequential sentences in the Bible. Why are you persecuting me?

Saul had never met Jesus of Nazareth. He had never struck him, tried him or voted against him; as far as we know he was not in Jerusalem during the trial. What he had done was drag Christians out of houses. And the voice from the light does not say why are you persecuting my people, or my church, or those who follow me. It says me.

Everything Paul later wrote about the church being the body of Christ is already lying in that pronoun, and he heard it before he had a theology to put it in. It cuts two ways and both of them matter. It means that the way a Christian treats another Christian is not a matter of church politics; Christ files it under his own name. And it means that whatever has been done to a believer — the exclusion, the cruelty, the years of it, the thing nobody else noticed — has not gone unrecorded, because it was not finally done to him at all. The Lord takes it personally, and he says so in the first sentence he ever speaks to Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Who are you, Lord?" And he said, "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. But rise and enter the city, and you will be told what you are to do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who are you, Lord? He says Lord before he has any idea who is speaking. The word could mean no more than sir, and a man flat on a road addressing a voice out of a light might reasonably reach for it — but the fall has already done its work, and by the end of the sentence it will mean everything it can mean.

Then five words which cost Saul everything he had: I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.

Take the two halves separately, because each is a demolition. I am Jesus — so the body is not in the tomb, the disciples were not lying, the movement is not a fraud, and everything Saul has done for the last year has been done to the Messiah of Israel. Whom you are persecuting — present tense, still going on, as of this morning. He is not being told about a mistake he once made. He is being interrupted in the middle of it, with the warrants still in his luggage.

And then, instead of a sentence, an instruction: rise and enter the city, and you will be told what you are to do. Not a word of rebuke, no accounting demanded, nothing about Stephen. He is told to get up and go and wait for instructions, like a man who has just been taken into someone's service. Which is exactly what has happened.

A note for anyone reading alongside an older Bible. The King James adds a sentence here that modern versions do not print: it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks, along with Saul's trembling question about what the Lord would have him do. The words are genuine — Jesus really did say them, and Luke records them when Paul retells the scene before Agrippa (26:14) — but they are not in the Greek manuscripts at this point. A copyist, knowing the fuller version from chapter 26, filled them in here. So nothing has been lost from Scripture; the saying has simply been returned to the place where Luke actually put it. The image itself is worth keeping: a goad was the farmer's spiked stick, and an ox that kicked back at it only drove the point deeper. Saul had been kicking for a while.

verseByVerse.quote: The men who were traveling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one. Saul rose from the ground, and although his eyes were opened, he saw nothing. So they led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the picture, and Luke draws it without a word of comment. A party of armed men on the Damascus road, standing in the dust with nothing to say, and their leader on the ground unable to see. They came out of Jerusalem as an escort. They go into the city leading a blind man by the hand.

Although his eyes were opened, he saw nothing. Luke chooses to put it that way round, and the irony is not lost on Paul either, who spent the rest of his life writing about veils and blindness and light shining into hearts. Here was a man who had never in his life been in any doubt about what he was looking at. He knew the law, he knew the tradition, he knew exactly who was in the right, and he could have set out his reasoning at any length required. His eyes are open and there is nothing in them.

And he is led by the hand — which is the detail to keep. The last time we saw Saul he was dragging people through doorways. He enters Damascus in the position of the people he came to arrest: helpless, dependent, going wherever somebody else takes him.

The first half of verse 7 has been a favourite of sceptics for a long time, and it deserves a straight answer. Luke says here that the men were hearing the voice but seeing no one. When Paul himself tells the story later in this same book, he says that those with him saw the light but did not hear the voice of the one speaking (22:9). Same author, same book, same event, and on the face of it a flat contradiction — which is why it turns up in every list of Bible errors ever compiled.

It dissolves in the Greek, and not by special pleading. The verb for hearing takes its object in different cases with different senses: with one case it means to hear a sound, with the other to hear with understanding — much as we distinguish hearing someone from catching what they said. Luke uses the first construction here and the second at 22:9. So the two sentences are saying precisely what any of us would say about the same afternoon: the men heard a noise but could not make out the words. Modern translations show this openly — the ESV renders 22:9 did not understand the voice — and the difficulty simply disappears.

The seeing works the same way. They saw the light, which is why they were struck speechless; they did not see the person who spoke, which is why Luke says they saw no one. And notice the pastoral point sitting underneath the grammar. The men beside him experienced the identical event — the same blaze, the same sound, the same road — and went away with nothing but a story about strange weather. Saul went away with a Lord. Proximity to revelation is not the same as receiving it, and the difference between the two was not in the light but in whom it was for.

verseByVerse.quote: And for three days he was without sight, and neither ate nor drank.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three days of nothing. No sight, no food, and — the detail people skim — no water. Three days without drinking is not a devotional exercise; in that climate it is the edge of what a body will take. This is not a man keeping a fast. It is a man who has stopped functioning.

Try to picture the room. He is in a strange city, in a borrowed house on a street called Straight, in the dark, with an escort outside who do not know what to do with him and a set of arrest warrants in a bag that nobody is going to use. Every certainty he possessed on the morning he left Jerusalem is gone — not weakened, gone — and the one thing he now knows for certain is that the people he was travelling to imprison were right about everything, and that he has spent his best years and his considerable gifts hunting the Messiah of Israel.

Verse 11 tells us what he was doing with the time. He was praying. Not, one imagines, in the confident, well-formed manner of a Pharisee who had prayed every day of his life. Something else, in a room, with no idea what to say.

The three days are worth noticing for the shape of them. He goes into darkness, everything he was dies there, and on the third day a man comes and he is raised up and washed. Paul would spend the rest of his life writing about being buried with Christ and raised with him, and about the old self having been crucified, and about a new creation in which the old has gone. He had lived it before he wrote a word of it, on the floor of somebody's guest room.

There is something here for anyone in the middle of a collapse of certainty — the person whose faith has come apart in his hands, or who has discovered that a thing he built a life on was not true, or who has been shown something about himself he cannot unsee. Saul's three days were not the end of him and did not feel like anything else at the time. It is worth knowing that Scripture's most spectacular conversion has a dark room in the middle of it, and that nobody in the house had the least idea what was going on.

One guard, because this sort of passage attracts imitators. Luke is not recommending three-day fasts, and there is no suggestion that Saul's abstinence achieved anything. The man was in shock. What the verse describes is a condition, not a technique.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, "Ananias." And he said, "Here I am, Lord." And the Lord said to him, "Rise and go to the street called Straight, and at the house of Judas look for a man of Tarsus named Saul, for behold, he is praying,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke introduces the most important minor character in the New Testament with five words: a disciple at Damascus named Ananias. No office. No title. He is not an apostle, not one of the seven, not an elder, not a prophet. He is a Christian who lives in the city, and God has decided to hand him the most consequential errand of the first century.

Paul fills in what Luke leaves out, when he tells the story in Jerusalem years later: Ananias was a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there. That is a description of a man with something to lose. He had a standing in the Jewish community of Damascus, and the errand he is about to be given would end it.

Here I am, Lord. Two words in Greek, and it is the answer Abraham gave on the mountain, and Jacob, and Moses at the bush, and Samuel in the dark, and Isaiah in the temple. It is not a promise to do the thing; Ananias has not been told what the thing is, and he will argue about it in three verses. It is simply the reply of a man who is available before he knows the assignment, which is a different and rarer disposition than willingness after the details are in.

Then the directions, and their ordinariness is the point. The street called Straight. It was a real road and it is still traceable — the long colonnaded thoroughfare that ran east and west through Roman Damascus, the sort of street every city had and everybody could find. The house of Judas. A man of Tarsus named Saul. A street, a householder, a name and a home town. God's guidance in this passage has an address on it.

And then the one piece of information the Lord offers about the man Ananias is being sent to: behold, he is praying.

It is worth noticing what is not said. Not he is safe now. Not he has repented and you will find him much changed. Not I have dealt with him. The single credential given for the most dangerous man in the province is that he is at that moment praying — which, from anybody else, would be no proof of anything at all. From the Lord who is speaking, it is the whole case.

verseByVerse.quote: and he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hands on him so that he might regain his sight."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has been at both ends of this the whole time.

While Ananias is being given a street name in one part of Damascus, Saul has already been shown a picture of a man called Ananias coming through a door and putting his hands on him. Neither of them arranged it. Neither of them knew the other existed a week ago. And when Ananias finally walks into that room, the blind man on the other side of it will have been expecting him by name.

That is a considerable kindness to both parties, and it is worth seeing which way it runs. For Saul, three days into the dark with nothing to hold, it is the first concrete thing he has been given: somebody is coming, and here is his name. For Ananias, it means he is not walking in cold. The man he is dreading has been told he is on his way and what he is coming to do.

There is an application here for the conversation a Christian is quietly dreading — the apology owed, the subject that has to be raised, the person who needs to be spoken to and will not welcome it. It is very easy to assume one is walking in entirely unprepared, into a room where nothing has been done. Sometimes a great deal has been done, at the other end, by somebody with access to both sides of the door.

One guard, because a promise can be manufactured out of this that Scripture does not make. It is not a guarantee that every difficult conversation has been divinely prepared, or that obedience will always turn out to be safer than it looked. Ananias's errand was genuinely dangerous and he was right to say so. What the verse establishes is narrower: that the God who sends people is already at work on the far side, and that the messenger is very rarely the first one there.

And notice how the Lord deploys it. This verse is not narration addressed to the reader; it is still part of what he is saying to Ananias, and it is the last thing he says before Ananias objects. In other words, it is offered as a reason. Go — and by the way, he is expecting you, and he already knows your name. The Lord is not simply issuing an order. He is reasoning with a frightened man, and the argument he uses is that the door has already been opened from the inside.

verseByVerse.quote: But Ananias answered, "Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem. And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ananias argues with God, and God does not rebuke him for it. That is the first thing to notice, and Luke reports the exchange without a syllable of disapproval.

Lord, I have heard from many about this man. He is not being difficult. He is stating the case as any sane member of that congregation would state it. Reports have been coming up the road from Jerusalem for months: houses entered, people taken, a young man from Tarsus at the centre of it. Ananias almost certainly knew names. Some of the refugees who had run to Damascus were sitting in his own meetings, and they had told him what they had seen.

And the second half of the objection is the sharper one. He has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name. All. Ananias is describing a warrant that has his own name inside it. He is not being asked to visit a difficult man; he is being asked to walk into a house and identify himself, by name and as a Christian, to the officer sent to arrest him.

Scripture has a small tradition of people who answered God back at the moment of calling. Moses produced five separate objections at the bush and God dealt with each. Gideon asked for the fleece twice. Jeremiah said he was too young. What distinguishes Ananias from Jonah is not that he kept his doubts to himself — he did not — but that he raised them in God's presence and then did what he was told. Jonah raised nothing and went to the harbour.

That is worth taking, because a certain kind of piety teaches people to suppress the objection and calls the suppression faith. It is not faith; it is usually fear wearing better clothes, and it tends to come out sideways later. Ananias tells God exactly what he thinks of the assignment, in plain words, with the reasons — and God answers him with an explanation rather than a reprimand. There is room in that conversation for a man to say what he actually thinks.

One phrase in the objection is worth a moment on its own: your saints. It is the first time in Acts that Christians are called this, and it means simply the holy ones, the people set apart for God. Ananias uses it of the men and women Saul had been hunting. Within a few years the man he is being sent to will be using the same word in letter after letter to describe ordinary congregations of fishermen and slaves and tradespeople — and once, describing himself, will say he is the very least of them.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Lord said to him, "Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel. For I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers the objection, and the answer is not reassurance. It is information.

He is a chosen instrument of mine. The word behind instrument is the ordinary one for a container or a piece of equipment — a jar, a pot, a vessel, the sort of word that turns up in an inventory. Saul is not being described as a hero, a champion or a great man. He is a receptacle that has been picked out, and the value is entirely in what it is for and who chose it. Paul evidently never forgot the word: writing to Corinth years later about the ministry he had been given, he says we have this treasure in jars of clay, so that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us. He is using the same term about himself, and he had heard it first in a sentence he was not present for.

Then the destinations, and they are the table of contents for the rest of the book. Before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel. The Gentiles are named first, which would have been an extraordinary thing to say in the year 34; the kings are Agrippa in chapter 26 and, by the end, Caesar's household; the children of Israel are the synagogue in every city, which is where Paul begins every time.

And then the sentence which is the reason this passage cannot be preached as a success story. For I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name.

It is joined to the commission by a conjunction, not separated from it by a paragraph. The calling and the cost arrive in the same breath, spoken to a third party before the man himself has been told anything. And there is an exchange in it that is hard to miss: Saul had spent a year making people suffer on account of that name, and the first thing said about his future is how much he will suffer for it.

What that meant in practice is not left to the imagination, because Paul eventually listed it. Five times he received thirty-nine lashes from his own people; three times he was beaten with Roman rods; once he was stoned and left for dead; three times shipwrecked, and a night and a day adrift at sea. Add hunger, cold, sleeplessness, and the daily pressure of anxiety for all the churches. That is the career being announced in verse 16, and God announces it as part of the good news he is giving Ananias to persuade him to go.

A guard is needed, because this can be turned into a formula. Not every calling carries this measure of suffering, and a Christian whose life has been comparatively gentle has not been overlooked or given a second-rate commission; Scripture nowhere makes hardship the proof of authenticity, and men have done real damage by implying it. But the verse is a permanent corrective to a way of speaking about the Christian life that has become almost standard — the presentation of Christ as the route to a better, smoother, more successful version of the life one already has. The Lord's own summary of what he was calling his greatest servant to was: he will carry my name a very long way, and it will cost him everything he has.

verseByVerse.quote: So Ananias departed and entered the house. And laying his hands on him he said, "Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus who appeared to you on the road by which you came has sent me so that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit." And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he regained his sight. Then he rose and was baptized;
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Ananias departed and entered the house. Six words for the bravest thing anybody does in this chapter. He had said what he thought, been answered, and gone.

And the first word out of his mouth is brother.

Stand in the doorway and weigh that. In the room is a blind man from Tarsus who arrived in Damascus with a warrant that covers Ananias by name. Somewhere in that house is a bag containing letters from the high priest. Ananias belongs to a congregation swollen with refugees who ran from this man, and he will have heard, over and over, what happened in Jerusalem — quite possibly from people who lost somebody. He has every reason to open with a question, or a condition, or at the very least a wary silence. He opens with a family word, and he uses it before Saul has said anything at all.

What follows is careful and generous. The Lord Jesus who appeared to you on the road by which you came has sent me — Ananias tells him he knows, and specifies the road, so that Saul understands he is not being humoured. Then the two things he has come for: sight, and the Holy Spirit.

It is worth registering who is doing this. Not Peter. Not John. Not an apostle at all, and not anyone whose name occurs anywhere else in the New Testament. The man who lays hands on Paul, restores his sight, tells him he is filled with the Spirit and baptises him is a disciple in a provincial city about whom nothing else whatever is known. Paul would insist for the rest of his life that he had not received his gospel from any man — and it is perfectly consistent, because what Ananias gave him was not a gospel. It was his eyes, a welcome, and water.

Immediately something like scales fell from his eyes. The word is one used of fish-scales and of flakes of shell, and it has a clinical ring to it; the doctor writing this reaches for the nearest physical comparison and marks it as a comparison — something like. Whatever came away, Luke will not pretend to know exactly what it was.

And then, with his sight barely back: he rose and was baptised. The first thing the man does when he can see again is get into the water. There is no interval, no period of assessment, no probation while the church works out whether it can trust him. He had been in the dark for three days and the moment the light came back he went and was washed.

verseByVerse.quote: and taking food, he was strengthened. For some days he was with the disciples at Damascus. And immediately he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues, saying, "He is the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And taking food, he was strengthened. Luke has not forgotten that this man has not eaten for three days. Before the theology there is a meal, and somebody in that house made it.

Then the sentence, and the geography in it is the joke Luke has been setting up since verse 2. Saul had carried letters addressed to the synagogues at Damascus, authorising him to search them for followers of the Way. He now walks into those same synagogues, with the same letters presumably still in his luggage, and preaches the thing he came to stamp out. One imagines the faces.

And what he preaches is worth weighing, because of how soon it is. He is the Son of God. Not: this man was a prophet, or a teacher, or even the Messiah — that comes three verses later. The very first recorded sermon of the apostle Paul, preached within days of his baptism by a man who had spent his adult life defending the oneness of God against every blasphemy, is that Jesus of Nazareth is God's Son. Whatever else his conversion did, it did not leave him working his way toward that conclusion gradually. He had met the person and drawn the only possible inference on the road. (cf. Gal. 1:16; 2 Cor. 5:17)

What did Saul mean by 'Son of God'? The title gathers up two streams of Scripture into one confession. First, it is a claim to full deity. To call Jesus God's own Son, in the unique sense, is to say he shares the very nature of God — which is exactly how his hearers understood it: Jesus was charged with 'making himself equal with God' because he called God his own Father (John 5:18; 19:7). 'Son' here speaks not of a beginning or of a lesser rank but of sameness of nature and eternal relation: as an earthly son shares his father's humanity, the divine Son shares the Father's deity, eternally — of one substance with him, 'begotten, not made.' Second, 'Son of God' was a royal, messianic title: the promised king of David's line was called God's son (2 Sam. 7:14; Ps. 2:7), so to say 'Jesus is the Son of God' is also to say he is the Christ, the anointed King — which is just where Saul's preaching goes next, 'proving that Jesus was the Christ' (v. 22). In Christ the two meet: the true Davidic King who is himself truly God.

One guard against misunderstanding. Scripture calls angels and even believers 'sons of God' (Job 1:6; John 1:12) — but those are sons by creation or by adopting grace. Jesus is the Son, the 'only-begotten' (monogenēs, John 3:16), Son by eternal right and by nature, not made a son and not adopted. We become sons only through him. So this short sentence is the gospel in miniature: the man Jesus, crucified and risen, is God the Son and the royal Messiah, worthy of all trust, worship, and obedience — and it is the very confession that saves, 'that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name' (John 20:31; cf. 1 John 4:15). And here is the wonder of the moment: the man who had set out to destroy everyone who made this claim is now the first in Damascus to make it.

verseByVerse.quote: And all who heard him were amazed and said, "Is not this the man who made havoc in Jerusalem of those who called upon this name? And has he not come here for this purpose, to bring them bound before the chief priests?" But Saul increased all the more in strength, and confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus by proving that Jesus was the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The synagogue's reaction is one of the more understandable in Scripture. They know exactly who this is and exactly what he came for, because the letters had been announced in advance and arrangements had presumably been made. And here he is, in the seat, saying the opposite of what he was sent to say.

The word they use of his career is a violent one: made havoc, a term used of sacking a city or laying waste to a country. It is not their invention either — Paul takes the same word and uses it of himself, twice, when he writes to the Galatians. He never softened the vocabulary. Whatever else he became, he did not become a man who described his past in careful language.

Then two verbs describing what he did next, and both are worth having.

Saul increased all the more in strength — the verb is the one Paul later uses of being strengthened by Christ, the word behind I can do all things through him who strengthens me. He is not describing natural confidence returning. Something was being supplied.

And proving that Jesus was the Christ. The Greek word means to bring things together, to knit or join them side by side — the image is of laying two things next to each other until the fit is obvious. That is precisely what Paul does in every letter and every sermon recorded of him: this text, and that event, laid alongside one another. The method of a lifetime was operating within a fortnight of his conversion, because the raw material — a first-class rabbinic training in the Scriptures — had been in place for twenty years and was now pointing the other way.

There is a caution here that the passage itself supplies if one keeps reading. Saul is formidable immediately, and he is also, within a few years, sent quietly home to Tarsus and not heard of again for the best part of a decade. The New Testament elsewhere warns against putting a recent convert into public leadership, lest he become puffed up — and the most gifted convert in the history of the church spent something like ten years in obscurity before anybody came to fetch him. Ability arrived at once. Deployment did not, and the interval was not an accident.

verseByVerse.quote: When many days had passed, the Jews plotted to kill him, but their plot became known to Saul. They were watching the gates day and night in order to kill him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When many days had passed. Luke's phrase is doing a great deal of quiet work: laid against Paul's own account, those days include a departure into Arabia and a return to Damascus, and the whole stretch comes to about three years. Luke is not concealing it; he is writing the story of a movement and moving at the movement's pace, and the timing is set out where it belongs at verses 26 and 27.

Then the plot, and there is a second witness to it. Paul describes the same episode in a letter and adds a detail Luke omits: the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city in order to seize him. Aretas was the Nabataean king whose territory ran south and east of Damascus, and his official was involved in the watch on the gates. So this was not merely a synagogue quarrel that turned nasty. Within three years of his conversion, Saul's preaching had become a matter for the civil authority of a neighbouring kingdom.

The two accounts fit together without strain, and the shape is familiar from this whole book: the complaint comes from one quarter and the muscle from another. It happened to Jesus in front of Pilate, to Paul again at Philippi and Thessalonica and Corinth. Religious objection supplies the charge; the state supplies the soldiers.

They were watching the gates day and night in order to kill him. Damascus was a walled city with a limited number of gates, and a watch on all of them, around the clock, is not a gesture. Somebody was paying for it.

And now set this beside chapter 8, three years earlier, and notice what has happened to the man. There, he was the one going house after house. There, he was the one with the authority, the letters and the men. Here he is the one being hunted through a city, unable to use the gates, dependent on a handful of frightened disciples to get him out alive. The transaction was quick and it was complete, and it is the pattern of everything that follows: for the next thirty years Paul is on the receiving end of precisely what he used to administer.

verseByVerse.quote: but his disciples took him by night and let him down through an opening in the wall, lowering him in a basket.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The most famous escape in the New Testament, and it is entirely undignified.

Picture the mechanics. The house is built into the city wall, which was ordinary enough in ancient cities; there is an opening — a window, probably. The basket is a large woven hamper, the kind used for carrying produce, big enough to hold a man if he draws his knees up. It is dark. A rope is tied on. And the future apostle to the Gentiles, the man who will stand in front of kings, is folded into a fruit basket and paid out over a wall by people who are hoping the rope holds.

He never forgot it, and what he did with the memory is the remarkable part. Years later, writing to the Corinthian church about the men who were undermining him with their credentials, he says that if he must boast he will boast of the things that show his weakness — and then he gives a list: labours, imprisonments, beatings, shipwrecks, hunger, the pressure of the churches. And the item he chooses to end on, the climax of the whole catalogue, is the basket. Of everything in a life that included visions of the third heaven, he selected as his boast the night he was lowered out of a window like a sack of figs.

That is not false modesty and it is not a joke. It is the deliberate destruction of a category. His rivals were competing on the strength of their standing; Paul answers by producing the single most humiliating moment of his career and putting it at the top of his own list of qualifications. He had understood something about how God works that they had not, and the basket was where he learned it.

One thing should be said plainly, because it releases a great many people from an unnecessary burden. Saul ran away. He did not stay and preach and take what came; he went over the wall at night and left the city. There is no hint of reproach in the text, and the Lord himself had told his disciples that when they were persecuted in one town they should flee to the next. Courage in Scripture is not the refusal to leave. Paul stood his ground on plenty of occasions and left quietly on others, and he seems to have had no rule about it beyond the work continuing.

And note who did it: his disciples. He has been a Christian for perhaps three years and there are already people in Damascus who are his. They put him in the basket, and they held the rope.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join the disciples. And they were all afraid of him, for they did not believe that he was a disciple. But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles and declared to them how on the road he had seen the Lord, who spoke to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He attempted to join the disciples. And they were all afraid of him.

It is the loneliest sentence in the chapter. The last time Saul was in Jerusalem he was emptying houses; the people now shutting their doors are the ones who got away, or whose relatives did not. Their fear is not weak faith. It is arithmetic. A man with his record turning up claiming to be one of them is exactly what an informer would do, and it would not be the first time somebody had tried it. Luke says they did not believe that he was a disciple, which is put charitably. They thought he was lying.

So here is Saul, three years after the road, no longer welcome in the synagogue and not admitted by the church, with a price on him in Damascus and nowhere at all to stand.

And then one man crosses the room. Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles. The verb means he took hold of him — he laid hands on the man everybody else was backing away from, and walked him in, and vouched for him out loud. It is the second time Luke has shown us this man and the second time he is doing the same thing: the first was a field sold and the money laid down without a speech, and this is a reputation put at risk on behalf of somebody with none. If Barnabas was wrong, he had just introduced an assassin to the entire leadership of the church.

It is worth saying plainly what the New Testament would look like without this paragraph. Nobody else moved. There is no indication that the apostles sent for Saul, or that the church debated it and came round. One man with no office beyond a nickname decided to believe a story that everybody else found incredible, and the entire Gentile mission came through that door.

Set this beside Paul's own account of the same visit and a question surfaces. Luke says Barnabas brought him to the apostles. Paul says that when he finally went up to Jerusalem he saw Cephas, and stayed fifteen days, and saw none of the other apostles except James the Lord's brother (Gal. 1:18-19). Plural in one, and pointedly not plural in the other.

They fit without strain once you see what each writer is doing. Luke is describing Saul's reception — that the church's leadership received him, which is the whole point of the paragraph — and uses the collective term for that body, as we might say a man was taken to meet the board when in fact two directors were in the office that week. Paul is under oath, so to speak: he is arguing to the Galatians that he did not get his gospel secondhand from Jerusalem, so he counts heads with deliberate precision and keeps the number as small as honesty allows. His case depends on it having been a short and limited visit; Luke's case depends on it having happened at all. And notice that Paul's two names are exactly the two who mattered for the introduction — Peter, the leading apostle, and James, the head of the Jerusalem church. Barnabas got him in front of the men whose word would settle it.

The timing fits the same way. Read alone, Luke's account gives the impression of a swift sequence, and he does not pause to say that three years in Arabia and Damascus lie between the road and this doorway (Gal. 1:17-18; and see v. 30). That is not concealment. Luke is writing the story of a movement and moves at the pace of the movement; Paul is writing his own defence and needs the calendar. Neither of them is telling you something the other denies.

verseByVerse.quote: So he went in and out among them at Jerusalem, preaching boldly in the name of the Lord. And he spoke and disputed against the Hellenists. But they were seeking to kill him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So he went in and out among them at Jerusalem, preaching boldly in the name of the Lord. The phrase in and out is an Old Testament way of describing somebody's ordinary comings and goings — it means he was simply part of the household now, moving about the city with them, no longer at the door.

Then Luke names the people he argued with, and the choice ought to stop a reader. He spoke and disputed against the Hellenists — the Greek-speaking Jews of the Jerusalem synagogues. That is the same circle Stephen had argued with in chapter 6, in front of whom Stephen could not be withstood, and whose response was to plant false witnesses and have him killed. Saul had been at that killing, holding the coats and approving.
