So he has walked straight back to the room where it happened and taken up the argument that got Stephen stoned, on Stephen's side, against Stephen's opponents. Luke does not comment. He simply records that they were seeking to kill him too, which by now the reader could have predicted.

A word on who 'the Hellenists' were (their fuller profile is at 6:1 and 6:9): the term (Hellēnistai) means Greek-speaking Jews — men of the diaspora, raised in the Greek language and culture, many with synagogues of their own in Jerusalem (such as the Synagogue of the Freedmen, 6:9). The word names a person's language and culture, not his faith: in 6:1 it labels Greek-speaking Jewish believers, whereas here — as with Stephen's opponents — it means unbelieving Greek-speaking Jews. And there is a sharp irony in Saul disputing with them: a man of Tarsus in Cilicia (6:9), he was himself a Hellenist, very likely once standing with this same circle against Stephen — and now he turns to plead the name of Jesus among his own former camp, and meets the very answer Stephen met.

And the last clause deserves counting. They were seeking to kill him. That is the second organised attempt on Saul's life in this one chapter — the Damascus gates in verse 24, and now Jerusalem — and he has been a Christian for about three years. He had been warned. What was said to Ananias about him was not that he would be protected but that he would be shown how much he must suffer for the name, and the instalments have started arriving before he has preached outside two cities.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the brothers learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus. The church takes charge of him and removes him — down to the coast, onto a boat, and home. It is worth noticing that the man who had just been prepared to argue himself to death in Jerusalem does not appear to have resisted. He went where the brothers put him.

And then the narrative simply stops carrying him. Saul does not appear again until chapter 11, when Barnabas travels to Tarsus to look for him and brings him to Antioch — and depending on how the years are counted, the gap is something in the region of eight to ten. Luke covers a decade of the most important life in the early church with half a sentence.

What was he doing? Not nothing. Paul says in his own account that he went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia, and that the churches of Judea kept hearing that the man who used to persecute them was now preaching the faith he had tried to destroy. Several of the beatings in his later catalogue have to fall somewhere, and this is the most likely stretch of road for them; so does the vision he describes as having happened fourteen years before he wrote about it. He was working. Nobody was writing it down.

Do the arithmetic on the man. He is converted at perhaps thirty. He goes home at about thirty-five, at the height of his powers, the most formidable mind in the movement, freshly commissioned by the risen Christ himself to carry the name to the Gentiles — and he spends his mid-thirties to his mid-forties in his home town, in a province nobody was watching, doing work that has left no record beyond one sentence in somebody else's letter.

That is worth sitting with by anybody whose most laborious years have produced nothing anybody else can see. It is not that the decade was a waiting room; there is no suggestion Paul spent it marking time until the real thing began. He was preaching, and the churches in Judea heard about it, and it counted. It is simply that the part of a life which turns out to matter most is very often the part nobody records — and that if Barnabas had not remembered where he lived, the whole of it would have been all we ever had of Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: So the church throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace and was being built up. And walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it multiplied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of Luke's hinge sentences, closing a section and opening the next — and there is a quiet irony in its placing. The church throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace. It gets its peace in the paragraph immediately after the church's chief persecutor has been converted and shipped home. The man whose arrival scattered it is gone, and the persecution he was driving has gone with him.

Note the geography as well, because Luke is quietly marking a target hit. Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria — that is the second and third stage of the commission given in the first chapter of this book, and it has now happened, largely by accident, through a persecution nobody wanted. Only the end of the earth is outstanding, and the man who will take it there has just gone home to Tarsus to wait.

And then the two phrases in which Luke chooses to describe a healthy church. Not its numbers, not its organisation, not its preaching: walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit. It is an unexpected pairing, and it is the whole character of the thing in five words.

On 'walking in the fear of the Lord,' see the fuller treatment at 5:11 — the reverent awe that draws near to God in love while never trifling with his holiness (the man at the hearth, who loves the fire and pulls his chair close, yet would never put his hand in it). Here it is worth dwelling on its companion phrase, 'the comfort of the Holy Spirit.' The word 'comfort' (paraklēsis) is far richer than our modern notion of soothing ease. It belongs to the same family as paraklētos — the name Jesus gave the Spirit, the 'Helper' or 'Comforter' he promised: 'I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever' (John 14:16). The root means to be 'called alongside' to give aid, and it sounds three notes at once: to console the troubled, to encourage the faint-hearted, and — as the old word 'comfort' (from the Latin for 'with strength') tells us — to make strong. So 'the comfort of the Holy Spirit' is no cosy ease; it is the personal presence of God's own Spirit coming alongside his people to console them in trouble, embolden them to witness, and strengthen them to stand and grow.

And mark the lovely pairing Luke sets down: fear and comfort, side by side — trembling reverence before the holy God, and the strong consolation of his Spirit. They are not rivals but partners; the same church that fears God is upheld by his Helper — and out of the two together it 'multiplied.'

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–43 — Peter's Ministry in Lydda and Joppa
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke leaves Saul in Tarsus and picks up Peter, and what follows is not an interlude. It is the approach road to chapter 10, and Luke has laid it out with the destination already in mind.

Peter is on a circuit through the coastal plain — territory he did not evangelise. The congregations he visits at Lydda and Joppa were planted by the refugees of chapter 8 and by Philip working his way up the coast, and he is going round churches that exist because of a persecution. At Lydda he finds Aeneas, eight years on a mat, and tells him that Jesus Christ heals him and to put his bedding away. At Joppa a woman called Tabitha dies, and the widows she had clothed send urgently for Peter without being able to say what they are asking for; and Peter puts the mourners out of the room, kneels down, and speaks two words in Aramaic that are one letter away from the two his Lord had spoken over Jairus's daughter.

Both miracles are performed in a name that is not Peter's, and Luke is careful to record that he says so aloud. Both produce faith across an entire district. And in both, the point being made is that the power at work in Jerusalem is at work out here too, among people the mother church neither reached nor organised.

Then the last verse, which looks like a stray domestic note and is in fact the hinge of the book. Peter stayed many days in Joppa with one Simon, a tanner. A tanner spent his working life among the skins of dead animals; the trade left a man permanently unclean under the law, and the stench put the workshop outside the town and downwind of it. The most scrupulous Jewish apostle in the church is lodging in a house that smells of death and defilement — and on its roof, in the next chapter, he will be shown a sheet full of unclean animals and told to eat. Luke put the tanner in first.
verseByVerse.theology:
Resurrection as the Power Behind Healing and New Life

The raising of Tabitha is told in a way that deliberately recalls the raising of Jairus's daughter — the mourners put outside, the taking of the hand, the command to rise, the girl presented back to her people. Peter is not improvising, and he is not exercising a power of his own; he is doing what he had watched being done, in the name of the one who did it and who was himself raised afterwards. That is why he kneels first. Reformed theology has read every healing and raising in Acts as a sign rather than a policy: a working sample of the new creation, offered in advance and on a small scale, of the day when everything sin and death have broken is put right permanently. Which is also why these events are rare rather than routine even in Acts. A sign that happened every time would not be a sign; it would be the arrangement, and the arrangement is still to come.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: When Tabitha died, the widows stood in the room holding up the coats and the dresses she had made, and Luke notes that she had made them while she was with them. That is what her ministry consisted of, and it is what the church had to show for her. Now: It is worth asking what would be held up. Not what would be said at the service, which is a different question and easier — but what could be carried into the room and shown.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as Peter went here and there among them all, he came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda. There he found a man named Aeneas, bedridden for eight years, who was paralyzed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Peter went here and there among them all. Luke's phrase describes a circuit — the apostle out of Jerusalem, going round from congregation to congregation on the coastal plain. It is the first glimpse in this book of what most Christian ministry actually consists of: travelling to see people who are already believers, in unremarkable towns, and staying a while.

And notice whose churches these are. Peter did not plant them. Lydda and Joppa lie in exactly the stretch of country the scattered believers of chapter 8 ran into, and Philip had preached his way through this plain from Azotus to Caesarea. The saints Peter is visiting are the fruit of a persecution and of refugees who could not stop talking. He arrives as a visitor to work somebody else began.

Lydda is the old town of Lod, sitting on the main road from Jerusalem down to the sea, about eleven miles from the port at Joppa. It was a market town on a trade route, which means that whatever happened there would be discussed by carriers and travellers within a day.

Then the man. Aeneas, bedridden for eight years, who was paralysed. He has a Greek name, and Luke does not say that he was a Christian; the phrase is that Peter found him, which is what you say about somebody you were not looking for.

Eight years is the detail to hold, because Luke gives numbers of this kind for a reason. It is long enough that everybody in a town that size knows the house, knows the family, and has stopped expecting anything. Whatever hope was expended in the first year had been spent by the third. Somebody had been washing him and turning him and carrying him for eight years, and had reorganised a life around it, and had long since stopped mentioning it.

One more thing about Aeneas is worth registering because of where this book is going. Luke tells us his name, his condition and the length of it, and says nothing whatever about his faith. He is not called a disciple, not said to have believed, and he is not recorded as speaking. He is simply a man Peter found. In two verses the mercy will arrive before any confession does, and within two chapters Peter will be standing in a Gentile house watching the same thing happen on a very much larger scale.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter said to him, "Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; rise and make your bed." And immediately he rose. And all the residents of Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you. Peter says the name before he says anything else, and the tense is present: not will heal, not can heal — is healing you, now, as I speak. He had learned this at a temple gate years earlier, when a crowd came running to stare at him and he had to shout them down. He does not wait to be misunderstood a second time.

Then the strangest instruction in the chapter: rise and make your bed.

The Greek can be read two ways — spread the table for yourself, or make up your bed — and the second is the likelier and much the better. Consider what it means as the first command given to a man who has not stood up since the reign of Tiberius. Not: run, or leap, or go and tell somebody. Roll up your mat. Tidy the thing away, because you will not be needing it. It is an ordinary domestic action, the sort a mother tells a child to do, and it is the exact gesture by which a man who has been ill for eight years signals that the illness is over. There is nothing to arrange around any more.

And immediately he rose.

Then Luke widens the shot: all the residents of Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord. Sharon is not a town but the whole coastal plain running north, so this is a district-wide result from one man getting off a mat in a market town on a main road. It should be read as Luke's summaries generally should — he is describing a movement across a region and not conducting a census — but the mechanism is easy enough to see. Everybody within a day's travel had known about Aeneas for eight years. He was the case that could not be argued with, and he was standing in the street.

And here a word is owed to the reader still on the mat, because a passage like this can be quietly cruel if it is left to speak alone. Aeneas was healed after eight years; a great many faithful people are not healed after eighty. Luke himself, a physician, writes in the same book about a man whose eyes never fully recovered and a colleague left behind ill at Miletus. Nothing in this chapter suggests that Aeneas had more faith than anybody else on the plain, or indeed any faith at all — he is not recorded as saying a word. What the passage establishes is not a method but an authority, and the authority has not diminished. The timing is not ours to hold, and the day is coming when the whole plain of Sharon gets up.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was in Joppa a disciple named Tabitha, which, translated, means Dorcas. She was full of good works and acts of charity. In those days she became ill and died, and when they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke does something here that he does nowhere else in the New Testament, and the Greek shows it where English cannot. He calls her a disciple — and he uses the feminine form of the word, which occurs in no other verse of the Bible. There was a perfectly serviceable masculine term he could have used, as he does of everybody else. For Tabitha he reached for a form nobody else ever needed.

Her name is given twice because she lived in a port. Tabitha in Aramaic and Dorcas in Greek both mean gazelle, and a woman with a working name in each language is a woman known in both halves of a mixed town.

Then the description, and it is worth weighing what Luke has decided to say about her. She was full of good works and acts of charity. Full of is his own particular phrase, and he has used it in this book of Stephen — full of faith and the Spirit, full of grace and power, working great wonders among the people. He now uses the same construction of a woman whose recorded output is coats. Luke evidently did not consider these to be different orders of achievement.

And then, in half a sentence: in those days she became ill and died.

No explanation is offered and none is available. She was full of good works and she got sick and died, in the middle of a chapter full of healings, in a town where an apostle was staying eleven miles away. Luke does not soften it and does not account for it. It is worth registering that the New Testament, which is often accused of promising too much, records the sudden death of its most useful woman in eight words and moves on.

The last detail is the one to notice. When they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room. In that climate burial followed death within the day; washing the body and laying it out was the first act, and interment ordinarily came next. They did the first and stopped. They put her upstairs, and they sent two men down the road. Nobody says why, and everybody knows why. They were hoping.

verseByVerse.quote: Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, urging him, "Please come to us without delay."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eleven miles between Lydda and Joppa: half a day on foot each way, which means the messengers have a day's round trip and a body upstairs in a warm climate. They send two men, which is the formal number for a delegation and also the practical number for a road, and the message they carry is four words long: please come to us without delay.

Now notice what the message does not say.

It does not say what for. It does not ask Peter to raise her; it does not mention prayer, or even name the woman. They have washed a corpse, declined to bury it, and sent for an apostle with an urgent request that says nothing about what they want him to do when he arrives. Luke, who could easily have told us what they were thinking, leaves the sentence exactly as short as they sent it.

It is one of the truest things in the chapter, because it is how people actually pray at the worst moments. Not with a clear petition properly framed, but with an urgent, half-formed sentence that cannot quite bring itself to ask for the thing it wants — partly because the thing is too large to say out loud, and partly because saying it would mean admitting how much is riding on the answer. Come quickly is very often the whole of it.

God is not put off by a badly drafted request. He had already told Moses that he heard the groaning of people who had not managed to compose a prayer at all. What these disciples had was a dead friend, a road, and a conviction they could not articulate that it was worth fetching the man who knew Jesus. That turned out to be sufficient.

And the town they are calling him to is worth a moment, because Luke's readers would have known its one famous story. Joppa is the port where a prophet, ordered to go and preach to Gentiles, went down to the harbour instead and took ship in the opposite direction. It is the place from which a man ran away from a call to the nations.

Peter is about to spend many days there. And on a roof in that same town he will be told three times to take and eat what he has spent his life refusing, and will say no three times, before getting up and going to a Gentile house. Luke does not point at the parallel and does not need to. Of all the ports on that coast, the call to the nations comes a second time at Joppa — and this time the man goes.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter rose and went with them. And when he arrived, they took him to the upper room. All the widows stood beside him weeping and showing tunics and other garments that Dorcas made while she was with them. But Peter put them all outside, and knelt down and prayed; and turning to the body he said, "Tabitha, arise." And she opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He goes, and the scene that meets him upstairs is the most affecting in the chapter. All the widows stood beside him weeping and showing tunics and other garments that Dorcas made while she was with them.

They are holding up the clothes. Not describing them — holding them out for Peter to look at, one after another, while they cry. It is the sort of detail nobody invents, and it is almost certainly what somebody in that room remembered forty years later when Luke asked.

And consider who these women were. A widow in that world without a son had no income, no legal standing to speak of, and nothing between her and destitution but charity. They are the same class of people whose neglect had caused the first crisis in the church three chapters back, when the Greek-speaking widows were being overlooked at the daily distribution. Here in a port town a woman had made it her business, personally, with her own hands, and the evidence is being waved in an upper room. Luke recorded the failure. He records the remedy too, and the remedy has a name.

Then Peter clears the room, and every move he makes is one he has seen before. He put them all outside — as his Lord had done in a house in Capernaum where a twelve-year-old girl lay dead and the mourners laughed at him. He turned to the body and spoke to it. And what he said, in Aramaic, was Tabitha koum — which is one letter away from Talitha koum, the two words Jesus had said to Jairus's daughter with Peter standing in the room.

He is doing what he watched being done. That is not imitation in any hollow sense; it is a man reaching for the only precedent he has, in the same language, in almost the same words, because he was there when it worked.

But one thing he does that his Lord did not, and it is the difference between them. He knelt down and prayed. Jesus put the mourners out and took the child's hand and told her to get up; there is no prayer in that account because there did not need to be. Peter has to ask. He kneels on the floor of a room containing a dead woman and requests something he has no power whatever to perform, and only then turns round and speaks.

It is a small distinction and the whole of apostolic ministry sits inside it. The words are nearly identical and the authority is entirely borrowed.

verseByVerse.quote: And he gave her his hand and raised her up. Then, calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He gave her his hand and raised her up. The last thing Peter does is the most ordinary — she has been dead and is now sitting on a bed, and a man puts out his hand and helps her to her feet, exactly as anyone would.

Then he opens the door. Calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive. They had been put outside a few minutes earlier in tears with an armful of clothes. Luke does not describe what happened next and there was no need.

Now the hard thing, which has to be said or the passage becomes an instrument of cruelty.

Tabitha was raised. Every other Christian who died in Joppa that year stayed dead. Luke records exactly two resurrections in the whole book of Acts and the deaths of a great many believers, including one of the Twelve, executed by Herod in chapter 12 with no rescue and no explanation — and the church was praying then too. Whatever this passage is, it is not a description of what God routinely does when his people ask, and no one should be handed it as though it were.

What it is, is a sign — which by definition is not the destination but a board at the roadside with the destination's name on it. Tabitha herself is the proof of that, because she died again. Whatever year it came, there was a second funeral in Joppa for the same woman, and that time nobody sent to Lydda. What she was given was not immortality. It was a few more years of making coats, and a demonstration, in one upper room on one afternoon, of what the God of the resurrection intends to do universally and at once.

Which is where the comfort actually lies, and it is worth reaching for rather than the shallower one. The point is not that God might do this again for the person you have lost. The point is that he has announced, in a room in a port town, in front of witnesses who told a doctor about it, what he means to do for everybody who belongs to him. The widows got their friend back for a while. They will get her back for good.

verseByVerse.quote: And it became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. And he stayed in Joppa for many days with one Simon, a tanner.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. The pattern of the whole section: the sign is not the point, the sign gets a hearing, and what people believe in is the Lord rather than the apostle.

And then the last verse of the chapter, which reads like a piece of travel administration and is nothing of the sort. He stayed in Joppa for many days with one Simon, a tanner.

Consider what a tanner was. He took the hides of dead animals and turned them into leather — scraping, soaking, and curing them in solutions that included urine and dung. The work brought him into permanent contact with carcasses, which under the law of Moses made him perpetually unclean, and the process produced a stench that carried. Later Jewish law codified what everybody already practised: a tannery had to be sited outside the town, and on the side away from the prevailing wind. A tanner's daughter was hard to marry off. A tanner's house was where the town ended.

And Peter, an observant Jew who will shortly tell the Lord to his face that he has never in his life eaten anything common or unclean, moves in and stays for weeks.

Luke has put that sentence at the end of the chapter deliberately, because of what happens at the beginning of the next. On the roof of that house, over that smell, Peter will fall into a trance and see a sheet let down full of every kind of unclean animal, and be told to kill and eat — and will refuse three times, and be told not to call common what God has made clean. The vision that opens the door to the Gentile world is given to a man who is already, without quite having noticed it, sleeping under a roof no scrupulous Pharisee would have entered.

That is generally how God moves people. Not by winning the argument first and relocating them afterwards, but by getting them into the house — and then asking the question, on the roof, in the morning, when the answer has already been half-conceded by the address on the letter.

It is worth asking whose house one would not stay in. Not in theory, where everybody is generous, but in practice — the address that would need explaining, the household whose habits or history or trade would make it awkward. Peter had not yet worked out his theology of clean and unclean; he had merely accepted an invitation from a man who worked with dead animals. The theology came later, on the roof, and it came to a man who was already in the building.

9.theology: Sovereign Grace in Conversion. The conversion of Saul is the New Testament’s clearest portrait of unconditional election and effectual calling. There is nothing in Saul that would attract God’s grace — he is actively persecuting the church, violently opposed to Christ, supremely confident in his own righteousness (Philippians 3:4–6). God chose him anyway. Not because of anything foreseen in him, but according to his own sovereign purpose — to display the fullness of his grace in the most unlikely vessel imaginable. Paul himself will later write that his conversion was designed to be a pattern, “an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life” (1 Timothy 1:16). If God can save Saul of Tarsus, he can save anyone. That is the point. The doctrine of election is not a closed door; it is the foundation of missionary confidence.
9.examples:
Then: A church that had watched Saul drag their brothers and sisters to prison now had to welcome him as a brother. Understandably, they were afraid. It took Barnabas — son of encouragement — to stand between the suspicious church and the new apostle and vouch for the reality of his conversion. The church that had prayed for boldness now needed faith to receive the answer.

Now: No one is beyond the reach of sovereign grace. The person who seems most violently opposed to the gospel may be the one God is about to apprehend. This is not a reason for naivety; it is a reason for prayer — the kind of prayer that believes God can stop any Saul on any road at any time. The church’s task is to be ready, like Ananias, to say “brother” when the moment comes.

10.title: The Gospel to the Gentiles
10.text: <sup>1</sup>At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion of what was known as the Italian Cohort, <sup>2</sup>a devout man who feared God with all his household, gave alms generously to the people, and prayed continually to God. <sup>3</sup>About the ninth hour of the day he saw clearly in a vision an angel of God come in and say to him, “Cornelius.” <sup>4</sup>And he stared at him in terror and said, “What is it, Lord?” And he said to him, “Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God. <sup>5</sup>And now send men to Joppa and bring one Simon who is called Peter. <sup>6</sup>He is lodging with one Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea.” <sup>7</sup>When the angel who spoke to him had departed, he called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among those who attended him, <sup>8</sup>and having related everything to them, he sent them to Joppa. <sup>9</sup>The next day, as they were on their journey and approaching the city, Peter went up on the housetop about the sixth hour to pray. <sup>10</sup>And he became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while they were preparing it, he fell into a trance <sup>11</sup>and saw the heavens opened and something like a great sheet descending, being let down by its four corners upon the earth. <sup>12</sup>In it were all kinds of animals and reptiles and birds of the air. <sup>13</sup>And there came a voice to him: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat.” <sup>14</sup>But Peter said, “By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean.” <sup>15</sup>And the voice came to him again a second time, “What God has made clean, do not call common.” <sup>16</sup>This happened three times, and the thing was taken up at once to heaven. <sup>17</sup>Now while Peter was inwardly perplexed as to what the vision that he had seen might mean, behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon’s house, stood at the gate <sup>18</sup>and called out to ask whether Simon who was called Peter was lodging there. <sup>19</sup>And while Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Behold, three men are looking for you. <sup>20</sup>Rise and go down and accompany them without hesitation, for I have sent them.” <sup>21</sup>And Peter went down to the men and said, “I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason for your coming?” <sup>22</sup>And they said, “Cornelius, a centurion, an upright and God-fearing man, who is well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation, was directed by a holy angel to send for you to come to his house and to hear what you have to say.” <sup>23</sup>So he invited them in to be his guests. The next day he rose and went away with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him. <sup>24</sup>And on the following day they entered Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends. <sup>25</sup>When Peter entered, Cornelius met him and fell down at his feet and worshiped him. <sup>26</sup>But Peter lifted him up, saying, “Stand up; I too am a man.” <sup>27</sup>And as he talked with him, he went in and found many persons gathered. <sup>28</sup>And he said to them, “You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation, but God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean. <sup>29</sup>So when I was sent for, I came without objection. I ask then why you sent for me.” <sup>30</sup>And Cornelius said, “Four days ago, about this hour, I was praying in my house at the ninth hour, and behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing <sup>31</sup>and said, ‘Cornelius, your prayer has been heard and your alms have been remembered before God. <sup>32</sup>Send therefore to Joppa and ask for Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging in the house of Simon, a tanner, by the sea.’ <sup>33</sup>So I sent for you at once, and you have been kind enough to come. Now therefore we are all here in the presence of God to hear all that you have been commanded by the Lord.” <sup>34</sup>So Peter opened his mouth and said: “Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, <sup>35</sup>but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him. <sup>36</sup>As for the word that he sent to Israel, preaching good news of peace through Jesus Christ (he is Lord of all), <sup>37</sup>you yourselves know what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed: <sup>38</sup>how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him. <sup>39</sup>And we are witnesses of all that he did both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. They put him to death by hanging him on a tree, <sup>40</sup>but God raised him on the third day and made him to appear, <sup>41</sup>not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead. <sup>42</sup>And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead. <sup>43</sup>To him all the prophets bear witness that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.” <sup>44</sup>While Peter was still saying these things, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word. <sup>45</sup>And the believers from among the circumcised who had come with Peter were amazed, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles. <sup>46</sup>For they were hearing them speaking in tongues and extolling God. Then Peter declared, <sup>47</sup>“Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?” <sup>48</sup>And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to remain for some days.
10.overview:
The tenth chapter of Acts is one of the pivotal moments in the history of redemption. God has been preparing two men simultaneously: a Roman centurion who prays and gives alms and fears the God of Israel, and a Jewish apostle on a rooftop in Joppa having a vision that overturns a lifetime of religious instinct. The God who governs all things is coordinating these two lives across thirty miles — because the gospel is about to cross the border that mattered most.

Peter’s vision is not primarily about food. It is about people. “What God has made clean, do not call common.” The dietary laws that had kept Israel separate from the nations were always pointing toward something — a people set apart for God. Now that people is being redefined around the Messiah, and the old boundary markers are being transformed. God is not lowering his standards; he is declaring that Gentiles, received through faith in Christ, are clean. They always could be. The wall between Jew and Gentile was never in God’s ultimate plan; it was a temporary steward until the seed came (Galatians 3:24).

The Spirit falls while Peter is still preaching. Not after an altar call. Not after theological instruction is complete. The sovereign Spirit comes when and where he wills, and what he produces in the house of Cornelius is praise. The Jewish believers who came with Peter are amazed. God is not. He planned this before the foundation of the world.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–48 — Cornelius and the Gentile Pentecost
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
This is the hinge of the book, and Luke gives it more room than any other single episode in Acts — forty-eight verses, and then he tells the whole thing over again in chapter 11 because the church could not take it in the first time.

It opens with a Roman officer at Caesarea who prays at the Jewish hours and gives money to Jewish poor, and an angel who tells him to send for a fisherman thirty miles down the coast. It proceeds by way of a vision on a roof that Peter refuses three times, a sheet full of animals he had never in his life eaten, and a sentence he cannot get round: what God has made clean, do not call common. And while he is still turning it over, three men are standing at the gate.

Then the thing Luke has been building toward since chapter 1. Peter walks into a Gentile house — and says so out loud, naming the barrier as he crosses it — and preaches a sermon he never finishes. The Spirit falls on the room while he is still speaking, on uncircumcised Gentiles who have kept none of the law, with the same tongues and the same praise as at Pentecost; and the Jewish believers who came with Peter as witnesses stand there astonished. Peter's response is a question nobody in the room can answer: can anyone withhold water?

Notice what the chapter does not contain. There is no debate, no council, no argument from Scripture, no vote. God simply does it, in front of six witnesses Peter had the foresight to bring, and the church spends the next several chapters catching up with what happened in a house in Caesarea on an afternoon when a preacher was interrupted.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Clean and the Unclean, and What the Food Laws Were For

The sheet is full of animals and the argument is about people, and Peter himself makes the translation at verse 28: God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean. The food laws had never been about digestion. They were about difference — a daily, three-times-a-day mechanism for keeping Israel visibly distinct from the nations around it, and they worked, which is why a devout Jew could not eat at a Gentile table without the whole arrangement collapsing. Reformed theology has read the vision as the retirement of a shadow rather than the repeal of a word: the separation was always temporary, always pointing forward, and its purpose was fulfilled the moment the middle wall of partition came down in Christ. What is striking is the order in which Peter learned it. He did not reason his way from Christology to table fellowship. He was given a command he found repellent, obeyed it under protest, and worked out the theology afterwards — which is worth remembering by anyone who assumes conviction always precedes obedience.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter needed a vision repeated three times, a direct instruction from the Spirit, three men at the gate and the Spirit falling in front of witnesses before he would accept what he had been told plainly at the ascension. And even then the church argued about it for a chapter and a half. Now: The instinct to take the gospel to people like ourselves is not usually held as a conviction; it is held as an assumption, which is why it survives so much preaching against it. Peter did not have an opinion about Gentiles that could be corrected. He had a lifetime of habit, and it took God three goes.

verseByVerse.quote: At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion of what was known as the Italian Cohort, a devout man who feared God with all his household, gave alms generously to the people, and prayed continually to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke introduces the man carefully, and every detail is chosen to make him the hardest possible case in the best possible way.

He is a centurion — a professional soldier commanding eighty men, the backbone of the Roman army and the rank at which the empire actually worked. He is stationed at Caesarea, the Roman administrative capital of Judea, a city built by Herod with a harbour, a theatre and a temple to the emperor. He is the occupation. Whatever a Jewish reader felt about Rome — the taxes, the standards, the crucifixions — Cornelius is the man who enforces it.

And then four things which make him, by any measure available to first-century Judaism, an exemplary human being. He is devout. He feared God with all his household, which means he had brought his family and his servants with him into it and not merely adopted a private opinion. He gave alms generously to the people — and the people in Luke's usage means the Jewish people, so a Roman officer was funding the poor of the nation he was garrisoning. And he prayed continually to God.

What he is not is a convert. He belonged to a recognised category — the God-fearer, the Gentile who attached himself to the synagogue, believed in the God of Israel, kept what he could of the moral law and gave to the poor, but had not been circumcised and so remained, formally, outside. There were many such men around Diaspora synagogues, and they occupied an uncomfortable middle ground: too Jewish for their Roman friends, never quite Jewish enough for the congregation.

So Luke has assembled the best Gentile in the empire. Sincere, generous, prayerful, respected by the very people he had power over, at the top of his profession, and bringing his whole household along with him. If moral seriousness and religious sincerity were enough, this is the man they would be enough for.

And the angel who arrives in the next verse does not tell him he is fine. He tells him to send thirty miles down the coast for a fisherman who has something to say to him. That is the whole argument of the chapter in its opening two verses, and it cuts in two directions at once. Nothing Cornelius had done had earned him anything — and God had noticed every bit of it, and was already moving.

verseByVerse.quote: About the ninth hour of the day he saw clearly in a vision an angel of God come in and say to him, "Cornelius." And he stared at him in terror and said, "What is it, Lord?" And he said to him, "Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
About the ninth hour of the day. Three in the afternoon, which is one of the Jewish hours of prayer — the hour of the evening sacrifice, when the smoke went up in Jerusalem and devout men everywhere turned toward it. A Roman officer in a Roman garrison town was keeping Jewish prayer times, and the angel arrived while he was doing it.

He saw clearly in a vision. Luke is being careful: not a dream, not an impression, not something he thought he saw. And Cornelius's reaction is not devotional pleasure. He stared at him in terror — the word is the ordinary one for fear, and it is the reaction of every person in Scripture who meets an angel, which is worth remembering by anybody whose picture of angels comes from Christmas cards. A professional soldier who had presumably seen a good deal was frightened rigid.

Then the message, and it is worth reading slowly because it has been misread in both directions. Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God.

The vocabulary is taken from the sacrificial system. A memorial was the portion of the grain offering that the priest burned on the altar, the part that went up as smoke — the token by which the whole offering came before God. So the angel is telling an uncircumcised Roman soldier, who had never brought a sacrifice and could not have brought one past the outer court, that his prayers and his money have gone up off the altar like an offering that God accepted.

That is an extraordinary thing to say, and it must not be flattened either way. It does not mean Cornelius had earned anything; the chapter exists precisely because he still needed a preacher, and the parallel account in chapter 11 records the part of the angel's message Luke leaves out here — that Peter would declare to him a message by which you will be saved. He was not saved yet. But neither is God indifferent to the groping of an honest man. The prayers of a Gentile who did not know the gospel went up, and were noticed, and were remembered, and God answered them by arranging a journey.

There is a great deal in that for anyone praying for a person who is nowhere near the faith — or for anyone who suspects that their own years of half-informed, badly-aimed prayer before they understood anything have simply evaporated. Cornelius's had not. They were on file, and God's answer to them was to send a man on a thirty-mile journey he did not want to make.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now send men to Joppa and bring one Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging with one Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea."
verseByVerse.commentary:
An angel is standing in the room, and what he brings is an address.

That is worth stopping over, because it is the most theologically loaded thing in the paragraph. Here is a genuine supernatural messenger, in a chapter full of divine intervention, speaking directly to a man who wants God — and he does not preach the gospel. He does not explain about Jesus, or the cross, or forgiveness. He gives a name, a town, a householder and a street: send to Joppa, ask for Simon called Peter, he is staying with Simon the tanner, the house is by the sea.

Angels in Scripture announce, warn, guide and rescue. They do not evangelise. The message by which a man is saved is put into the mouths of other men, and it always has been; God's settled arrangement is that the news travels on human breath, from someone who has it to someone who has not. It would have been simpler to let the angel say it. He is already in the room, he has Cornelius's undivided attention, and there would have been no need for anybody to walk anywhere. Instead the whole apparatus of heaven is deployed to get a fisherman onto a road.

Which is a considerable dignity conferred on ordinary Christians, and a considerable responsibility. Nobody else has been given the job.

Then the detail of the directions, which is almost comic in its specificity. The angel knows that there are two men named Simon in the story and distinguishes them. He knows the second one's trade. He knows the house is by the sea — which it was, because tanneries had to be, for the water and to keep the smell downwind of the town. God's guidance in this chapter has a postcode.

And notice what Cornelius is not told. Not why. Not what Peter will say, or what will come of it, or that this errand will crack open the whole future of the church. He is told to send for a man, and that is all, and he sends. Most obedience arrives in exactly that condition: enough instruction to act on and nothing whatever by way of explanation.

verseByVerse.quote: When the angel who spoke to him had departed, he called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among those who attended him, and having related everything to them, he sent them to Joppa.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the angel who spoke to him had departed — and then, immediately, action. Luke does not record any interval. Cornelius does not sleep on it, does not consult anybody, does not wait to see whether the impression fades by morning. The angel goes and he calls for staff.

Look at whom he sends: two household servants and a soldier, and Luke troubles to tell us the soldier was devout. That is a small window into what this man's household was actually like. Verse 2 said he feared God with all his household, and here is the corroboration — one of the men under his command shared his faith, closely enough that Cornelius could pick him for an errand of this kind and know he would understand it.

And what he does before they leave is the sentence to notice. Having related everything to them. He did not send them with an instruction; he sent them with the whole story. The angel, the hour, the message, the fear — all of it, told to two servants and a private soldier before they set off. A senior officer, in a rigidly hierarchical profession, sat his subordinates down and told them what had happened to him while he was praying.

It is a small thing and it explains a great deal about the reception Peter gets four days later. When those men arrive in Joppa they are able to give an account of Cornelius that persuades an apostle to travel; and when Peter reaches Caesarea he finds not a curious individual but a room full of relatives and friends who have been assembled and briefed. That happened because a man who had received something extraordinary told the people around him instead of keeping it to himself.

The distance to Joppa is about thirty miles down the coast — a day and a half on foot. They will go, arrive, stay a night, and come back with Peter, and Cornelius will spend four days waiting on the strength of one conversation with a stranger in bright clothing. Whatever else this is, it is not a man taking a small risk.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day, as they were on their journey and approaching the city, Peter went up on the housetop about the sixth hour to pray. And he became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while they were preparing it, he fell into a trance
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke does something here that he does all through this chapter: he cuts between the two ends of the story and lines up the timing so the reader can see the machinery. The next day, as they were on their journey and approaching the city — the messengers are perhaps an hour away — Peter went up on the housetop about the sixth hour to pray.

The roof was the coolest and most private place in an eastern house: flat, reached by an outside stair, used for sleeping in hot weather and for drying things. It was where a man went to be alone. And the sixth hour is noon, which was not one of the fixed hours of prayer — nine and three were. Peter has gone up to pray at an hour nobody required of him, which tells you something about him that no sermon in this book does.

Then the entirely unspiritual detail that Luke, being Luke, refuses to leave out. He became hungry and wanted something to eat. It is noon, he has been up since dawn, the meal is being cooked downstairs and he can presumably smell it. And in the gap between the hunger and the food arriving, God speaks.

It would be easy to make too much of that and it would be a pity to make nothing of it. God does not appear to have chosen the moment at random. A man who is hungry, on a roof, waiting for lunch is a man in whose mind the subject of food is already open — and what is about to come down out of the sky is a sheet full of animals with an instruction to kill and eat. The revelation arrives in the vocabulary Peter's body has just supplied.

It is worth registering how ordinary the setting is. The most consequential vision in the book of Acts, the one that opens the church to the entire non-Jewish world, is given to a man on a roof, in a borrowed house that smelt of tanning, at midday, while he was waiting for something to eat. Nothing had been arranged; he had simply gone up to pray as he did most days, and stayed there long enough to get hungry.

verseByVerse.quote: and saw the heavens opened and something like a great sheet descending, being let down by its four corners upon the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He saw the heavens opened. Luke uses that phrase very sparingly and always at a moment when something changes permanently — at the Jordan when the Spirit came down on Jesus, and in a council chamber when Stephen looked up and saw the Son of Man standing. It is not decorative language. It means the boundary has been crossed from the other side.

And what comes through it is a household object. Something like a great sheet — and note the something like, which is Luke's habitual honesty when a witness is describing an unfamiliar thing by the nearest familiar one. It was not a sheet. It was whatever it was, and a sheet is what it resembled: a large square of cloth, of the sort that would have been lying about on that very roof, the kind used for drying and carrying.

It is let down by its four corners upon the earth. Four corners is a phrase with a history — the prophets speak of God gathering the outcasts of Israel from the four corners of the earth, and the four corners are a standard way of saying everywhere, from every direction, the whole inhabited world. Peter is watching something being lowered toward him that is held at the four points of the compass, and it will be full of every kind of living creature. The shape of the vision is announcing its subject before a word is spoken.

And the direction of travel is the thing to hold. It comes down. Peter does not go up, is not caught away, is not given a tour of anything. He is on a roof and heaven descends to where he is standing, which is exactly what the rest of the chapter is about: God moving toward people who could not have come to him, and doing it on their own roofs, at lunchtime.

One small thing about the word Luke chose, which is the sort of detail that suggests somebody was describing this rather than composing it. The term he uses for the sheet means a piece of fine linen, and in Greek writers it can carry the sense of a ship's sail. Peter is a fisherman, lying on a roof in a port, within sight of the harbour at Joppa. Of all the shapes a large square of cloth held at four corners might have suggested to him, that one had been in front of his eyes every working day of his life.

verseByVerse.quote: In it were all kinds of animals and reptiles and birds of the air. And there came a voice to him: "Rise, Peter; kill and eat."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All kinds of animals and reptiles and birds of the air. The three categories are the ones Genesis uses at the creation and Leviticus uses when it draws the lines, and Luke lists them in a way that makes clear the sheet is not a selection. It is the whole zoo. Clean and unclean together, in one cloth, on Peter's roof — the pig beside the sheep, the vulture beside the pigeon, and creeping things which were unclean without exception and about which there had never been any argument at all.

Then the voice, and it gives an order rather than an invitation. Rise, Peter; kill and eat.

Feel the force of that on a man of Peter's upbringing. The verb translated kill is the word for slaughtering an animal, so it is not merely eat what is put in front of you; it is do the butchering yourself. He is being told to get up, take a knife, and prepare a meal out of creatures he had been taught before he could walk were an offence to God.

And it was not a marginal scruple. The food laws were where Jewish identity had been defended at the cost of blood within living memory of Peter's grandparents. Under the Greek persecution, mothers had watched their sons killed rather than eat pork; the books that recorded it were read and treasured. To a Jew of the first century, refusing unclean food was not a dietary preference. It was what martyrs had died for, and everybody knew the stories.

So the command is not a gentle stretching of a habit. It is an instruction to do the specific thing that faithful Israelites had gone to their deaths refusing to do — and it comes from heaven, in a vision, from a voice Peter will address as Lord.

Which is why the next verse contains one of the most understandable refusals in Scripture, and why God has to say it three times.

One guard, and it needs stating because this passage gets pressed into service for arguments it was not given for. The vision is regularly produced to settle questions about what Christians may eat, and it does bear on that — the New Testament is clear elsewhere that no food is unclean in itself, and Mark says as much in an aside. But Peter himself tells us what the vision was for, and he tells us in verse 28, and it is not a menu. God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean. The animals were the vehicle. The freight was people.

Which means the passage is being used most faithfully not when it is settling a dispute about diet, but when it is dismantling the far more durable habit the food laws existed to enforce — the sorting of human beings into those one can sit down with and those one cannot. That habit long outlived the dietary code, and it has never needed a Bible verse to keep it going.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said, "By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
By no means, Lord.

Two words in Greek and they will not go together. The first is the strongest negative the language has — not I would rather not but absolutely not, under no circumstances. The second is Lord. Peter has said, in a single breath, never and master, and the sentence contradicts itself before he has finished it.

It is not the first time he has done it, either, and Luke's readers who had his Gospel would have heard the echo. In a boat on Galilee, after a catch of fish, Peter had said depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord. At a supper table he had said you shall never wash my feet. On a road to Jerusalem, when Jesus told him what was going to happen there, he took him aside and said far be it from you, Lord. It is a recognisable habit in a particular man: he is the disciple who tells Jesus what will not be happening, and who calls him Lord while doing it.

And the reason is not stubbornness. Look at what he actually says: I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean. That is a lifetime's record laid out as evidence, and every word of it is to his credit. He is not saying he does not want to. He is saying that in fifty years, under pressure, in poverty, travelling, as a fisherman working alongside Gentiles on a lake with a mixed shoreline, he has never once done it. He is defending God's own law, which he has kept at cost, and he is defending it against God.

That is the situation worth sitting with, because it is more common than it looks. The thing Peter cannot let go of is not a sin. It is an obedience — a genuine one, in a real command, kept faithfully for decades. What has changed is not that God has grown lax; it is that the command had a purpose, and the purpose has arrived, and Peter is holding on to the scaffolding after the building is up.

Most Christians who are stuck are not stuck on something disreputable. They are stuck on something that was once right, and was kept at cost, and has quietly become the thing they will not let God touch. Peter's by no means, Lord is not the sentence of a rebel. It is the sentence of a good man defending a good thing at the exact moment God is moving past it.

verseByVerse.quote: And the voice came to him again a second time, "What God has made clean, do not call common." This happened three times, and the thing was taken up at once to heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What God has made clean, do not call common.

Note the tense and the agent. Not what I am now permitting but what God has made clean — the thing has already been done, elsewhere, and Peter's part is simply to stop describing it wrongly. He is not being asked to change a rule. He is being told that a fact has altered and his vocabulary is out of date.

And the correction is aimed at his mouth. Do not call common. The problem the voice addresses is not what Peter eats but what he says about people, and within thirteen verses he will have made the translation himself in front of a room full of Gentiles: God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean.

Nor is this the law being contradicted. Jesus had already said it, in a sentence Mark records with an editorial note attached — that what goes into a man cannot defile him, and that in saying so he declared all foods clean. Peter had been standing there. He had heard it and had not drawn the conclusion, which is worth knowing by anyone who assumes that hearing good teaching is the same thing as being changed by it. He needed it said again, from heaven, three times, with livestock.

This happened three times. It is the same number as a charcoal fire in a courtyard and three questions on a beach, and it is hard to believe Peter missed the resonance. Three times he had denied; three times he had been restored; three times now he refuses and is corrected. God appears to know exactly how many repetitions this particular man requires.

Then, abruptly, the thing was taken up at once to heaven — and no explanation is given. The vision does not conclude with an application. It simply stops, leaving a man on a roof holding a command he has refused, a sentence he cannot argue with, and no idea what any of it is for. That is where verse 17 finds him, and it is where a great deal of Christian experience actually happens: the instruction has been received and the meaning has not arrived, and the only thing to do is go on standing there until somebody knocks at the gate.

verseByVerse.quote: Now while Peter was inwardly perplexed as to what the vision that he had seen might mean, behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon's house, stood at the gate and called out to ask whether Simon who was called Peter was lodging there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Inwardly perplexed as to what the vision that he had seen might mean. The word is a strong one — thoroughly at a loss, completely unable to see through it. Luke is not describing a man who has grasped a great truth and is savouring it. He is describing bafflement, and he says it twice, because the next verse adds that Peter was still pondering when the Spirit spoke.

That is a useful thing to have on record. The apostle Peter received a direct revelation from heaven, repeated three times for emphasis, and did not know what it meant. He was not being slow. The vision was genuinely opaque, and it was designed to be — it was about food and it was not about food, and there was no way to get from the sheet to the Gentiles by thinking harder. The interpretation was going to arrive by other means.

And it is already at the gate. Behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon's house, stood at the gate and called out. Luke's timing is exact and he wants it noticed: while the vision is still fresh enough to be unresolved, the answer to it is standing in the street asking for Peter by name.

Notice how the meaning is going to be delivered. Not by further revelation, and not by a better idea occurring to Peter on the roof. It arrives as three men with a message, an address, and a request — which is to say, as circumstances. Peter will understand the sheet by obeying the knock, and not before.

This is worth holding by anyone who has been given something by God that they cannot yet make sense of — a conviction, a burden, a text that will not leave them alone, a strong impression with no obvious application. The temptation is to sit with it until it clarifies. Peter was perplexed on a roof and the explanation was downstairs, and he would never have worked it out up there. Some things are only understood at the point where they are acted on.

verseByVerse.quote: And while Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, "Behold, three men are looking for you. Rise and go down and accompany them without hesitation, for I have sent them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three separate parties are being moved in this chapter and none of them can see the others. Cornelius has an angel and an address. The three messengers have a road and an errand. Peter has a sheet full of animals and no idea what it is for. Here, for the first time, the wiring becomes visible: the Spirit said to him, Behold, three men are looking for you.

The information is precise — the number, the fact that they are searching, and then the instruction. Rise and go down and accompany them without hesitation, for I have sent them.

That last clause is the hinge of the chapter and Peter never lets go of it. When he is hauled in front of the Jerusalem church a chapter later to explain what he has done, this is what he produces: the Spirit told me to go with them. He does not argue from the vision, or from theology, or from the evident sincerity of Cornelius. He says he was sent, and that ends the discussion.

The phrase rendered without hesitation is worth a moment, because it is doing more than steadying his nerves. The verb means to be divided, to discriminate, to make a distinction between one thing and another — and it is the same root Peter uses in his report at Jerusalem, and the same idea again at the council in chapter 15, where he says God made no distinction between us and them. So the Spirit's word to Peter on the stairs is not merely do not dither. It is do not sort these men into a category. The instruction names the exact reflex that was about to operate, and forbids it before it can.

And notice the sheer economy of what Peter is given. He is not told who Cornelius is, or what the vision meant, or what is going to happen in Caesarea, or that this afternoon will change the shape of the church for ever. He is told there are three men downstairs, to go with them, and that they were sent. That is the whole briefing, and it turns out to be enough, because the one thing in it that matters is the last four words.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter went down to the men and said, "I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason for your coming?" And they said, "Cornelius, a centurion, an upright and God-fearing man, who is well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation, was directed by a holy angel to send for you to come to his house and to hear what you have to say."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter goes down and opens with a flat, practical sentence — I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason for your coming? — and it is worth noticing that he has not been told the reason. The Spirit gave him the instruction and withheld the explanation, and Peter is now going to get it from three strangers at a gate.

Their answer is a small masterpiece of diplomacy, and every clause is chosen for the man they are talking to.

Cornelius, a centurion — they lead with the awkward fact rather than hiding it. An upright and God-fearing man — the two things a Jewish hearer would most want to know, in the right order. Who is well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation — that is, the people you are worried about offending already think highly of him; there are references available, and they are from your own community. And finally the clincher: was directed by a holy angel to send for you. Not he would like a word. He was told to fetch you, from heaven.

These three men have made the case as well as it could be made, which suggests they had rehearsed it on the road, which suggests they knew exactly how unlikely their errand was. Two servants and a soldier walked thirty miles to ask a Jewish holy man to come and stay in a Roman officer's house, and they went with a prepared argument.

And the last phrase of their speech is the one to sit with: they have come to hear what you have to say. That is the whole invitation. Not to be healed, not to be advised, not to be impressed. A household has been assembled thirty miles away and is waiting, and what they want is words.

It is not a common request. Most preachers spend their lives trying to get people to listen; here is a man who sent servants on a two-day round trip to secure a hearing for a message he had not heard yet and could not have described. Whatever Peter was feeling as he came down those stairs, he was walking toward the most willing audience of his life.

verseByVerse.quote: So he invited them in to be his guests. The next day he rose and went away with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three things happen in this one verse and two of them are quietly enormous.

The first: he invited them in to be his guests. Peter takes two Gentile servants and a Roman soldier into the house and puts them up for the night. That means beds, and it means a meal, and a meal means a table — which is precisely the thing a devout Jew did not do with Gentiles, and precisely the thing the vision had been about an hour earlier. Luke does not comment. He simply records that the man who had said by no means, Lord before lunch had Gentiles eating in his lodgings by supper.

It is worth noticing how fast that went. Peter did not resolve his theology first and then act on it; the theology is not resolved until verse 28, and he says as much. He obeyed a plain instruction, one step at a time, and understood it afterwards. And the first step was not preaching to Gentiles. It was having them in the house.

The second: the next day he rose and went away with them. Not that afternoon — Joppa to Caesarea is thirty miles and the men had already walked it. He gave them a night's rest first, which is a small kindness Luke did not have to record and did.

The third is the shrewdest thing anybody does in this chapter: some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him. In the retelling at Jerusalem we learn there were six of them, and we learn it because Peter had them standing beside him when the church demanded an explanation.

He knew what was coming. A man does not take six witnesses on a pastoral visit. Peter understood that whatever happened in Caesarea was going to be examined, contested and possibly disbelieved, and that his own word would not be enough — so he arranged, before he set out, for six other men to see it with their own eyes. It is not timidity and it is not politics. It is a leader anticipating the church's real difficulty and taking the trouble, in advance, to make his account checkable.

verseByVerse.quote: And on the following day they entered Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends. When Peter entered, Cornelius met him and fell down at his feet and worshiped him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends.

He has spent four days on this. The angel came on a Tuesday afternoon, if you like; the messengers walked a day and a half; they stayed a night; they walked back. And in the meantime Cornelius has been going round Caesarea inviting people to his house to hear a man he has never met say something he cannot describe.

Consider what that took. He is a serving officer in a garrison town, and he has told his extended family and his friends — probably including brother officers — that an angel appeared to him while he was praying and told him to send for a Jewish fisherman from Joppa. He had no idea what Peter was going to say. If nothing had come of it he would have looked ridiculous in front of everybody whose opinion mattered to him, and would have gone on looking ridiculous for years.

And notice the instinct. The first thing this man does with something from God is fill a room. He does not receive it privately and consider passing it on later; he assumes from the outset that whatever is coming is too large to keep, and he goes and fetches the people he loves. The whole Gentile mission begins in a house full of somebody's relatives, because a Roman soldier could not think of a reason to hear this alone.

Then Peter arrives, and Cornelius does the wrong thing. He met him and fell down at his feet and worshipped him.

It is worth being fair to him. He is not a theologian. What he knows is that four days ago an angel stood in his house and told him to send for this man, and here the man is; and in the world Cornelius grew up in, when something from heaven turns up you get on the floor. His error is an error of enthusiasm and reverence, made by a man who has been waiting four days and does not know quite what he is dealing with. It is corrected in the next verse, immediately and kindly, and Luke does not hold it against him.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter lifted him up, saying, "Stand up; I too am a man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter lifted him up, saying, Stand up; I too am a man.

Four words in Greek, and they are the whole of Christian ministry stated as a sentence. Not you are embarrassing me, not this is inappropriate. I too am a man — the same kind of thing you are, on the same side of the floor, made of the same material.

And he does not simply say it. He lifted him up — reaches down, takes hold of a Roman centurion who is lying on the ground in front of him, and puts him back on his feet. The correction is physical and it is instant, and it happens before a word of the gospel has been preached in that house. The first thing Peter does in the first Gentile home to hear the gospel is pick a man up off the floor.

Luke has a habit of setting scenes like this against each other, and the reader is meant to notice. Two chapters later a king in this same city of Caesarea will accept exactly the acclaim Peter has just refused — the crowd will shout that it is the voice of a god and not of a man, and Herod will take it, and Luke records what happened to him in a single unsparing verse. The two scenes are set in the same town, a few years and a few pages apart: a fisherman on his feet saying I am only a man, and a king on a throne saying nothing at all.

It should also be said that Peter is doing something harder than it looks. Cornelius's reverence was genuine, and it was directed at a man who had walked thirty miles to help him; refusing it risked chilling the room before anything had begun. There is a kind of false humility that deflects with one hand and enjoys the compliment with the other, and it is much more comfortable than what Peter does here, which is to end the transaction on the spot.

Every ministry that lasts is built on this refusal, and every one that collapses has stopped making it somewhere. The apostle who is about to be the instrument of the most important sermon in the book will not be knelt to in a doorway, because the treasure and the jar are two different things and he has never been in any doubt which one he is.

verseByVerse.quote: And as he talked with him, he went in and found many persons gathered. And he said to them, "You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation, but God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter walks in, sees a room full of Gentiles waiting for him, and opens by naming the barrier.

That is the remarkable thing about this speech and it is easily missed. He does not pretend the difficulty is not there. He does not begin with something warm and general and hope nobody raises it. He says, in the first sentence, to a roomful of people it applies to: you yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation. They did know. Every person in that house had lived with it, and the God-fearers among them had felt it most — welcome at the synagogue door and not past it.

Two things are worth getting right about the barrier itself. The first is that Peter's word for unlawful is not the word for the law of Moses; the Torah nowhere forbids a Jew to enter a Gentile house. What had grown up was a dense hedge of custom and interpretation around the purity laws, hardened by centuries of pressure, until entering such a house was simply not done — which is why Peter can call it unlawful in ordinary speech and be perfectly understood. The second is that it had a real purpose once. A people surrounded by empires that swallowed nations whole survived by not eating with them.

And then the pivot, and Peter makes the translation himself: but God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean.

The vision was about animals. Peter says it was about persons — and he had not been told that. Nobody on the roof explained the parable to him; the voice said what God has made clean do not call common, and left. Between the roof and this doorway, somewhere on thirty miles of coast road with three Gentiles for company, Peter worked out what he had been shown. Obedience came first, at the gate in Joppa; the understanding caught up on the journey.

It is worth asking what a congregation would sound like if it did this — named its own barrier out loud, in front of the people on the other side of it, before saying anything else. Peter's honesty here is the reason the room believed him. He had not come to tell them the division never existed. He had come to tell them who had ended it.

verseByVerse.quote: "So when I was sent for, I came without objection. I ask then why you sent for me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So when I was sent for, I came without objection.

It is a straightforward sentence and it is not quite the whole truth, and Peter knows it. He had objected. He had said by no means, Lord, and had gone on saying it until God had repeated himself three times. What he means is that once he was actually sent for — once the men were at the gate and the Spirit had spoken — he raised nothing. The arguing was finished on the roof. From the moment the knock came he simply went.

The Greek word behind without objection is the negative of the term the Spirit had used at verse 20: do not discriminate, make no distinction. Peter is reporting back in the vocabulary he was given. He was told not to sort these men into categories, and he is telling the room that he did not.

Then the question, and it is a good deal more courteous than it looks on the page. I ask then why you sent for me.

He does not walk in and start preaching. He has a vision, an instruction from the Spirit and the full authority of an apostle, and the first thing he does in that house is ask a question and wait for the answer. He is giving Cornelius the floor in his own home — inviting him to say what has happened at his end, in front of the relatives and friends he has assembled, before anything else is said.

What follows is Cornelius's account of the angel, told out loud to a room that has been waiting four days for it. And the effect of Peter's question is that when the sermon finally comes, everybody present already knows that this meeting was arranged from heaven at both ends. Peter could have asserted that. Instead he asked, and let his host establish it.

There is a small lesson in it for anybody who arrives somewhere with something to say. The apostle with the revelation began by asking the Roman soldier to explain himself, and listened to the answer, and only then opened his mouth.

verseByVerse.quote: And Cornelius said, "Four days ago, about this hour, I was praying in my house at the ninth hour, and behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing and said, 'Cornelius, your prayer has been heard and your alms have been remembered before God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cornelius tells it back, and Luke lets him — which means the angel's message appears twice in one chapter, once as it happened and once as the man himself reports it. That is not padding. Luke wants the reader to have it from both ends, and he will give it a third time in the next chapter when Peter recounts the whole affair in Jerusalem.

And it is when the three tellings are laid side by side that something important surfaces — something this chapter, twice, leaves out.

Here and at verse 4, the angel's message is that Cornelius's prayers and alms have been remembered before God, and that he should send for Peter. That is all.
