John the Baptist is brought in as the last signpost (vv. 24–25); the sermon turns from history to the room — to us has been sent the message of this salvation (v. 26); and the death and burial are set out with the charge that Jerusalem condemned him without cause and so fulfilled the very prophets it read every Sabbath (vv. 27–29). God raised him, and the witnesses are alive and can be asked (vv. 30–31). Three Scriptures then carry the argument: Psalm 2 for his installation as Son (vv. 32–33), Isaiah 55 and Psalm 16 for a body that did not decay — which cannot be David's, since David's did (vv. 34–37).

The application, and the warning. Verses 38–39 are the first plain statement of justification by faith in Acts, and Habakkuk 1:5 is the sting in the tail (vv. 40–41): God is doing a work in your days that you will not believe even when you are told.

What it cost. They beg for more the following week (v. 42), and are urged to continue in the grace of God (v. 43). The next Sabbath almost the whole city turns out, and the synagogue leadership, seeing the crowds, is filled with jealousy (vv. 44–45). Paul and Barnabas answer with Isaiah 49:6 and turn to the Gentiles (vv. 46–47) — not a change of plan but a share in the Servant's own commission. The Gentiles rejoice, those appointed to eternal life believe, and the word spreads through the whole region without the missionaries (vv. 48–49). Then the expulsion, arranged quietly through the leading women and men of the colony (vv. 50–51). And the last sentence of the chapter belongs not to the apostles but to the converts they had to leave behind: filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit (v. 52).
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification by Faith in Paul's First Sermon

Paul's climactic statement in vv. 38–39 is the first explicit statement of justification by faith in Acts: let it be known to you that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses. The word the ESV renders freed is dikaioutai, justified — a courtroom word, the word for a judge declaring a man to be in the right. The law cannot issue that verdict; faith in the crucified and risen Jesus receives it. This is the heart of Paul's theology, already fully formed in his first recorded sermon — the gospel that will generate the letters to the Galatians and Romans. And it is not preached softly: the same sermon that announces the amnesty ends on Habakkuk's word to scoffers, be astounded and perish (vv. 40–41).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: 'The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of God.' The widespread hunger for the gospel was met with jealousy from the Jewish leaders, who spoke against Paul. Their opposition drove the explicit turn to the Gentiles. Now: The pattern repeats whenever the gospel meets institutional religion: those who should be most receptive are sometimes least so, while those outside the religious establishment respond with open hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Paul and his companions set sail from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia. And John left them and returned to Jerusalem, but they went on from Perga and came to Antioch in Pisidia. And on the Sabbath day they went into the synagogue and sat down.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Paul and his companions — and something has changed that Luke does not stop to explain. Until this point it has been Barnabas and Saul, in that order, every time: the church set apart Barnabas and Saul (v. 2), the proconsul summoned Barnabas and Saul (v. 7). From here on it is Paul, and the man who fetched him out of obscurity in Tarsus, who vouched for him in Jerusalem when nobody else would touch him, and who was the senior partner in every earlier sentence, has become part of the phrase and his companions.

Luke records the change and passes no comment on it. There is no meeting, no vote, no explanation. The gifts sorted the order out, and Barnabas — who had every reason to mind — appears not to have minded. It is one of the quietest and hardest things in the New Testament: a man overtaken by somebody else's growth, who goes on walking beside him.

Then: And John left them and returned to Jerusalem. Nine words, and no reason given. It is worth saying plainly that we do not know why, because a great deal of confident guessing has been done here. The suggestions are reasonable and not one of them is in the text: the road ahead was hard and dangerous; the coastal plain of Pamphylia was malarial, and Paul later reminds these very churches that it was a bodily ailment that brought him to them in the first place (Gal. 4:13); his cousin Barnabas had just slipped to second place; the mission was turning toward Gentiles faster than a Jerusalem boy had bargained for. Take your pick. Luke will not help you.

What Luke does record is the cost. Two chapters on, this departure — and Paul calls it desertion — breaks up the partnership. Paul will not take him, Barnabas will not go without him, and the two men who walked out of Antioch together in verse 3 separate over it (15:36–41). One young man goes home early, and the consequences are still running fifteen chapters later.

And then the end of the story, which is the reason to be careful how we read the middle of it. Mark reappears in Paul's letters, and in the last letter Paul ever wrote, from a Roman prison with his own execution close, he asks for him by name: Get Mark and bring him with you, for he is very useful to me for ministry (2 Tim. 4:11; see also Col. 4:10; Philem. 24). The man who could not be relied on for one journey became the man the apostle wanted with him at the end.

If you have a Perga in your own history — a work you began and did not finish, a post you left, a moment when you simply went home — notice that Luke puts it in verse 13 and does not close the file. The record of the desertion is in Scripture forever. So is the request for him at the end.

The two who remain go up. Perga is on the coast; Pisidian Antioch is about a hundred miles inland and three and a half thousand feet up, over the Taurus mountains, on roads Paul later summarises in four words — danger from rivers, danger from robbers (2 Cor. 11:26). Luke gives the crossing half a sentence. Most of the cost of the missionary journeys is in the half-sentences.

And then a clause smaller still, which matters more than it looks: on the Sabbath day they went into the synagogue and sat down. They sent no word ahead. They asked for nothing. Two travel-stained strangers came in, found a place, sat down among the congregation like anybody else, and waited to see whether they would be asked. The most consequential sermon of Paul's recorded ministry begins with two men sitting down and keeping quiet.

verseByVerse.quote: After the reading from the Law and the Prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent a message to them, saying, "Brothers, if you have any word of encouragement for the people, say it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The service runs its course — the prayers, the scroll of the Law lifted and read, the passage from the Prophets after it. Then the rulers of the synagogue notice the two visitors and send a message down to them, and what they send is not an invitation to a special meeting but the ordinary courtesy of that room: if you have any word of encouragement for the people, say it.

The phrase is worth holding for a moment. A word of encouragement — in Greek a logos parakleseos, the very phrase the writer to the Hebrews uses of his own long letter (Heb. 13:22). It means a word that comes alongside and strengthens. It is what a synagogue expected from a visitor, and it is the ancestor of the sermon. The rulers are being generous, and they are being entirely routine. They are asking for a few warm words on the readings.

They have no idea what they have asked for. Within a fortnight this congregation will have split, the whole city will be at the door, and the two visitors will have been run out of the district by the leading families of the colony. Nobody in the room plans any of it. A polite formality, offered to strangers as a matter of form, is the hinge the entire chapter turns on — which is very often how God gets a door opened, and is worth remembering the next time you are handed something small and routine to do.

A word on 'the reading from the Law and the Prophets,' since it shaped the scene. The service centred on two readings: one from the Law (the five books of Moses) and one from the Prophets (a chosen passage, the Haftarah — the reading Jesus stood to give from Isaiah, Luke 4:16–20). After them came a 'word of exhortation,' open to any competent man present — exactly the door opened to Paul. Its roots run to Moses, who commanded the Law be read aloud to the people (Deut. 31:10–13), and to Ezra, who read it to the gathered nation 'and gave the sense, so that the people understood' (Neh. 8:8). The synagogue itself (the word means 'gathering') grew up during and after the Babylonian exile: with the temple gone and the people scattered, Jews met locally to hear and study God's Word. The Law was read in order over a fixed cycle, the prophetic reading chosen to match, often with an Aramaic paraphrase for those who no longer spoke Hebrew.

And do Jews still do this? Yes, with striking continuity. To this day the Torah is read aloud from a handwritten scroll on the Sabbath (and Mondays, Thursdays, and festivals), on the annual cycle that ends and begins again each year at Simchat Torah ('rejoicing in the Torah'), still paired with a prophetic reading and a teaching — the very practice Luke describes, kept now as two thousand years ago. And it is the church's inheritance too: the public reading of Scripture followed by exposition is the pattern Paul charged Timothy to keep — 'devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, to teaching' (1 Tim. 4:13) — the shape of Christian worship ever since. The deep irony here: the Law and the Prophets had just been read aloud, and Paul rises to show that every line was pointing to the Jesus he is about to preach (Luke 24:27, 44). The reading set the table; Paul served Christ from it.

verseByVerse.quote: So Paul stood up, and motioning with his hand said: "Men of Israel and you who fear God, listen. The God of this people Israel chose our fathers and made the people great during their stay in the land of Egypt, and with uplifted arm he led them out of it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He stands up. In a synagogue the teacher normally sat to expound — Jesus sat down in Nazareth before he began (Luke 4:20) — and Paul stands, motioning with his hand, which is the posture and the gesture of a public speaker in the Greek world. Luke notices that hand twice more before the book ends, on the barracks stairs and in front of Agrippa (21:40; 26:1). It is a small thing, and it tells you what kind of man is about to speak: a Jew of the Scriptures who has spent his life in Greek cities and knows how to hold a room.

And his first sentence names two congregations, not one: Men of Israel and you who fear God.

The second group needs explaining, because they are all over this chapter and much of this book. The God-fearers were Gentiles who had attached themselves to the synagogue. They believed in the God of Israel, kept the Sabbath, came to the readings, tried to live by the moral law — and had not been circumcised, and so had not become Jews. They were the most sympathetic hearers in the ancient world and the most frustrated. Picture a man who has been coming to that building for twenty years. He knows the psalms by heart. He has heard the promises to Abraham read aloud perhaps a thousand times, and every one of those times he has understood that they were being read out to somebody else's family and that he was welcome to listen. Cornelius was one of these men (10:2). So was Lydia (16:14), and Titius Justus, whose house stood next door to the synagogue in Corinth (18:7).

Paul puts them in his opening sentence. Before a word of the sermon proper, the man on his feet has told the back of the room that this is addressed to them too. So when the Gentiles of this city respond as fast as they do in verse 48, it is not a sudden lurch. The ground had been ploughed for years by the synagogue itself, and Paul knew it.

Then the history begins — and notice the verb it begins with. The God of this people Israel chose our fathers. The sermon opens on God's choosing. It will also end on God's choosing: as many as were appointed to eternal life believed (v. 48). Every man in that room would have said amen to the first without blinking. What split the congregation a week later was not whether God chooses. It was whom.

And where did the choosing get them? He made the people great during their stay in the land of Egypt. Read that slowly. The multiplying of the promised family did not happen in the promised land. It happened in a foreign country, under a king who was trying to stop it, through years the Bible describes as bitter with hard service — the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied (Exod. 1:12). God's promise to Abraham made its greatest visible progress during the four centuries that looked, from the inside, like the promise having been forgotten.

If you are in a season you did not choose and would not have chosen, that is not a decorative thought. It is the shape of the first thing Paul says about God in the first sermon of his we possess. And then: with uplifted arm he led them out of it (Exod. 6:6; Deut. 4:34) — the arm bared and raised, the way a man raises his arm to strike. Israel did not slip out of Egypt unnoticed in the night. God took his people out with his sleeve rolled up.

verseByVerse.quote: "And for about forty years he put up with them in the wilderness. And after destroying seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave them their land as an inheritance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For about forty years he put up with them in the wilderness.

It is a blunt rendering, and very probably the right one, though the manuscripts here are divided by a single letter. One reading gives a verb meaning to bear with someone's manners, to endure their behaviour — hence put up with. The other, one letter different, means to carry as a nurse carries a child, and it is the word Moses used of these same forty years: the LORD your God carried you, as a man carries his son (Deut. 1:31). Translations divide here, and honest scholars divide with them. What is worth noticing is that both are true of that wilderness, and neither is flattering to Israel. Either God spent forty years enduring them or he spent forty years carrying them, and the reason he had to do either is the same reason.

Measure the forty years, because put up with is not a compliment and the Bible does not intend it as one. Within weeks of hearing God's own voice at Sinai they were dancing round a golden calf. They complained about the food and the water, wept for the fish and the cucumbers of the country where they had been slaves, and twice proposed appointing a leader to take them back to it. God's own summary is that they put him to the test ten times (Num. 14:22). The generation that saw the sea open died in the sand.

And here is the thing to sit with: he did not leave, and he did not pretend. God is nowhere recorded as saying that they were doing rather well under the circumstances. He put up with them. If you have ever suspected that God stays with you only because he has not looked closely, this verse is better news than that. He has looked, the assessment is in, and he is still walking at the pace of the slowest man in the column.

Then, in the next breath, he gave them their land as an inheritance. An inheritance is not a wage. Nobody in Scripture earns an inheritance; it comes to you because of who your father is. Moses made sure they could not misunderstand it — not because of your righteousness (Deut. 9:5). Forty years of being put up with, and then a country, handed over.

'Destroying seven nations' — Paul passes over it in a phrase, but it is one of the hardest things in Scripture, and an honest reader feels its weight: how could a good God order the destruction of the Canaanites? We must not be glib — the loss of life is real and grievous. But several truths, held together, show this is not the arbitrary cruelty it is often imagined to be.

First, it was judgment, not ethnic hatred. Israel had no general warrant to harm Gentiles — she was even to offer peace to distant cities (Deut. 20:10). This was a bounded act of justice on particular nations for particular, appalling sin. God said so: four centuries earlier he told Abraham his descendants would wait, 'for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete' (Gen. 15:16) — holding back judgment four hundred years. And the sin? Among other things, burning their own children alive in sacrifice (Deut. 12:31; Lev. 18:21), with entrenched idolatry and cultic prostitution — until the land itself, defiled, 'vomited out its inhabitants' (Lev. 18:24–25). This is the wrath of a holy God against great and violent evil, long endured.

Second, it was not favouritism toward Israel. God twice tells them this is 'not because of your righteousness... but because of the wickedness of these nations' (Deut. 9:4–6), warning that if Israel does the same, the land will vomit them out too (Lev. 18:28) — and centuries later it did, in the exile. The standard is God's holiness applied impartially, not ethnic preference; that dismantles the charge of 'tribal genocide.' And mercy stood open throughout: Rahab the Canaanite was spared through faith and stands in the Messiah's own bloodline (Josh. 6:25; Matt. 1:5). The issue was never race but allegiance.

Third, underneath the objection lies a question it skips. We assume the Canaanites had a right to life that God violated. But Scripture holds that God is the Author and rightful Lord of all life (Deut. 32:39), and that every one of us has already forfeited life through sin (Rom. 6:23). On that reckoning, what needs explaining is not that God judges sin, but that he is so patient, and that anyone is spared at all. The Canaanites were not innocents struck down by a capricious deity but guilty people under the just sentence of a Judge who had waited centuries. (On the hardest part, the children, Scripture gives no glib answer; we rest in the One of whom Abraham asked, 'shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?' (Gen. 18:25), trusting his mercy toward little ones — as David did for his own child, 2 Sam. 12:23 — and refusing to pretend we see more than we do.)

And finally, most importantly for a Christian: this was a unique, one-time event — Israel as a covenant nation executing God's judgment in a particular land. It is emphatically not a model for today. Jesus refused the sword ('my kingdom is not of this world; if it were, my servants would fight,' John 18:36); the church's weapons 'are not of the flesh' (2 Cor. 10:4); we love our enemies and leave vengeance to God (Matt. 5:44; Rom. 12:19). No one may invoke Joshua to justify violence in Christ's name. Rather, the conquest is a sober, localized preview of the final judgment. And here the gospel speaks its deepest word: at the cross the judgment we all deserve fell on Jesus — the same holy God who judged Canaan 'did not spare his own Son' (Rom. 8:32) but laid our condemnation on him, so that wrath and mercy met. The only refuge from judgment, as for Rahab, is faith in the God of Israel, now revealed in Christ. That is just where Paul's sermon is heading: all this history runs to a Saviour (v. 23).

verseByVerse.quote: "All this took about 450 years. And after that he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All this took about 450 years. A reader with a study Bible will already have seen a footnote, because this is one of the well-known chronological knots in the New Testament, and it is better untied than stepped over.

The difficulty is this. If the 450 years covers the period of the judges — which is how the older printed Greek text reads, and how the King James renders it, after that he gave unto them judges about the space of four hundred and fifty years — then the sum will not come out. First Kings 6:1 puts 480 years between the exodus and the fourth year of Solomon, and 450 years of judges alone leaves no room for the wilderness, the conquest, Samuel, Saul, David, and the first four years of Solomon on top.

The better attested reading, which is what the ESV translates, attaches the number to what has just been said rather than to what follows: all this — the growth in Egypt, the exodus, the wilderness, the dividing of the land — took about 450 years. Then the sum works, and works neatly: about four hundred years in Egypt (Gen. 15:13; Acts 7:6), forty in the wilderness, and roughly ten to take and divide the land. Four hundred and fifty, near enough. The apparent contradiction turns out to be a question of which clause the number belongs to.

And note the word Paul actually uses: about. He is a preacher giving a congregation the shape of their own history, not a chronicler filing dates. The wider case for Luke's care as a historian was set out at 5:37–38 and does not need repeating here; this is simply another place where a charge dissolves on inspection.

Now the sentence that follows, which is easy to read past: and after that he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet.

He gave them. Consider what that word means, given what the book of Judges actually contains. This is the bleakest stretch in Israel's history — a spiral in which the nation goes after other gods, is handed over to an oppressor, cries out, is rescued, and then does the whole thing again, round after round, each one worse than the last, until the book's own closing verdict is that everyone did what was right in his own eyes (Judg. 21:25). And God's response, through three centuries of it, was to go on giving.

Look at what he gave, too, because it is not a roll of heroes. A left-handed assassin. A woman, because no man would go. A frightened man threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it from the enemy. The son of a prostitute, thrown out by his own family. A strong man who could not govern his own appetites and died blind, grinding grain for the people he had been sent to deliver. That is God's provision for the worst period of Israel's life: not better men, but the men who were there, taken up and used.

If you have ever looked at the leadership God has actually provided you — in your church, in your family, in the mirror — and privately concluded that he could have done better, the book of Judges was written for you. He was not doing his best with poor material. He was demonstrating, over three hundred years, that the deliverance never depended on the deliverer.

And then, until Samuel the prophet. Paul disposes of three centuries in eleven words, because he is in a hurry. The whole recital has been running downhill toward one name, and it is not Samuel's.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years. And when he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king, of whom he testified and said, 'I have found in David the son of Jesse a man after my heart, who will do all my will.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul.

Two clauses, and the whole tragedy of 1 Samuel 8 is folded into the space between them. They asked. God gave. And what the older account tells us, which Paul's sentence does not, is that the asking was itself the sin: they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them (1 Sam. 8:7). Samuel told them in advance what a king would cost — your sons for his army, your daughters for his kitchens, a tenth of everything, and one day you will cry out because of the king you chose, and the LORD will not answer you. They heard the whole list and said: nevertheless, we will have a king.

So God gave them one. He gave them precisely what they insisted on, and the giving was not approval. There is a verse elsewhere that says it exactly: he gave them what they asked, but sent a wasting disease among them (Ps. 106:15).

That is worth stopping on, because most of us have quietly learned to read an answered prayer as a divine endorsement, and Scripture will not let us. Some of what you have been given, you were given because you would not stop asking for it. The test is not whether the door opened; some doors open because you leaned on them. Before you take an opening as approval, ask whether you would still have wanted this if God had said no first — and whether you gave him a real chance to.

The son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years. The forty is Paul's, not the Old Testament's. The Hebrew of 1 Samuel 13:1 has been damaged in transmission and no longer gives Saul's regnal years at all, which is why the modern versions carry a gap and a footnote there. Josephus, writing a generation after Paul, also reckons forty, so Paul is repeating the received figure of his day rather than inventing one.

And there is something in that verse the men in the synagogue would have caught instantly, though Paul says nothing about himself and does not need to. A Saul. Of the tribe of Benjamin. Standing in front of them, a dozen verses after Luke told us his name is now Paul, is a Saul of the tribe of Benjamin (Phil. 3:5; Rom. 11:1) who spent his early career being everything a tall, impressive, self-directed Benjamite could be, and was removed from it on a road. He does not draw the line. He tells the story of the first Saul and moves on to David, and every man in the room knew the preacher's name.

And when he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king. The commendation Paul quotes is two Scriptures joined — a man after his own heart from 1 Samuel 13:14, and I have found David my servant from Psalm 89:20 — and it raises the question every honest reader of the Old Testament ends up asking out loud.

How can God call David a man after his own heart? This is the man who took another man's wife; who, when the pregnancy could not be hidden, tried to manoeuvre the husband home to cover it; and who, when the husband proved too loyal to go, had him posted where the fighting was heaviest and the line pulled back from him. Adultery finished off by murder by memorandum. And this is God's man?

Three things, and they matter.

First, the sentence was spoken long before Bathsheba, and it is not a character reference. God says it in 1 Samuel 13, at the moment Saul is rejected, and its emphasis falls on the seeking rather than on the man found: the LORD has sought out a man after his own heart. It describes God's choice. I have found in David — the finding is God's verb, and David is its object.

Second, what actually separates the two kings is not that one sinned and the other did not. It is what each did when he was caught. Saul, confronted over Amalek, argued: the people did it, the animals were meant for sacrifice, and in any case he had obeyed. He was still explaining when Samuel walked away. David, confronted by Nathan with a story and one sentence — you are the man — said four words: I have sinned against the LORD (2 Sam. 12:13). No lawyer, no context, no blame shifted. And then he wrote it up, set it to music, and handed it to the choirmaster, so that the whole nation could sing his worst hour back to him forever (Ps. 51). That is not a man protecting his reputation. That is a man who cared more about being right with God than about being thought well of.

Third, who will do all my will is measured against the man he replaced. Saul had one plain instruction at Amalek and kept the best of the livestock. David's life, for all its wreckage, ran in the direction God pointed; he never went after other gods, and that is precisely the measurement the books of Kings apply to every later king in the line.

So if you are afraid your failures have disqualified you, notice that God's chosen king has a murder in his file. And if you are tempted to use that as cover, notice what it cost him: a dead child, a fractured house, a son in armed rebellion, and a psalm he had to sing in public for the rest of his life. God's man is not the man who never falls. He is the man who cannot stay down, because God will not leave him there.

The question this verse puts to you is not whether you have sinned. It is narrower than that, and you can answer it from this week: what did you do the last time you were found out?

verseByVerse.quote: "Of this man's offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Of this man's offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised.

This is the sentence the whole recital has been walking toward, and the last three words carry the weight: as he promised.

Set the promise where it was made. It is night, and David is settled at last — the wars are over, he is living in a house of cedar, and it strikes him that the ark of God is still under canvas. He proposes to build a temple. God's answer, through Nathan, declines the offer and returns it multiplied: you will not build me a house; I will build you one. I will raise up your offspring after you... and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever... your throne shall be established forever (2 Sam. 7:12–16).

Now measure that promise against what had actually become of it by the time Paul stood up in Pisidia.

Four hundred years after Nathan, Nebuchadnezzar's army broke into Jerusalem. The last king of David's line, Zedekiah, was caught fleeing and brought to Riblah. They killed his sons in front of him, and then they put out his eyes — so that the last thing he ever saw was the end of the dynasty (2 Kgs 25:7). He was led away in chains, and no son of David sat on a throne in Jerusalem again. Not under the Persians. Not under the Greeks. Not under the Maccabees, who were priests and not David's house. Not under Herod, who was an Idumean and knew it, and killed his own family to keep what he had taken. Some six hundred years, and the royal line had run down into a joiner's shop in a village of a few hundred people in the hills of Galilee.

Any reasonable observer would have called that promise dead. It had not merely been delayed. It had been publicly falsified, on a scale everybody could see, for two dozen generations.

And a travelling tentmaker stands up in a provincial synagogue and says: as he promised. Not as he intended. Not as we still hope. As he promised — and here he is.

Notice the verb, too. God brought a Saviour to Israel. He did not offer them the possibility of one, or make salvation available in principle. He led one in, in a body, to a particular people, at a particular date, under a named governor.

And notice the title, which had a rival in that town. Pisidian Antioch was a Roman colony, refounded by Augustus and settled with discharged legionaries, and Saviour was a word the empire used of its emperor on inscriptions and coins — the man who ended the civil wars and gave the world peace. Paul walks into a town full of old soldiers and old loyalties and hands the title to a crucified Galilean. Everyone in the room understood that there was only room for one.

What this verse asks of you is simple and rather searching. Name the promise of God you have quietly written off — not denied, just shelved, because of how long it has been. Then look again at how late this one was, and how completely kept.

verseByVerse.quote: "Before his coming, John had proclaimed a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel. And as John was finishing his course, he said, 'What do you suppose that I am? I am not he. No, but behold, after me one is coming, the sandals of whose feet I am not worthy to untie.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why does John the Baptist appear in a sermon preached seven hundred miles from the Jordan, to a congregation of Anatolian Jews and Gentile God-fearers, some fifteen years after John was executed?

Because they had heard of him. That is not a guess: Luke shows us the evidence twice, both times in this same mission field. At Ephesus Paul finds twelve men who had received John's baptism and had never so much as heard that there is a Holy Spirit (19:1–7); and Apollos turns up in the same city, a learned Alexandrian Jew, accurate about Jesus as far as he went, knowing only the baptism of John (18:25). John's movement had travelled the trade routes into the diaspora and arrived without its ending. There were synagogues across the empire where the Baptist was honoured as the last of the prophets and nobody knew what had happened next.

So Paul is not padding a sermon with background. He is standing exactly where a real gap in his hearers' knowledge sits, and closing it: yes, John — and here is what John himself said he was for.

Then look at what Luke chose to preserve. As John was finishing his course. The word is dromos, a runner's track, the distance a man has been set to cover. Paul will use it of himself twice — I do not account my life of any value... if only I may finish my course (20:24), and at the very end, I have finished the race (2 Tim. 4:7).

Now put that word against the facts. John's course finished in a cell in Herod's fortress, cut short in the dark because a girl danced well at a birthday party and her mother wanted a head on a dish. He had been left in that cell long enough to send word out asking whether he had backed the right man after all. By every measurement we normally use, it was a wasted, unfinished, humiliating end.

Scripture calls it finishing his course. That is not sentiment; it is a different way of measuring. A course is finished when the distance you were given has been run, not when you have arrived somewhere impressive. If you are afraid that your life is going to end mid-sentence — a work half done, a family not yet safe, something somebody else will have to pick up — this is the word you need. God does not measure a life by where it stopped. He measures it by whether the ground assigned to you was covered.

And what did John say at the height of his influence, with crowds coming out to him and delegations sent to ask who he was? What do you suppose that I am? I am not he.

He spent his greatest capital on a denial. And then the picture: the sandals of whose feet I am not worthy to untie. The rabbis had a saying that a disciple should do for his teacher anything a slave would do, with one exception — he must not loosen his master's sandal, because that was too degrading a thing to ask of a free Israelite. John reaches for the one job a disciple was excused and says he is not fit for it.

This is the pattern for everybody whose work is preparatory, which is to say nearly everybody. The parent whose child will go further. The teacher whose pupil will be the better preacher. The man who trained his own replacement and now watches him do it better. I am not he is not false modesty. It is accuracy, and it is the most liberating sentence a servant can say, because the moment you stop being the point you stop having to be impressive.

Ask yourself honestly which you would find harder: to be told your ministry had failed, or to be told it had succeeded and that its entire value lay in making somebody else visible. John was told the second, and called it his joy.

verseByVerse.quote: "Brothers, sons of the family of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, to us has been sent the message of this salvation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Something happens to the pronouns here, and it is the moment the sermon stops being a history lesson.

For ten verses Paul has spoken in the third person. God chose our fathers; he brought them out; they asked for a king; he raised up David. Then: Brothers, sons of the family of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, to us has been sent the message of this salvation. To us. Not to them, back there. To the people in this room, this morning.

Every sermon has to make that turn or it is a lecture, and this is how Paul makes it — not by raising his voice, but with a pronoun.

Notice that he names both groups again, in the same order as verse 16. He opened with Jews and God-fearers, and now, at the point of application, he names them both and puts them inside a single word: us. There is no smaller circle for the Gentiles at the back. Nothing in this sermon has been for the born Israelites only.

Consider what that does to a God-fearer hearing it. He has spent years in the position of a guest at somebody else's family reading of a will. The promises were read aloud in his hearing every Sabbath and were addressed to a household he could not enter without a knife. And now a visiting rabbi, speaking with the full authority of the Scriptures that have just been read, says: to us. Not you may listen. Not you may hope. Sent to us.

Look at the verb, too. The message has been sent — passive, and the sender is not named for the good reason that no naming is needed. It did not develop. It was not discovered by clever men, or arrived at by anyone thinking hard about God. It was dispatched. The word behind our word apostle is inside that verb. Somebody sent this, deliberately, to a particular address.

This salvation, too — not salvation in general, not a religious idea of rescue, but this one: the specific, dated, local thing that happened to a named man under a named governor, which Paul is about to describe in five verses. Christianity is not a theory about how people get saved. It is a report of something done.

Here is the test. If somebody asked you who the gospel was sent to, you would probably answer, without thinking, something like everyone, or people who need it. Both true, and both a way of standing at a polite distance from it. Paul's sentence is narrower and much harder to get out of: it was sent to us. Which means it was put into your hands, addressed, by name — and you have signed for it.

verseByVerse.quote: "For those who live in Jerusalem and their rulers, because they did not recognize him nor understand the utterances of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him. And though they found in him no guilt worthy of death, they asked Pilate to have him executed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Read the middle clause again, and then look around the room Paul is standing in: the utterances of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath.

The prophets had been read aloud in that synagogue perhaps twenty minutes earlier. It is what got Paul on his feet in the first place (v. 15). He is not offering the congregation a general fact about Jerusalem's religious habits. He is describing them. The men who missed the Messiah were men who did exactly what this congregation had done before he stood up — in a building like this one, on a day like this one.

That is the sting, and Paul does not have to point it out.

Then the sentence that ought to stop anyone who reads it carefully. They did not understand the prophets, and so they fulfilled them by condemning him. Their blindness did not frustrate the Scriptures. It carried them out. Every step the authorities took to shut this business down had been written down centuries earlier: the betrayal price, the false witnesses, the silence under accusation, the sentence, the cross, the tomb. They were not derailing God's plan. They were the instrument of it, and they did not know.

Which raises the obvious question, and Scripture does not dodge it. If they were fulfilling prophecy, were they guilty? Paul answers in the very next breath, and the answer is yes: they found in him no guilt worthy of death, they asked Pilate to have him executed. Two clauses, and everything is in the gap between them. This was not a court that got it wrong. This was a court that got it right and asked for the execution anyway. Luke's Gospel has Pilate say three separate times that he finds no guilt in the man (Luke 23:4, 14, 22).

So both things stand: they acted in ignorance, and they are answerable. Peter had already held those two together in Jerusalem itself, and that ground was covered at 3:17; it does not need going over again. But notice that Paul does not use their ignorance to excuse them, and he does not use God's sovereignty to either. He says they did not know, and he says they had no case and asked for the death anyway, and he lets the two sentences stand side by side without softening either one.

Now the part aimed at us. Almost everyone reading this quietly assumes he would have known better. It is very hard not to; we have the end of the story and they did not. So be exact about who these people were. They were the most Scripture-soaked population on earth. They read it in the language it was written in. They had it read publicly every week of their lives. They lived in the city where it was kept and worked in the building where the promises were housed. And they looked straight at the fulfilment and saw a blasphemer.

Familiarity with the Bible is not the same thing as recognition of Christ. You can read a chapter every morning for thirty years and be no nearer. That is not an argument for reading less; it is a reason to pray before you read, because the difference between them and us was never that we are cleverer.

And here is a test you can actually run, because it exposes the mechanism. The rulers had a reason to misread the prophets: recognising this man would have cost them their standing, their income and their control of the temple. So ask what a plain reading of Scripture would cost you — in your marriage, your money, your reputation among people whose good opinion you value. And then ask, honestly, whether that happens to be a passage you have found unusually difficult to be sure about.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they had carried out all that was written of him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had carried out all that was written of him. All of it — and it is worth refusing to leave that vague, because Paul certainly did not.

Sold for thirty pieces of silver, which were flung down in the temple and spent on a field (Zech. 11:12–13). The shepherd struck and the sheep scattered (Zech. 13:7). Silent in front of his accusers, like a sheep before its shearers (Isa. 53:7). Hands and feet pierced, his clothing divided by lot while men stood and stared (Ps. 22:16–18). Numbered with transgressors, one on either side (Isa. 53:12). Given sour wine for his thirst (Ps. 69:21). Not one of his bones broken, like the Passover lamb (Ps. 34:20; Exod. 12:46). And a grave with a rich man (Isa. 53:9) — which is exactly where this verse ends up.

These were not obscure texts that could be bent into shape afterwards. They were in the scrolls in that synagogue's own cupboard, and Paul is preaching to men who could go and check him.

There is a small thing in the grammar worth clearing up, since a careful reader will trip on it. Paul says they took him down and they laid him in a tomb — and the they of the previous verse were the rulers who asked Pilate to have him killed. In fact it was Joseph of Arimathea who went and asked for the body, with Nicodemus and about seventy-five pounds of spices, and a tomb Joseph had cut for himself (Luke 23:50–53; John 19:38–42). Paul is compressing, speaking of Jerusalem as a single actor, the way we say that a city did something. He is not correcting the Gospels; he is summarising in one clause what took them a paragraph.

And do not hurry past the burial. It is in the sermon, and it is in the creed — crucified, dead, and buried — and it is there because the burial is the notary's seal on the death. A man who is buried has been handled, examined, wrapped, carried and shut in by people with no interest whatever in pretending. Every theory that Jesus merely fainted on the cross and revived in the cool of the tomb has to explain how a man in that condition, sealed behind a stone he could not have reached from the inside, presented himself three days later as the conqueror of death. The stone was moved from the outside. Somebody had to move it, and it was not the occupant working the door.

Why 'the tree' here, and not 'the cross'? The word is xylon, which means simply 'wood' or 'timber' — a beam, a stake, a tree. The apostles use it of the cross on purpose (also 5:30; 10:39; Gal. 3:13; 1 Pet. 2:24), to sound a deliberate echo of the Law: 'if a man... is hanged on a tree... a hanged man is cursed by God; you shall bury him the same day' (Deut. 21:22–23). To call the cross a 'tree' is therefore to load the word with meaning: Jesus hung where the accursed criminal hung, bearing the curse of God in our place — as Paul spells out, 'Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, for it is written, Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree' (Gal. 3:13). And notice the precise fit right here: they 'took him down from the tree' and buried him at once, fulfilling that very command not to leave the body on the tree overnight. The word is no loose synonym; it preaches the heart of the cross — he took our curse. (Some also hear a quiet echo that the curse which entered the world by a tree in Eden was undone on a tree at Calvary — a lovely thought, though the plain reference is Deuteronomy's curse.)

verseByVerse.quote: "But God raised him from the dead, and for many days he appeared to those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are now his witnesses to the people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But God raised him from the dead.

Track the subjects of the verbs for a moment, because Paul has built this. In verses 27 and 28 the subject is they: they did not recognise him, they did not understand, they condemned him, they found no guilt, they asked Pilate. In verse 29 it is still they: they carried it out, they took him down, they laid him in a tomb. Men are doing everything — and what men do reaches its natural end in a sealed tomb, which is where every human story has always finished.

Then the subject changes. But God. Two words, and the direction of the whole history reverses. The tomb is the last place in the paragraph where men are the subject of the verbs.

Now the evidence, and notice how careful Paul is with it. He does not say the resurrection was felt, or that the disciples came to a new understanding of things. He gives duration, movement, and named witnesses.

For many days he appeared. Luke has already given us the number: forty (1:3). This was not one shattering moment in a garden at dawn that could be put down to grief and poor light. It was six weeks.

To those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem. The same men, the whole way. They were with him in the north, they walked south with him, they were there when it went wrong. Their testimony spans the entire story; they are not late arrivals who turned up after the interesting part.

And then the phrase that carries the argument: who are now his witnesses to the people. Now. Present tense. Paul is speaking some fifteen years after the event, in a city a long way from Judea, and the men he is citing are alive at that moment and can be found and questioned. It is exactly the move he makes in writing to Corinth — more than five hundred saw him at once, most of whom are still alive (1 Cor. 15:6). That is a strange sentence to write unless you positively want your readers to go and check.

There is something else here worth noticing. Paul had his own encounter with the risen Christ, and it is the best story he owns; Luke will tell it three times before this book is finished. He does not use it. He rests the resurrection on the testimony of the Twelve — men he had been hunting at the time — and puts the weight on witnesses rather than on his own experience. That is the right way round, and it is the opposite of how most of us argue for our faith.

Which matters for the reader who feels his own experience of God is too thin to rest anything on. Your assurance does not stand on the vividness of what happened to you. It stands on what happened to Jesus, in public, in front of people who could be named, in a city where the authorities had every motive to produce a body and never did.

verseByVerse.quote: "And we bring you the good news that what God promised to the fathers, this he has fulfilled to us their children by raising Jesus, as also it is written in the second Psalm, 'You are my Son, today I have begotten you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we bring you the good news. The verb is euangelizometha, and this is the first time in Acts we hear Paul use gospel language of his own preaching. Notice what its content turns out to be. Not advice, not a philosophy, not a technique for living better — a report that a promise has been kept.

And kept to whom? What God promised to the fathers, this he has fulfilled to us their children. The fathers were given the promise. The children were given the thing. Abraham died holding a word from God about a family he could not see; a man sitting in the third row of a synagogue in Asia Minor is handed the fulfilment. Hebrews puts it exactly: they died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar (Heb. 11:13, 39–40). We are the generation that took delivery of what they signed for.

Then the proof text — and it needs a guard, because read carelessly it will teach a reader something the Bible does not: You are my Son, today I have begotten you (Ps. 2:7), applied to the resurrection.

Taken flatly, that sounds as though Jesus became the Son of God on Easter morning — that he was a man whom God promoted, adopted, upgraded. That teaching has a name and a long history, and it is wrong. Four things put it out of court.

First, look at the psalm Paul is quoting. Psalm 2 is a coronation psalm. Its scene is a king being installed while the nations rage, and the today in it is the day of enthronement, not the day of anybody's conception. Israel's kings were addressed as God's son at their accession — I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son (2 Sam. 7:14); I will make him the firstborn (Ps. 89:27). The language is throne language from the start.

Second, Paul says elsewhere precisely what the resurrection did to Jesus's sonship, and he chooses his verb with care: he was declared to be the Son of God in power... by his resurrection from the dead (Rom. 1:4). Declared, not created. The resurrection published a fact; it did not manufacture one.

Third, the New Testament has the Son in place long before there was anything to raise him from. God has spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed the heir of all things, through whom also he created the world (Heb. 1:2) — and Hebrews then quotes this very psalm three verses later (Heb. 1:5) without the least embarrassment. God sent forth his Son (Gal. 4:4), which is not something anyone can do with a son he does not yet have.

Fourth, the identical guard is needed at Peter's Pentecost sermon, where God has made him both Lord and Christ (2:36), and it is worked out at that verse. The two stand or fall together, and the answer in both places is the same: enthronement, not manufacture.

So what changed on the third day? Not who Jesus is. What changed is who knows it. On the Friday the public verdict on him was that he was a blasphemer, justly executed, and heaven had said nothing. On the Sunday God said something — and what he said was: this is my Son, here is the proof, and I am putting him on the throne.

One small curiosity for the interested reader. A few old manuscripts of Acts have Paul cite this as the first psalm rather than the second, which is not a blunder but a memory of an older Jewish way of counting, in which our Psalms 1 and 2 were read as a single opening piece. It changes nothing, and it is a quiet witness to how carefully these texts were copied — awkward details and all.

If you have ever wondered what God thinks of Jesus, you are not left to guess. He said it out loud, in an empty tomb, in a way that cannot be argued with, and the sentence he used was: You are my Son.

verseByVerse.quote: "And as for the fact that he raised him from the dead, no more to return to corruption, he has spoken in this way, 'I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David.' Therefore he says also in another psalm, 'You will not let your Holy One see corruption.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul now sets two Old Testament texts side by side, and to a modern reader the join looks arbitrary — a line from Isaiah about David's blessings, then a line from a psalm about a body that does not decay, and somehow the two are supposed to prove a resurrection. It is worth seeing what he is actually doing, because it is not sleight of hand.

The two texts share a word. Isaiah 55:3 promises the holy and sure blessings of David; Psalm 16:10 says you will not let your Holy One see corruption. In the Greek Bible these congregations used, the same root stands behind holy in both places — hosios. Linking two passages by a shared term was a recognised method of Jewish exposition, and every trained man in that synagogue would have followed the move without needing it explained. Paul is not lifting verses out of context. He is arguing in the way his hearers had themselves been taught to argue, and inviting them to go and read both passages.

And the argument itself is tight. God swore David an everlasting covenant, and Isaiah calls its benefits sure — the word means reliable, guaranteed, the sort of thing you could take into a court. But how sure can a covenant be if the man it was made with is in a tomb, and everyone who inherits it ends in a tomb as well? A dynasty of corpses is not an everlasting kingdom. If the promises to David are to be sure, at some point somebody in that line has to stop dying. Which is why Paul reaches for the second text.

Now hold on to the phrase he puts in front of them both: no more to return to corruption. That is the clause which separates Easter from every other raising in the Bible, and it is a distinction most Christians have never been taught to make.

The widow's son at Nain sat up and spoke — and one day was buried again. Jairus's daughter got up and was given something to eat, and grew old, and died. Lazarus came out of the tomb still bound in his grave clothes, and somewhere in Judea there is dust that used to be Lazarus. Every one of those was a reprieve, a postponement, a body handed back on loan. Death let them go and then took them.

Jesus was not resuscitated. He was raised — no more to return to corruption — out the far side of death and beyond its reach, into a body that will not wear out and cannot be reclaimed. Death has no second claim on him.

And that is why the Christian's grave is not a postponement either. What is promised to us is the same kind of thing: this perishable body must put on the imperishable (1 Cor. 15:53–54). If Jesus had merely been revived, the best any of us could hope for would be more time. Because he was raised past corruption, what waits for the believer is not a longer loan but a body given outright.

verseByVerse.quote: "For David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep and was laid with his fathers and saw corruption, but he whom God raised up did not see corruption."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the argument's last step, and it is an argument, not an assertion: Psalm 16 cannot be about David, because David decayed.

Peter had made the identical point at Pentecost, and he made it with a piece of evidence lying on the ground in front of him — his tomb is with us to this day (2:29). You could walk to it. Paul, seven hundred miles away, has nothing to point at, so he argues it from the text and from a fact nobody in the room would dispute: David died, was buried with his fathers, and his body did what bodies do. Two apostles, the same psalm, the same conclusion, each preaching it to the congregation actually in front of him. The comparison is worth making, because it shows how these men worked: the gospel does not change between Jerusalem and Pisidia, but the way of putting it does.

Do not rush past the description of David's life, though, because it is one of the quietly weightiest sentences in the New Testament: David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep.

The Greek can be turned two ways, and the older versions turn it the other way — that David served his own generation by the will of God. Both readings are true and both are humbling, and either way the boundary in the sentence is the same: in his own generation. Not in every generation. Not in ours.

David did not fix Israel. He left a divided family, an unbuilt temple, a census plague, and a son who would undo a good deal of what he had built. He did what God gave him to do in the years he was given, and then he stopped. That was enough, and it is recorded as enough.

If your own work feels small and local — a congregation of forty, a family, a class of children, one difficult relative — this is the sentence to keep. You are not asked to serve the purpose of God in history. You are asked to serve it in your own generation, which is the only one you have been issued with. Nobody in Scripture is ever commended for the size of his sphere.

And then Paul refuses to be sentimental about the end of it. Fell asleep, and was laid with his fathers, and saw corruption. The man after God's own heart rotted in the ground. Scripture does not flinch and does not decorate.

But he whom God raised up did not see corruption. Now notice what that does to the gentle word Paul used a moment earlier. Christians call death sleep. We put it on gravestones. It is a lovely word, and it is only usable because one body in the history of the world went into a tomb and did not decay. Take verse 37 away and fell asleep is a euphemism. Leave verse 37 where it stands and it is a description.

verseByVerse.quote: "Let it be known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let it be known to you therefore. Everything up to this point has been argument — the history, the promise, the death, the witnesses, the two psalms. This is the conclusion drawn from it, and the whole sermon has been climbing toward these two verses.

And the first thing to notice is the verb: forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you. Not offered on conditions. Not made available to suitable applicants. Proclaimed — the word for a herald standing in a public square reading out what the king has decided. There is a world of difference between a notice explaining how to apply for a pardon and a herald announcing that one has been granted. Paul is not describing a process the synagogue might enter. He is reading out an amnesty.

Then the sentence that will fill two of his letters: by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses.

The English says freed. The Greek word underneath it is dikaioutai — justified — and this is its first appearance in Acts and the earliest recorded use of it by Paul anywhere. It is a courtroom word. To be justified is not to be improved, cleaned up, or given a fresh start. It is to have a judge declare, formally and on the record, that you are in the right.

Stage it, because the picture is what makes it land. A man is in the dock. He did it. The evidence is in, the witnesses were credible, his own counsel has stopped pretending. And the judge, who has read every page of it, says: not guilty. And the reason is not that the file was thin, and not that the judge is easy-going, and not that the offence turned out to matter less than it seemed. The reason is that the sentence has already been served by somebody else, and the court holds the receipt. That is justification. It is why Paul can put everyone who believes in the same sentence as freed from everything, and it is what the Reformers spent their lives on.

Now the other half, which the men in that synagogue felt far more sharply than we do: from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses.

What could the law of Moses not do? Be specific here, because the general answer — that nobody keeps it perfectly — is true and is not the whole of it. The law had an elaborate machinery for sin: sacrifices, washings, a priesthood, a day of atonement once a year. But that machinery had a limit written into it, and every Israelite knew exactly where the limit was. The offerings covered sins committed unwittingly, in ignorance, by mistake. For the sin done deliberately, with the eyes open and the hand raised, the law made no provision whatever: the person who does anything with a high hand... shall be cut off from among his people (Num. 15:30–31). There was no offering to bring. A man could stand in the temple courts with his best lamb and there was nothing in the book that would take it.

David knew that better than anybody. He had committed adultery and arranged a killing, both with his eyes wide open, and when he came to write it up he said so out loud: you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it; you will not be pleased with a burnt offering (Ps. 51:16). He was not being poetic. He was a king with unlimited access to the altar, saying that the altar had nothing for him.

And now look at what Paul has just spent ten verses doing. He has walked this congregation through the story of David — chosen, commended, the man after God's own heart, the man the promise was made to — and then says, at the top of his voice, that in Jesus there is a freeing from precisely the things the law of Moses could not free you from. He never draws the line between the two. He does not have to. He has told them the story, they know the psalm, and they can hear a thousand-year-old question being answered in their own synagogue.

So the offer here is not for tidy people who have fallen a little short. It is aimed at the high-handed sin — the one you did not drift into, the one you chose. The one nothing has ever touched: not resolutions, not service, not an unbroken run of Sundays, not a hundred confessions of the same thing. Name it, privately, now. That is what Paul means by everything from which you could not be freed.

And note the width of the door: everyone who believes. Not everyone who improves, or qualifies, or has the right ancestry — which is a startling thing to say in a room half full of men who had been told for years that their ancestry was the problem. Believes. That is the whole entry requirement, and it is deliberately the one thing a beggar can do as easily as a benefactor.

This is Galatians and Romans in embryo, in the first sermon of Paul's that we possess, years before either letter was written. He did not develop this doctrine under pressure from opponents. He preached it the first time he opened his mouth in a synagogue, because it is not his theory. It is the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: "Beware, therefore, lest what is said in the Prophets should come about: 'Look, you scoffers, be astounded and perish; for I am doing a work in your days, a work that you will not believe, even if one tells it to you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has just announced an amnesty. He ends by telling them what happens to men who laugh at one.

The quotation is Habakkuk 1:5, and its original setting is what gives it teeth. Habakkuk had been complaining — properly, out loud, in the way the Bible permits — that God was doing nothing about the corruption of Judah. How long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear? God's answer is not comfort. It is this verse: look, be astounded, for I am doing a work in your days that you would not believe if you were told.

And what was the work? Babylon. God's answer to Judah's wickedness was to raise up the Chaldeans and let them come, and Habakkuk was so appalled by the answer that he spends the rest of the chapter arguing with it. The unbelievable work in the original was a judgment nobody would credit until the siege ramps were up against their own walls.

Now hear Paul use it. God has done another unbelievable thing in your days — this time a rescue and not a ruin, a crucified man raised and forgiveness proclaimed in his name. The warning is not this might be true, so do be careful. It is: your fathers were told in advance about a work of God they refused to credit, and it arrived anyway, and it flattened the city. Do not make that mistake twice. And do not assume that because this word is good news it can safely be laughed at.

Notice too that Paul is quoting the Greek Old Testament his hearers used, which reads you scoffers, where the Hebrew we translate from reads look among the nations. In an unpointed Hebrew text the treacherous and the nations are a single consonant apart, and both traditions are ancient. He preaches from the Bible that is on the table in front of them, which is what a good preacher does.

And then the word he chooses to end on: perish. That is where the first recorded sermon of the apostle to the Gentiles lands. Not on an invitation to consider the claims of Christ at one's leisure. On astonishment and perishing. A gospel that has lost the ability to say that word is not the gospel Paul preached — and the kindness of a warning is exactly proportional to the danger it names. Nobody shouts at a man about a fire that is not burning.

But be careful who this is aimed at, because the wrong reader will take it home. It is a warning to scoffers — men who hear, understand, and treat the thing as beneath serious attention. The frightened Christian who reads this verse at midnight and wonders whether it describes him should notice something simple: a scoffer is not troubled by warnings. That is what makes him a scoffer. The alarm you feel is itself evidence that the description has not fastened on you.

So the real question the verse puts is not whether you feel certain. It is whether you have been told and are declining to act on it. And if you have read this far, the first half of that is already settled.

verseByVerse.quote: As they went out, the people begged that these things might be told them the next Sabbath. And after the meeting of the synagogue broke up, many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas, who, as they spoke with them, urged them to continue in the grace of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they went out, the people begged that these things might be told them the next Sabbath.

The verb is one of continuing action — they kept on asking, all the way out of the door, a crowd of them; and what they asked for was not a discussion or a private word but the same thing again. Say it to us again next week.

Sit with what that meant. They could not take a copy home. There was no record of the sermon, no way to hear it a second time, no Gospel to read it against; the New Testament did not exist and would not for years. They had heard the most important thing they would ever hear, once, and now they had seven days to hold it in their heads with nothing but memory and each other. That is why they begged. We carry more sermons in our pockets than we will ever listen to, and beg for none of them, and it is worth asking honestly which of us is in the worse position.

And keep this verse where Luke put it, because he is setting something up. This is the same congregation that will be filled with jealousy two verses from now. Between the begging and the jealousy lies one week, and Luke does not tell us what happened in it. He tells us only two things: that a great many people wanted to hear more, and that when the next Sabbath came the crowd was too large and too Gentile. Enthusiasm for the word of God and hostility to it can live in the same building seven days apart — and sometimes in the same person.

Meanwhile, some did not wait for next week. Many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas — and the word is the ordinary one for following a teacher, the discipleship word. Note who these are: not the Gentile God-fearers at the edge of the synagogue but people from inside it — born Jews, and Gentiles who had gone the whole way into Judaism, circumcision included. The first fruit of this mission comes out of the synagogue, not around it.

And what did the two missionaries say to their brand-new converts, walking along the street with them? Not a programme. Not a list of things to start doing. Luke says they urged them to continue in the grace of God — and the tense is again the continuing one; they kept urging it, the whole way. The first pastoral instruction ever given in that city was not do more. It was: stay.

What does it mean 'to continue in the grace of God'? 'Grace' is God's free, undeserved kindness to sinners in Christ — salvation as a gift, never a wage, never earned. To continue in it (the word means to remain, to abide, to hold fast) is to go on living every day on that same footing of free grace on which you first came in. You were welcomed home freely, with empty hands; continuing in grace means staying there — not slipping back onto the treadmill of trying to make God love you by being good enough, and not despairing when you fail, as though grace had run out. It is the very thing Paul urges on the Colossians: 'as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him' (Col. 2:6). The way in is the way on.

Picture the prodigal son. He came home expecting to earn his keep as a hired servant, and instead the father ran to him, put the robe on him, and welcomed him as a beloved son — sheer grace. Now imagine that son, a week later, quietly slinking off to the servants' quarters to start earning his place after all. That is exactly what it looks like to drift out of grace. 'Continue in the grace of God' means: stay at the Father's table as a freely-loved child. Keep coming to Christ with empty hands; keep drawing on his daily mercy for strength, forgiveness, and growth (grace is not just the door you enter by but the room you live in — 'grow in the grace... of our Lord Jesus Christ,' 2 Pet. 3:18). And keep going — persevere, do not give up. Lest this make you anxious about whether you can hold on, remember what was said at Colossians 1:23: the call to continue is real, yet the God who began this grace is the one who keeps us in it; we persevere because he preserves us. Even our continuing is grace.

verseByVerse.quote: The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord. But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and began to contradict what was spoken by Paul, reviling him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Almost the whole city. Pisidian Antioch was a Roman colony of some size, and whatever building the synagogue occupied, it did not hold the town. Picture the courtyard full, the street outside full, people standing on walls. And understand where they came from, because nobody organised this. There was no advertising and no second meeting arranged. What there was, all week, was a few hundred God-fearers going home to Gentile neighbours and Gentile relatives and saying: you will not believe what a man said in the synagogue on Saturday.

That is still how it happens, and it is worth noticing that the largest response in this chapter came through people whose names Luke never gives, doing something nobody commissioned them to do.

But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy.

Two things must be said about that sentence, and neither cancels the other. The first is that Luke cannot possibly mean the Jewish people as such. The preacher is a Jew. So is Barnabas. So are the converts of verse 43, and so is every Christian in the story so far. Luke means the leadership of that synagogue, in that city, on that morning. The church's long and shameful habit of reading sentences like this one as a verdict on a race is a misuse of Scripture that has cost innumerable lives, and the man speaking here is the man who wrote that he could wish himself accursed for the sake of his own people (Rom. 9:3).

The second is that the jealousy is not hard to understand, and we should not pretend it is alien to us. These were men who had kept a minority faith alive in a pagan colony, at real cost, for generations. They had built the congregation, maintained the scrolls, and taught the God-fearers whatever those Gentiles knew about the true God. Last Sabbath the synagogue was theirs. This Sabbath it is full of people who have come to hear two strangers who arrived on foot a fortnight ago with nothing.

And notice what they were jealous of. Not error — they never do answer Paul's argument, then or later. They were jealous of a crowd. Luke says precisely what set it off: they saw the crowds.

Here is the test, and it is a nasty one to run honestly. Think of the last time God did something obviously good through somebody whose success made your own work look small — the neighbouring church that grew while yours did not, the younger man who preaches better than you, the colleague who was handed the thing you had been quietly working toward. What was the first thing you felt, before you corrected it? Not what you said. What you felt. That feeling is in this verse, and in this verse it ends with a man being driven out of a city.

And watch how the opposition degrades. First they contradict — that is at least an argument, and an argument can be answered. Then they are reviling him, and Luke's word for it is the one behind our word blasphemy: abuse, slander, the tearing down of a man instead of an answer to what he said. Both verbs are continuous. This went on.

It is a reliable sign, and you can use it in both directions. When a case moves from the argument to the man, the argument has been lost. And when it is your own tone that has moved from the argument to the man, it is worth asking what you are actually defending.

verseByVerse.quote: And Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly, saying, "It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you. Since you thrust it aside and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles. For so the Lord has commanded us, saying, 'I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly. The word is the great Acts word for open, unguarded, free speech — the thing the church prayed for when the threats started in Jerusalem and was given on the spot (4:29–31). It does not mean loudly. It means without editing.

It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you. Necessary is Luke's word for divine obligation — the same word he uses for the Christ who must suffer. This order was not tact, and not a strategy for finding sympathetic hearers. It was owed. The promises were made to this people; the Messiah came from them; the Scriptures were kept by them. To have gone anywhere else first would have misrepresented what God had actually done. It is what Paul later compressed into a single phrase: to the Jew first and also to the Greek (Rom. 1:16).

And here a guard is needed, because we are turning to the Gentiles has been read for centuries as though God had finished with Israel on that Sabbath in Pisidia. He had not, and Paul demonstrates it with his feet. He says this here; he says it again in Corinth (18:6); he says it again in Rome, in the closing scene of the book (28:28) — and in between, on arriving in each new city, the first place he goes is the synagogue. He said it three times because each time it was a local verdict on a local refusal, not a final verdict on a people. His own answer to the question is flat: has God rejected his people? By no means! For I myself am an Israelite (Rom. 11:1).

Then the sentence that ought to be uncomfortable: since you thrust it aside and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life.

Look at who does the judging. Not Paul. Not God, not yet. You judge yourselves. Nobody in that synagogue stood up and said, I am unworthy of eternal life. What they said was something far more ordinary — not from him; not on those terms; not now. Paul tells them that this is the same sentence, written out in full. A refusal is a verdict, and the man who gives it has passed it on himself.

That is worth carrying out of the first century, because most refusals of Christ are not defiant. They are polite, reasonable and postponed. And Paul's point is that the politeness does not alter what has been decided. If a man is handed the only bread there is and says, thank you, not just now, he has settled the question of whether he will eat, however courteously he put it.

Then the Scripture, and this is the most remarkable move in the chapter: For so the Lord has commanded us, saying, I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.

That is Isaiah 49:6, and in Isaiah it is spoken to the Servant — that is, to the Messiah. Simeon understood it that way when he held the baby in the temple and called him a light for revelation to the Gentiles (Luke 2:32). And Paul takes a text about Christ and says the Lord commanded us — meaning himself and Barnabas, two tired men who have just been shouted down in a provincial synagogue.

He is not confusing himself with the Messiah. He is saying something that ought to steady every ordinary Christian who has ever felt that mission is somebody else's department: the church's task is not a separate assignment running alongside Christ's. It is a share in his. What the Servant was sent to do, his people are now doing in him — which is why Paul can call himself an ambassador and say that God makes his appeal through us (2 Cor. 5:20).

And notice which verse of Isaiah he chose, because it is precisely the one that carries the argument. The full sentence runs: it is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob... I will make you as a light for the nations. God himself says that restoring Israel alone would be too small a commission. Paul has just been accused of abandoning his people's hope. He answers by producing the one verse in which God calls that hope, taken by itself, not big enough.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the Gentiles heard this, they began rejoicing and glorifying the word of the Lord, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed. And the word of the Lord was spreading throughout the whole region.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the Gentiles heard this, they began rejoicing and glorifying the word of the Lord.

Heard what, exactly? That the door stood open to them, by name, from a Jewish preacher, out of a Jewish prophet, in a Jewish building, on the very morning the leadership of that building was in the act of shutting them out. These were people who had spent years at the edge of somebody else's promise. Now a man with the Scriptures open has told them that the promise was addressed to them all along, and that God said so seven hundred years ago.

Luke's verbs are continuous: they kept on rejoicing. And notice what they glorified. Not Paul, whom they had every reason to make much of — the word of the Lord. The verb is one normally kept for glorifying God himself, and Luke lets it fall on the message.
