When people are genuinely converted, the thing they cannot stop praising is what they heard, not the man they heard it from.

And the result: the word of the Lord was spreading throughout the whole region — again the continuous tense; it went on spreading. Which is worth pausing on, because in two verses' time Paul and Barnabas are expelled from that district. They are not the ones spreading it. Pisidian Antioch sat on a Roman road at the head of a wide upland region of villages and market towns that Paul never visited, and the gospel reached them anyway, carried by people whose names nobody wrote down, going home and telling their families. The missionaries were removed. The word was not.

But between the rejoicing and the spreading Luke sets down a single clause, without explanation and without apology, and Christians have been arguing about it ever since: as many as were appointed to eternal life believed.

Why is this one of the strongest verses in Scripture for election? Three things give it force. 'Appointed' (tetagmenoi) is a perfect passive participle — a completed action done to them by another, and the unnamed agent, as so often, is God (the 'divine passive'): 'as many as had been appointed [by God] to eternal life believed.' The order is decisive: the appointment comes first and the believing follows — faith is the fruit, God's prior choice the root. And the context sharpens it: two verses earlier the unbelieving Jews 'judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life' (v. 46) — rejection at their own door — while the believing Gentiles are those 'appointed to eternal life.' Luke sets the two side by side without embarrassment: responsibility in unbelief, grace in belief. It fits a steady pattern — 'all that the Father gives me will come to me' (John 6:37); 'you do not believe because you are not among my sheep' (John 10:26); 'the Lord opened her heart' (Acts 16:14); Eph. 1:4–5; Rom. 8:29–30.

How do our non-Reformed brothers read it? Godly, Bible-loving Christians who are not Calvinist honour this verse and read it mainly two ways. First, some take the participle as middle voice, 'as many as had disposed themselves toward eternal life' — describing the people's own receptivity rather than a prior decree. (The form can be middle or passive; Reformed readers answer that, given Luke's usage and the contrast with v. 46, the passive with God as agent is far more natural — but the middle is honestly held.) Second, the classic Arminian reading affirms a genuine appointing grounded in God's foreknowledge: foreseeing who would freely believe, God appointed those to eternal life (Rom. 8:29). Election is real, but conditioned on foreseen faith, so free will is preserved. A few read it corporately — the destiny of the believing people as a body, entered by faith.

And it must be held in charity. What unites us comes before what divides: every side believes salvation is by grace through faith in Christ alone, that God is sovereign and good, that sinners are truly responsible, and that the gospel must be freely offered to all — exactly what Paul is doing here. The difference is over how God's sovereignty and our believing fit together. In honesty, many even non-Calvinist scholars grant the plain passive is the most natural sense of the Greek; but this is an in-house disagreement among brothers who love the same Lord and Bible, to be carried with humility, not point-scoring. And note what the verse does not do: it does not make God the author of anyone's unbelief (v. 46 lays that on the rejecters), nor does it dampen evangelism — in Acts, election runs right alongside the most tireless preaching the world has seen. Rightly held, it humbles the believer, banishes boasting, and turns assurance into worship: if I believe, it is because grace appointed me, sought me, and opened my heart.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Jews incited the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city, stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and drove them out of their district. But they shook off the dust from their feet against them and went to Iconium.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the Jews incited the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city.

Luke is being precise, and the precision tells you exactly how it was done. The synagogue could not touch Paul and Barnabas directly; they had broken no law, and in a Roman colony you do not simply remove people. So the pressure went round another way. Women of rank held a genuinely prominent place in the civic and religious life of the cities of Asia Minor, and a good number of them were the synagogue's own God-fearers — devout, respected, and married to the men who ran the colony. The leadership went to the women; the women went to their husbands; the husbands were the magistrates.

Not a mob, then. A word in the right drawing rooms, and by the end of the week the missionaries were put out of the district by due process. That is what most opposition to the gospel has actually looked like down the centuries: not violence but influence, applied quietly by people who never have to raise their voices, arriving as a decision from an office that never explains itself.

There is a small, hard irony in it as well. The women are called devout. They were the fruit of the synagogue's own patient work among the Gentiles — and they were used to expel the men who had just told them the promises were theirs.

But they shook off the dust from their feet against them and went to Iconium.

This is not a gesture Paul invented in temper. It is an instruction, given by Jesus to his own men when he sent them out: if a town will not receive you, shake the dust from your feet as a testimony against them (Luke 9:5; 10:11). And it carried a meaning everybody present would have caught. A Jew returning from Gentile territory would shake the dust off at the border, refusing to carry pagan soil into the holy land. To do it to a Jewish community was to say something very hard indeed: in this matter, you are the ones on the outside.

Two guards are needed here, because the verse gets misused. First, it is not permission for an ordinary Christian to write people off in a huff. It was done by apostles, under an explicit command from Christ, after a full and public hearing, and only when the answer had become a settled and organised refusal. Second, look at what they did not do. They did not curse anybody. They did not organise resistance, appeal to Rome, or write to the colony. They did not stay to have the last word. The gesture is not revenge; it is a transfer of responsibility — you have been told, and it is now yours.

Then: and went to Iconium. Eighty miles down the road, and they start again. Which is the whole answer to the question of what a Christian does when a door is shut in his face. You do not stop; you relocate. An expulsion from one town has never yet been anything but the introduction of the gospel to the next.

And this town stayed with Paul. Thirty years later, writing his last letter from a Roman cell to a young man who had grown up further down that same road, he lists it by name: my persecutions and sufferings that happened to me at Antioch, at Iconium, and at Lystra (2 Tim. 3:11). He never forgot it. He also never once suggested it had been a mistake to go.

verseByVerse.quote: And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter's last sentence, and look who it is about. Not Paul. Not Barnabas. And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.

The disciples are the ones left behind. Take stock of their position. They are converts of a few weeks in a Roman colony that has just formally expelled their teachers. The synagogue — which for the Gentiles among them was the only religious home they had ever known — is now closed to them. The leading families of the city have shown what they are prepared to do. There is no church building, no elder, no letter from Paul, and no New Testament to read. They have a few weeks of teaching, each other, and God.

And they were filled with joy. Not coping. Not bearing up. Not relieved it had not been worse. Filled — and the tense says they went on being filled, not that it happened once on the day the apostles left.

Notice how the sentence is built, because the order explains it. Joy first, then the Holy Spirit — but the second is the source of the first. If Christian joy were a mood produced by circumstances, this verse could not exist; the circumstances here are unambiguously bad. It is not manufactured out of the situation. It arrives with a Person.

And that has to be guarded, or it will be used to beat people. This is not a command to feel cheerful, and it is not a denial of grief. Paul knelt on a beach and wept with the Ephesian elders (20:36–38). Jesus wept at a grave. The Christian position is not joy instead of sorrow but, as Paul put it, sorrowful, yet always rejoicing (2 Cor. 6:10) — two things at once; and anyone who has buried a believer knows exactly what that means and how it is possible.

So do not test yourself by asking whether you are happy. Ask a narrower question, which is actually answerable: is there anything in your life at the moment that is gladness you cannot account for from your circumstances? Any residue of contentment your situation does not explain and does not deserve? That, and not cheerfulness, is what this verse is describing, and it has a name and an address — filled with the Holy Spirit.

Antioch got rid of the preachers. It could not get the joy out of the town.

13.theology: Election and Evangelism. Acts 13:48 is the Reformed doctrine of election stated with apostolic directness: the believing of the Gentiles in Pisidian Antioch is grounded in their prior appointment to eternal life. This is not fatalism — it does not prevent preaching; it undergirds it. Paul and Barnabas preach with everything they have, to everyone who will listen, in the synagogue and in the streets. They do not know who is appointed; they preach to all. And God, through the preaching, brings to faith those he has appointed. Election is the guarantee that the mission will not ultimately fail: there are sheep in every flock that God is calling, and the voice of the gospel will reach them. This is the ground of missionary confidence in every hostile city.
13.examples:
Then: Barnabas and Saul, sent out from a worshipping, fasting, praying church, arriving in city after city with nothing but the word and the Spirit — and the word going out, and the appointed ones believing, and the disciples filled with joy even when expelled. The first missionary journey is a portrait of how the kingdom advances: through weakness and proclamation and sovereign grace.

Now: The church sends when it worships. Mission flows from the presence of God, not from strategic planning. The Antioch church was not looking for a missionary project; they were seeking God — and God spoke. The question for every congregation is not “what is our mission strategy?” but “are we in the kind of sustained, attentive, fasting prayer in which the Spirit can speak?” When he speaks, we must be ready to send our best.

14.title: Suffering and Strengthening
14.text: <sup>1</sup>Now at Iconium they entered together into the Jewish synagogue and spoke in such a way that a great number of both Jews and Greeks believed. <sup>2</sup>But the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the brothers. <sup>3</sup>So they remained for a long time, speaking boldly for the Lord, who bore witness to the word of his grace by granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands. <sup>4</sup>But the people of the city were divided; some sided with the Jews and some with the apostles. <sup>5</sup>When an attempt was made by both Gentiles and Jews, with their rulers, to mistreat and to stone them, <sup>6</sup>they learned of it and fled to Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and to the surrounding country, <sup>7</sup>and there they continued to preach the gospel. <sup>8</sup>Now at Lystra there was a man sitting who could not use his feet. He was crippled from birth and had never walked. <sup>9</sup>He listened to Paul speaking. And Paul, looking intently at him and seeing that he had faith to be made well, <sup>10</sup>said in a loud voice, “Stand upright on your feet.” And he sprang up and began walking. <sup>11</sup>And when the crowds saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in Lycaonian, “The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!” <sup>12</sup>Barnabas they called Zeus, and Paul, Hermes, because he was the chief speaker. <sup>13</sup>And the priest of Zeus, whose temple was at the entrance to the city, brought oxen and garlands to the gates and wanted to offer sacrifice with the crowds. <sup>14</sup>But when the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard of it, they tore their garments and rushed out into the crowd, crying out, <sup>15</sup>“Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men, of like nature with you, and we bring you good news, that you should turn from these vain things to a living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them. <sup>16</sup>In past generations he allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways. <sup>17</sup>Yet he did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness.” <sup>18</sup>Even with these words they scarcely restrained the people from offering sacrifice to them. <sup>19</sup>But Jews came from Antioch and Iconium, and having persuaded the crowds, they stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead. <sup>20</sup>But when the disciples gathered about him, he rose up and entered the city, and on the next day he went on with Barnabas to Derbe. <sup>21</sup>When they had preached the gospel to that city and had made many disciples, they returned to Lystra and to Iconium and to Antioch, <sup>22</sup>strengthening the souls of the disciples, encouraging them to continue in the faith, and saying that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God. <sup>23</sup>And when they had appointed elders for them in every church, with prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord in whom they had believed. <sup>24</sup>Then they passed through Pisidia and came to Pamphylia. <sup>25</sup>And when they had spoken the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia, <sup>26</sup>and from there they sailed to Antioch, where they had been commended to the grace of God for the work that they had fulfilled. <sup>27</sup>And when they arrived and gathered the church together, they declared all that God had done with them, and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. <sup>28</sup>And they remained no little time with the disciples.
14.overview:
The pattern of the first missionary journey is by now familiar: the Word is proclaimed, some believe, others oppose, the apostles are driven out, and they preach in the next city. At Lystra, the pattern intensifies. Paul heals a lame man and the crowd, speaking in Lycaonian, decides that the gods have come down. They want to sacrifice oxen to Barnabas and Paul. The apostles tear their garments — the Jewish gesture of horror at blasphemy — and push back into the crowd to preach the living God who made heaven and earth. They scarcely hold back the sacrifice.

And then the same crowd stones Paul. The speed of the reversal is breathtaking: one moment they are bringing garlands and oxen; the next, stones. The crowd that wanted to worship Paul drags his body out of the city, supposing him dead. And Paul gets up and walks back into the city. He does not leave the region; he does not change his message; he goes on to Derbe and comes back through Lystra and Iconium and Antioch, strengthening the disciples.

What he tells them on the return journey is the sentence that threads through the whole of Acts: “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God.” Not may — must. Suffering is not the exception for the follower of Jesus; it is the road. The kingdom does not come without the cross — not for the King, and not for those who follow him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–28 — The First Journey Continues and Returns
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
This chapter finishes the first missionary journey and brings the two men home. It falls into three parts, and the middle one is the strangest scene in Acts.

Iconium (vv. 1–7). The same shape as Pisidian Antioch: they go to the synagogue, a great number of Jews and Greeks believe, and the opposition organises — but here it works by poisoning the mind of the city against them (v. 2). What is unexpected is the response: they stay a long time, and the Lord goes on attesting the word of his grace with signs (v. 3). Only when the hostility hardens into an attempt to stone them do they leave, and they leave on an instruction of Jesus rather than in fear (vv. 4–7).

Lystra (vv. 8–20). A man crippled from birth is healed (vv. 8–10), and a Gentile town with no Scripture and no framework draws the only conclusion available to it: the gods have come down. Barnabas is Zeus, Paul is Hermes, and the priest of Zeus arrives at the gates with garlands and oxen (vv. 11–13). The apostles tear their clothes and run into the crowd, and what follows is the first sermon in Acts preached to people who know nothing at all — no Abraham, no Moses, no promise; only rain, harvests, food and gladness, which God has been giving them all along as a witness to himself (vv. 14–18). Then opponents arrive from the two towns behind them, and the same crowd stones Paul and drags him out for dead. He gets up and walks back in (vv. 19–20).

The return (vv. 21–28). Derbe, and then — astonishingly — back through Lystra, Iconium and Antioch, the three towns that had just tried to kill them, to strengthen the disciples and tell them plainly that the road into the kingdom runs through many tribulations (vv. 21–22). Elders are appointed in every church, with prayer and fasting, and the congregations are handed over to the Lord (v. 23). Then Pisidia and Pamphylia, a sermon in Perga — the town they had passed straight through on the way out — and the harbour at Attalia (vv. 24–25), and the voyage back to the church that had commended them to the grace of God for the work now finished (v. 26). They gather the congregation and report — not what they achieved but what God did, and that he has opened a door of faith to the Gentiles — and they stay a long while (vv. 27–28). The next thing that happens is chapter 15, and it is an argument about how wide that door should be.
verseByVerse.theology:
Suffering as the Path into the Kingdom

Paul and Barnabas's declaration in v. 22 — 'through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God' — is not pessimism but theology: the path of the crucified Lord is the path of his followers. Reformed theology insists that suffering is not a sign of God's absence but often a sign of his presence and approval: the servant who shares his Lord's cross shares his Lord's resurrection. The 'must' (dei) is the divine necessity — the same 'must' applied to Christ's suffering in Luke 24:26. The pattern of dying and rising is the pattern of life in the kingdom.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul was stoned and dragged out of Lystra for dead, then got up and went back into the city the next day. The courage required to re-enter the city where you were nearly killed is the courage of the man who has nothing to fear from death. Now: The willingness to re-enter dangerous territory — to continue faithful witness after suffering for it — is the distinctive quality of those whose security is not in this world's preservation of their lives but in Christ's resurrection that awaits them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now at Iconium they entered together into the Jewish synagogue and spoke in such a way that a great number of both Jews and Greeks believed. But the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They entered together into the Jewish synagogue and spoke in such a way that a great number of both Jews and Greeks believed.

Two things in that sentence. The first is that they went to the synagogue — in Iconium, eighty miles after the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch had had them expelled from the district. Paul had announced there, publicly and with a prophet's text behind him, that he was turning to the Gentiles (13:46). And the next building he walks into is a synagogue. That is what the turn to the Gentiles actually meant in practice, and anyone who reads 13:46 as a resignation from his own people should read this verse straight afterwards.

The second is Luke's curious phrase: they spoke in such a way that a great number believed. He does not say they spoke faithfully, or at length, or with power. He says they spoke in such a way — a comment on the manner of it, on how the thing was put. There is such a thing as saying true things badly, and these two did not.

Then verse 2. The unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the brothers. The word behind poisoned is the ordinary word for harming or ill-treating, used here of what was done to the Gentiles' minds rather than to the missionaries' bodies. Luke's picture is of an audience being made bitter — worked on, over time, by people with access to them.

And notice what the opposition does not do. It does not answer the preaching. It goes round it, to people who have not heard it yet, and gets there first.

That is a particular kind of injury, and it is worth naming for the reader who has suffered it, because most of us have. There is no defence against it, because it does not happen where you are. You discover it only in its effects: rooms that go quiet, an invitation that stops coming, a coolness in somebody who used to be warm and will not say why. You cannot answer a charge that was never put to you, and the attempt to try makes you look exactly like the man they were warned about.

So what did these two do about it? Nothing, so far as Luke records. No defence, no letter to the synagogue, no month spent repairing the damage. The next verse tells you what they did instead: they stayed, and went on speaking, for a long time. Some slander can only be outlived — and the outliving is done by going on doing the work in front of everybody, for years if necessary, until the account people were given stops matching the man they can see.

verseByVerse.quote: So they remained for a long time, speaking boldly for the Lord, who bore witness to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they remained for a long time.

Read that against the verse before it. The city has just been deliberately turned against them. And the word Luke uses to join the two sentences is so — therefore. The poisoning of the city is given as the reason they stayed.

That is the reverse of the instinct. When a place goes cold on us we start looking at the timetable. These men treated the hostility as evidence that something was happening worth opposing, and dug in.

Be careful with it, though, because the same chapter has them running from this same city three verses later, and a reader could take either verse as the rule. Neither is. What decided it was not their comfort but the state of the work: while there was preaching to be done they stayed under pressure, and when the pressure became a plot to kill them they left, on Jesus's own instruction. Courage is not the same thing as staying, and prudence is not the same thing as leaving. The question in both verses is what serves the work.

Speaking boldly for the Lord, who bore witness to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands.

Notice which way round that sentence runs. It is not that the apostles bore witness to the Lord, though of course they did. It is that the Lord bore witness to them — or more exactly, to the word they were preaching. They spoke; he testified that what they said was so.

And notice precisely what the signs are said to authenticate. Not the men. The word of his grace — the message, named by its content: that God gives what nobody has earned. The wonders are attached to that and underwrite that. Which is worth holding on to in a Christian world where the miraculous is sometimes offered as a credential on its own. A ministry full of wonders and empty of grace is not the thing this verse describes; the signs here are a signature at the bottom of a particular document.

There is a quiet comfort in it for anyone who has felt the loneliness of saying something true that nobody wants to hear. Two men were being systematically discredited in Iconium, and the record says the Lord Jesus went on publicly backing what they said. He is not neutral about his own word. He may not vindicate it on the timetable you would choose — Paul is stoned two towns later and no sign prevents it — but the word of his grace has never yet gone out unattended.

verseByVerse.quote: But the people of the city were divided; some sided with the Jews and some with the apostles. When an attempt was made by both Gentiles and Jews, with their rulers, to mistreat and to stone them,
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the people of the city were divided; some sided with the Jews and some with the apostles.

Luke is unembarrassed about this, and it is worth stopping on, because it is not a result any of us would put in a newsletter. Two good men preached the gospel in Iconium with great effect, and the measurable outcome was that the town split in half.

The gospel does that, and Jesus said it would, in terms nobody has ever found comfortable: do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? No, I tell you, but rather division (Luke 12:51). Not because Christians are quarrelsome, though we often are, but because the message puts a question that cannot be left lying. A man can be neutral about most claims. He cannot be neutral about the claim that a particular executed Jew is the Lord of his life.

Then a small word with a long argument behind it: the apostles. Luke has just called Barnabas an apostle, and he does it again at verse 14. Everywhere else he keeps the word for the Twelve.

It repays a moment, because Christians are told confidently both that there are no apostles now and that there are, and the word is doing two different jobs in the New Testament. In its strict sense an apostle is one of the men who had seen the risen Christ and been commissioned by him personally as an eyewitness and a layer of foundations — the Twelve, with Paul added as one untimely born (1 Cor. 15:8). That office cannot be repeated, and the reason is built into the qualification: the man had to have seen him (1:21–22), and a foundation is laid once (Eph. 2:20). In its wider sense the word simply means one who is sent, and the New Testament uses it freely — of Barnabas here, of Epaphroditus, whom Philippi sent to Paul (Phil. 2:25), of the men Paul calls the messengers of the churches (2 Cor. 8:23). In that sense the church has always had them, and mostly calls them missionaries, which is the same word arriving through Latin instead of Greek.

So when somebody claims the title today, the useful question is not whether the word may be used but which of the two things is being claimed. A sent one, yes, and thank God for them. A man whose word stands beside Scripture because he saw the risen Christ, no. That door closed when the last of them died, and it is a mercy that it did: a church that can still be given new foundational revelation is a church that can be told anything.

Then verse 5, and the alliance is the thing to see. Both Gentiles and Jews, with their rulers. Two communities that agreed on almost nothing found something they could agree on. It is the pattern of the trial itself, where Herod and Pilate became friends with each other that very day (Luke 23:12). Opposition to Christ has a remarkable power to unite people who would not otherwise sit in the same room, and it is one of the stranger backhanded testimonies to who he is.

verseByVerse.quote: they learned of it and fled to Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and to the surrounding country, and there they continued to preach the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They learned of it and fled.

Somebody told them. A plot involving the rulers of a city and both its communities was known in advance to two travelling preachers, which means that among the divided people of verse 4 there was at least one person on the inside who got word out. Luke does not name him, and never finds out what it cost him. This book is quietly full of people like that.

And they ran. It is worth saying plainly that this is not a lapse. Jesus commanded it — when they persecute you in one town, flee to the next (Matt. 10:23) — and did it himself more than once (Luke 4:30; John 8:59). There is a strain of Christian thinking in which leaving is always weakness and staying is always faith, and this verse is flatly against it. The mission is the point, not the missionary's reputation for nerve.

But now hold verse 6 next to verse 20, where the same man, having been stoned and dragged out of Lystra as a corpse, gets up and walks straight back into the town. One chapter, one apostle, two opposite decisions. So the rule cannot be flee, and it cannot be stay.

What decides it in both places is the work. He leaves Iconium because staying would end the preaching; he re-enters Lystra because there are new disciples in it who have just watched their teacher killed and need to see him on his feet. So if you are weighing whether to leave something hard — a post, a church, a situation — the question this chapter puts is not whether you would be braver to stay. It is what happens to the work if you go, and what happens to it if you do not. That is a question you can answer without having to grade your own courage, which is just as well, because nobody grades his own courage accurately.

Then the destination: Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and to the surrounding country.

Lystra is only about twenty miles from Iconium, but Luke's phrase marks the thing that mattered — it was over a boundary, in Lycaonia, and therefore outside the reach of the Iconian magistrates while remaining in the same region. Twenty miles was enough, provided they were the right twenty miles.

And it is a step down in the world. Iconium was a substantial Greek-speaking city; Lystra was a small Roman colony in rough hill country whose people, as verse 11 will show, still shouted in Lycaonian when they were excited. Paul is moving steadily away from the places where his education is worth anything.

Then the clause that carries the weight: and there they continued to preach the gospel. They arrive as fugitives from a stoning, in a backwater whose language they do not speak, and they start again. Not recovered, and then preached. Fled, and preached.

verseByVerse.quote: Now at Lystra there was a man sitting who could not use his feet. He was crippled from birth and had never walked. He listened to Paul speaking. And Paul, looking intently at him and seeing that he had faith to be made well,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke slows right down for this man and gives three descriptions where one would have done: he could not use his feet, he was crippled from birth, and he had never walked. The last is the one that costs something. Not injured, not declining — a man who had never in his life taken a step, and had spent all of it watching everybody else do it.

Then: He listened to Paul speaking. The tense is continuous. He was listening — not one sermon overheard from the roadside but a man who kept coming back to hear, in the open air of a town with no synagogue and no Scripture in it. Whatever he was making of it, he wanted more of it.

And Paul, looking intently at him and seeing that he had faith to be made well.

This sentence has done a great deal of damage in the church, and it has to be handled carefully, because a wounded reader will get it wrong in one particular way.

Read carelessly, it says the healing happened because the man's faith was sufficient — from which it follows, with awful logic, that where healing does not happen the faith was not sufficient. That is what people are told. It is told at bedsides. And it is not what this verse says.

Look at who is doing the seeing. Paul, looking intently at him — the same verb Luke used of him a chapter ago, staring at Elymas — and seeing. What Paul saw was not printed on the man's face for anyone to read. It was shown him. This is not an apostle assessing a candidate's spiritual performance and finding it up to standard; it is an apostle being given to know, in that moment, what God intended to do in that man. And the faith he sees is itself something God has been producing through the preaching the man kept coming back to hear.

Then test the doctrine against the rest of the book, which is the surest way to settle it. The man at the temple gate asked for money and expected nothing else, and was healed anyway (3:6). Aeneas had been bedridden eight years and is not recorded as saying a word (9:34). Dorcas was dead (9:40). Malchus was in the act of helping to arrest Jesus when his ear was put back on, and it is Luke who tells us so (Luke 22:51). If healing ran on the sufferer's faith, half the healings in Scripture could not have happened.

And then the hardest evidence of all, which ought to settle it for good. Paul himself asked three times to be relieved of something and was told no (2 Cor. 12:8–9). He left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Tim. 4:20). He told Timothy to take a little wine for his frequent ailments rather than healing him (1 Tim. 5:23). The apostle who read this man's faith in a Lystran street could not read his own way out of a thorn.

So if you are ill, or someone you love is, and you have been made to feel that the failure is yours — that if you could only believe harder the thing would lift — put this verse down and pick it up the other way round. It does not say that faith produces healing. It says that on one particular afternoon in one particular town, God let his apostle see what he was about to do. Your not being healed is not a report card on your faith. If it were, Paul failed his.

verseByVerse.quote: said in a loud voice, "Stand upright on your feet." And he sprang up and began walking.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Said in a loud voice, Stand upright on your feet. And he sprang up and began walking.

Consider what is actually being asked of the man. He has never stood. He has no idea what standing feels like — no learned sense of balance, no memory of how weight shifts from one leg to the other, none of the ten thousand small corrections a body makes without being told. Somebody who has been off his feet for a single year needs months to walk again after the cause is removed, because walking is a skill and the body forgets it. This man had never had the skill to forget.

And he sprang up. Not stood carefully. Not was helped upright and shuffled a few steps between two men. He jumped. What he was given in that second was not a repair to a mechanism; it was everything a person normally acquires over the first two years of his life and then practises for the rest of it, handed over complete.

Now notice something that is not in the sentence, because it explains everything that goes wrong next.

Peter, at the temple gate, said in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk (3:6), and the crowd that came running was preached at about the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob before anybody had time to misunderstand. Here Luke records no name at all. Paul says five words in a loud voice, and a town with no Scripture in it is left to interpret what it has seen out of the only religious vocabulary it possesses.

Which is why the next verse goes so badly wrong, and it is a lesson worth carrying well beyond Lystra. A miracle by itself teaches nobody anything. It compels attention, and then people explain it with whatever they already believe. Jerusalem had the Scriptures and reached for the God of Israel. Lystra had Zeus and reached for him. The event was the same; the two towns drew opposite conclusions from it, and neither drew a conclusion the event had supplied.

So a remarkable thing happening is not, on its own, evidence that God has done it, nor evidence of what he meant by it. The apostles never once treat a sign as self-explanatory; every one of them in this book is followed within minutes by somebody standing up and saying what it meant. Where that explanation does not follow, the crowd supplies its own — and this crowd is already sending for oxen.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the crowds saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in Lycaonian, "The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!" And Barnabas they called Zeus, and Paul, Hermes, because he was the chief speaker.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!

The reaction looks wild until you know the local story, and then it becomes almost inevitable.

There was a legend attached to these hills, and the Roman poet Ovid had written it up a generation before Paul walked into the town. Zeus and Hermes came through this country disguised as travellers, looking for somewhere to stay, and were turned away from a thousand doors. One household took them in — an old couple, Baucis and Philemon, poor enough to have almost nothing to offer, who killed their only goose for the strangers. The gods revealed themselves, turned the couple's cottage into a temple, and drowned the entire district that had refused them.

That is the story these people grew up on. It is set in their own countryside. And it has a moral with teeth: when two strangers turn up and something impossible happens, you do not want to be the household that got it wrong.

So the shouting in verse 11 is not simple enthusiasm. It is fear with a long memory, and it explains why the priest comes at a run with cattle instead of convening a meeting about it.

Luke's ear is exact here too. They cried out in Lycaonian — the old country language, not the Greek Paul had been preaching in. Under strain people revert to the tongue they think in. And the detail quietly explains the delay: Paul and Barnabas go on standing there while a sacrifice is organised around them, because they cannot understand a word of it. They find out what is happening when the animals appear.

Then the roles, which are worth having. Barnabas is Zeus — the senior god, the presence, the one you do not address directly. Paul is Hermes, the messenger who runs the errands, because he was the chief speaker. So the man doing all the talking is taken for the junior deity, and the quiet one beside him for the god. Luke, who has spent the previous chapter recording that Paul had taken over the leadership of this mission, does not comment. He simply lets you notice that a crowd looking for greatness looked straight past the man in the middle of it.

There is something in that for anyone who has been sized up wrongly — passed over on the strength of a manner, or promoted on one. The people of Lystra got both men wrong, in opposite directions, on the same afternoon. Neither verdict survived the week.

verseByVerse.quote: And the priest of Zeus, whose temple was at the entrance to the city, brought oxen and garlands to the gates and wanted to offer sacrifice with the crowds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the priest of Zeus, whose temple was at the entrance to the city, brought oxen and garlands to the gates and wanted to offer sacrifice with the crowds.

Set the scene properly, because this is where a misunderstanding turns into a crisis.

Zeus-before-the-city was the town's own guardian — the god whose shrine stood outside the walls, watching the road, so that every trader and traveller passed him on the way in. He was not an abstraction to these people. He was the local authority responsible for the weather, the harvest, and whether Lystra had a good year.

And his priest is now at the gate with oxen — full-grown cattle, the most expensive offering the town could make, not a pair of pigeons — and with garlands, the woollen wreaths wound about the animals' heads and horns before they were killed. The garlands mean the beasts are already dedicated. This is not under discussion. It is under way.

Two men have been preaching in that town for a few days about the true God. In the space of about ten minutes, the most impressive religious act in the town's calendar is being arranged in their honour, by the professional in charge of it, at public expense, with the whole population delighted about it.

It is worth asking what makes this moment so dangerous, because on the face of it a misunderstanding by ignorant people looks harmless enough — embarrassing, but correctable. It is dangerous because it is flattering, and because it is sincere. Nobody here is working an angle. These people are grateful, and frightened, and they have brought the best they have.

And that is the easiest thing in the world to let run. Not to endorse it — nobody endorses it. Simply to be slow about correcting it. To reflect that they will understand better in time, that this is not the moment, that the crowd is finally listening and it would be a pity to lose them. Very nearly every scandal of Christian celebrity has begun in a version of this room: not a man claiming to be more than a man, but a man declining, for a while, to interrupt people who were treating him as though he were.

What happens next takes a handful of words in Greek, and it is a large part of the reason we are still reading about these two.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard of it, they tore their garments and rushed out into the crowd, crying out, "Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men, of like nature with you, and we bring you good news, that you should turn from these vain things to a living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They tore their garments and rushed out into the crowd.

Take the two actions separately, because both are deliberate and both cost something.

Tearing your clothes was the Jewish sign of unbearable grief, or of horror at blasphemy — it is what the high priest did at what he took to be blasphemy from Jesus (Mark 14:63). Paul and Barnabas are not making a gesture the Lystrans will understand; nobody in that crowd knows what a torn robe means. They are doing what a Jew does when he hears God insulted, in a town where it will simply look odd. That is what they thought of the honour being offered them.

And they rushed out into the crowd. Not onto a platform, and not away. Into it — shoving into a mass of excited people in order to get physically between them and the altar.

Then the sentence itself: We also are men, of like nature with you. The Greek is homoiopatheis, of the same feelings, the same sufferings. Not merely the same species — the same aches, the same fears, the same capacity to be hurt. Within a few days Paul will be lying outside that same gate under a heap of stones, and the town will have its proof.

The question of what a man does when he is offered honour that belongs to God has already been put in this book, and it was answered the other way by a king in Caesarea who kept his robes on and said nothing (12:22–23); the working of it out is there and does not need repeating. But notice what makes Lystra harder than Caesarea. Herod's flatterers were buying grain and everybody in the theatre knew it. These people mean it. They are not manipulating anybody; they are overwhelmed with gratitude and have brought oxen. It is far easier to refuse worship from a man working an angle than from a man who simply wants to say thank you in the only currency he has, and who will be hurt when you will not take it.

Then look at how they preach, because this is the first sermon in Acts addressed to people with no Bible at all. No Abraham, no Moses, no exodus, no prophets — not even one God to start from. Peter at Pentecost could quote Joel. Paul in the synagogue could quote the Psalms and expect the room to follow. Here there is nothing to quote. So they begin where these people actually are.

Turn from these vain things to a living God. Vain is the prophets' word for idols — empty, hollow, nothing there (Jer. 2:5; 10:15). And living is the whole contrast: the gods of Lystra had to be fed by a priest, and this one made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them. That last phrase is straight out of the Psalms, and they do not say so, because saying so would have meant nothing here. They just say the thing.

Which is the model, and it is more demanding than it looks. They did not open with justification and they did not open with Genesis 12. They took the one real point of contact a pagan farming town had — the sky, the fields, the food on the table — and they used it. And having found the point of contact, they did not soften the demand by a syllable: turn. It is the same word Peter used in Jerusalem. The starting place moved. The call did not.

verseByVerse.quote: "In past generations he allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In past generations he allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways.

That is a stark sentence, and it raises the question this whole scene has been circling: what about all the people who never heard?

It is not an abstract question here. Lystra is standing in front of Paul as an instance of it — a town that has been sacrificing to Zeus for centuries with no prophet, no Scripture and no summons. And it is one of the two or three questions most likely to be put to a Christian by somebody he loves.

Take what Scripture actually says, and refuse both of the comfortable answers.

First, nobody is judged against a light he was never given. Paul's own developed argument is that Gentiles who do not have the law are judged by what they did have — the work of the law written on their hearts, their conscience accusing or else excusing them (Rom. 2:14–16). Whatever the outcome in any individual case, God is not weighing a man against a revelation he withheld from him. That is worth saying to anyone whose real fear is that God is unfair.

Second, they are not innocent. Paul is equally firm that what can be known about God is plain from what has been made, so that people are without excuse — and the charge he brings is not ignorance but suppression: knowing something of God and not honouring him or giving thanks (Rom. 1:19–21). The very next verse is about to make the same point in kinder language. God had been sending Lystra rain the whole time. Nobody in that town had been left with nothing.

Third, the Judge is good. Abraham's question — shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just? (Gen. 18:25) — is one of those questions that is answered in the asking, and it is the answer Scripture actually gives to the anxious. You are not being asked to certify the eternal state of people you have never met. You are being asked whether the God who did not spare his own Son can be trusted with them.

And then refuse the false comfort in both directions. This verse gives no ground for supposing the nations are safe in their ignorance: Paul's whole point is that the era of overlooking has ended and a summons has now arrived, which is exactly what he tells Athens in almost these words (17:30). And it gives no ground for the flat assertion that everyone who never heard is certainly lost, which Scripture nowhere states in that form. The honest position is that God has told us plainly how he deals with those who have heard, has not published his arrangements for the rest, and has instead put a job in our hands: how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching? (Rom. 10:14).

Which is the real force of the verse where it stands. Paul does not raise the past generations to settle a puzzle. He raises them to tell a crowd in a small Anatolian town that the waiting is over — and that the summons has arrived in the street they are standing in.

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet he did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness." Even with these words they scarcely restrained the people from offering sacrifice to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet he did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness.

Look at what Paul chooses. He is speaking to farmers on the Anatolian uplands, and he does not reach for the stars, or the intricacy of the body, or the moral law within. He reaches for rain, harvest, dinner, and being glad.

That is a remarkable list, and the last item is the most remarkable of all. God's witness to himself in a pagan town included gladness — the pleasure of a good meal, the ease that settles on people when there has been enough and the year has gone well. Paul stands in front of idolaters and tells them that their happiness was evidence.

And notice who had been fed. The rain fell on the fields of a town that had built a temple to Zeus at its gate and paid a priest to keep him satisfied — and God sent the rain anyway, season after season, for as long as anyone could remember. The people now leading oxen up to the wrong god had eaten every day of their lives at the table of the right one.

Then verse 18, which is deliberately anticlimactic: even with these words they scarcely restrained the people from offering sacrifice to them.

Scarcely. This is one of the great short sermons in Acts, delivered by an apostle at the top of his powers in an emergency — and Luke's verdict on it is that it only just worked. They got the sacrifice stopped by the skin of their teeth. Luke does not even say the crowd was persuaded; only that it was restrained.

There is an honesty in that which the church needs. The best answer, given at the right moment by the right man, may only just hold — and this crowd, a few days later, picked up stones. If you have said the true thing as well as you knew how and watched it barely land, you are in good company. Luke thought the barely was worth writing down.

This verse is one of Scripture's clearest windows onto common grace. 'Common' means not cheap but given to all in common — the goodness God shows every creature, believer and unbeliever alike: the rains and fruitful seasons, the food and gladness here; and beyond, life and breath (Acts 17:25), the restraint of evil, the skill and kindness and beauty found even among those who do not know God, and the patience that delays judgment to leave room for repentance. Jesus grounds it in the same gifts: God 'makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust' (Matt. 5:45; cf. Ps. 145:9; James 1:17). The astonishing thing Paul presses on these idolaters is that God had been feeding them, gladdening them, and watering their fields all along — lavishing kindness on people building altars to other gods.

Two things must be kept clear. First, common grace is not saving grace: genuinely grace, undeserved kindness, but it blesses this life without, by itself, reconciling anyone to God — the redeeming grace given in Christ is a greater thing, granted to those who believe. (To confuse them is to imagine everyone is saved because everyone enjoys God's sunshine.) Second, see what it is for: it is a 'witness' (v. 17) — daily goodness testifying that God is real and kind, leaving people 'without excuse' (Rom. 1:20) and meant 'to lead you to repentance' (Rom. 2:4). The tragedy is to take the gifts and ignore the Giver (Rom. 1:21). And the lesson is warm and practical: every good thing you enjoy — the rain on your garden, the harvest, the meal on the table, the laughter of friends, the sun on your back — is a gift from the open hand of a good God, a daily knock pointing past the gift to the Giver. It teaches you to give thanks for everything, see God's hand everywhere, and love even your enemies as God does, doing good to all (Matt. 5:44–45).

verseByVerse.quote: But Jews came from Antioch and Iconium, and having persuaded the crowds, they stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead. But when the disciples gathered about him, he rose up and entered the city, and on the next day he went on with Barnabas to Derbe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Jews came from Antioch and Iconium.

Look at the distances before anything else. Iconium is some twenty miles from Lystra. Pisidian Antioch is around a hundred. Somebody organised this — messages sent, a journey of several days made deliberately over hill roads, by men whose entire purpose in travelling was to finish in this town what they had started in their own.

It is one of the ugliest sentences in Acts, and it is quietly instructive. Hatred will make an effort that indifference never makes. These men walked a hundred miles to break up a meeting.

And having persuaded the crowds, they stoned Paul.

The same crowds. Luke does not soften it and does not explain it. The people who a few days earlier had to be physically restrained from worshipping this man now throw stones at him until he stops moving. Nothing had changed except who had been talking to them.

That is worth knowing about crowds, and about what their approval is worth. A reputation handed to you by people who do not know you can be taken back by people who do not know you, and the same afternoon's excitement supplies both. It is also worth knowing about ourselves. These were not monsters by the standards of their town. They were ordinary, frightened, easily led people who had just been told a persuasive story by men who sounded as though they knew.

Then: dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead. They were not pretending. A stoning is not a beating; it is an execution, and this one was carried far enough that the men doing it stopped, looked, and concluded the job was finished. Paul mentions it exactly once, in a list of things he had survived — once I was stoned (2 Cor. 11:25) — and writing to the Galatians, whose churches these are, he says he bears the marks of Jesus on his body (Gal. 6:17). Whatever those marks were, some of them were made here.

But when the disciples gathered about him, he rose up and entered the city.

Two things, and the second one is the find.

The first: Luke, who is a careful writer, does not say that Paul was raised from the dead. He says the crowd supposed he was dead, and that he got up. It may have been a miracle; it may have been a man surviving what should have killed him. Luke declines to say, and it is a mark of his honesty that he leaves the reader without the more impressive version — the more so since he is quite willing to report a raising when he believes one happened (9:40; 20:9–12).

The second: the disciples gathered about him. There were disciples in Lystra. In the middle of the disaster, Luke mentions in passing that the preaching had worked, and that a small group of brand-new believers is now standing in a ring round the body of their teacher outside the town wall — which took some nerve, with the crowd not yet dispersed.

And it is very likely that one of them was a boy called Timothy. Lystra was his town; Paul finds him there on the next journey and takes him along (16:1–2). Years later, writing to him for the last time, Paul reminds him of the persecutions he endured and names Antioch, Iconium and Lystra — the three towns of this chapter, in this order (2 Tim. 3:11; the same sentence is quoted at 13:50–51). He writes as though Timothy needs no explanation. The likeliest reason he needs none is that he was there.

So the young man who became Paul's closest colleague — a man frightened by temperament, who had to be told more than once not to be — may well have begun by watching his hero dragged out of town as a corpse. And signed on anyway.

And on the next day he went on with Barnabas to Derbe. Not convalesced. The next day, and about sixty miles on foot.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had preached the gospel to that city and had made many disciples, they returned to Lystra and to Iconium and to Antioch, strengthening the souls of the disciples, encouraging them to continue in the faith, and saying that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Read verse 21 as a route, and it stops being a travel note.

They preach at Derbe and make many disciples there, and Derbe is the far end of the journey — out near the pass that leads home. From Derbe the road east through the Cilician Gates would have brought them to Tarsus in a few days and to Syrian Antioch not long after: downhill, familiar, and safe. And instead they turn round.

They returned to Lystra and to Iconium and to Antioch. Name them in order. Lystra is where Paul had been stoned and left for dead a few weeks earlier. Iconium is where both communities and their rulers had agreed to stone him. Antioch is where the leading families of the colony had had the two of them expelled from the district. He goes back to all three, in reverse order, deliberately.

Ask what for, because it is not to preach — the preaching has been done. Luke gives three participles: strengthening the souls of the disciples, encouraging them to continue in the faith, and saying that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God. They are going back to make sure that what they started can stand without them.

And that is a judgment about what the work actually is. It would have been perfectly defensible to write to those churches, or to send somebody, or to reckon that a man recently stoned has earned the road home. Paul walks back into the town where it happened, and the reason is in the third participle.

Because think what those young churches had just watched. Their teachers had been talked out of one town, chased out of another, and very nearly killed in a third. Every convert in those cities was facing the obvious question: is this what following Jesus is going to be like? And Paul's answer, delivered in person, on legs that had recently been stoned, was yes.

Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God. Notice that he says we, not you. He is not issuing a warning from a safe distance; he is describing a road he is standing on, to people who had seen him on it. That is the strengthening. He does not tell them it will get easier. He tells them that the difficulty is the road and not a diversion from it — which is the only kind of comfort that survives contact with real trouble, and the reason it works is that it removes the second wound. Suffering hurts. Suffering plus the suspicion that it means God has gone is unbearable, and it is the second half Paul is taking away. He says the same to Rome, that suffering produces endurance, endurance character, and character hope (Rom. 5:3–4), and to Timothy without any softening at all: all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted (2 Tim. 3:12).

'Made many disciples' — worth pausing on, because we easily lose the very idea of a disciple. The word (mathētēs) means a learner, an apprentice — not one who collects information but one who attaches his whole life to a master, learns his teaching and his way of living, and sets out to become like him: 'everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher' (Luke 6:40). Jesus made it costly and total — 'let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me' (Luke 9:23) — yet also the ordinary identity of every believer: 'disciple' was the word for a Christian before the name 'Christian' existed (Acts 11:26).

That is where the modern church stumbles. We can reduce the faith to a single decision — getting people 'converted' — and forget that the commission is to 'make disciples... teaching them to observe all that I have commanded' (Matt. 28:19–20). A disciple is not an optional upgrade for keen Christians; it is simply what a Christian is — a lifelong apprentice of Jesus. Paul and Barnabas did exactly this: not counting converts and moving on, but returning to strengthen the disciples and appointing elders to watch over them (vv. 22–23). The reminder is bracing and freeing: you were not saved to make one decision and drift, but to follow — to walk after Jesus as a learner, for the rest of your life.

'We must enter the kingdom of God' — and you may be puzzled: did we not already enter it? Paul says God 'has transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son' (Col. 1:13, past tense) — yet here entering is still future. Both are true; this is the 'already and not yet.' God's saving reign in King Jesus comes in two stages. It already arrived at his first coming — 'the kingdom of God has come upon you' (Matt. 12:28) — and every believer is already under its reign, enjoying its blessings (forgiveness, the Spirit, sonship). And it is not yet consummated: its full glory waits for his return, when he reigns openly and makes all things new, and in that sense we will yet 'enter' or 'inherit' it (Matt. 25:34; 1 Cor. 15:50; 2 Tim. 4:18). Same kingdom, two stages — the 'already' real but partial, the 'not yet' full and final. (See on Col. 1:13; 4:11.)

So Paul speaks both ways as his point requires: to assure us of what is already ours by grace, he says we have been placed in the kingdom; to press us on in hope — as here — he points to the kingdom we have yet to enter. Picture a decisive battle already won, the outcome settled, while the victory parade still lies ahead; or dawn — the sun truly risen, the full blaze of noon still to come. And notice why he raises the future entrance here: to frame the 'many tribulations' as the appointed road home. The trials are not a sign we have lost the kingdom; they are the path into its fullness — 'provided we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him' (Rom. 8:17).

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had appointed elders for them in every church, with prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord in whom they had believed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they had appointed elders for them in every church.

The verb deserves a note before anything else, because it has been fought over. Cheirotoneo originally meant to stretch out the hand — that is, to vote by a show of hands in an assembly — and by the first century it had worn down to mean simply to appoint or designate. Congregationalists have leaned on the older sense and episcopalians on the later one, and the honest answer is that a single verb will not settle a system of church government. What the sentence plainly says is that Paul and Barnabas did the appointing, that they did it in every church without exception, and that no congregation was left without it.

And consider the timing, which is the astonishing part. These churches were a few months old at most. Some had been founded, opposed and abandoned inside a fortnight. Every member was a convert of that same year — men and women who had been idolaters or synagogue attenders in the spring and were now being set apart to lead a congregation. There was no training college, no probationary decade, no New Testament to study, and in Lystra the whole church had recently watched its founder stoned.

Paul did not conclude from any of this that it was too soon. He concluded that a church without elders was a church he could not leave, and so he raised leaders out of the material actually in front of him. The alternative — keeping the churches dependent on himself until somebody sufficiently impressive turned up — would have felt far safer and would have been fatal.

Then: with prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord in whom they had believed.

The word behind committed is the one used of depositing something valuable with somebody else for safekeeping. It is the word Jesus used from the cross: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit (Luke 23:46). Paul and Barnabas are handing over something that was never theirs to keep, to the only one who can keep it, and they do it fasting — going without food while they pray, which is what serious men did before a step that could not be taken back.

And then they walked away. That is the part worth sitting with. They left congregations of new believers, in hostile towns, under brand-new elders, with no means of finding out for months how any of it was going. What made that bearable is in the last clause: the Lord in whom they had believed. Not the elders they had appointed, good men though those may have been. The churches were left with the Lord, because the churches had always been his.

Anyone who has had to hand something over — a work, a congregation, a child, a parent — knows the difference between resignation and entrusting. Resignation lets go because it has run out of options. Entrusting lets go into hands it can name. The test is simple enough to run: when you think about the thing you cannot control, are you bracing for the worst, or have you actually put it somewhere?

Was this simply what these two men happened to do, or a mandate? That they appointed elders 'in every church' shows it was fixed practice, and the rest of the New Testament confirms it: Paul left Titus in Crete to 'appoint elders in every town' (Titus 1:5), a church without them being 'not yet in order.' Every church we meet has them — Ephesus (Acts 20:17), Peter's readers (1 Pet. 5:1), James's (James 5:14), Philippi's 'overseers and deacons' (Phil. 1:1). Two things. First, three words name the same office from different angles: elder (presbyteros, maturity), overseer/bishop (episkopos, oversight), and pastor/shepherd (poimēn, care) — all used of the same men (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5, 7; 1 Pet. 5:1–2). Second, it is always elders, plural — a team, not a lone ruler. Shared leadership is the apostolic norm.

What authority does that give them, and what does it not? Elders have real, God-given authority: to lead or 'rule' (1 Tim. 5:17), to teach and guard sound doctrine (Titus 1:9), to shepherd and watch over souls (Acts 20:28); and the flock is to 'obey your leaders and submit to them' (Heb. 13:17). But it is strictly bounded. It is derived: they are under-shepherds serving the Chief Shepherd (1 Pet. 5:4), tending 'the church of God,' not their own (Acts 20:28). It is Word-bound: they minister Scripture's authority, so they may not bind consciences with rules God has not given (the error of Col. 2) — they declare God's Word, they do not legislate. And it is not the right to dominate: 'not domineering... but being examples' (1 Pet. 5:3); they lead as servants, not lords (Mark 10:42–45), and will 'give an account' to God (Heb. 13:17). Real authority, but servant-authority — Christ-derived, Scripture-limited, accountable, never tyrannical. The elders are no little popes.

And what qualifies a man for it? The two lists (1 Tim. 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9) stress character, not talent. The umbrella is 'above reproach' — a life giving no just handle for accusation. Under it: faithful in marriage (a 'one-woman man'), self-controlled, sober-minded, gentle and not violent, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money, hospitable, upright, holy, 'not a recent convert' (mature, lest he be puffed up). He must manage his own household well — 'if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?' (1 Tim. 3:5) — and be 'well thought of by outsiders.' Only one item is an ability, not a trait: he must be 'able to teach,' holding firm to sound doctrine 'to give instruction... and to rebuke those who contradict' (1 Tim. 3:2; Titus 1:9) — the chief thing distinguishing an elder from a deacon. The lesson humbles: an elder is not the most gifted or successful man in the room, but a man of proven Christlike character who knows and can teach the truth — nearly everything on the list is simply the mature Christian life, on display in one fit to model it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they passed through Pisidia and came to Pamphylia. And when they had spoken the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they passed through Pisidia and came to Pamphylia. And when they had spoken the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia.

Two sentences of itinerary, and one of them is a quiet piece of repair.

Perga is where the journey went wrong. It is the town they landed at on the way out, and it is where John Mark left them and went home (13:13). Luke records at the time that they simply went on from Perga — no preaching mentioned, nothing planted there. They had passed straight through it and up into the mountains, a man short.

Now, coming back the other way, they stop and preach. The place that had been nothing but the scene of a disappointment gets the gospel on the return leg.

Luke makes no comment, and it would be easy to make too much of it. But it is worth noticing how much of God's work is done on the second pass. The road travelled in discouragement is travelled again, and this time something is planted in it. Very little in the Christian life is gone through only once, and the place where you failed, or were failed, is very often the place you are brought back to with something to give.

The rest is unglamorous, and it is the actual substance of the mission. Pisidia and Pamphylia are the mountain country and the coastal plain — the same Taurus crossing as before, in reverse, and the same fever-ridden lowland at the bottom of it. Then Attalia, the working harbour a few miles west of Perga, where they wait for a ship going east.

Reckon up what Luke has covered in two chapters: well over a thousand miles of walking and sailing, the best part of two years, five cities evangelised, one man stoned. Almost none of it is scenes. Most of a life given to God looks like verses 24 and 25 — getting to the next place, speaking there, and going on. If you have ever felt that your own discipleship is short of moments and long on plodding, this is what the plodding looks like in Scripture when it is written down by somebody who was there.

verseByVerse.quote: and from there they sailed to Antioch, where they had been commended to the grace of God for the work that they had fulfilled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And from there they sailed to Antioch, where they had been commended to the grace of God for the work that they had fulfilled.

They go home. And Luke identifies home not by its geography but by what had happened there at the start: this is the place where they had been commended to the grace of God.

Turn back to that scene for a moment. A congregation fasted and prayed and laid hands on its two best men and let them go (13:1–3) — and having done that, there was nothing else it could do. They could not send messages. They had no way of knowing whether the two were alive. Every event in these two chapters — the blinded magician, the expulsion from Antioch, the crowd with the oxen, the stoning — reached the sending church for the first time in the next verse, long after it was all over.

So what had that church actually done when it commended these men to the grace of God? It had put two people somewhere it could not follow them, and left them there, and gone on praying. That is what the phrase means when it is not a formula. It is what a parent does at a door. It is what a congregation does at an airport. It is what any of us does with somebody we love and cannot help — and this verse is here to say that it is not a gesture. The ship came in, and both men were on it.

Then the last phrase, which is a small masterpiece of accounting: for the work that they had fulfilled. Not attempted. Not begun. Not made a good start on. The commission of 13:2 — the work to which I have called them — is closed out here with the same word, completed. Between those two sentences lie a hundred miles of mountain road, a stoning, and churches in five cities.

Very few of us ever get a sentence like that written about anything we have done. But notice what made it possible, because it is available. The work was defined by the one who gave it, not by the men doing it. They had not set out to evangelise the world, or to reach a figure, or to keep going until they felt it was enough — which is a race with no finishing line and is how a great many earnest Christians exhaust themselves. They had been sent for a work. When it was done, they came home.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they arrived and gathered the church together, they declared all that God had done with them, and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. And they remained no little time with the disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they arrived and gathered the church together, they declared all that God had done with them.

The report is given standing in front of the congregation that sent them, and its grammar is the whole point: all that God had done with them. Not what they had done for God. Not even what they had achieved with his help. God is the subject of the sentence and the two of them are the instrument he used. Luke has bracketed the entire journey with the same claim — commended to the grace of God at one end, all that God had done at the other.

That is not modesty, and it is not a pious way of talking. It is accuracy, and it is also the only kind of report a sending church can safely be given. A congregation that hears what its missionaries have accomplished will begin, quietly, to assess them, and the next report will have to be better than this one. A congregation that hears what God has done will begin to pray.

And how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles.

The image stayed with Paul for the rest of his life: a wide door for effective work at Ephesus, with many adversaries (1 Cor. 16:9); a door opened for him at Troas (2 Cor. 2:12); a request from prison that God would open a door for the word (Col. 4:3).

Notice who opens it. Not the missionaries. They had walked through a door; they had not made one, and they are careful to say so in the same breath as the report of their own two years' work. And notice what kind of door it is — not a door of opportunity or of success, but a door of faith. What God had made possible was that Gentiles could come in on the same terms as anyone else, by believing, without first becoming something they were not.

Which is precisely the sentence about to cause the worst crisis in the church's history. Every word of that report was true and welcome in Antioch — and within a short time men would come down from Judea to say that the door had been opened too wide, and that these Gentiles must be circumcised. Luke sets the two chapters side by side without a joint. The report of an opened door is followed immediately by an attempt to narrow it, and that is a pattern worth expecting rather than being wounded by: the clearest work of God tends to be followed, quite soon, by an argument about it inside the church.

And they remained no little time with the disciples. Luke's understatement — a good long while. After two years on the road, five churches and a stoning, the record of the greatest missionary journey yet undertaken ends with two tired men staying put for months with their own congregation.

There is a permission in that for anyone who has come to believe that faithfulness means never stopping. The Spirit who said set apart for me Barnabas and Saul is the same Spirit under whose hand they now sit still in Antioch and do nothing remarkable. Rest, in this book, is not a lapse in obedience. It is part of the shape of it.

14.theology: Suffering as the Path of the Kingdom. Acts 14:22 is the New Testament’s clearest statement that suffering is the appointed means by which the people of God enter the kingdom. This is not peripheral; it is structural. The cross was not a detour on the way to the resurrection; it was the way. And the church that follows a crucified Lord is called to the same road. Paul writes later that he fills up in his flesh “what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions for the sake of his body” (Colossians 1:24) — not that Christ’s atoning work was incomplete, but that the suffering of Christ is reproduced in his body, the church, as the gospel goes forth into the world. The church that suffers for the name is the church that looks most like its Lord. And it is the church that the watching world cannot ultimately explain away.
14.examples:
Then: Paul, stoned and left for dead outside Lystra, rising and walking back into the city, going on to Derbe the next morning. Returning through Lystra and Iconium and Antioch — the cities that had tried to kill him — to strengthen the believers he left behind. Appointing elders, committing them to God with prayer and fasting, and sailing home to report everything God had done. This is what faithful looks like.

Now: The Western church has largely lost the theology of suffering. We expect the Christian life to be comfortable, and when it is not, we assume something has gone wrong. Acts 14 says the opposite: tribulation is the appointed road, and the God who walked it first walks it with his people. The suffering church is not the failing church; it is often the most faithful church — and, in God’s strange economy, the most fruitful.

15.title: The Jerusalem Council
15.text: <sup>1</sup>But some men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.” <sup>2</sup>And after Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and debate with them, Paul and Barnabas and some of the others were appointed to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and the elders about this question. <sup>3</sup>So, being sent on their way by the church, they passed through both Phoenicia and Samaria, describing in detail the conversion of the Gentiles, and brought great joy to all the brothers. <sup>4</sup>When they came to Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the church and the apostles and the elders, and they declared all that God had done with them. <sup>5</sup>But some believers who belonged to the party of the Pharisees rose up and said, “It is necessary to circumcise them and to order them to keep the law of Moses.” <sup>6</sup>The apostles and the elders were gathered together to consider this matter. <sup>7</sup>And after there had been much debate, Peter stood up and said to them, “Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe. <sup>8</sup>And God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us, <sup>9</sup>and he made no distinction between us and them, having cleansed their hearts by faith. <sup>10</sup>Now, therefore, why are you putting God to the test by placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?
