<sup>11</sup>But we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will.” <sup>12</sup>And all the assembly fell silent, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul as they related what signs and wonders God had done through them among the Gentiles. <sup>13</sup>After they finished speaking, James replied, “Brothers, listen to me. <sup>14</sup>Simeon has related how God first visited the Gentiles, to take from them a people for his name. <sup>15</sup>And with this the words of the prophets agree, just as it is written, <sup>16</sup>‘After this I will return, and I will rebuild the tent of David that has fallen; I will rebuild its ruins, and I will restore it, <sup>17</sup>that the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by my name, says the Lord, who makes these things <sup>18</sup>known from of old.’ <sup>19</sup>Therefore my judgment is that we should not trouble those of the Gentiles who turn to God, <sup>20</sup>but should write to them to abstain from the things polluted by idols, and from sexual immorality, and from what has been strangled, and from blood. <sup>21</sup>For from ancient generations Moses has had in every city those who proclaim him, for he is read every Sabbath in the synagogues.” <sup>22</sup>Then it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole church, to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas. They sent Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas, leading men among the brothers, <sup>23</sup>with the following letter: “The brothers, both the apostles and the elders, to the brothers who are of the Gentile nations in Antioch and Syria and Cilicia, greetings. <sup>24</sup>Since we have heard that some persons have gone out from us and troubled you with words, unsettling your minds, although we gave them no instructions, <sup>25</sup>it has seemed good to us, having come to one accord, to choose men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul, <sup>26</sup>men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. <sup>27</sup>We have therefore sent Judas and Silas, who themselves will tell you the same things by word of mouth. <sup>28</sup>For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay on you no greater burden than these requirements: <sup>29</sup>that you abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality. If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell.” <sup>30</sup>So when they were sent off, they went down to Antioch, and having gathered the congregation together, they delivered the letter. <sup>31</sup>And when they had read it, they rejoiced because of its encouragement. <sup>32</sup>And Judas and Silas, who were themselves prophets, encouraged and strengthened the brothers with many words. <sup>33</sup>And after they had spent some time, they were sent off in peace by the brothers to those who had sent them. <sup>35</sup>But Paul and Barnabas remained in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord, with many others also. <sup>36</sup>And after some days Paul said to Barnabas, “Let us return and visit the brothers in every city where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, and see how they are.” <sup>37</sup>Now Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark. <sup>38</sup>But Paul thought best not to take with them one who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work. <sup>39</sup>And there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus, <sup>40</sup>but Paul chose Silas and departed, having been commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord. <sup>41</sup>And he went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.
15.overview:
The first great theological crisis of the church comes from within. Men from Judea arrive in Antioch teaching that Gentile believers must be circumcised to be saved. This is not a secondary issue — it is the gospel itself at stake. If Gentiles must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses in order to be saved, then Christ alone is not enough. The cross is not sufficient. Grace is not free. Paul and Barnabas see this immediately and oppose it with everything they have.

The Jerusalem Council is the church’s first great doctrinal assembly — and what it produces is not a compromise but a clarification. Peter says it most plainly: neither we nor our fathers have been able to bear the yoke of the law. Why lay it on the Gentiles? We believe we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus — just as they will. The playing field is level at the foot of the cross. There is one way of salvation for Jew and Gentile alike: grace through faith in the Lord Jesus.

James confirms with Amos: God always intended to take a people for his name from the Gentiles. This is not deviation from the old covenant; it is its fulfilment. The letter goes out. The Gentile churches are freed from the burden of circumcision. The gospel is clarified, codified, and sent. And then, quietly, Paul and Barnabas fall out over John Mark, and the mission continues in two streams — which means God uses even the sharp disagreements of his servants to multiply the advance of his kingdom.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
This is the hinge of the book, and the question it settles decides what Christianity is going to be. Must a Gentile become a Jew in order to be saved, or is faith in Jesus Christ enough on its own? It is not a boundary dispute. If circumcision is added to faith as a condition of salvation, then Christ's death was not sufficient, and grace is no longer grace.

The crisis (vv. 1–5). Men come down from Judea to Antioch teaching that without circumcision you cannot be saved. Paul and Barnabas fight them — Luke's phrase is no small dissension — and the church sends a delegation to Jerusalem, preaching the whole way and welcomed at the other end (vv. 3–4). There the objection is put formally by believers of the party of the Pharisees (v. 5).

The debate (vv. 6–21). After much argument Peter stands up and appeals to what God did in Cornelius's house a decade earlier: God gave them the Spirit, made no distinction, and cleansed their hearts by faith (vv. 7–9). Then his conclusion, which is the most radical sentence in the chapter — the law is a yoke nobody has ever carried, and we shall be saved by grace just as they will (vv. 10–11). Barnabas and Paul report the signs God did among the Gentiles and the room goes silent (v. 12). James sums up: Peter's testimony agrees with the prophets, and Amos had said God would rebuild David's fallen tent so that the nations should seek him (vv. 13–18). His ruling is that the Gentiles must not be troubled, but should be asked to abstain from four things for the sake of shared life with Jewish believers who hear Moses read every Sabbath (vv. 19–21).

The letter (vv. 22–29). The apostles and elders, with the whole church, choose Judas Barsabbas and Silas to carry the decision in person. The letter disowns the men who had unsettled Antioch, commends Barnabas and Paul as men who have risked their lives, and states the verdict in the most audacious formula any church has ever used: it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us.

The relief (vv. 30–35). The letter is read aloud to the whole congregation and they rejoice at its encouragement. Judas and Silas, both prophets, stay a while and strengthen the church with many words, and are sent off in peace — the chapter that opened in dissension closing this stage of it in peace. Then Paul and Barnabas settle to the ordinary work of teaching and preaching in Antioch, with many others also, none of whom Luke names.
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification by Faith Alone — the Council's Theological Verdict

Peter's speech in vv. 8–11 is the clearest statement of justification by faith alone in the book of Acts: 'God made no distinction between us and them, having cleansed their hearts by faith... we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will.' The Gentiles are saved the same way the Jews are — by grace through faith, not by law observance. This is the verdict that Paul will develop in Galatians and Romans. The Jerusalem Council is the communal confirmation of what the Spirit had demonstrated in Cornelius's house.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Jerusalem Council produced a letter of pastoral decision rather than a theological treatise — practical guidance that allowed Jew and Gentile to live together in one community. Now: The church continues to face questions about what is required for full membership in the people of God. The council's method — testimony, Scripture, deliberation, pastoral wisdom — remains the model for ecclesial discernment on divisive questions.

verseByVerse.quote: But some men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers, "Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved." And after Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and debate with them, Paul and Barnabas and some of the others were appointed to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and the elders about this question.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.

Weigh that sentence, because almost everything in it is right. It assumes Jesus is the Messiah. It assumes he died and rose. It assumes these Gentiles must be saved and wants them saved. It is not the sentence of an unbeliever, and the men saying it were not pretending. What it does is add one condition — and that is all it takes.

This is worth grasping, because Christians tend to picture false teaching as a denial. It very rarely is. Heresy that matters is almost always an addition, made by sincere people, to a set of true statements. The most dangerous sentence in the New Testament is not one that contradicts the gospel. It is one that agrees with it and then says and.

Why does one word matter so much? Because of what it does to the whole. Suppose salvation is ninety-nine parts God's grace and one part your compliance. That one part is now the part everything hangs on — the joint that can fail — and your standing before God rests, in the end, on you. Paul saw this instantly and wrote to these very churches in the most violent language he ever used: if you accept circumcision, Christ will be of no advantage to you... you are severed from Christ (Gal. 5:2–4). Not damaged. Severed. A gift with a condition attached is not a gift, and a rescue you have to help with is not a rescue.

No small dissension and debate. Luke is being dry; he means a furious row. And notice that Paul had it. There is an instinct in Christians, and it is usually a good one, that peace is the higher value and a man who argues has failed. This verse says otherwise. On the gospel itself, refusing to fight is not gentleness; it is desertion.

But watch how precisely Paul aims. In the very next chapter he will take a young man with a Greek father and circumcise him himself (16:3), and to the Galatians he says he would not let Titus be circumcised for a moment (Gal. 2:3–5). Same rite, same apostle, opposite decisions — because in one case it was a free choice made for the sake of the mission, and in the other it was being demanded as a condition of salvation. That distinction is the whole of Christian wisdom about secondary things: what you may cheerfully do for love, you must refuse absolutely the moment somebody makes it necessary.

Then: Paul and Barnabas and some of the others were appointed to go up to Jerusalem. The verb is passive; the church did the appointing. And there is something striking in Paul submitting to it. This is the man who insists his gospel came to him from no human being (Gal. 1:11–12), and he does not need Jerusalem's permission to preach. He goes anyway — because being right on your own is not the same as the church being settled, and the unity of the whole was worth a journey of some three hundred miles on foot.

Here is the question to put to yourself before reading on. Almost every Christian has an unspoken and. Something added, privately, to faith in Christ — a habit, a level of feeling, an achievement, a version of the past put right — without which you do not quite believe God has accepted you. Name it. That is your circumcision, and this chapter was written about it.

verseByVerse.quote: "So, being sent on their way by the church, they passed through both Phoenicia and Samaria, describing in detail the conversion of the Gentiles, and brought great joy to all the brothers. When they came to Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the church and the apostles and the elders, and they declared all that God had done with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Being sent on their way by the church. The word means equipped and provisioned for a journey — Antioch paid for it. They are not slipping off to defend themselves; they are going as the congregation's representatives, at the congregation's expense.

And look at what they did on the road. They are travelling to a hearing about whether the Gentiles they have converted are really saved, and they spend the journey describing in detail the conversion of the Gentiles through Phoenicia and Samaria. Not marshalling arguments. Telling the story, at length, in every church they passed. Men on the way to a tribunal turned the trip into a preaching tour.

And it landed: they brought great joy to all the brothers. Notice who those brothers were. Samaria is where Philip preached and where Peter and John had to come down and see for themselves (8:14). Phoenicia is where the refugees of the persecution had fled and first spoken to Greeks (11:19). These were the congregations who had themselves been outside the circle most recently — and they are the ones who receive the news with unmixed gladness. People who have just been let in are rarely the ones who want the door narrowed.

Then Jerusalem, and Luke is careful: they were welcomed by the church and the apostles and the elders. The mother church received them warmly. Whatever the men of verse 1 were, they were not Jerusalem's voice, and the letter will say so in writing (v. 24). The problem is a faction, not an institution — which is worth remembering before writing off a whole church because of who turned up from it.

And they declared all that God had done with them — the same sentence Luke used of the report at Antioch (14:27), and it means the same thing there and here: God is the subject; they are the instrument.

One question hovers over this visit and is worth settling honestly, because a reader with a study Bible will meet it. Is this the visit Paul describes in Galatians 2, where he went up to Jerusalem, laid his gospel before the pillars, and they added nothing to it? Many think so: the cast is identical (Paul, Barnabas, Peter, James, John), the issue is identical, and so is the outcome. Others place Galatians 2 at the earlier famine visit (11:30), chiefly because Paul is listing his Jerusalem visits precisely in order to prove his independence, and it would be odd for him to skip one — which would also mean Galatians was written before this council rather than after it.

The honest position is that it is not certain, and that very little rests on it. On either reading the two accounts say the same decisive thing: Paul submitted his gospel to the Jerusalem leadership, and they added nothing to it. (The one place the two men later clashed in person — Peter withdrawing from the Gentile table at Antioch, Gal. 2:11–14 — is dealt with at 11:2–3 and does not need going over again.)

verseByVerse.quote: "But some believers who belonged to the party of the Pharisees rose up and said, 'It is necessary to circumcise them and to order them to keep the law of Moses.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But some believers who belonged to the party of the Pharisees rose up.

Read that description twice, because Luke has put two words together that most of us keep well apart. Believers. And Pharisees. These are not opponents of the church who have infiltrated it. They are converted men, inside it, who love the God of Israel and have now come to trust his Messiah — and they are the crisis.

Try to feel the case from where they were standing, because contempt for them will stop you learning anything. These were men raised to believe that the boundary of God's people was marked in the flesh, by God's own command to Abraham, four hundred years before Moses and never once withdrawn. They had kept the law at genuine cost. Some of them had probably been beaten for it. And they are now being asked to receive as full members of the covenant people men who were sacrificing to idols eighteen months ago and who still, as far as anyone can tell, eat whatever is put in front of them. Their objection is not malice. It is a lifetime of conviction meeting a new fact.

And the man who will argue hardest against them had been one of them. Paul was a Pharisee, son of a Pharisee, and said so under oath years later (23:6; Phil. 3:5). He is not refuting a position he finds strange. He is refuting the one he used to hold, which is why he does it so exactly and with so little patience.

It is necessary to circumcise them. Necessary — the word Luke uses through his Gospel and this book for divine obligation, the must that stood over the cross. They are not saying it would be wiser or safer or more consistent. They are saying God requires it. Nothing smaller would have needed a council.

So where does this live now? Not in circumcision; nobody is arguing about that. It lives wherever the church quietly attaches to salvation a mark that Christ did not attach. A particular translation. A conversion story of the right shape, with a date. A style of worship, a position on secondary doctrine, a political allegiance, a manner of speaking, a family arrangement. None of these need be stated as a condition; they only have to function as one.

Here is a test you can run this week, and it is uncomfortable. Think of the marker you privately treat as necessary. Now picture meeting, in heaven, somebody who trusted Christ and got that thing wrong all his life. If you find in yourself a hesitation — a small unwillingness, a sense that surely there would have to be some qualification — you have found your circumcision, and this chapter is about you and not about first-century Judea.

And a guard, because the opposite error is just as available: this does not mean nothing matters. The council itself is about to lay down four things (v. 29) and Paul will spend his letters on how Christians ought to live. The entire chapter turns on keeping two questions apart — what is required in order to be saved, and what is required in order to live together. Collapse them in either direction and you get a false gospel or a lawless church.

verseByVerse.quote: The apostles and the elders were gathered together to consider this matter. And after there had been much debate, Peter stood up and said to them, "Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles and the elders were gathered together to consider this matter. And after there had been much debate...

Sit with that for a moment, because it is not how most Christians imagine the early church working. The first council in the history of the faith, on the most important question it would ever face, with apostles in the room — and it was a long argument. No voice from heaven. No prophecy settling it at the outset. Men talked, and disagreed, and went on talking.

And this same meeting produced the sentence it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us (v. 28). So the Spirit's verdict came at the end of a hard debate rather than instead of one. That is worth having if you have been taught to expect God's guidance to arrive as a feeling, or to treat the need for argument as evidence that something has gone wrong. Here is the apostolic pattern, in order: evidence of what God has actually done, tested against Scripture, argued out in the open, decided together, and then owned. Nobody in this room had a dream.

Peter stood up. And this is the last we hear from him. The man who preached at Pentecost, who opened the door to Cornelius, who has carried the first half of this book, speaks once more and then leaves the narrative altogether — his exit was noted at 12:17. He goes out not with a miracle but with an argument for somebody else's freedom.

In the early days God made a choice among you. Peter is putting a date on it. Cornelius was perhaps ten years earlier, and the whole Jerusalem church had heard the report and given its verdict at the time: then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life (11:18). They had already settled this. And here they are, a decade on, arguing about it again.

Which is not a first-century failing. A church can formally agree something, mean it, and then discover ten years later that the agreement never reached the place where convictions actually live. What is being resisted at this council is not new information. It is the cost of what they already believed.

And notice the grammar of Peter's claim, made in a room where his own authority is one of the pressures: God made a choice... that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear. God chose; Peter's mouth was the instrument. He has the strongest personal precedent in the room and he takes no personal credit for it, which is precisely why the precedent carries.

verseByVerse.quote: "And God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us, and he made no distinction between us and them, having cleansed their hearts by faith."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them.

The word is kardiognostes — heart-knower — and it is rare enough to be worth tracing. It occurs twice in the whole New Testament, and both times in Acts. Here, and at 1:24, when the eleven had to choose between two men and prayed you, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which one of these two you have chosen.

Both times the church has to make a decision about who is in. Both times it reaches for the same name for God, and the reason is the same: men can see the outside of a person and God can see the rest. In a debate about whether a mark in the flesh is required, Peter names God by the attribute that makes the flesh irrelevant.

And then the evidence, which is not an argument but a fact: God gave them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us. Not a lesser measure, not a provisional instalment pending regularisation. The same. Peter is saying, in effect: you may debate whether these people qualify, but God has already moved in, and he did it without waiting for our decision.

He made no distinction between us and them. The verb is the one the Spirit used to Peter on the roof and the one the circumcision party turned against him afterwards — the wordplay is set out at 11:2 and needs no repeating. What matters here is the tense. God made no distinction. It is done. The question before the council is not whether to admit the Gentiles but whether to reimpose a distinction God has already removed.

Then the clause that wins the argument: having cleansed their hearts by faith.

Peter chooses that verb deliberately. It is the word from the sheet let down from heaven — what God has made clean, do not call common (10:15). He is quoting his own vision back to the council without saying so.

But look where the cleansing happened. Not the body: the heart. And that is exactly the organ the Old Testament always said was the problem. Moses told Israel to circumcise the foreskin of your heart (Deut. 10:16). He promised that one day God himself would do it — the LORD your God will circumcise your heart... so that you will love him (Deut. 30:6). Jeremiah said the whole nation was uncircumcised in heart (Jer. 9:26). Ezekiel had God promising a new heart I will give you, and a new spirit I will put within you (Ezek. 36:26).

So here is what Peter has actually said. The party of the Pharisees is asking for the sign. God has already given the thing the sign pointed at. They want the knife on the body of men whose hearts have been cut by God himself.

And the last two words carry it: by faith. Not by ritual, not by descent, not by effort, not by a probationary period of good behaviour. The instrument by which a heart is made clean is empty-handed trust — which is why it is available to a Roman centurion, and why it is available to you tonight, and why no committee anywhere has ever been able to add a step to it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now, therefore, why are you putting God to the test by placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now, therefore, why are you putting God to the test?

That is a serious charge and Peter aims it at the most orthodox men in the room. The phrase belongs to the wilderness — it is what Israel did at Massah, and what God's own summary of those forty years accuses them of (the wilderness generation is treated at 13:18). Peter tells the party of the Pharisees that they are repeating it.

How? Because to put God to the test is to demand that he do it your way after he has shown you his. God has already acted: he gave the Spirit, he cleansed the hearts, he made no distinction. To require circumcision now is to inform God that his method was insufficient — and to do it while calling yourself a defender of his law.

Then the image: a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear.

Consider who is speaking and where. Peter is an observant Jew, standing in Jerusalem, in front of Pharisees, and he says: none of us has ever managed it. Not our fathers. Not us. Not me. He does not say the law is bad — he says it is a weight no one in the history of his nation has carried, and that the honest record of Israel is a thousand years of proving it. The generation that received it broke it before Moses got down the mountain; the nation that was given the land was deported out of it for the same reason.

And every serious person knows the feeling from the inside, whatever his religion. You can manage the outside. You cannot manage the inside — and the law asked for the inside, which is what makes it unbearable. A rule about murder can be kept. A rule about what you want can not.

So Peter's argument runs: you are proposing to lay on these Gentiles a burden that has crushed every one of us who has ever tried to carry it, and to do it in the name of kindness.

And then the sentence that turns the whole council over, and it is easy to read past. But we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will.

Read the order of it. Peter does not say that the Gentiles will be saved the way we are. He says that we will be saved the way they are. The Gentiles have become the standard, and the Jewish believer is measured against them.

Nothing in the chapter is more startling. The people with the covenant, the patriarchs, the temple, the prophets, the law and the pedigree are told by the apostle to the circumcision that their salvation is the same bare grace as that of an uncircumcised Roman officer converted the day before yesterday. Every advantage still exists — Paul will list them all in Romans 9 and call them real — and not one of them contributes anything at the point of being saved.

Which cuts in both directions, and the second is the comfort. If everything you have that makes you a better candidate counts for nothing here, then everything you have that makes you a worse candidate counts for nothing here either. The Christian of forty years and the convert of last Tuesday are saved by the identical mechanism, and neither has the smallest advantage over the other in it. There is one door, it is very low, and everybody goes through it on the same terms.

verseByVerse.quote: "And all the assembly fell silent, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul as they related what signs and wonders God had done through them among the Gentiles. After they finished speaking, James replied, 'Brothers, listen to me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And all the assembly fell silent.

Six verses earlier there had been much debate. Now nobody speaks. Luke puts the two states of that room side by side and lets the silence do the work: the argument has run out of road, and the men who were shouting are listening.

And notice the order of the names — Barnabas and Paul. Ever since the proconsul's house it has been Paul first, every time. In Jerusalem the old order comes back, because in Jerusalem Barnabas is the trusted man: the Levite who sold his field for the church (4:36–37), the one man willing to vouch for Saul when everybody else was frightened of him (9:27), Jerusalem's own emissary to Antioch (11:22). Luke's word order is tracking the room, and it is the sort of detail a man makes up only if he was there.

What the two of them do is also worth noticing. They do not argue theology; Peter has done that. They report. What signs and wonders God had done through them among the Gentiles — facts, laid before the assembly as evidence.

And that gives the council's method, which is a model worth keeping. Testimony first — what has God actually done? Then Scripture — James is about to say the prophets agree with it (v. 15). Then judgment (v. 19). Experience is admitted as evidence and is never made the authority; Scripture decides, and had Amos not agreed, no quantity of signs would have settled the question. That order guards a church in both directions: against deciding doctrine from stories, and against being so afraid of stories that it cannot see what God is plainly doing in front of it.

Then: After they finished speaking, James replied.

Which James? Not the apostle — that James was executed with a sword at 12:2. Not the son of Alphaeus, of whom we know almost nothing. This is the brother of Jesus, and the fact deserves a moment.

He grew up in the same house. He watched his older brother at the carpenter's bench and at family meals for the best part of thirty years, and he did not believe a word of it: not even his brothers believed in him (John 7:5). When the family came to take Jesus away because they thought he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21), James was presumably among them. Then Jesus was crucified — and then, Paul tells us in a bare line, he appeared to James (1 Cor. 15:7). We are told nothing about that meeting. We only see the result: the brother who thought he was mad is now the leading man of the Jerusalem church, presiding over the decision that his brother is the Saviour of the world.

If you are praying for somebody in your own family who has heard it all and believes none of it — who knows the Christian at close quarters and is unimpressed — James is your verse. It took a resurrection. But it happened, and he was in the house the whole time.

One more thing, stated plainly and without heat, because readers ask. Peter speaks here, and James rules. Whatever weight one gives Peter's leadership elsewhere, in this room the summing-up belongs to the head of the local church, and the decision is taken by the apostles and elders with the whole church (v. 22). That is what the text shows. It is worth noticing, and it is not worth quarrelling over.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Simeon has related how God first visited the Gentiles, to take from them a people for his name.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simeon has related how God first visited the Gentiles, to take from them a people for his name.

Three things in one sentence, and each is doing careful work.

First, the name. James calls him Simeon — the Hebrew form, not Peter, not even the usual Greek Simon. In a room debating whether Gentiles must become Jews, James refers to the man who argued for Gentile freedom by his most Jewish name. He is not conceding an inch of the argument. He is signalling to the party he is about to rule against that the case did not come from an outsider. That is how a wise man wins a disagreement inside a family: he takes away every reason to dismiss the messenger before he takes away the argument.

Second, the verb: God visited the Gentiles. In the Greek Old Testament that word is not neutral; it is what God does when he comes to rescue. He visited Sarah and she conceived (Gen. 21:1). He visited his people in their slavery and Israel bowed and worshipped (Exod. 4:31). Zechariah, holding his newborn son, sang that the Lord God of Israel has visited and redeemed his people (Luke 1:68). It is the homecoming word, the word for God turning up on behalf of his own. James takes it and puts it on the nations.

Third, and most provocative of all: a people for his name. The Greek Old Testament keeps two words carefully apart — laos, the people, meaning Israel; and ta ethne, the nations, meaning everybody else. James has just taken the word reserved for Israel and applied it to men taken out of the nations. In eleven words he has called Gentiles a visited people who bear God's name.

It would have been difficult to say anything more inflammatory to the men of verse 5, and he says it gently, in their own vocabulary, from their own Scriptures.

And note the small word that keeps it honest: from them. Not all of them. God is taking a people out of the nations, which is remnant language, and it guards two errors at once — the idea that everyone is swept in regardless, and the idea that the church has simply replaced Israel. What is happening is what was always promised: out of every nation, a people, called by his name.

verseByVerse.quote: "And with this the words of the prophets agree, just as it is written, "'After this I will return, and I will rebuild the tent of David that has fallen; I will rebuild its ruins, and I will restore it,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And with this the words of the prophets agree.

Notice which way round that is. James does not say the prophets predicted this and therefore we must accept it. He says the testimony and the prophets agree — the Scriptures are the fixed point, and what Peter, Barnabas and Paul have reported is being measured against them. Had Amos not agreed, no number of signs and wonders would have settled the matter. The council's whole doctrine of authority is in that one verb.

Then the quotation, and the picture in it is better than most of us notice. The tent of David that has fallen. Amos does not say the house of David or the throne of David. He says the booth — the word for a temporary shelter, the kind of thing thrown up out of branches in a vineyard at harvest and taken down again afterwards. The dynasty that was promised an everlasting throne is described by the prophet as a garden hut, and a collapsed one.

And God's answer is not to replace it with something grander. I will rebuild the tent of David that has fallen; I will rebuild its ruins, and I will restore it. He goes back to the fallen shelter and puts that up again.

Now the difficulty, which the honest reader will meet the moment he turns to Amos, and which is worth facing squarely rather than stepping over. James is quoting the Greek Old Testament, and at the crucial point it does not read like the Hebrew. Amos 9:12 in our English Bibles, translated from the Hebrew, says the purpose is that they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations who are called by my name. James quotes it as that the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord. Edom has become mankind, and possessing has become seeking.

Three things settle it. First, the differences are exactly the kind that arise between two ancient copies rather than the kind a translator invents: in Hebrew written without vowels, Edom and mankind are the same three consonants, and possess and seek differ by a single letter. The Greek translators were working from a Hebrew manuscript and read the consonants one way; the text behind our Old Testament read them another. Second, James is speaking to a Greek-speaking church from the Bible they actually used, which is what Paul did in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch (13:41) and what any preacher does.

Third, and decisively: his argument survives on either text. Even in the Hebrew, the restored kingdom of David includes all the nations who are called by my name — Gentiles bearing God's name inside David's rebuilt house, which is precisely the point in dispute. The council did not smuggle the Gentiles in through a variant. Both texts have them there; the Greek simply says it more warmly.

So James can settle a question about the present from a prophet of the eighth century BC. The tent of David is being rebuilt now, in the risen Son of David, and the proof that the rebuilding is under way is standing in the room: Gentiles seeking the Lord, exactly as Amos said they would when it happened.

Here too brothers read the prophecy differently, and it is worth noting kindly. On the amillennial / Reformed reading taken above, the 'rebuilding of David's fallen tent' is being fulfilled now in the risen Son of David and the ingathering of the Gentiles into his church — which is exactly why James cites it to settle the question. Our dispensational friends, by contrast, generally take Amos's rebuilt tent of David to await a future, literal restoration of national Israel and the Davidic throne in the millennial kingdom; on their reading James is not declaring the prophecy fulfilled today but showing that the present Gentile ingathering is in harmony with the prophets ('after this I will return and rebuild'), the church age being a foretaste of what Christ will yet establish at his return. Both honour the prophets and rejoice that Gentiles are saved by grace, apart from becoming Jews — the very point of the council; the difference belongs to the larger, family conversation between amillennial and dispensational readings of God's future for Israel, and should be carried with charity.

verseByVerse.quote: "'that the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by my name, says the Lord, who makes these things'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
That the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord.

This is the purpose clause, and it answers a question most readers never think to ask: why is the tent of David rebuilt at all? Not so that Israel may have a king again for its own sake. The prophet gives the reason, and the reason is other people — that the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord. The throne is restored so that those who were never under it can come in.

That single line is the answer to the whole council. If the King was raised up for the sake of the nations, then requiring the nations to become Israelites first has the prophecy backwards.

And all the Gentiles who are called by my name. The Hebrew idiom underneath is more concrete than the English: it is literally that God's name has been called over them. It is what is said of the temple — this house, which is called by my name (1 Kgs 8:43) — and of Jerusalem, and of Israel itself. To have God's name called over something is to have it publicly marked as his property, the way a man's name over a door tells you whose house it is.

Now put that against what the party of the Pharisees was asking for. They wanted a mark. They wanted something visible on the Gentiles' bodies to show they belonged. And Amos says God has already put his own name on them — which is the strongest mark there is, and there is no room on a man for a better one.

Says the Lord. James does not finish on his own authority, and he is about to hand down a ruling. The last voice in his quotation is God's.

And there is a word here for the Christian who does not feel that he belongs — who sits in church suspecting he is tolerated rather than wanted, or who came in late, or from the wrong background, or with a history he would rather nobody knew. Belonging, in this verse, is not established by how you feel about the family. It is established by whose name has been called over you. That was done to you; you did not do it, and you cannot undo it by feeling unworthy of it. The Gentiles in Amos are not told to earn the name. They are told it is already on them.

verseByVerse.quote: "'known from of old.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you are reading this with a Bible open you may be looking at a very short verse and wondering whether something has gone missing — particularly if you grew up with the King James, where verse 18 is a whole sentence: Known unto God are all his works from the beginning of the world. Many people have that line by heart. The ESV gives you three words, and attaches them to the end of Amos's quotation: God is the one who makes these things known from of old.

This is worth explaining rather than passing over, because a reader who notices a gap and is given no account of it will quietly conclude that somebody is hiding something.

The longer sentence stands in the mass of later Greek manuscripts, which is the text the King James translators worked from. The shorter reading is in the oldest and best copies we have. On the shorter reading, the words are still part of what God says through the prophet; on the longer, they become a separate remark of James's own about God's omniscience in general.

Now notice something that ought to be reassuring. The shorter reading — the one the modern versions print — is actually the stronger one for James's argument. A general statement that God knows everything he does would be true but loose. What the better text says is sharper: God made these things known from of old. This particular thing. The ingathering of the nations was published centuries in advance, and the council is not deciding a new policy but catching up with an old announcement.

And take the general point away with you, because it will meet you again in the footnotes of any modern Bible. Nothing in the Christian faith is at stake here. God's eternal knowledge of all his works is taught plainly elsewhere — in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me (Ps. 139:16); declaring the end from the beginning (Isa. 46:10); chosen in him before the foundation of the world (Eph. 1:4). Whichever reading is in your Bible, the doctrine stands; only the address of the proof text moves. That is what the great majority of textual variants are like, and the footnotes exist because translators are being honest with you rather than because the ground is shifting.

So to the verse itself. From of old. This was not a change of plan. God did not revise his policy on the Gentiles somewhere in the middle of the first century in response to how the mission was going. The men in that room are discovering something that had been written down centuries earlier, in a book they had heard read aloud every Sabbath of their lives — the very tragedy Paul laid at Jerusalem's door at 13:27, except that this time they see it.

And there is comfort in the phrase for anybody whose life has not gone to plan. The parts of your life that look like improvisation — the detour, the years that came to nothing, the door that shut — are being handled by someone who does not improvise. Known from of old is a sentence about a plan that was already old when you were born.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Therefore my judgment is that we should not trouble those of the Gentiles who turn to God, but should write to them to abstain from the things polluted by idols, and from sexual immorality, and from what has been strangled, and from blood.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore my judgment is. The word is judicial — James is not offering a view, he is handing down a decision. So it matters enormously what the decision actually is, and the first thing it does is take something away.

That we should not trouble those of the Gentiles who turn to God.

Before one requirement is named, the ruling is: stop making it hard for them. And the verb is stronger than trouble suggests in modern English — it means to harass, to pile difficulty on somebody, and it appears nowhere else in the New Testament. James's formal judgment is that the Gentile converts were being harassed by the church, and that it must stop.

Turn that on ourselves for a moment, because it is not a first-century problem. It is entirely possible to harass people toward Jesus. To attach to the gospel a cloud of expectations — about dress, vocabulary, background, politics, family shape, how quickly the drinking stops, how soon the story can be told tidily — none of them stated as conditions, all of them functioning as conditions; and then to wonder why people who genuinely turned to God do not stay. The first ruling the church ever issued about how to treat new believers begins with the words do not trouble them, and it is not a soft sentiment. It is a verdict against a church that had been doing it.

And notice what James calls them while he is at it: those of the Gentiles who turn to God. That is the conversion word, and he uses it as settled fact. In the act of ruling on the question, he grants the disputed point — they have turned to God — and he says it before he says anything at all about their behaviour. The order is the whole gospel in miniature: they are in, and then we talk about how to live.

But should write to them to abstain from the things polluted by idols, and from sexual immorality, and from what has been strangled, and from blood.

Having lifted the burden, James does lay down four things — and a reader who has followed the argument this far is entitled to ask what they are doing there at all.

If the food laws are abolished, why forbid blood and strangled meat? First, hold on to what the council had just decided: Gentiles are saved by grace, not by keeping the law (15:11) — so these are not kosher rules smuggled back in, nor conditions of salvation. Why ask them, then? For love and unity. Jewish believers were revolted by these things — meat offered to idols, and the eating of blood (which strangled meat retains). Scripture had forbidden blood since Noah, long before Moses (Gen. 9:4; Lev. 17), out of reverence for the life in it. For Jew and Gentile to sit at one table and be one church, the Gentiles — free in conscience — were asked to surrender a few things that would deeply wound their brothers: liberty limited by love (Rom. 14). And all four cluster around the pagan temple — idol-meat, blood, strangled animals, ritual immorality were the stuff of idol-feasts — so the decree also keeps new converts clear of their old idolatry. It is not 'back to the law'; it is 'love your brother, and stay clear of idols.'

But doesn't Paul later allow food offered to idols (1 Cor. 8–10)? No contradiction, once two questions are distinguished. (1) Eating as an act of worship, at a temple feast — Paul forbids it as flatly as the council: 'flee from idolatry... you cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons' (1 Cor. 10:14, 21). On idolatry, Paul and James are identical. (2) Eating meat that merely happened through a temple and is now sold in the market or served at a private meal — this Paul treats as neutral ('an idol has no real existence,' 8:4; 'eat whatever is sold in the meat market,' 10:25), permitted, governed only by love: do not eat if it would wound a weaker brother (8:9–13). So Paul is not overturning the decree but applying its same two principles — flee idolatry, let love limit liberty — with more nuance. The ruling was a wise unity measure for a raw Jewish–Gentile church; its permanent heart — no idolatry, no sexual immorality, freedoms surrendered for love — never changes, even as the specific abstentions from blood and strangled meat are generally understood to belong to that moment (most Christians today do not observe them, seeing the reverence-for-blood fulfilled in the blood of Christ once shed). The thread from James to Paul is one: keep clear of idols, and love your brother more than your dinner.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For from ancient generations Moses has had in every city those who proclaim him, for he is read every Sabbath in the synagogues.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For from ancient generations Moses has had in every city those who proclaim him, for he is read every Sabbath in the synagogues.

This is the reason James gives for the four abstentions, and it is honestly one of the more puzzling sentences in Acts. Careful readers have taken it three ways, and it is better to say so than to pretend the verse is obvious.

Some read it as being about the Jewish believers: Moses is preached in every city, so in every city there are Christians of Jewish background who hold these scruples deeply — which makes the four abstentions the minimum floor on which a mixed congregation can actually eat together. Some read it as being about the Gentiles: anyone who wants the law of Moses can hear it any Sabbath he likes, so the church has no need to impose it — the synagogue is already doing that job. And some read it as a reassurance to the party of the Pharisees that this ruling does no dishonour to Moses, who goes on being read every week regardless.

The first reading fits the ruling's stated purpose best and is the one most take, though the second is attractive and not to be dismissed. But notice that on any of the three, the shape of James's reasoning is the same, and it is the point worth carrying.

He does not ground the four abstentions in the Gentiles' own holiness. He does not say these things will defile you, or damage you, or displease God in themselves. He grounds them in other people — in the existence of believers, in towns these Gentiles will never visit, who hear Moses read every Sabbath and would be unable to sit at a table where blood was served.

So the Gentile Christians of Antioch are being asked to give something up for the sake of men they have not met and will not meet. Not because those men are right — the council has just declared they are not right about circumcision. Because they are brothers.

That is the hardest form of Christian love and much the commonest: surrendering a liberty you are entitled to, for somebody whose scruple you do not share and privately think mistaken. It is the principle the payload of the previous verses works out from Romans 14, and it costs more than the grand sacrifices because nobody notices you doing it and there is no credit in it.

Here is the test, and it is a short one. Name a freedom you are genuinely entitled to — you have thought it through, you are right, and Scripture permits it — that you have actually given up, in practice, because it would have wounded a particular Christian you know. If nothing comes to mind, this verse has not yet reached you.

verseByVerse.quote: Then it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole church, to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas. They sent Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas, leading men among the brothers, with the following letter: "The brothers, both the apostles and the elders, to the brothers who are of the Gentile nations in Antioch and Syria and Cilicia, greetings."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole church.

The congregation is in the sentence. The apostles had the authority, the elders had the oversight, and the whole church is named alongside them in the sending. Luke does not explain the mechanics and it is not worth manufacturing a system out of a clause; but he tells us the decision was not simply handed down from a room upstairs.

And then a piece of pastoral wisdom that is easy to walk past. They had a letter. They could have sent the letter. Instead they chose men from among them and sent them to Antioch with it.

Think about the difference. A ruling that arrives as a document is a verdict; you read it, and then you are alone with your questions and with whatever tone you imagined in it. A ruling that arrives in the hands of two respected men who will stay for weeks and answer anything you ask is a pastoral act. Antioch had been unsettled by men who came with words. Jerusalem answers with men who came with words — and the entire difference is that these were sent.

Look, too, at who was chosen. Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas, leading men among the brothers. Both Jerusalem men. Both, so far as we can tell, Jewish. The delegation carrying a verdict in favour of Gentile freedom is drawn entirely from the side that had most to lose by it — which meant that nobody in Antioch could say the Gentiles had voted themselves a privilege, and nobody in Jerusalem could say the decision had been carried by outsiders. It is the sort of care that costs nothing and prevents years of trouble.

Remember the second name. Silas has come to Antioch to deliver a letter and go home. Within twenty verses he will be Paul's partner on the second missionary journey, and before long he will be singing in a Philippian cell at midnight and producing his Roman citizenship the morning after (16:25, 37). Men are forever setting out on errands that turn into their life's work.

Then the letter itself, and its first word settles the question it was written to answer: The brothers, both the apostles and the elders, to the brothers who are of the Gentile nations. Brothers, on both ends of the address. Not converts, not adherents, not Gentile believers pending regularisation. Before a single clause of argument, the salutation has conceded everything the Judaizers were contesting.

And one small fingerprint for the interested reader. The Greek word for greetings here is the ordinary opening of a Greek letter — and in the whole New Testament it appears in exactly three places: in this letter, in a Roman officer's despatch at 23:26, and in the opening line of the letter of James. The man who drafted this one seems to have written another.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Since we have heard that some persons have gone out from us and troubled you with words, unsettling your minds, although we gave them no instructions, it has seemed good to us, having come to one accord, to choose men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since we have heard that some persons have gone out from us and troubled you with words, unsettling your minds, although we gave them no instructions.

That is the most powerful church in the world putting it in writing that men who had used its name had no authority to do so.

And notice the honesty of the wording. They do not deny that the men came from them. From us is conceded in the same breath as the disowning. What they deny is the commission. That is exactly the right shape for an institution that has been misrepresented, and it is rarer than it ought to be — the standing temptations being either to defend your own because they are your own, or to pretend they were never anything to do with you.

Then the description of the damage, and Luke's vocabulary is not gentle. The word behind unsettling is one used of dismantling a building or stripping a town: they took your minds apart.

Sit with what the injury actually was. Not immorality. Not a split. Unsettled minds. People who had been sure they belonged to God were no longer sure — and that is the characteristic wound of adding anything to the gospel. It does not usually make people worse; it makes them uncertain. And an uncertain Christian cannot love freely, or give freely, or speak of Christ freely, because a part of him is permanently occupied with checking whether he is in. Everything else runs at half power. Anyone who has lived a season without assurance knows precisely how much of life it eats.

Having come to one accord. The phrase is Luke's word for the church's Spirit-given unity — the same word used of the upper room and of the prayer meeting after the first arrests (1:14; 4:24). And here is the thing worth noticing about where he puts it: eighteen verses after much debate (v. 7), and twenty-three after no small dissension (v. 2). They did not reach one accord by leaving the subject alone. The unity is on the far side of the argument, not instead of it — which is the only kind that holds.

Our beloved Barnabas and Paul. The two men whose ministry the Judaizers had been quietly undermining are named in an official document with an adjective of affection. And Barnabas first again — in a Jerusalem letter, the Jerusalem order.

verseByVerse.quote: "'men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. We have therefore sent Judas and Silas, who themselves will tell you the same things by word of mouth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

The Greek is stronger than risked: they have handed over their lives, given themselves up. And when this letter was read aloud in Antioch, that sentence was not a compliment about people far away. The two men were standing in the room. Every person listening could see them, and some of them knew what Paul had looked like when he got back from Lystra.

That is what makes the commendation weigh anything. Jerusalem is not saying these are sound men whose theology we have checked. It is saying: these are the men who have already paid for this gospel with their bodies, and the people telling you they are wrong have paid nothing.

And note what they risked their lives for — not for a doctrine of Gentile inclusion, not for a mission strategy, but for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. The name is the thread running through this whole chapter. God is taking a people for his name (v. 14). The Gentiles are called by his name (v. 17). These men have handed over their lives for the name. And the question the council exists to answer is simply whether that name is enough by itself — which is answered, in a way, by noticing what men will die for.

We have therefore sent Judas and Silas, who themselves will tell you the same things by word of mouth.

The written word and the living voice, sent together and deliberately. They anticipated that a letter can be read with a hostile tone supplied by the reader, or quoted in parts, or explained away by whoever gets to it first. So they sent two men who would say the same things out loud, in the room, and could be asked follow-up questions.

It is a small thing and it is worth copying. If something has gone wrong at a distance — a misunderstanding in a family, a quarrel in a church, a message that landed badly — a letter will very often make it worse, because the reader supplies the voice. Send a person if you possibly can.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay on you no greater burden than these requirements: that you abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality. If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us.

That is the most audacious sentence any church body has ever written about its own decision, and it has been quoted ever since to justify a great deal that it will not bear. So it is worth being exact about what makes it available here.

Three things stand under it, and remove any one and the formula collapses. The Spirit had already acted publicly and visibly, before any of them voted — he fell on Cornelius's household, and Peter's entire argument is that God went first (v. 8). Scripture agreed, and James said so in as many words (v. 15). And apostles were in the room, men holding a commission that is not repeatable. A committee with none of those three has no business borrowing this sentence.

But look at the order of the words, because that is where the guard is. The Holy Spirit, and us. They do not write we have decided, and we trust the Spirit approves. Nor do they write the Spirit has spoken and we merely wrote it down — which would have sounded far more impressive and would have been a lie, because they had argued for hours and Luke says so. Both halves are in the sentence, joined by a plain and, and Christians ever since have wanted to delete one or the other: some claiming a directness God did not give them, others reducing the church's decisions to human management with a prayer at the start.

This is what it looked like when the early church got guidance right. Evidence of what God had actually done, tested against Scripture, argued out in daylight, decided together, and then owned. Nobody had a dream. And afterwards they were willing to put their name next to the Spirit's — which is a far more sobering thing to do than to claim a private impression.

To lay on you no greater burden than these requirements. Note the honesty: it is a burden, and they say so. They do not pretend the four things cost nothing. What they promise is that nothing further will be added — which was the whole anxiety of the Gentile churches, and remains the anxiety of anyone who suspects the requirements will keep coming.

Now something worth doing with a pencil, because Luke gives this decree three times in his book and the wording moves. James speaks it (v. 20); the letter writes it (v. 29); and years later, when Paul comes back to Jerusalem for the last time, James quotes it back at him (21:25). Set the three side by side.

James's spoken ruling was: things polluted by idols, sexual immorality, what has been strangled, blood. The letter reads: what has been sacrificed to idols, blood, what has been strangled, sexual immorality. Two changes, and both are instructive. First, the letter tightens the opening phrase — James said things polluted by idols, which is broad enough to cover almost anything connected with a temple, and the letter says what has been sacrificed to idols, which is a specific and checkable thing. That is what happens when a spoken ruling is put into a document by people who know it will be read by strangers in another country.

Second, the order changes: sexual immorality moves from second place to last, so that the three food matters stand together. And it is the letter's order that sticks — it is exactly the order James himself uses when he quotes the decree at 21:25, years afterwards. Which also settles a question a thoughtful reader will have been carrying: the decree did not quietly lapse once feelings cooled. A decade or more later the Jerusalem church still regarded it as standing.

If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell. And notice how it ends. No threat, no penalty, no warning about what happens otherwise. The most important letter of the first century closes by telling a nervous congregation that they will do well.

verseByVerse.quote: "So when they were sent off, they went down to Antioch, and having gathered the congregation together, they delivered the letter. And when they had read it, they rejoiced because of its encouragement."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having gathered the congregation together, they delivered the letter.

Read to everybody, at once, out loud. Not circulated among the leadership first, not summarised from the front by somebody who had already seen it. The people whose minds had been unsettled heard the answer with their own ears at the same moment as everyone else.

Now stand in that room, because the whole chapter has been building to this and it is the point at which a doctrine becomes a person's own relief.

You are a Gentile in Antioch. A year or two ago you were sacrificing to gods you had grown up with, and then you heard about Jesus and you believed it, and something in you came alive that you had no words for. Then men arrived from Jerusalem — from the place it all came from, from the church of the apostles — and they said that you were not, in fact, saved. That there was a further thing, and until it was done you were outside. Your own teachers could not settle it and went away to ask, and you have spent the intervening months not knowing whether you belong to God.

And now a letter is read aloud, from the apostles and the elders, and its first word is brothers, and it says the men who unsettled you were never sent, and that nothing further is required of you.

They rejoiced because of its encouragement. The word is the same one the synagogue rulers used when they invited Paul to give a word of encouragement (13:15) — something that comes alongside and strengthens. It is what a letter can be when it says the right thing.

And notice what produced the joy. Nothing was added to these people. They received no new experience, no gift, no vision, no fresh instruction. Something was taken away — a doubt — and the result was a congregation in tears of relief. Most of the deepest joys of the Christian life are like that: not additions, but the removal of something that had been standing between you and what you already had.

So it is worth asking whether you are carrying an unsettled mind of your own — some question about whether God has really accepted you that you have never put into words and never had answered. The Christians at Antioch got theirs settled in writing, from the apostles, and wept with relief. You are holding rather more of it in writing than they were.

verseByVerse.quote: "And Judas and Silas, who were themselves prophets, encouraged and strengthened the brothers with many words. And after they had spent some time, they were sent off in peace by the brothers to those who had sent them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judas and Silas, who were themselves prophets.

Jerusalem did not send two couriers. It sent two prophets, and they did not hand over the letter and catch the next ship. They stayed.

And what Luke tells us they did is the plainest description in the New Testament of what a prophet in the early church actually did with his time: they encouraged and strengthened the brothers with many words.

That deserves attention, because the word prophet now conjures something quite different — prediction, private revelation, a man announcing what is about to happen. There is some of that in Acts; Agabus forecasts a famine and later a binding (11:28; 21:11). But here, in the one place where Luke tells us at length what two named prophets did in a local church, the answer is: they talked to people for a long time and left them stronger. Paul's own definition matches it exactly — the one who prophesies speaks to people for their upbuilding and encouragement and consolation (1 Cor. 14:3). Three notes, and not one of them is prediction.

With many words. Luke's cheerful admission that it took a while. This was not a striking sentence delivered over somebody at the end of a meeting. It was hours of talking to frightened people, probably repeating himself, in a church that had been badly shaken and needed to hear the same thing several times before it went in.

Which is a comfort to anybody who suspects his own ministry is unremarkable. The treatment that healed the first church to be wounded by a false gospel was two men staying on for a few weeks and talking to people at length.

They were sent off in peace. Hold that against the opening of the chapter. It began with no small dissension and debate (v. 2) and ran through much debate (v. 7), and now men are sent home in peace. Luke has framed the whole council between those two words, and the peace at the end is not the peace of a subject nobody raised. It is what was left when the thing was fought out properly and settled.

verseByVerse.quote: But Paul and Barnabas remained in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord, with many others also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the verse itself, an oddity most readers will have noticed: your Bible goes straight from verse 33 to verse 35. There is a footnote at the bottom of the page, and it is worth reading, because the missing verse is a small and unusually clear window on how we came to have the New Testament we have.

Verse 34 exists in the King James — Notwithstanding it pleased Silas to abide there still — and in the manuscripts behind it. The modern versions put it in the margin, noting that some manuscripts insert But it seemed good to Silas to remain there, because it is absent from the oldest and best copies we have.

Now ask why anybody would add such a sentence, because the answer is disarming. Look at verse 33: Judas and Silas were sent off, back to the men who had sent them. Then look at verse 40: Paul chooses Silas and departs. A copyist reading those in sequence sees a snag — how can Paul take a man who has gone home to Jerusalem? — and supplies a line to keep Silas in Antioch.

That is the shape of the great majority of textual variants, and it should steady rather than alarm you. The scribe was not inventing doctrine, or protecting a party, or smoothing away something inconvenient. He was tidying a narrative wrinkle, in good faith. And we can see him doing it, because the copies without his tidy-up have survived; the evidence is all still on the table, which is precisely why the footnote is there. Nothing whatever is at stake in verse 34 — Luke was quite capable of leaving a gap between a departure and a return, and Silas may simply have gone and come back, or delayed his going. (The one place in Acts where a footnoted verse carried real weight is 8:37, and it is handled there.)

So to verse 35. Paul and Barnabas remained in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord, with many others also.

The greatest theological crisis in the history of the church has just been resolved, and this is the next sentence: two men stayed put in their own congregation and taught. Councils are rare. Teaching is daily.

And then the clause that ought to be famous and is not. With many others also. Luke names none of them. There were, in Antioch, a large number of people teaching and preaching the word of the Lord, and not one of their names has come down to us. They were doing the same work as the two men whose names fill this book, in the same city, in the same weeks. The record of them is three words.

If you have ever measured your own service against the people whose names are known and concluded that yours does not count, notice that Luke's sentence puts the many others in the same clause as Paul and Barnabas, with the same verbs, and simply does not distinguish. The distinction is ours, not his, and not God's.

One more thing, and Luke does not draw attention to it. This is the last time Paul and Barnabas appear together as partners. The next paragraph is the quarrel.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–41 — The Parting of Paul and Barnabas
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke has just recorded the church surviving its worst doctrinal crisis by argument, Scripture and agreement. He follows it immediately with two of its best men falling out so badly that they cannot work together, and the subject is not doctrine at all. It is whether to give a young man a second chance.

What happened. Paul proposes revisiting the churches (v. 36). Barnabas wants to take John Mark (v. 37). Paul refuses, on the ground that Mark had withdrawn in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work (v. 38). The disagreement is sharp — Luke's word is the one behind our paroxysm — and they separate: Barnabas takes Mark to Cyprus, Paul takes Silas and is commended by the church to the grace of the Lord (vv. 39–40), and goes through Syria and Cilicia strengthening the churches (v. 41).

What Luke does not do. He does not say who was right. There is no narrator's verdict, no hint, no rebuke of either man. The reader's strong wish to be told is a wish Luke declines, and any commentary that supplies the answer is supplying something Scripture withheld.

Both men had a real case. Barnabas is looking at a young man who can be recovered — which is what he has always done, for Saul most of all (9:27). Paul is looking at a commission the Holy Spirit named (13:2), and at towns where he had already been stoned once, and he wants to know that the man beside him will still be there when it gets bad.

What it cost, and what it did not. Something was genuinely lost: two men who had been stoned and mobbed together never appear side by side again in this book, and Scripture does not pretend otherwise. But it did not become permanent. Years later Paul mentions Barnabas to the Corinthians as a fellow worker, in passing and without a shadow (1 Cor. 9:6), and speaks warmly of Mark as Barnabas's cousin (Col. 4:10). Two teams went out where one had gone before. Both of those things are true, and the second does not cancel the first.
verseByVerse.theology:
God's Sovereignty Over Human Conflict

Reformed theology sees in the Paul-Barnabas conflict the characteristic pattern of God's providence: working through human failure and disagreement to accomplish more than perfect human unity might have achieved. The separation produces two missionary teams instead of one. John Mark, the subject of the dispute, will prove his worth — Paul himself will later commend him (2 Timothy 4:11; Colossians 4:10). God does not waste the failures of his servants; he works through them, around them, and despite them.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Barnabas took Mark and sailed to Cyprus — his home, the place that knows him — to restore the man he believes in. Paul took Silas through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches. Both were faithful; both bore fruit. Now: The church's disagreements, when they do not touch the gospel itself, can produce multiplication rather than division if those who disagree remain committed to the mission rather than to winning the argument.

verseByVerse.quote: "And after some days Paul said to Barnabas, 'Let us return and visit the brothers in every city where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, and see how they are.' Now Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us return and visit the brothers in every city where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, and see how they are.

The last clause is the whole man. Paul is not proposing new territory, and he is not proposing a preaching tour. He wants to know how they are. This is somebody who has been driven out of most of those towns, and what is on his mind a year later is whether the people he left behind are all right.

Keep that in view through everything that follows, because the quarrel is about to make both men look small, and the sentence that starts it is one of the kindest in Acts.

Now Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark. Luke drops it in without comment, and any reader who has been paying attention knows at once what is coming, because he told us at 13:13 that Mark had left them and gone home.

But before the argument, look at Barnabas — not this decision, but his whole recorded life, because it is all one thing.

He first appears selling a field and laying the money at the apostles' feet, and Luke pauses to say the apostles had nicknamed him Son of Encouragement (4:36–37). He appears next at the moment when a recently converted persecutor arrived in Jerusalem and the whole church was afraid of him and would not have him near: but Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles (9:27). Years later, when the work at Antioch needed a teacher, it was Barnabas who went to Tarsus to find the man everyone else had forgotten (11:25–26). And when he arrived at an unauthorised congregation of Gentiles that no apostle had planted, he looked at it and saw the grace of God and was glad (11:23).

Every one of those is the same act. Barnabas's entire biography is taking a chance on somebody other people had written off.

And now the irony, which Luke does not point out and does not need to. The man refusing to take a chance on Mark is a man whose entire ministry exists because Barnabas took a chance on him. Strike 9:27 out of the record and there is no Paul in this story at all; he is a suspect ex-persecutor whom nobody would vouch for. He is now declining to do for a young man exactly what was once done for him.

That is not said in order to convict Paul, whose case is serious and comes in the next verse. It is said because it is one of the most human things in the New Testament. It is very possible to have been rescued by a kindness, to be genuinely grateful for it all your life, and to be entirely unable to see the same situation when it turns up in front of you with somebody else's name on it.

And one honest complication, which Luke leaves for us to find elsewhere: Mark was Barnabas's cousin (Col. 4:10). Paul knew that. It does not make Barnabas wrong — a man may be right about somebody and partial to him at the same time, and most of us are both at once — but it is part of the picture, and pretending otherwise would make the scene tidier than it is.

verseByVerse.quote: "But Paul thought best not to take with him one who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Paul thought best not to take with them one who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work.

Now Paul's case, and it is stronger than it is usually given credit for.

Start with the verb Luke chooses for what Mark did. It is not left, which is how the account at 13:13 puts it. It is a heavier word — to stand off from, to desert, to fall away — and it is the verb from which the noun apostasy comes. Whether that is Luke's assessment or Paul's own word reported, it is the strongest term available, and it tells you how Paul had been carrying this for two years.

Then look at how precisely he states the charge, because he does not say what we might expect. He does not say Mark was unreliable, or young, or homesick, or frightened. He says he had not gone with them to the work.

That word — the work — is the point, and it reaches back. It is the word the Holy Spirit used in the sentence that started all of this: set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them (13:2). It is the word used again when the two of them came home, of the work that they had fulfilled (14:26). Paul's objection is not that a young man let him down personally. It is that a man walked out on a commission the Holy Spirit had named, and that the same commission is now being proposed again.

And note the tense: Paul thought best not to is a continuous form. He kept insisting. This was not a remark made once in irritation; it was a position he held through the argument.

So the two of them are not looking at the same thing at all. Barnabas is looking at a person, and asking what will become of him. Paul is looking at a commission, and asking what will become of it. Both objects are real, both men are right about the object they are looking at, and neither can see why the other will not be reasonable.

Anyone who has sat on a church committee, or in a family, where two people of unquestioned goodwill could not be reconciled, has watched this exact thing. It is worth saying plainly that Scripture does not tell you which of them was right. The pressure you feel to award the decision is a pressure Luke deliberately declined, and it is probably the most useful thing this passage does to us — because our instinct in every such conflict is that one party must be the problem, and Luke will not let us have it.
