What we do get, later, is that each of them turned out to be right about something. Barnabas was right about Mark, and Paul himself eventually says so in as many words — the whole of that is set out at 13:13 and does not need repeating. And Paul was right that the second journey would need men who would not go home: within a chapter Silas is in the inner cell of a Philippian prison with his feet in the stocks.

verseByVerse.quote: "And there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus, but Paul chose Silas and departed, having been commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other.

Luke's word is paroxysmos, from which we get paroxysm — a violent flaring, a fit. He does not soften it, and he does not apologise for it.

There is one other place in the New Testament where that noun appears, and it is worth knowing: let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works (Heb. 10:24). The word behind stir up is this one. The same heat that tears two missionaries apart in Antioch is the thing Christians are commanded to provoke in each other. Passion is not the problem in either verse; what it is aimed at is.

Now, what to do with this passage, because it is usually handled badly in both directions.

The common comfort is that God used the quarrel to double the mission — one team became two, and twice the ground was covered. There is something in that, and Luke does let us see both men going on to fruitful work. But it must not be allowed to become approval. Luke reports a rupture between two men who had been mobbed and stoned together, and the plain fact is that they never appear working side by side again in this book. Something real was lost. A reader who is estranged from a Christian brother is not helped by being told that these things generally work out for the best; he is helped by seeing that the Bible records one that hurt, and does not tidy it.

And then the genuine hope, which is better than the tidy version because it rests on evidence rather than on optimism. It did not become permanent. Years afterwards, writing to Corinth about the rights of an apostle, Paul asks: Or is it only Barnabas and I who have no right to refrain from working for a living? (1 Cor. 9:6). It is a throwaway line, and that is exactly what makes it valuable. Long after the split, Paul assumes the Corinthians know Barnabas, puts their two names in one clause, and treats him as a fellow worker in good standing, without a shadow on it. And when he mentions Mark to the Colossians he identifies him, warmly, as the cousin of Barnabas (Col. 4:10) — which means he was still close enough to the family to be using the family relations as shorthand.

So: a real break, and not a permanent one. That is a more useful pattern to carry than either the sentimental version or the despairing one.

Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus. Look where he takes him. Cyprus is Barnabas's own home (4:36), and it is the first leg of the very journey Mark abandoned — the island they worked before they crossed to the mainland where he turned back. Barnabas does not take him somewhere new and easy. He takes him back over the ground where it went wrong and walks it again with him.

That is what restoring somebody actually looks like when a person does it rather than talks about it. Not a conversation and a fresh start elsewhere, but going back to the place of the failure and doing it properly, in company, at cost to yourself. Barnabas gave up the greatest partnership of his life for it, and it worked.

But Paul chose Silas and departed, having been commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord. Two things. The church at Antioch commended Paul — they did not treat the quarrel as disqualifying, and they did not take sides publicly. And they used the same words over him as when he first went out (14:26), which is where that phrase is worked through.

One guard as Barnabas leaves the book here. Luke follows Paul from now on, and we hear of Barnabas no more. That is the shape of Luke's narrative, which is travelling toward Rome; it is not a verdict on the man. Do not mistake the camera angle for the assessment of God — a great deal of the best work in the church is done by people the story stops following.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.

Cilicia is Tarsus. It is Paul's home province, and this is the first and almost the only time we are told there were churches in it.

Stop on that, because Acts never records their founding. Nobody planted them in any scene Luke has given us. The likeliest explanation is sitting in the gap between two earlier verses: when the Jerusalem believers put Saul on a boat to get him out of danger, they sent him off to Tarsus (9:30), and he disappears from the narrative until Barnabas goes and fetches him (11:25). That is somewhere around a decade, and Luke tells us nothing whatever about it.

This verse is the trace. Congregations existed in Cilicia, and the man walking round them now is the man who spent his obscure years there. Nobody wrote up those years. There is no account of the preaching, no list of converts, no story of a riot or a healing. There is a participle in a travel note, ten years later, and churches on the ground.

That is worth having if the most obscure stretch of your own life is the one you cannot see any fruit from. Paul's decade in Tarsus produced churches that Scripture mentions once, in passing, without crediting anyone. It was not a holding pattern before the real ministry started.

Strengthening. Luke has now used that word three times in twenty verses — of Paul and Barnabas going back through the towns that had expelled them (14:22), of Judas and Silas staying on in Antioch (15:32), and now of Paul walking home through his own province. It is plainly a thing he thinks the church needs more of than it gets. And in the very next chapter we learn what part of it consisted in: he was carrying the council's letter and delivering it as he went (16:4). The theology of chapter 15 arrives in the churches on foot.

And consider how the second missionary journey begins — the journey that will reach Philippi, Thessalonica, Athens, Corinth and Ephesus, and produce most of the letters in your New Testament. Not with a vision. Not with a commissioning service. It begins with a man who has just lost his closest friend over an argument he could not win, walking through his home province, propping up small churches nobody has heard of.

Luke never resolves the quarrel. He simply goes on with the story, which is what the two men did.

15.theology: Justification by Grace Alone through Faith Alone. Acts 15 is the original council on justification. Peter’s summary — “we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will” — is the thesis of the Reformation stated by an apostle. The Judaizers were not wicked men; they were sincere believers who thought obedience to the law was necessary for salvation. But sincerity does not make a false gospel true. The council’s verdict is decisive and irreversible: the Gentiles are saved through grace, and so are the Jews. The law cannot save. It never could. The law was given to demonstrate the need for grace, not to provide an alternative to it. The cross of Christ is sufficient, complete, and alone — and any addition to it, however well-intentioned, is a subtraction from it.
15.examples:
Then: A church divided over the most fundamental question imaginable: what must a person do to be saved? The answer came not from compromise but from clarity, grounded in Scripture (James’s citation of Amos) and confirmed by experience (Peter’s witness to Cornelius, Barnabas and Paul’s report from the Gentile mission). The church that settles this question rightly can face every other challenge. The church that gets it wrong has nothing left to offer.

Now: The Judaizer error never stays buried. It reappears in every generation dressed in different clothes: the idea that grace plus something — baptism, church membership, moral effort, liturgical compliance — constitutes salvation. The Jerusalem Council’s answer is permanent and non-negotiable: the grace of the Lord Jesus alone. The church’s task in every generation is to say it clearly, defend it stubbornly, and live it joyfully.

16.title: Into Macedonia
16.text: <sup>1</sup>Paul came also to Derbe and to Lystra. A disciple was there, named Timothy, the son of a Jewish woman who was a believer, but his father was a Greek. <sup>2</sup>He was well spoken of by the brothers at Lystra and Iconium. <sup>3</sup>Paul wanted Timothy to accompany him, and he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Greek. <sup>4</sup>As they went on their way through the cities, they delivered to them for observance the decisions that had been reached by the apostles and elders who were in Jerusalem. <sup>5</sup>So the churches were strengthened in the faith, and they increased in numbers daily. <sup>6</sup>And they went through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. <sup>7</sup>And when they had come up to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them. <sup>8</sup>So, passing by Mysia, they went down to Troas. <sup>9</sup>And a vision appeared to Paul in the night: a man of Macedonia was standing there, urging him and saying, “Come over to Macedonia and help us.” <sup>10</sup>And when Paul had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go on into Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them. <sup>11</sup>So, setting sail from Troas, we made a direct voyage to Samothrace, and the following day to Neapolis, <sup>12</sup>and from there to Philippi, which is a leading city of the district of Macedonia and a Roman colony. We remained in this city some days. <sup>13</sup>And on the Sabbath day we went outside the gate to the riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down and spoke to the women who had come together. <sup>14</sup>One who heard us was a woman named Lydia, from the city of Thyatira, a seller of purple goods, who was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul. <sup>15</sup>And after she was baptized, and her household as well, she urged us, saying, “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come to my house and stay.” And she prevailed upon us. <sup>16</sup>As we were going to the place of prayer, we were met by a slave girl who had a spirit of divination and brought her owners much gain by fortune-telling. <sup>17</sup>She followed Paul and us, crying out, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you the way of salvation.” <sup>18</sup>And this she kept doing for many days. Paul, having become greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.” And it came out that very hour. <sup>19</sup>But when her owners saw that their hope of gain was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers. <sup>20</sup>And when they had brought them to the magistrates, they said, “These men are Jews, and they are disturbing our city. <sup>21</sup>They advocate customs that are not lawful for us as Romans to accept or practice.” <sup>22</sup>The crowd joined in attacking them, and the magistrates tore the garments off them and gave orders to beat them with rods. <sup>23</sup>And when they had inflicted many blows upon them, they threw them into prison, ordering the jailer to keep them safely. <sup>24</sup>Having received this order, he put them into the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks. <sup>25</sup>About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them, <sup>26</sup>and suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken. And immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone’s bonds were unfastened. <sup>27</sup>When the jailer woke and saw that the prison doors were open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped. <sup>28</sup>But Paul cried out with a loud voice, “Do not harm yourself, for we are all here.” <sup>29</sup>And the jailer called for lights and rushed in, and trembling with fear he fell down before Paul and Silas. <sup>30</sup>Then he brought them out and said, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” <sup>31</sup>And they said, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.” <sup>32</sup>And they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all who were in his house. <sup>33</sup>And he took them the same hour of the night and washed their wounds, and he was baptized at once, he and all his family. <sup>34</sup>Then he brought them up into his house and set food before them. And he rejoiced along with his entire household that he had believed in God. <sup>35</sup>But when it was day, the magistrates sent the police, saying, “Let those men go.” <sup>36</sup>And the jailer reported these words to Paul, saying, “The magistrates have sent to let you go. Therefore come out now and go in peace.” <sup>37</sup>But Paul said to them, “They have beaten us publicly, uncondemned, men who are Roman citizens, and have thrown us into prison; and do they now throw us out secretly? No! Let them come themselves and take us out.” <sup>38</sup>The police reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Roman citizens. <sup>39</sup>So they came and apologized to them. And they took them out and asked them to leave the city. <sup>40</sup>So they went out of the prison and visited Lydia. And when they had seen the brothers, they encouraged them and departed.
16.overview:
Europe receives the gospel through a series of divine redirections. Paul plans to go east; the Spirit says no. He plans to go north; the Spirit of Jesus does not allow it. He arrives at the edge of the continent — Troas, on the Aegean shore — with every plan closed, and there in the night a Macedonian man appears: “Come over and help us.” The call to Europe is not strategic analysis; it is a vision in the night and obedience the next morning.

What awaits in Philippi is three conversions that could not be more different from one another: a wealthy businesswoman, a demonised slave girl, and a Roman jailer on the verge of suicide. Lydia’s conversion is quiet — the Lord opens her heart, she attends to Paul’s words, she is baptised. The slave girl’s deliverance is dramatic — a command in the name of Jesus, and the spirit leaves. The jailer’s conversion is desperate — a man in the ruins of his career, trembling, asking the question that matters most: what must I do to be saved?

The answer to the jailer is the simplest and most complete in the New Testament: “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.” Not believe and do. Not believe and perform. Not believe and be circumcised. Believe. The gospel is that simple, and that enough.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — Timothy, the Macedonian Call, and Lydia
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The second journey opens quietly and ends up changing the map. Four things happen in fifteen verses, and none of them was planned by the men involved.

Timothy joins (vv. 1–3). At Lystra — the town where Paul had been stoned — he picks up a young disciple with a Jewish believing mother and a Greek father, well spoken of by two churches. And Paul circumcises him. He is at that moment carrying a letter from Jerusalem saying circumcision is not required, which is exactly why he is free to do it: what may never be conceded as a condition may be chosen for the sake of the mission.

The decrees delivered (vv. 4–5). Town by town they hand over the council's decision, and Luke records the result — the churches strengthened in the faith and increasing in number daily. The theology of chapter 15 arrives on foot.

Two closed doors and one open one (vv. 6–10). The Holy Spirit forbids Asia; the Spirit of Jesus refuses Bithynia; and they end up at Troas, on the coast, out of options. There a vision comes at night of a Macedonian pleading for help — and at verse 10 Luke's pronouns change to we, because the author has joined the party. Note that they had to conclude what the vision meant; even a vision needed a judgment.

Europe (vv. 11–15). Philippi is a proud Roman colony, and it cannot muster the ten Jewish men needed for a synagogue. So the gospel enters Europe at a women's prayer meeting outside the gate, with the missionaries sitting down on the riverbank. The vision had shown a man of Macedonia; the first convert is a foreign businesswoman from Thyatira, and Luke says plainly who did it — the Lord opened her heart. She is baptised with her household, presses her hospitality on the team until they give in, and the first church in Europe meets in her house.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit's Direction of Mission

The second missionary journey is notable for the Spirit's specific prevention and redirection: 'they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia... the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them' to go to Bithynia. The door to Europe opens only because two Asian doors close. Reformed missiology sees here the sovereignty of the Spirit over missional geography: the Spirit is not merely the empowerer of human initiative but the director of the mission's course. The church's task is to be obedient to both open doors and closed ones.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Lydia's household was the first European church — gathered in a businesswoman's home around the word of God and the Lord's Supper. Now: The church continues to be built wherever the Lord opens hearts — in homes as often as in purpose-built buildings, through business relationships as often as through formal religious programs.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul came also to Derbe and to Lystra. A disciple was there, named Timothy, the son of a Jewish woman who was a believer, but his father was a Greek. He was well spoken of by the brothers at Lystra and Iconium."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul came also to Derbe and to Lystra.

Lystra. Stop there for a moment before meeting Timothy, because Luke expects you to remember what happened in that town. It is where a crowd tried to sacrifice oxen to Paul and, a few days later, stoned him and dragged him out of the city for dead (14:19). He is walking back into it, on purpose, for the second time.

And what he collects there is the best thing he ever got out of any city.

A disciple was there, named Timothy, the son of a Jewish woman who was a believer, but his father was a Greek.

Every clause of that is doing something. He is already a disciple — converted on the first journey, in the aftermath of the stoning, which makes it very likely he was one of the young men standing round Paul's body outside the wall. His mother is a Jewish believer; Paul later names her and her mother, Lois and Eunice, and tells Timothy that the faith he has lived in dwelt first in them (2 Tim. 1:5). Three generations, and the men are missing from the account entirely.

Because the father was a Greek, and the tense Luke uses suggests he was dead by now. He had certainly not been a believer, and he had not allowed his son to be circumcised, which tells you which way the household had leaned while he was alive. So Timothy grew up in a home divided down the middle — a Jewish mother teaching him the Scriptures from infancy (2 Tim. 3:15), a Greek father who wanted none of it, and a boy belonging fully to neither community. To the Jews of Lystra he was the son of a mixed marriage, uncircumcised, irregular. To the Greeks he was his mother's son, and odd with it.

That matters more than it looks, because it is exactly the shape of the church Paul is building. The man who will carry more of Paul's correspondence and receive two of his letters was formed by belonging to two worlds and being fully at home in neither, until the gospel gave him a third.

If you have grown up between things — a divided home, two cultures, a family where the faith came down one side only and was resisted on the other — Timothy is in Scripture partly for you. The thing that made him awkward is the thing that made him useful.

He was well spoken of by the brothers at Lystra and Iconium. Two churches, eighteen miles apart, and both of them volunteered the same verdict. Paul did not interview him; he asked around, and the answer came back from people who had watched him grow up. That is still the soundest way anybody has found to identify a man for ministry: not what he says about himself, and not how he performs, but what the people who have known him for years say when they are asked.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul wanted Timothy to accompany him, and he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Greek."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul wanted Timothy to accompany him, and he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places.

Read that with chapter 15 still open and it looks impossible. Paul has just won a public fight against men who said Gentiles must be circumcised. He is at this moment carrying the letter that settles it. And the first thing he does on the road is circumcise his new colleague.

The apparent contradiction dissolves once you see two things, and the second is the one usually missed.

First, the principle. What may never be conceded as a condition may be freely chosen as a courtesy — and the moment somebody makes it a condition, it must be refused absolutely. Paul held both ends of that at once, and the pair of cases that proves it is set out at 15:1. The point here is that it is the letter in his bag that makes this possible. Because Jerusalem has ruled that circumcision saves nobody, Paul is free to circumcise a man without the act meaning anything about salvation at all. Settle the doctrine and you are at liberty in the practice. Leave the doctrine unsettled and every practical decision becomes a battle.

Second — and this is the part that is usually skipped — Timothy was not a Gentile. In Jewish reckoning a child's standing followed the mother, and his mother was a Jewess. Timothy was a Jew. An uncircumcised Jew, which was not a mild irregularity but a standing scandal, and one his own town knew about: they all knew that his father was a Greek. Titus, who was a Gentile through and through, was not circumcised and Paul would not hear of it (Gal. 2:3). Timothy's case is not the same case. This is not a Gentile being made to conform. It is a Jew whose Jewishness had been left incomplete by a father who wanted no part of it.

And the reason given is entirely missional: because of the Jews who were in those places. Paul's method in every town is to start in the synagogue. An uncircumcised companion at his elbow would have ended that conversation in the first five minutes, in every city, for the rest of the journey — not over the gospel, but over a distraction.

Now consider what it cost the man himself, because we read the verse as a decision of Paul's and it was an operation on Timothy. He was an adult. There was no anaesthetic. There would have been days of pain, some risk, and then a long walk. His first recorded act as a missionary is to submit to that, for the sake of getting a hearing among people who had looked down on him his whole life for the very thing he was now having corrected.

Which is a searching thing to put next to our own ideas of what serving Christ costs. Timothy gave up his comfort and his body before he had preached a sermon, and he did it for people who had not asked him to and would probably never know. The question it puts is not whether you would die for Christ, which is a question most Christians will never be asked. It is whether you would accept an unnecessary personal cost, unremarked, to remove a small obstacle between somebody else and the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: As they went on their way through the cities, they delivered to them for observance the decisions that had been made by the apostles and elders who were in Jerusalem. So the churches were strengthened in the faith, and they increased in numbers daily.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they went on their way through the cities, they delivered to them for observance the decisions that had been reached by the apostles and elders who were in Jerusalem.

Here is what happened to the Jerusalem Council. It went into a bag and was carried around Galatia on foot by two men and a young apprentice, and read out in one small congregation after another.

That is worth pausing on, because we are inclined to think of doctrine as settled when the argument is won. It was not settled when James gave his judgment, or when the letter was drafted, or even when it was read aloud in Antioch. It was settled in Iconium when a handful of frightened Gentile believers, who had heard the rumours and had no way of checking them, watched Paul unfold a document from the apostles telling them they were already in.

And notice which churches these are. Derbe, Lystra, Iconium, Pisidian Antioch — the exact towns of the first journey, and the towns most likely to have been visited by the men who went out from us and unsettled everybody (15:24). The letter is being taken to precisely the addresses where the damage was done. Somebody had thought about where it needed to go.

Then Luke's summary, and it is one of his periodic progress notes: So the churches were strengthened in the faith, and they increased in numbers daily.

Take the two halves in order, because the order is an argument. They were strengthened in the faith first — made solid in what they believed — and then they grew. Luke does not present these as two separate blessings that happened to arrive together. The so at the head of the sentence ties them to the delivery of the decrees.

A church that does not know where it stands cannot grow, because it has nothing steady to invite anybody into, and its members are too busy checking their own footing to look outward. Remove the doubt and both things follow at once. It is the same movement as in Antioch, where the letter was read and the congregation rejoiced (15:31): assurance comes first, and then a church has something to give away.

So if you have wondered whether doctrinal precision is the enemy of evangelistic warmth — whether time spent getting the gospel exactly right is time stolen from telling people about it — here is Luke's answer in one sentence, and he puts the causal word in the middle of it.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they went through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. And when they had come up to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia... but the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them.

Two closed doors in two verses, and both of them shut by God.

Feel the strangeness of it first, before drawing any comfort. These men are doing exactly what they were commissioned to do. Asia is a populous Roman province with great cities in it — Ephesus among them — and they are forbidden to preach there. Bithynia is a rich province on the Black Sea, and the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them. There is no suggestion of sin, no rebuke, no correction of a wrong motive. Two good men with a right aim are stopped twice.

And Luke does not tell us how. Not a word about the mechanism — no vision, no prophet, no illness, no closed road. Every commentator has a theory and every theory is a guess. Luke's silence here is worth as much as his information elsewhere, because it stops us turning the episode into a method. If we knew how the Spirit forbade them, we would immediately start looking for the same signal in our own lives and grading each other on our ability to detect it.

Then the phrase, which is unusual enough to have been noticed for centuries: the Spirit of Jesus. Luke has called him the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of the Lord, and simply the Spirit; this is the only place in Acts where he is called the Spirit of Jesus. Paul will use close relatives of it — the Spirit of Christ (Rom. 8:9), the Spirit of his Son (Gal. 4:6), the Spirit of Jesus Christ (Phil. 1:19).

And it appears exactly where the direction of the mission is being taken out of the missionaries' hands. That is not decoration. The one who is steering is the same Jesus who said you will be my witnesses... to the end of the earth, and he is doing the steering personally. The men on the road are not executing a strategy they devised and asking God to bless it. They are being moved.

Now the pastoral use of this, and it needs a guard on both sides.

The comfort is real: a closed door may be the hand of God, and the fact that a good and reasonable plan has failed is not evidence that God has stopped paying attention. Everything you can see says Asia, and the answer is no, and the no is not a punishment.

The guard is that these men did not know that at the time. We read verses 6 and 7 already knowing about verse 9, and that ruins the experience of them. Standing on that road, they had two refusals and no explanation, no destination, and no assurance whatever that anything was being led towards. They found out later. Almost everybody finds out later, and a good many never find out at all.

So do not turn this into a rule that every setback is a redirection with a Macedonia waiting behind it. Some closed doors are simply closed, and Scripture does not promise you the explanation. What it shows you here is that the Lord of the mission is capable of steering by refusal, and that two of the best men who ever lived spent an unknown number of weeks walking in what felt like the wrong direction with no idea why.

verseByVerse.quote: "So, passing by Mysia, they went down to Troas."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So, passing by Mysia, they went down to Troas.

Eight words, and they cover a long, dispiriting walk.

Look at the map they were working with. Refused Asia to the south-west. Refused Bithynia to the north-east. What is left is the road running north-west, and they take it — through country Luke does not even say they preached in — until they run out of land. Troas is on the coast. There is nowhere further to go without a boat.

That is the position: two apostles, a young colleague, several hundred miles behind them, no commission for anywhere they can reach on foot, standing on a beach.

And it is worth saying plainly that at that moment nothing in their situation looked like guidance. It looked like failure. The strategy had collapsed, the obvious fields were shut, and they had been walking for weeks toward a place they had no reason to go to. Anyone who has kept obeying while everything visible was going wrong knows exactly what that road felt like, and knows too that hindsight is no help while you are on it.

Then consider what Troas actually was, because they could not see this either. It is the port beside the ruins of Troy, the crossing point between two continents, and the place from which any ship for Macedonia would sail. Every refusal had been moving them toward the one town in the world from which Europe was two days away.

There is something else here that they could not possibly have known. Troas is where Luke joins them. In two verses the pronouns will change from they to we, and the man who wrote a quarter of the New Testament walks into the story at the town they arrived at because everywhere else was forbidden.

So the two noes did not merely reroute a mission. They put an apostle and a historian in the same room. Neither of them knew that when they got there, and neither of them chose it.

Which is the only honest way to take comfort from this verse. Not that your closed doors are certainly leading somewhere you will get to see — they may not be, and Scripture does not promise it. But that the God who shut Asia and Bithynia was, the whole time, arranging a meeting on a beach that neither man would have thought to ask for.

verseByVerse.quote: And a vision appeared to Paul in the night: a man of Macedonia was standing there, urging him, "Come over to Macedonia and help us." And when Paul had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go on into Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And a vision appeared to Paul in the night: a man of Macedonia was standing there, urging him, Come over to Macedonia and help us.

After two refusals and no explanation, a request. And notice that it is a request — not an order, not a rebuke for having gone the wrong way, not a strategy briefing. A man stands there and asks for help.

Then look at what happens in the next sentence, because it is easy to miss and it is the most important thing in the paragraph for anyone who has ever wanted God to make something plain.

Concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them.

Concluding. The word means to put things together, to reason to a conclusion, to work it out. Even after a night vision of a man pleading with him by name, Paul did not simply know what to do. The vision had to be interpreted, and the team did it together — note the plural — and what they arrived at was a judgment, not a certainty handed down. The man in the dream had not said preach the gospel. He had said help us. Working out that the help meant the gospel was the missionaries' own conclusion.

That should reset most of what Christians expect from guidance. Here is the clearest, most dramatic, most unambiguous piece of direction in the New Testament outside the Damascus road — and it still required sanctified reasoning by a group of people talking it over in the morning. If Paul had to conclude, you are not failing when you have to conclude.

And notice the speed: immediately we sought to go on into Macedonia. Having reasoned it out, they moved the same day. Long deliberation and instant obedience are not enemies; here they are consecutive.

Now the pronoun, which is one of the quiet marvels of the New Testament. Up to verse 9 the narrative runs they. From verse 10 it is we sought, we made a direct voyage, we remained. The author has joined the party at Troas and has said so by changing a pronoun and nothing else.

He never explains it. He never introduces himself, never says how he met them, never once writes I, and never names himself anywhere in either of his two books — and between them they make up about a quarter of the New Testament. The only place Luke appears in his own history is inside the word we.

Two things follow. The first is historical: from here on, large stretches of Acts are the report of somebody who was in the boat, and the sober, unshowy way he reports himself is part of why he is believed. The second is a matter of temperament, and it is a rebuke to the way most of us tell the story of what God has done with us. A man was present at the founding of the church in Europe, sailed with Paul, survived the shipwreck, and stayed with him to the last cold months in Rome when everyone else had gone — Luke alone is with me (2 Tim. 4:11). And in his own account of all of it he is a pronoun.

verseByVerse.quote: "So, setting sail from Troas, we made a direct voyage to Samothrace, and the following day to Neapolis, and from there to Philippi, which is a leading city of the district of Macedonia and a Roman colony. We remained in this city some days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So, setting sail from Troas, we made a direct voyage to Samothrace, and the following day to Neapolis.

Luke the traveller shows here. A direct voyage renders a nautical expression — they ran before the wind, straight across, no tacking. Two days. On the return journey later, the same crossing against the wind takes five (20:6). Somebody on that boat noticed the difference and remembered it for thirty years.

It is a small thing and it is worth having, because it is the sort of detail nobody invents. And it is the sort of thing a man notices when he is glad to be going.

Then Philippi, and Luke gives it two credentials: a leading city of the district of Macedonia and a Roman colony.

A colony was not simply a town with Romans in it. It was a piece of Rome transplanted — founded to settle discharged legionaries, governed under Roman law, its citizens holding Roman citizenship, its magistrates styled like Rome's, its people exempt from certain taxes and immensely proud of the whole arrangement. Philippi had been made one after the battle fought on that plain in which Antony and Octavian destroyed the assassins of Julius Caesar, and it had been settled twice over with veterans. It was, in its own estimation, Italy in Macedonia.

Hold that beside what is about to happen. The gospel's first European address is the proudest, most self-consciously Roman town in the province — and it will be entered through a woman's prayer meeting, held outside the gate because the city could not muster a synagogue. Within a chapter the men of that colony will beat two Jews without trial, and then discover, to their horror, that the Jews were Romans and they were not entitled to.

Luke puts the city's Roman standing in the introduction because the whole story turns on it twice — once when the charge is customs not lawful for us as Romans (v. 21), and once when it costs the magistrates their dignity in the street (v. 39).

We remained in this city some days. A flat sentence, and it means they were looking for a way in and had not yet found one. There is no synagogue to preach in. For several days the mission to Europe consists of three or four men walking round a strange town waiting for the Sabbath.

verseByVerse.quote: "And on the Sabbath day we went outside the gate to the riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down and spoke to the women who had come together."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And on the Sabbath day we went outside the gate to the riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer.

Take that sentence apart, because every clause is a step down.

Outside the gate. Not in the city. Foreign cults were often required to keep their meetings beyond the walls of a Roman colony, and in any case there was nothing inside to go to.

Where we supposed there was a place of prayer. They were not sure. They had been in the town some days and were reduced to guessing where a handful of Jews might gather on a Sabbath, and going out to see.

And behind all of it lies a fact Luke leaves you to work out: Philippi had no synagogue. It took ten Jewish men to constitute one. The leading city of the district, a Roman colony of some thousands, could not produce ten Jewish men.

And we sat down and spoke to the women who had come together.

So this is how Christianity arrived in Europe. Not in the forum, not in a basilica, not before the magistrates. A few travellers walked out of a side gate on a Saturday morning, found a group of women praying by a river, sat down on the bank, and started talking.

Notice even the posture. In the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch Paul stood up and motioned with his hand, in the manner of a public speaker addressing a hall (13:16). Here he sits down. It is the ordinary posture of a Jewish teacher, and it is also simply what you do when you join a small group on a riverbank. The same man, the same message, and an entirely different register — because the room was different, and he could tell.

There is a lesson in that which the church keeps having to relearn. The apostles had no platform in Philippi and did not wait for one. They did not hire a hall, or hold out for a hearing before somebody important, or decide that a handful of women was too small a return on a two-day sea crossing and several hundred miles of walking. They went where people were praying and sat down among them.

And here is the thing worth measuring. Out of that riverbank conversation came the church at Philippi — the congregation that alone supported Paul when no other church did (Phil. 4:15–16), that sent him money in prison, that he called his joy and his crown. The single warmest letter in the New Testament was written to the people who started as the women at the river.

If your own service to God feels absurdly small in proportion to the effort it took to get there — a handful of people, a conversation nobody will hear about, an evening that produced nothing you can point to — this verse is the shape of most of what God actually does. Nobody at that riverside knew they were founding the church in Europe.

verseByVerse.quote: One who heard us was a woman named Lydia, from the city of Thyatira, a seller of purple goods, who was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul. And when she was baptized, and her household also, she urged us, saying, "If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come to my house and stay." And she prevailed upon us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One who heard us was a woman named Lydia, from the city of Thyatira, a seller of purple goods, who was a worshiper of God.

Luke tells us four things about the first person in Europe to believe the gospel, and together they make a portrait of somebody no strategist would have picked.

She is a woman, in a world where that meant her testimony carried little weight in a court and her name would not normally appear in a history. She is from Thyatira — which is in Asia, the province the Spirit had just forbidden them to preach in. They were stopped from going to her country, and she had already come to theirs. She is a seller of purple goods, which was the luxury trade: the dye came from shellfish, took vast quantities to produce, and clothed magistrates and emperors. Thyatira was famous for it, and a woman running that business at a distance from home was a person of means, with a house big enough for a household and, shortly, for a church. And she is a worshiper of God — one of the God-fearers, a Gentile who had attached herself to the God of Israel without becoming a Jew.

So the vision showed a man of Macedonia asking for help, and the first person helped is a foreign businesswoman. Luke sets the two side by side within five verses and offers no comment at all. God answered the request in the dream with somebody outside every category in it.

Then the sentence that explains everything: The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul.

That phrase, 'the Lord opened her heart,' is one of Scripture's clearest pictures of what the Reformed call effectual calling: Lydia believed because God first opened her heart — grace the cause, faith the fruit. Paul preached (the means), but only the Lord could open the heart (the power); a closed heart no sermon can pry open. (Arminian brothers say grace opened her heart while leaving her free to refuse; the Reformed read the opening itself as the decisive work that brings faith to be — see 13:48.) For you it is pure comfort and humility: if you believe, it is because God opened your heart — so no boasting, all thanks.

'She was baptized, and her household as well.' What was her household? In the first century a household (oikos) was far larger than our 'nuclear family' — servants and slaves, employees, dependents, sometimes extended kin, all under one roof and authority. Lydia seems a woman of means heading her own house (no husband mentioned), so 'her household' likely means her servants and dependents, perhaps children — though Luke gives no roster.

And did they all believe, or were they simply baptized? Honestly, the text does not say: Luke records that Lydia believed ('the Lord opened her heart') and that her household was baptized, but nothing explicit about the household's faith. That silence is why this is one of the 'household baptism' texts in the friendly baptism disagreement (see on 2:39). Believer's-baptist readers fill the gap from the other households said to believe and rejoice (the jailer's, v. 34; Crispus's, 18:8), concluding Lydia's household believed and were baptized as believers, Luke compressing. Covenant-baptist readers note that only Lydia's faith is mentioned, yet the whole household is baptized on the head's faith — the old covenant pattern (Gen. 17), including dependents and any little ones. Scripture leaves the gap; each side fills it from its view of the sign. What is beyond dispute, and a comfort, is that God loves to save not lone individuals but whole households: the conversion of one is so often the open door of grace to a home (cf. v. 31). Pray, then, for your whole household.

And then the last thing she does, which is the first recorded act of any Christian in Europe. If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come to my house and stay. And she prevailed upon us.

Look at how she frames it. She does not offer hospitality; she puts her new standing on the table and makes them rule on it. If you have judged me faithful — the sentence dares them to say that her conversion was real and then decline to eat at her table. A woman baptised that morning has understood, within hours, that being received by Christ means being received by his people, and she will not let the two come apart.

She prevailed upon us. The word means she forced the issue, pressed until they gave way. They said no, or hesitated — Paul was careful about being kept at anybody's expense, and it is the one thing he mentions about this very church afterwards, that Philippi alone was allowed to support him (Phil. 4:15). And she overruled him. It is the only place in Acts where somebody argues Paul down and wins, and it is a new convert of a few hours.

So the first church in Europe met in that house, and it began because a woman would not take no for an answer about having people to stay. Not a strategy, not a building fund, not a preaching licence. A door held open until the missionaries walked through it.

Which is worth saying to anyone who has concluded that they have no ministry because they cannot teach, or lead, or speak in public. Lydia's contribution to the New Testament is a room. The letter to the Philippians exists because of what she did with her house.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–40 — Prison and Earthquake in Philippi
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Everything in this section runs on one night, and Luke gives the hours: an arrest in the afternoon, a public flogging, the inner cell by evening, singing at midnight, an earthquake, a conversion, a meal before dawn, and an apology from the magistrates when it was light.

The girl and the owners (vv. 16–24). A slave girl with a fortune-telling spirit follows the missionaries for days shouting something that is almost true, and Paul — worn down rather than serene — turns and commands the spirit out. Her owners' income goes with it, and that, not doctrine, is what starts the riot. The real grievance is dressed up for the magistrates as a threat to Roman order, the crowd joins in, and two men are stripped, beaten with rods without trial, and locked in the innermost cell with their feet in the stocks.

Midnight (vv. 25–34). Backs open, legs fixed apart, and they are praying and singing — with the other prisoners listening. The earthquake unfastens everyone's chains, not only theirs. The jailer, liable with his own life for the prisoners, draws his sword, and Paul stops him: we are all here. Nobody had run. Then the question — what must I do to be saved? — and the answer that contains no doing in it at all. He washes the wounds he was responsible for and is washed himself the same hour; then food in his house, and a household rejoicing before daylight.

Morning (vv. 35–40). The magistrates send word to let them go quietly, and Paul refuses to be got rid of quietly. He and Silas are Roman citizens, beaten publicly and uncondemned, and he requires the magistrates to come themselves. They come, frightened, and apologise. Then the two men walk out of the prison and go to Lydia's house, see the brothers, encourage them, and leave — the last thing they do in Philippi being pastoral rather than triumphal.
verseByVerse.theology:
Midnight Praise and the Ministry of Suffering

Paul and Silas pray and sing hymns at midnight — after being stripped and beaten with rods — and the other prisoners listen. The praise is not despite the suffering but in it: the same Spirit who fills the church for witness fills the suffering church for worship. Reformed theology sees in this midnight scene the confirmation of what Paul will later write: 'we rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance' (Romans 5:3). The songs at midnight are the most powerful proclamation the prisoners that night will ever hear.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The jailer asked 'What must I do to be saved?' — the question of Pentecost (2:37) repeated in a Philippian prison. The answer is the same: 'Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.' Now: The gospel's answer to the question of salvation is always the same: not circumcision, not ritual, not moral achievement, but faith in the Lord Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "As we were going to the place of prayer, we were met by a slave girl who had a spirit of divination and brought her owners much gain by fortune-telling. She followed Paul and us, crying out, 'These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you the way of salvation.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
We were met by a slave girl who had a spirit of divination and brought her owners much gain by fortune-telling.

Before anything else, notice what she is. Luke gives her no name, and he gives her three owners' worth of ownership: she is a slave, she is possessed, and she is an income. Three things have hold of her and not one of them is her own. She is the most thoroughly owned human being in the book of Acts.

And she is the first person the gospel meets on the way to the place of prayer in Europe.

The 'spirit of divination' translates the Greek pneuma pythōna — literally a Python spirit. In ancient Greek religion, the Python was the great serpent that guarded the sanctuary at Delphi before Apollo killed it and claimed the site; thereafter, the Delphic priestess (the Pythia) was said to speak her oracles under the inspiration of the Python's spirit. The Pythian oracle at Delphi was the most prestigious in the ancient world — Greek cities, kings, and generals consulted it before major military campaigns and political decisions. Slave girls with Python spirits were therefore Delphic-style commercial oracles of the highest value, and their owners made substantial fortunes from their prophetic services. Paul's encounter at Philippi is thus a direct confrontation with the dominant prophetic tradition of the Greek world — Apollo's oracle, in miniature, following the apostles through a Macedonian street.

The girl's testimony is formally true — Paul and his companions are servants of the Most High God proclaiming salvation — but its source is demonic. This is the most dangerous kind of false witness: accurate content, corrupt source. A Delphic-style oracle endorsing Paul would associate the apostolic mission with the occult establishment, potentially drawing curiosity-seekers rather than genuine converts, and tying the gospel to the very prophetic system it was displacing. Paul is not annoyed at the content but at the source and its implications.

There is one more thing in her words, and it is the practical reason the shouting had to stop. These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you the way of salvation. To a Jewish ear, the Most High God is a title for the God of Israel. To a Greek ear in a Macedonian colony, it was a title people used of Zeus. And the Greek behind the way of salvation has no article: a way of salvation. One among the several on offer in any Roman town.

So her testimony was not merely true-from-a-bad-source. Heard by the crowd it was actually endorsing something else: two more travelling holy men, agents of the high god under whatever name, with one more route to blessedness for sale. Every word could be agreed to by a pagan without changing a single thing he believed.

That is worth carrying out of Philippi, because it is the commonest way the gospel is neutralised now — not by contradiction but by warm agreement on slightly different terms. Christ is affirmed as one of the great spiritual teachers. The message is praised as a path to meaning. Nothing is denied and nothing is left.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this she kept doing for many days. Paul, having become greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, 'I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.' And it came out that very hour."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And this she kept doing for many days.

Many days. That is the first thing to account for, and most readers pass it. Paul did not act at once. Day after day this girl trailed the missionaries through the streets shouting after them, and day after day he let it run.

Then: Paul, having become greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit.

The word means worn down, exasperated, at the end of his patience. Luke could have written that Paul was moved with compassion, or grieved in his spirit, and he wrote that Paul was thoroughly fed up. This is not a serene apostle exercising cool authority at a chosen moment. It is a tired man who has finally had enough, swinging round in the street — and God used it, and Luke recorded it without tidying it.

That is worth having, because we tend to imagine that God only works through us when our motives are pure and our composure is intact. Here the most famous exorcism in Acts is done by a man at the end of his temper.

I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her. And it came out that very hour.

Note where the authority sits. Paul does not reason with it, bargain with it, or require anything of the girl — no faith, no consent, not even her attention. He names a name, and the thing that had held her for years leaves within the hour. Whatever else is uncertain about this territory, the New Testament is never uncertain about the outcome of that particular collision.

And now the question Luke does not answer, which ought to be asked out loud rather than quietly filled in. What became of her?

She is not said to have believed. She is not said to have been freed. So far as the text goes, she is still a slave the next morning — and now a slave who has stopped earning, owned by furious men who have just lost a fortune. In the world's accounting, her position that evening was worse than the day before.

Luke leaves her there. He does not tell us that she joined the church at Lydia's house, and it would be pleasant to say so, and we do not know. What we know is that she was the one person in the story who was not consulted about anything and the only one whose ending is withheld.

It is worth resisting the urge to close that. The Bible frequently rescues somebody and then declines to tell us how it turned out, and a reader who has watched a real deliverance leave someone with a harder life afterwards — the addiction broken and the debts still there, the marriage saved and the reputation gone — needs to know that Scripture is not embarrassed by that. The spirit came out. Everything else about her was still difficult. Both of those are in the verse.

This raises the question of exorcism today. (On the reality of demons — real, personal, evil beings — see 5:15–16.) The Reformed position is cautious and Christ-centred, for scriptural reasons. (1) The dramatic commanding of demons clusters in the unique era of Christ's ministry and the apostolic founding, among the authenticating signs of the kingdom (see 5:12). (2) Strikingly, the Epistles, which teach the church to fight the devil, never establish an 'office of exorcist,' never list it among the gifts (Rom. 12; 1 Cor. 12; Eph. 4), and give no ritual of deliverance; they relocate the warfare to ordinary weapons — 'resist the devil, and he will flee' (James 4:7); 'put on the whole armour of God... stand' (Eph. 6:10–18); 'resist him, firm in your faith' (1 Pet. 5:8–9). (3) A true believer, indwelt by the Spirit, cannot be possessed (owned): 'he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world' (1 John 4:4; John 10:28–29) — harassed from without, but not inhabited. (4) And blaming sins on demons evades repentance, when Scripture lays sin at our own heart and flesh (James 1:14; Mark 7:21–23). So deliverance comes through the gospel (conversion transfers us out of the domain of darkness, Col. 1:13), prayer, and Christ's authority humbly invoked when genuinely needed — never a technique, a specialist, or a spectacle.

Other views, answered kindly. The Roman Catholic church keeps a formal rite of exorcism by an authorised priest; we honour its seriousness but find no such office or fixed ritual in Scripture. Much of the Pentecostal/charismatic world practises 'deliverance ministry,' often casting demons out of Christians and naming 'spirits' behind particular sins; we affirm the reality of the demonic and the zeal to help, but answer that a believer cannot be possessed (1 John 4:4), that the Epistles prescribe resisting and the armour, and that treating besetting sins as demons undercuts the call to repent and mortify the flesh (James 1:14). At the other extreme, liberal/naturalistic readers reduce 'demon-possession' to ancient mental illness; this we reject, for Scripture distinguishes the sick from the demonised (Mark 1:32–34) and treats demons as real persons subject to Christ. The two ditches (as at 5:16): do not deny the demonic, and do not see a demon behind every sin and sickness.

For you, then: you need not fear demons, nor go hunting for a deliverance minister. If you are in Christ, the strongest Being in the universe lives in you, and at the cross Christ has already 'disarmed the rulers and authorities' (Col. 2:15; see 10:38). Your warfare is daily and ordinary — resist the devil in faith, put on the armour, feed on the Word, pray, walk in holiness, lean on the church — and he flees. Do not excuse your sins as someone else's spirits; fight them as your own, by the Spirit, resting in your Lord's finished victory. (In settings of overt occult darkness, sober missionaries do meet real demonic confrontation; even there the remedy is the same — the gospel and the name of Christ, humbly.)

verseByVerse.quote: "But when her owners saw that their hope of gain was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers. And when they had brought them to the magistrates, they said, 'These men are Jews and they are disturbing our city.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when her owners saw that their hope of gain was gone.

There is the motive, stated in the first clause, before any charge is laid. Nobody in Philippi objected to the theology. A girl had been set free and the accounts had changed.

Luke's phrasing is exact and unlovely: their hope of gain went out of her when the spirit did. He does not say they lost a servant, or a daughter, or even a valuable slave. What left the room, as far as they were concerned, was an income stream.

And this is the shape of a great deal of opposition to Christianity, then and since. It is not usually argued; it is funded. When the gospel changes what people do with their money, their bodies or their time, somebody's revenue falls, and the objection that arrives afterwards will be dressed in principle and will never mention the accounts. The same thing happens on a larger scale at Ephesus, where a silversmith calls a public meeting about the honour of the goddess and the first thing he says in private is from this business we have our wealth (19:25).

Then watch the charge get built, because it is a small masterpiece of misrepresentation.

They seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers. Note who is seized, and who is not. Paul and Silas — the two Jews. Timothy, whose father was Greek, and Luke, who is almost certainly a Gentile, are left alone, and Luke's we quietly drops out of the narrative until Paul comes back through Philippi years later. The mob knew who it wanted.

These men are Jews and they are disturbing our city. Not a word about the girl. Not a word about money. Two accusations instead: an ethnic one and a civic one.

The ethnic one was live currency in a Roman colony at that moment. Claudius had recently expelled the Jews from Rome — Luke mentions it two chapters later, when Paul meets a couple who had been thrown out (18:2) — and a Roman town full of veterans would have been in exactly the mood to hear it. The men who had been living off a possessed child reached for the nearest available prejudice, and it was to hand.

And the civic one is the charge that will be used against Christians for the next three hundred years: disturbing our city. Not that the message is false. That it is inconvenient — that things were quieter before. It is a complaint that never has to prove anything, and it is unanswerable, because the gospel really does disturb a city where a girl can be owned and worked.

verseByVerse.quote: "'They advocate customs that are not lawful for us as Romans to accept or practice.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They advocate customs that are not lawful for us as Romans to accept or practice.

Count the words doing the work: for us as Romans. That is the whole accusation, and in Philippi it was the one sentence guaranteed to land.

Rome tolerated Judaism. It was an ancient national religion with its own customs, legally recognised, and Jews were excused the emperor's rites on that ground. What Rome did not tolerate was a foreign cult recruiting Roman citizens out of their own religion. You could be a Jew; you could not make a Roman into one.

So the charge is technically shrewd. It concedes that these men are Jews and their religion is legal, and then says they are exporting it to people who are not entitled to receive it. It is aimed at magistrates in a colony whose entire identity was that they were Romans a long way from Rome, in a town settled with veterans who had been given land here for their loyalty. Tell those men that two foreigners are undermining Roman custom in their own market square and you will not need evidence.

And there is a bitter irony sitting inside it that nobody in the square could see. The two men in the dock are Roman citizens themselves. The accusers are appealing to Roman privilege against men who hold more of it than they do, and the magistrates are about to break Roman law comprehensively in the act of defending it. That will be discovered in the morning, and the fear in verse 38 is the sound of it landing.

Then the deeper thing, which outlives the legal detail. The charge was, in its way, accurate. Christianity did advocate customs a Roman could not simply add to his existing life. A man who confessed Jesus is Lord in a colony where the loyal formula was Caesar is lord had not adopted a new interest; he had changed allegiance, and everything from his household gods to his trade guild dinners to the civic festivals would eventually feel it.

Which is why the complaint has never really gone away. The gospel is welcome as long as it is one more thing a person has. It becomes intolerable at the point where it starts reorganising what he already had. If your faith has never inconvenienced any arrangement in your life, it is worth asking honestly whether anybody could bring this charge against you at all.

verseByVerse.quote: "The crowd joined in attacking them, and the magistrates tore the garments off them and gave orders to beat them with rods. And when they had inflicted many blows upon them, they threw them into prison, ordering the jailer to keep them safely."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd joined in attacking them, and the magistrates tore the garments off them and gave orders to beat them with rods.

Notice how fast this is. There is no hearing. Nobody calls the girl, or the owners, or any witness. The prisoners are not asked to answer, and Luke records not one word from either of them. Between the accusation in verse 21 and the flogging in verse 22 there is nothing at all.

The magistrates tore the garments off them — the clothes are ripped away in public, in the market square, in front of the crowd that has just been shouting. Then the rods. These were the lictors' rods, the bundle of birch carried in front of a colony's magistrates as the visible sign of their authority to punish. A Roman flogging with rods was not a formality; it opened the back, and men died of it.

And when they had inflicted many blows upon them. Many. Luke, who was probably somewhere in that crowd, does not give a number and does not spare us the word.

Paul refers to this day twice in his letters, and both references are worth having because they tell you what it actually cost. To Corinth, listing what he had survived: three times I was beaten with rods (2 Cor. 11:25) — this was one of the three. And to the Thessalonians, about what happened next: though we had already suffered and been shamefully treated at Philippi, we had boldness in our God to declare to you the gospel of God in the midst of much conflict (1 Thess. 2:2). He walked from this to Thessalonica and preached there with the marks still on him.

The word he uses to the Thessalonians is not injured. It is shamefully treated — outraged, insulted. What stayed with him was not only the pain but the public stripping of two men who had done nothing, in front of a town, by officials who never asked them a question.

And it is important to say plainly that this was injustice, and that Scripture calls it that. There is a way of reading these stories which turns every wrong into a divine arrangement so quickly that the wrong disappears. God did use this night, magnificently. He also did not need the magistrates to break their own law to do it, and Luke does not pretend otherwise. The earthquake does not make the flogging right.

They threw them into prison, ordering the jailer to keep them safely. No charge recorded, no sentence, no term. Two bleeding men are put away with an instruction about security and no instruction about anything else.

verseByVerse.quote: "Having received this order, he put them into the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having received this order, he put them into the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks.

The jailer is introduced doing his job and slightly exceeding it. He was told to keep them safely. He puts them in the innermost cell and puts their feet in the stocks as well.

Both details are worth knowing exactly, because the scene at midnight depends on them.

The inner prison is the windowless interior room — no light, no air moving, the floor of it filthy, and the smell of it the thing ancient writers mention first. It is where you put a man you have been told to keep, and it is as far from the street as the building goes.

And the stocks were not simply a lock for the ankles. The Roman device was a heavy timber with a row of holes, and the point of the row was that the legs could be forced wide apart and fixed there. It was used as a punishment in its own right, not merely a restraint: hours in it produced cramp that became agony, and there was no way to shift position, and no way to lie down properly, and no way to reach your own back.

So hold the whole picture, because Luke has built it deliberately and we are about to be told what these two men were doing in it. Backs laid open by rods and untreated. Legs forced apart and clamped. Locked in the dark in the innermost room of a Roman jail in a foreign city, with no charge, no trial, no sentence, and no reason to think the morning would be any better.

That is the setting of verse 25, and every word of this verse exists to make verse 25 almost unbelievable.

One more thing about the man turning the key. He does not know who he is guarding. He has been handed two prisoners at the end of a long day and given an order, and he carries it out with a little extra thoroughness, the way a careful official does. Within about six hours he will be on the floor in front of them asking how to be saved, and by daylight he will have washed the wounds that his own thoroughness left untended tonight.

verseByVerse.quote: About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them, and suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken. And immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone's bonds were unfastened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God.

Put that sentence on top of the last one and refuse to hurry past the join. Backs opened by rods and never cleaned. Feet clamped apart in a timber. The inner cell, in the dark, at midnight, with no charge and no prospect. And they are singing.

Both verbs are continuous — they were praying and going on praying, singing and going on singing. This was not one defiant snatch of a psalm. It went on long enough to be noticed down the corridor.

And what they sang was almost certainly the psalms, which is worth knowing, because the psalms are full of exactly this. Men in the dark asking how long, and telling God the truth about it, and then turning to praise before anything has changed. Paul and Silas did not have to manufacture a mood. They had a hymnbook written for nights like this one.

Then the detail Luke keeps, and it is the one that changes the scene from private piety into something else: and the prisoners were listening to them. The word suggests close, deliberate attention — leaning in, straining to catch it. Luke uses it nowhere else in the New Testament.

Consider what those men were used to hearing at midnight in that room, and then consider hearing this.

Now a guard, because this verse is regularly used as a stick. It is not a command to feel like singing, and it is not a measurement you have failed. Paul himself writes elsewhere that he was so utterly burdened beyond our strength that we despaired of life itself (2 Cor. 1:8), which is the same apostle describing the opposite experience without any embarrassment. Scripture gives you Philippi at midnight and it also gives you Gethsemane, and the psalm that ends darkness is my closest friend (Ps. 88). If tonight you can only manage the praying half of verse 25, you are still inside the verse.

What the singing does show is where the joy was anchored. Nothing whatever in their circumstances had improved, and nothing was going to before the earthquake, which they did not know was coming. So the gladness was not a response to their situation. It came from somewhere the magistrates could not reach.

And suddenly there was a great earthquake... and immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone's bonds were unfastened.

Read the last clause again. Everyone's. Not Paul's and Silas's. Every door in the building and every chain on every prisoner in it.

They had been praying for themselves, presumably, and singing where others could hear. What arrived was an answer that took in every man in the prison, including men who had never asked for anything. God's reply to the two who prayed was wider than the two who prayed — which is a thing worth remembering about the prayers you make for your own situation, in a house where other people can hear you.

verseByVerse.quote: When the jailer woke and saw that the prison doors were open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped. But Paul cried out with a loud voice, "Do not harm yourself, for we are all here."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the jailer woke and saw that the prison doors were open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself.

He wakes to an earthquake and an open building, and he reaches for his own sword before he reaches for a light. That reflex needs explaining, because it looks like panic and it was arithmetic.

Under Roman practice a guard who lost his prisoners took their sentence himself. This book has already shown it happening: when Peter got out of prison in Jerusalem, Herod examined the sentries and ordered them put to death (12:19), and Luke recorded the cost without softening it. This man knows how that goes. What is waiting for him in the morning is an execution, preceded by disgrace. Falling on his own sword was the respectable Roman way out of exactly that, and by the standards he had been raised in it was the honourable thing to do.

So the man about to die is not a monster and not a coward. He is a middle-ranking official who has done his job well, been overtaken by something outside anybody's control, and worked out in about four seconds that his life is over.

But Paul cried out with a loud voice, Do not harm yourself, for we are all here.

Take the two halves separately, because both are astonishing.

First, Paul saw him. In a pitch-dark cell, from the innermost room, a man with his feet in the stocks somehow knew what was happening in the doorway and what it meant, and shouted before the sword went in. He was paying attention to somebody else at the one moment when nobody would have blamed him for thinking about himself.

Second, and far harder: we are all here.

Every door was open. Every chain was off. They had been beaten without trial by the authorities of that town, they had every legal grievance a man could have, and the building had just been opened by an act of God which any reasonable person would have read as a summons to walk out. Nobody moved. Not Paul, not Silas, and not one of the other prisoners — men with no faith at all and every reason to run.

Luke does not explain that, and it is the quietest miracle in the chapter. Something had been going on in that prison for the previous few hours, and the men who had been listening in verse 25 stayed where they were in verse 28.

And notice what the gospel does for this man first. Before a word is said about God, before he asks anything, before he knows who these people are — his life is saved, in the plainest physical sense, by a prisoner who did not use his freedom. The first thing Christianity did for the jailer at Philippi was stop him killing himself.

If you have ever wondered what use your obedience is when it is invisible and costs you an obvious advantage, here is the answer in one verse. Paul stayed in a cell he could have walked out of, and a man he had never spoken to was alive in the morning because of it.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the jailer called for lights and rushed in, and trembling with fear he fell down before Paul and Silas. Then he brought them out and said, 'Sirs, what must I do to be saved?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the jailer called for lights and rushed in, and trembling with fear he fell down before Paul and Silas.

Watch the reversal in the room. A few hours ago this man locked two prisoners in the dark and clamped their feet. Now he is calling for torches so he can see them, running into his own inner cell, and going down on the floor in front of the men he put there.

And he is trembling. Not with relief that his prisoners are safe, though they are. Luke has already told us he was ready to die a moment earlier and did not tremble then. Something else has got hold of him between the sword and the torches.

Then he brought them out and said, Sirs, what must I do to be saved?

It is the best question in the New Testament, and it is worth asking honestly what he meant by it, because the answer he gets is bigger than the question he asked.

On the face of it he may have meant something quite immediate. Saved was an ordinary word — saved from drowning, from illness, from a sentence. He is a man whose prison has just fallen down around him, who was seconds from suicide, and who may simply have been asking how he gets out of this alive.

But there is more in it than that, and the evidence is in the room. His prisoners are all present, so his immediate danger has already passed — Paul told him so in the previous verse. He is not asking how to escape execution; that is settled. And these are the men the whole city had been hearing about for days, because a slave girl had been following them through the streets announcing that they proclaimed a way of salvation (v. 17). He has almost certainly heard her. He has certainly heard them singing at midnight with their backs in ribbons.

So the question is probably both, and that is exactly how such questions arrive. An earthquake shook the walls and it shook something else, and a man who had never asked anything of the sort found the words in his mouth at two in the morning.

Now notice the form of it: what must I DO? That is the instinct of every religious person who has ever lived, and it is the instinct of every irreligious one too the moment he is frightened. Tell me the task. Give me the requirement and I will meet it. It is the same question the crowd asked at Pentecost (2:37) and the rich young ruler asked Jesus, and it is the question the whole of chapter 15 has just been fought over.

He is a practical man in a uniform, and he wants the procedure. What he is about to be handed has no procedure in it at all.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they said, 'Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they said, Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.

He asked what he must do. The answer contains no doing in it at all.

That is the first thing to see, and it is the whole gospel in the grammar. There is one verb: believe. Not believe and be circumcised, which is what men had been arguing for in Jerusalem a few months earlier. Not believe and make restitution to the two men you had flogged, which he would very reasonably have expected. Not believe and reform your life first, which is what most people privately assume is meant. One verb, and its object is a person.

And notice that the object is a person and not a proposition. Believe in the Lord Jesus — not believe that something is the case. The difference is the difference between knowing a bridge will hold and standing on it. A man can be entirely persuaded of every article of the faith and have trusted nobody.

Then the Lord Jesus, and both words are chosen. Jesus is the name of the man from Nazareth who was executed a few years ago — a fact, a date, a person you could have met. Lord is the word this jailer used every day of his working life about Caesar, and it is the confession that will eventually cost Christians in this colony their standing and sometimes their lives. He is being told to transfer his allegiance, and the man saying it has the marks of the local magistrates' rods on his back to show what that can cost.

Now the promise: and you will be saved. Future, and certain. Not you may be, not you can hope to be. The answer to a terrified man at two in the morning is a plain statement of outcome.
