So when and where every nation — and every person — lives is no accident of blind chance (the Epicurean's view) nor of impersonal Fate (the Stoic's), but the appointment of the living, personal God who writes the timeline of history and draws the map of the world (Deut. 32:8, 'he fixed the borders of the peoples'; Dan. 2:21, 'he changes times and seasons; he removes kings and sets up kings'). Empires rise and fall on his schedule, not their own — a humbling word to proud Athens, and a steadying one for us when the headlines look out of control: history is not adrift; God reigns over it.

And mark why he does it (the next words): 'that they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him.' God arranges the times and places of the nations with a gracious, missionary aim — so that people might seek and find him, 'for he is actually not far from each one of us.' This lands very personally. Your own century, your country, your town, the family you were born into — none of it is random. The God who sets the seasons of empires set your time and place on purpose, that you would seek him and find him (cf. Esther 4:14, 'for such a time as this'; Ps. 139:16). Where and when you live is not an accident; it is an appointment — a kindness designed to bring you home to the God who is near.

verseByVerse.quote: "'for "In him we live and move and have our being"; as even some of your own poets have said, "For we are indeed his offspring."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For in him we live and move and have our being; as even some of your own poets have said, For we are indeed his offspring.

Paul quotes two pagan poets to a pagan audience, and both quotations were written about Zeus.

The first is traditionally credited to Epimenides, a Cretan sage; the second is from the Phaenomena of Aratus, a poem about the stars — and Aratus came from Cilicia, which is Paul's own province. He is quoting a local poet from home to men in another country.

So what is he doing, and how far does it license us to go?

Notice first what he does not do. He does not say the poets were right about Zeus. He does not treat their religion as another road to the same place; he is nine verses from telling them to repent. He takes a true sentence out of a false frame and puts it in the true one. Pagans said something accurate about the dependence of every living thing on God, and got the name of the God wrong, and Paul keeps the accurate part and corrects the address.

He does it elsewhere too. Writing to Titus about Crete, he quotes the same Epimenides again — and this time the line is an insult about Cretans, and Paul says flatly that this testimony is true (Titus 1:12–13). He is quite willing to say that an unbeliever has told the truth.

That gives Christians a settled way of handling the culture they live in, and it avoids two errors. One is the instinct to treat everything outside the church as poison, which Paul plainly did not think and could not have preached this sermon if he had. The other is the modern habit of quoting whatever is popular in order to seem approachable, which is not what is happening here either — Paul uses two lines and then turns them against the whole religious system the poets belonged to. He is not borrowing credibility. He is taking territory.

Now the content, because it is not decoration. In him we live and move and have our being is not pantheism — Paul has just spent two verses insisting God is distinct from what he made. It is total creaturely dependence: the life you are living at this moment is on loan, moment by moment, and so is the breath you are taking while you read the sentence.

And we are indeed his offspring is the hinge into the next verse. Paul lets it stand — in the sense that every human being is God's creature and bears his stamp — and then he is about to turn it round on them with considerable force. If we are his offspring, then whatever God is like, he is at least as alive as we are. And that is exactly what a statue is not.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Being then God's offspring, we ought not to think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and imagination of man. The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Being then God's offspring, we ought not to think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and imagination of man.

Here is the argument, and it is devastating precisely because it is so simple. If we are God's offspring — living, thinking, choosing — then God is at least that. And a thing made of metal or rock is not.

Turn it round and the absurdity is exposed. The image is supposed to represent the greater and is made by the lesser. A living creature manufactures a dead object and then bows to it. Whatever is true of God, he cannot be less alive than the man holding the chisel.

And note the two words Paul puts at the end: the art and imagination of man. The idol is not merely stone; it is stone plus a human idea. Somebody decided what the god should look like, and then made it look like that. Which means the worshipper is, in the end, kneeling to his own conception — and the god will never require anything of him that he did not first think of himself.

That is why idolatry is so durable, and why the modern version is not statues. Nobody reading this keeps a figure of Athena. But the manufacture of a god out of the art and imagination of man is a live industry, and it is generally done in the first person: a God assembled out of the attributes we approve of, who is offended by the sins we do not commit and relaxed about the ones we do. It is a much more comfortable arrangement than the one Paul is preaching, and it has exactly the defect he names here. It cannot say anything to you that you did not put in it.

The test is uncomfortable and it is short. When did the God you believe in last contradict you?

The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent.

Overlooked does not mean excused. The word means passed over, let go by without pressing the matter — the same patience Paul described to the farmers at Lystra, where God sent rain and harvests to people who did not know him, and where the whole question of those who never heard is set out at 14:16. This is the other end of that patience. It has an expiry date, and the date has passed.

But now. Something has happened in history that changes the standing of every person alive, whether or not they have heard of it — and Paul is about to say what it was.

Then the four words that would have struck this audience hardest: he commands all people everywhere.

Not invites. Not recommends to those who find it congenial. God commands, which means repentance is not a religious option for the temperamentally devout but an order issued to everyone. And all people everywhere, said to a council that divided the human race into Greeks and barbarians and was rather sure which half mattered. The universality Paul established in verse 26 — one man, every nation — comes back here as a universal summons. If we all came from one, we are all answerable to one.

And notice that this is the first word of demand in the entire sermon. Paul has talked about creation, providence, nearness and poetry for eight verses, and only now, having taken the ground from under the idols, does he tell them to turn round.

verseByVerse.quote: "'because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead.

Every clause here is calculated, and to an Athenian every clause is an impossibility.

He has fixed a day. Not a cycle, not an endless recurrence of ages, which is how the Greeks thought about time. A date, already set, in a diary that is not ours. Nothing about it is contingent on whether the Areopagus finds the idea plausible.

He will judge the world in righteousness. The Epicureans in the audience believed that death ends the matter and there is nothing to fear; that is the comfort their whole system was built to give. Paul removes it in six words.

And it is worth saying that judgment is not only a threat. To a room of philosophers it lands as one. But a fixed day when the world is finally assessed in righteousness is, for anyone who has been genuinely wronged, the only hope there is. Every human court is partial, late, or bought. This one will not be. Nothing done in the dark to a person nobody defended will go unaddressed — which is why Scripture speaks of the coming judgment as something creation waits for rather than dreads.

By a man whom he has appointed. This is the point at which the sermon stops being philosophy. God will judge the world through a human being. Not through fate, not by a principle, not by weighing souls on a cosmic scale — by a man, with a name, who lived at a particular address and can be identified.

And there is mercy in that arrangement which is easy to miss. The one who will assess a human life has lived one. He knows from the inside what it is to be tired, poor, betrayed and afraid. The judge is not an outsider to the conditions he is judging.

And of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead.

The word for assurance is pistis, which usually means faith, but in the courts and the market it meant a guarantee, a proof, the security you offer to make a claim credible. God has posted a bond. The resurrection is not offered here as a comforting doctrine but as the evidence for the appointment — the public demonstration that the man in question is the one.

And to all. Not to insiders, not to the initiated, not to those with the right temperament. It is a fact placed in the open, and Paul is telling the most sceptical audience in the world that they already have everything they need to check it.

So the sermon that began with an altar to a god nobody could name ends with a man everybody can. That is the whole distance the gospel travels: from the unknown god to the named, dated, risen one.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked. But others said, 'We will hear you again about this.' So Paul went out from their midst."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked.

The room had been perfectly civil until this word. Creation, providence, the unity of the human race, even the summons to repent — all of it was strange but discussable. The resurrection is where an audience that would listen to anything stopped listening.

And it is worth knowing why, because it was not stupidity. Educated Greeks did not want the body back. The body was the problem — the weight, the appetites, the decay; and death, on the best Greek view, was the soul's release from it. To announce that a man had been raised bodily was not to offer them a hope. It was to propose returning a prisoner to his cell.

There is a line that makes the moment sharper still. In the Eumenides of Aeschylus — a play set at the founding of this very council, and known to every educated Athenian — Apollo declares that when the dust has drunk up a man's blood, once he is dead there is no rising again. That is the Athenian creed on the subject, spoken on the Areopagus in their own literature. Paul stands on the same ground and contradicts it.

But others said, We will hear you again about this. The second response, and it is the most common one in any century. Not refutation. Postponement. It may have been sincere; some of them may have meant it, and at least one member of that council believed before the day was out. But a subject can be kept permanently open, and Felix will do the same thing to Paul at greater length a few chapters later, sending for him often and deciding nothing (24:25–27).

So Paul went out from their midst. He did not stay to soften it. He had reached the resurrection, which was the thing he came to say, and when it was refused he left.

Now a question that hangs over this chapter and should be dealt with, because it is often raised. Was Athens a failure that Paul learned from? The suggestion is that he over-reached with philosophy and poetry, got a poor return, and afterwards resolved to do it differently — I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified (1 Cor. 2:2), written from Corinth, the very next city.

It is a tidy theory and there are reasons to doubt it. Paul did preach Christ crucified and risen at Athens — that is precisely what they mocked; he was not withholding the offensive part. Luke, who chose what to include, gives this speech more space than almost any other and presents it as a model of preaching to people with no Bible. And the contrast Paul draws in 1 Corinthians is not with contextualisation but with polished oratory and human cleverness as a means of persuasion — a warning about method, written to a church that was addicted to celebrity preachers.

What is fair to say is that Athens was hard ground and Luke does not pretend otherwise. There is no church at Athens in the New Testament, no letter to the Athenians, and no return visit recorded. Some places take a long time. That is not the same as having done it wrong.

verseByVerse.quote: "But some men joined him and believed, among whom also were Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris and others with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But some men joined him and believed.

That but is doing a great deal of work. The mockery was real, the deferral was real, and Luke records both without softening them — and then he tells you what else happened in the same room.

He names two people.

Dionysius the Areopagite. That is a member of the council itself — one of the men who had summoned Paul to explain himself, sitting in judgment on whether this teaching should be allowed a hearing in Athens. The court examined the gospel and one of the judges came over.

And a woman named Damaris. Luke does not tell us who she was and we should not invent her. What is worth noticing is that he keeps her name at all. This is the most male setting in the book — an ancient council of elders in a city where respectable women were not generally in such gatherings — and the two converts Luke chooses to name are a member of the aristocracy and a woman.

And others with them. Unnumbered and unnamed, and that is the whole harvest of the most celebrated sermon in Acts.

Set it against the ledger. At Thessalonica, a great many. At Berea, many. At Corinth, where he goes next, so many that God tells him in a vision to keep speaking because I have many in this city who are my people (18:10). At Athens, two names and some others.

And Luke writes it down. He does not pad it, does not explain it away, and does not suggest that the seed sown will surely spring up later. He gives the honest figure.

That honesty is worth more to a discouraged Christian than any amount of encouragement. The best-prepared, most intelligent, most carefully aimed sermon in the New Testament, preached by an apostle in the intellectual capital of the world, produced a handful of people. If your own work has produced a handful of people, you are not below the apostolic standard. You are on it.

And consider what a handful turned out to be. A councillor of the Areopagus is in the New Testament by name, nineteen centuries after the men who laughed at him have disappeared without one. Nobody remembers who mocked. We know who believed.

17.theology: General Revelation and the Necessity of the Gospel. Acts 17 contains the New Testament’s most developed account of what theologians call general revelation: the knowledge of God available to all humanity through creation and conscience (Romans 1:18–20). Paul acknowledges the Athenians’ religious instinct as genuine — they are groping toward God. But groping is not finding. General revelation creates the question; the gospel alone provides the answer. The God who made all nations from one man, who determined their times and boundaries, who is not far from any of us — this God has now spoken definitively in a man he raised from the dead. The times of ignorance are over. The command is universal: all people everywhere must repent. General revelation without the gospel leaves no one saved; it only leaves everyone without excuse.
17.examples:
Then: Paul in Athens, spirit provoked, standing before the intellectual elite of the ancient world with nothing but the story of a crucified and risen Jew. Some mock. Some believe. He moves on. The church in Athens is small, but Dionysius and Damaris are there — and the gospel is in Europe to stay.

Now: The contemporary West is increasingly like Athens: intellectually sophisticated, spiritually restless, full of altars to unnamed gods, suspicious of exclusive truth claims. The Areopagus sermon is the model for engagement: begin where people are, affirm what is true in their searching, and then announce the resurrection without apology. The resurrection is still the scandal. It is also still the only answer to the altar inscribed “To the unknown god.”

18.title: Corinth
18.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Paul left Athens and went to Corinth. <sup>2</sup>And he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome. And he went to see them, <sup>3</sup>and because he was of the same trade he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers by trade. <sup>4</sup>And he reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath, and tried to persuade Jews and Greeks. <sup>5</sup>When Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, Paul was occupied with the word, testifying to the Jews that the Christ was Jesus. <sup>6</sup>And when they opposed and reviled him, he shook out his garments and said to them, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.” <sup>7</sup>And he left there and went to the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshiper of God. His house was next door to the synagogue. <sup>8</sup>Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord, together with his entire household. And many of the Corinthians hearing Paul believed and were baptized. <sup>9</sup>And the Lord said to Paul one night in a vision, “Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, <sup>10</sup>for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many in this city who are my people.” <sup>11</sup>And he stayed a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them. <sup>12</sup>But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews made a united attack on Paul and brought him before the tribunal, <sup>13</sup>saying, “This man is persuading people to worship God contrary to the law.” <sup>14</sup>But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, “If it were a matter of wrongdoing or vicious crime, O Jews, I would have reason to accept your complaint. <sup>15</sup>But since it is a matter of questions about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves. I refuse to be a judge of these things.” <sup>16</sup>And he drove them from the tribunal. <sup>17</sup>And they all seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the tribunal. But Gallio paid no attention to any of this. <sup>18</sup>After this, Paul stayed many days longer and then took leave of the brothers and set sail for Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila. At Cenchreae he had cut his hair, for he was under a vow. <sup>19</sup>And they came to Ephesus, and he left them there, but he himself went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews. <sup>20</sup>When they asked him to stay for a longer period, he declined. <sup>21</sup>But on taking leave of them he said, “I will return to you if God wills,” and he set sail from Ephesus. <sup>22</sup>When he had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the church, and then went down to Antioch. <sup>23</sup>After spending some time there, he departed and went from one place to the next through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples. <sup>24</sup>Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, competent in the Scriptures. <sup>25</sup>He had been instructed in the way of the Lord. And being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John. <sup>26</sup>He began to speak boldly in the synagogue, but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately. <sup>27</sup>And when he wished to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. When he arrived, he greatly helped those who through grace had believed, <sup>28</sup>for he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus.
18.overview:
Corinth is the last place a fastidious missionary would choose. It is the Las Vegas of the ancient world — a great port city famous for commerce, vice, and the worship of Aphrodite. Paul arrives from Athens, where the reception was mixed, and he comes, as he later writes, “in weakness and in fear and much trembling” (1 Corinthians 2:3). He finds Aquila and Priscilla, works with them at their trade, preaches every Sabbath, and waits.

Then the Lord speaks in the night: “Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you… I have many in this city who are my people.” This is the doctrine of election turned into pastoral comfort. God already has people in Corinth — people who are his, who will be gathered by the proclamation of the gospel. Paul does not need to manufacture a harvest; he needs to be faithful, and God will bring in what is his. He stays a year and a half. The church at Corinth — with all its chaos, all its gifts, all its problems — is born.

The chapter closes with Apollos — eloquent, fervent, scripturally competent, but knowing only the baptism of John. Priscilla and Aquila take him aside privately and explain the way of God more accurately. They do not embarrass him publicly; they instruct him privately. And Apollos, genuinely humble, receives the teaching and goes on to powerfully confute the opponents of the gospel. The church grows not only by addition but by the deepening of those already in it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Corinth and the Return to Antioch
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul arrives in Corinth alone, discouraged and short of money, and stays a year and a half — the longest he had settled anywhere. Corinth was a boom town: levelled by Rome, refounded a century later, a port on both seas, rich, new, and with a reputation for vice so settled that to Corinthianise had been slang for debauchery for generations. It is the least promising ground in the book and it produces one of the great churches.

The workshop (vv. 1–5). He meets Aquila and Priscilla, driven out of Rome by an imperial edict, and moves in with them because they share his trade. For weeks the mission to Corinth runs on leatherwork six days a week and argument in the synagogue on the seventh — until Silas and Timothy arrive from Macedonia with money and Paul is freed to give himself wholly to preaching.

The break and the vision (vv. 6–11). The synagogue turns on him; he shakes out his garments, takes Ezekiel's watchman language on his lips, and moves next door — literally next door, to the house of Titius Justus. Then the synagogue's own ruler believes, and the Lord speaks to Paul at night: do not be afraid, go on speaking, I have many in this city who are my people. He stays eighteen months.

Gallio (vv. 12–17). A united attack brings Paul before the proconsul's tribunal on a charge worded to sound Roman. Gallio will not even let him answer: this is a dispute about words and names and your own law, and he refuses jurisdiction and clears the court. The crowd then beats the new synagogue ruler in front of the bench and Gallio pays no attention. The ruling protects the mission across the province for years, and it was given by a man with no interest in the gospel whatever.

Home (vv. 18–22). Paul sails for Syria with Priscilla and Aquila, having cut his hair at Cenchreae under a vow. He leaves the couple at Ephesus, reasons briefly in the synagogue there, declines an invitation to stay, promises to return if God wills, and goes on to Caesarea, Jerusalem and Antioch. The second journey ends where it began.
verseByVerse.theology:
Tent-Making Ministry and the Support of Proclamation

Paul's tent-making partnership with Aquila and Priscilla is the first explicit mention of Paul's manual labor as a means of supporting his missionary work. Reformed theology has often discussed whether 'tentmaker ministry' (self-supported missionary work) is a normative apostolic pattern or a situational adaptation. Paul's own letters suggest the latter: he worked with his hands to avoid being a burden on new churches and to model the dignity of labor, but he accepted support from established communities (Philippians 4:15–16). The Corinthian mission itself was eventually supported by the arrival of Silas and Timothy from Macedonia (v. 5).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Gallio decision — the Roman proconsul's dismissal of the Jewish charge against Paul — established a legal precedent protecting Christian preaching as an internal Jewish dispute. Now: God continues to use civil authorities and legal processes to protect the gospel's proclamation, even when those authorities have no understanding of or sympathy with the gospel. Providence works through the decisions of those who know nothing of its purposes.

verseByVerse.quote: "After this Paul left Athens and went to Corinth. And he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome. And he went to see them,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this Paul left Athens and went to Corinth.

Fifty miles west, and a complete change of world. Athens was a university town living on its past; Corinth was money. Rome had destroyed the old city and left it in ruins for a century, then refounded it as a colony for freedmen and veterans, and by Paul's day it was the administrative capital of the province and one of the richest ports in the empire, with a harbour on each sea and the traffic of both passing through it. It was about a hundred years old and behaved like it.

Its reputation was appalling and had been for centuries; the Greeks had a verb, to Corinthianise, which meant to live like that. Whatever you have heard about the immorality of Corinth is roughly what a first-century reader would have assumed.

So Paul walks out of the most cultured city in the world, where he got a handful of converts, into the most notorious, alone and with no contacts. It is worth remembering how this looked at the time, because he tells us: I was with you in weakness and in fear and much trembling (1 Cor. 2:3).

And he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome.

That expulsion is datable and it is one of the places where the New Testament and Roman history touch. The biographer Suetonius, writing some seventy years later, records that Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome because they were continually making disturbances at the instigation of Chrestus. Chrestus was a common slave name and was also, in ordinary speech, almost indistinguishable from Christus. What a Roman official at a distance would have seen, if the gospel had reached the Jewish quarter of Rome, is exactly what Acts has shown us in city after city: the synagogue in an uproar over a man called Christ.

If that is right — and it is the most natural reading — then the edict that threw Aquila and Priscilla out of their home was a piece of imperial policy made in ignorance about a quarrel the emperor did not understand, concerning the very gospel that was about to be preached in Corinth.

And notice what it produced. Luke never records their conversion, and never calls them converts of Paul's; they simply appear as believers, which suggests there were already Christians in Rome years before Paul wrote to them. Claudius emptied the Jewish quarter of Rome, and in doing so delivered to a lonely and frightened apostle in Corinth the two most useful colleagues he would ever have. They will house him, work beside him, cross the sea with him, teach Apollos, risk their necks for him, and host churches in at least three cities.

They did not choose to come. They were deported. And it is worth saying to anybody whose life has been rearranged by a decision taken somewhere else, by people who never considered them: the most fruitful partnership in the New Testament began with a forced removal.

verseByVerse.quote: "and because he was of the same trade he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers by trade."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And because he was of the same trade he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers by trade.

The word covers work in leather and in the coarse cloth woven from goats' hair that tents were made of — a trade of the awl and the knife, hard on the hands, and unglamorous. Cilicia, Paul's home province, was known for that cloth.

He had it because his family were observant Jews, and it was a settled principle among the rabbis that a man should teach his son a trade; the teachers of Israel were not a salaried class. So Paul the Pharisee, trained under Gamaliel, had also been trained to cut leather, and in Corinth it kept him alive.

Now consider what that means for the shape of these months, because it is easy to read Acts and imagine a full-time evangelist. In the ancient city the working day began at first light and ran until the light went. Paul was at the bench for it. He tells this very church that he worked with our own hands (1 Cor. 4:12), and reminds the Thessalonians of our labour and toil: we worked night and day, that we might not be a burden to any of you (1 Thess. 2:9). Years later, saying goodbye to the Ephesian elders, he holds them up: these hands ministered to my necessities and to those who were with me (20:34).

So the church at Corinth was planted by a man who preached on the Sabbath and made tents the other six days, and who did the two things in the same room. A workshop in that world was open to the street; customers came, apprentices worked, neighbours stopped. A great deal of the conversation that founded this church almost certainly happened over the bench, with both men's hands busy.

Two things follow, and they matter in opposite directions.

The first is for anyone who has ever felt that his working life is what he does when he is not serving God. Paul's trade was not an interruption of his ministry, and it was not merely a way of funding it. It put him among ordinary working people on their own terms, gave him a reason to be in the city, and made him impossible to accuse of being in it for the money — a charge he had to answer more than once at Corinth.

The second is a guard, because this passage gets used to argue that paid ministry is a compromise. Paul did not think so. He argued at length that the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel, and then said he had not used that right (1 Cor. 9:14–15). It was a right he waived, in a particular city, for particular reasons — which is the opposite of a rule that nobody should be supported.

And it is worth noticing where the friendship came from. Not a shared theology, not a shared background — he was from Tarsus and they were from Pontus by way of Rome — but a shared trade. God's provision for Paul's loneliness in Corinth arrived looking like a job.

verseByVerse.quote: And he reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath, and tried to persuade Jews and Greeks. When Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, Paul was occupied with the word, testifying to the Jews that the Christ was Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath, and tried to persuade Jews and Greeks.

Both verbs are the continuous kind — he kept reasoning, kept trying to persuade, Sabbath after Sabbath, for as long as they would have him. This was not a campaign. It was a routine, worked at week after week by a man who spent the other six days cutting leather.

And notice the honesty of the second verb. He tried to persuade. Luke does not say he persuaded them. Some weeks nothing happened, and Luke's Greek admits it.

When Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, Paul was occupied with the word, testifying to the Jews that the Christ was Jesus.

Something changes when the two men arrive, and Luke's word for it is strong: Paul was occupied — gripped, held fast, constrained. It is the word used of being seized by a fever, or hemmed in on every side. From this point he is not fitting the gospel round the working day.

What changed? Luke does not say here, but Paul does. Writing to Corinth about this very period, he says: when I was with you and was in need, I did not burden anyone, for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my need (2 Cor. 11:9). Silas and Timothy came from Philippi and Thessalonica, and they came with money.

So the sequence is plain. Money arrived from two poor churches several hundred miles away, and an apostle put down his tools and preached full time in the biggest city in Greece.

That is worth holding on to, because giving to Christian work is one of the more abstract things a believer does. Here it is not abstract at all. The Macedonians were not wealthy — Paul says elsewhere that they gave out of extreme poverty and beyond their means (2 Cor. 8:2–3). What their gift bought was hours: the hours Paul would otherwise have spent at a bench, converted directly into hours in front of people. The church at Corinth exists partly because Christians in Philippi went without something.

And note the content he was so gripped by, because Luke states it in one clause: testifying to the Jews that the Christ was Jesus. Not that Jesus was a Christ, or a good man, or a way. That the Christ — the one they had been waiting for, argued about, and prayed for every Sabbath in that building — was this particular man. Everything else Paul preached hangs off that identification.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they opposed and reviled him, he shook out his garments and said to them, 'Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.' And he left there and went to the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshiper of God. His house was next door to the synagogue."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they opposed and reviled him, he shook out his garments and said to them, Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent.

The gesture first. He shakes out his cloak — the same kind of prophetic sign as shaking the dust from the feet, which is set out at 13:51, and it says the same thing: I have nothing of yours on me and I carry nothing away.

But the words are not from that scene at all, and they repay knowing, because they are the key to a question that troubles a great many Christians.

Your blood be on your own heads. I am innocent. That is the language of Ezekiel 33, and it belongs to one image: the watchman on the wall. God sets a man to watch, and an army is coming. If the watchman sees the sword and does not blow the trumpet, and somebody is taken, his blood I will require at the watchman's hand. But if he blows the trumpet and the people do not take warning, then his blood shall be upon his own head... but you will have delivered your soul (Ezek. 33:4–6).

Look carefully at what the watchman is and is not responsible for. He is responsible for blowing the trumpet. He is not responsible for whether anybody comes inside the walls. Those are two different things, and Ezekiel keeps them rigorously apart.

Paul has been in that synagogue every Sabbath for weeks. He has reasoned, argued, answered, and been reviled for it. And what he says, in effect, is: the trumpet has been blown. His conscience is clear — not because he succeeded, but because he spoke.

That distinction is worth more than almost anything else in this chapter to the reader who carries a private grief about somebody unconverted — a father, a brother, a child who has heard it all and wants none of it. There is a burden that belongs to you and a burden that does not, and the two get mixed together until a person is worn out praying under the weight of an outcome he was never given charge of. You are answerable for the trumpet. You are not answerable for the walls.

And note the guard on the other side, because this is not a licence to give up on people. Paul says this to a synagogue that had turned hostile after months, not to someone who had said no once. And read what he does next.

From now on I will go to the Gentiles. And he left there and went to the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshiper of God. His house was next door to the synagogue.

Next door. He walks out of the building and sets up the Christian meeting immediately on the other side of the wall, in the house of a God-fearer who had presumably been sitting in that synagogue listening to him.

There is a certain steel in that, and it is not spite. Every Sabbath from now on, the congregation that threw him out will arrive to find the singing going on next door, and some of their own number in it — including, in the very next verse, their own ruler. Paul has said that he is going to the Gentiles. He has not gone anywhere. He is standing where they cannot miss him, which is exactly what a watchman does.

verseByVerse.quote: "Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord, together with his entire household. And many of the Corinthians hearing Paul believed and were baptized."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord, together with his entire household.

Read that immediately after verse 6, because Luke has put it there on purpose. Paul has just shaken out his garments at that synagogue and declared himself clear of it. And the first convert Luke names afterwards is the man who ran it.

The ruler of a synagogue was not a rabbi but the official responsible for the building and the services — who read, who spoke, what happened on the Sabbath. He was, in other words, the man who had been giving Paul the platform for those weeks, and quite possibly the man who had to withdraw it. He is a person of standing in the Jewish community of the province's capital, with everything to lose, and he believes.

Paul remembered it. Writing back to this church a few years later, when they were quarrelling about whose party they belonged to, he says he is thankful he baptised almost none of them — except Crispus and Gaius (1 Cor. 1:14). He did that one himself.

And there is a thread here that runs to the end of the chapter, which is worth following, because Luke does not point it out. Crispus is the ruler of the synagogue in verse 8. By verse 17 the ruler of the synagogue is a man called Sosthenes — so they replaced him, as they would have to. And when Paul writes to Corinth, the letter opens: Paul... and our brother Sosthenes (1 Cor. 1:1). If that is the same man, and it is a fair guess, then that synagogue lost two rulers in a row to Jesus Christ, and the second one is standing beside Paul when he writes the letter.

And many of the Corinthians hearing Paul believed and were baptized.

Many. In the town whose name was a byword for vice. Paul lists later what some of them had been — a catalogue of the sins that city was famous for — and then writes the sentence that has carried more people out of their past than almost any other in Scripture: and such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified (1 Cor. 6:11).

Were. If you have a history that you assume disqualifies you, that verb was written to the church founded in this verse.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the Lord said to Paul one night in a vision, 'Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many in this city who are my people.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the Lord said to Paul one night in a vision, Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent.

You do not tell a man not to be afraid unless he is. That is the first thing in this verse and it should not be hurried past. Somewhere in those early months at Corinth, the apostle Paul was frightened enough that the Lord Jesus came to him at night to say so.

And he had reason. He had been flogged at Philippi, run out of Thessalonica by night, chased out of Berea, ignored at Athens, and he was now in a city where the synagogue had just turned on him. He tells the Corinthians plainly how he arrived: in weakness and in fear and much trembling (1 Cor. 2:3). The man who wrote most of the New Testament knew what it was to want to stop.

Then notice what the Lord actually commands, because it is not what we would expect. Not rest. Not go somewhere safer. Go on speaking and do not be silent — the same instruction twice, once positively and once negatively, which is how you speak to somebody who is on the edge of stopping. The cure for the fear is to keep doing the thing that caused it.

And then three reasons, and each one is precise.

For I am with you. Not I will protect your reputation, or your comfort. Presence.

And no one will attack you to harm you. Now read that clause very carefully, because it is easy to misquote and the difference matters enormously. It does not say nobody will attack him. People do attack him — in three verses' time there is a united assault and he is dragged before the tribunal. What is promised is that no attack will land as harm.

That is not a lesser promise; it is a truer one, and it is the shape of every promise of this kind in Scripture. Paul was not given a quiet eighteen months. He was given eighteen months in which what happened to him could not stop what God was doing through him. And in due course, in this same country, the promise ran out and he was arrested and eventually executed — which is not a failure of the word given here, because this word was given about Corinth and about now.

Which is worth saying to anyone who has claimed a verse like this and then been hurt by something. God's assurances of protection in Scripture are almost always attached to a work and a season, and they promise that the work will not be defeated. They do not promise that you will not be touched.

Then the third reason, and it is the strangest and best of them: for I have many in this city who are my people.

'I have many in this city who are my people' — spoken of Corinthians who had not yet believed. Notice how God's election here does not cool evangelism but fires it: because God has a chosen people in Corinth who will come to faith through the preaching, Paul can keep speaking, unafraid, certain his labour will not be wasted. Election does not make sowing pointless; it makes the harvest sure, for the Lord gathers his own through the gospel preached (cf. 13:48; 2 Tim. 2:10, 'I endure everything for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain salvation'). It is the discouraged evangelist's deepest comfort: somewhere in your 'city' are people God means to save, and your faithful witness is the means he will use.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he stayed a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he stayed a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.

Eighteen months. Set that against the rest of the book and the number is extraordinary. Three Sabbaths at Thessalonica. A few weeks at Berea. Days at Athens. Everywhere in the first two journeys, Paul plants and is moved on, usually by force. Here he stops.

And Luke puts the verse immediately after the vision, which is the explanation. The promise in verses 9 and 10 was not an emotional comfort; it was permission to put down roots. A man being hunted from town to town does not build. A man who has been told that nothing will land as harm and that there are many in this city who belong to God can unpack.

Now consider what eighteen months of a settled apostle actually produced, because it is a great deal more than one church.

He was teaching, continuously — Luke's verb is the one for sustained instruction rather than proclamation. Not eighteen months of evangelistic addresses; eighteen months of taking a mixed congregation of Jews, God-fearers and converted pagans through the Scriptures. Whatever the Corinthians later got wrong, and they got a remarkable amount wrong, they had been thoroughly taught.

He also wrote from here. The two letters to the Thessalonians belong to this stay — the earliest of Paul's letters we possess, and among the earliest documents in the New Testament. They were written by a tentmaker in a rented room in Corinth to a church he had been driven away from and could not get back to, and they are in every Bible on earth.

And there is a lesson in the sheer length of it for anybody impatient with slow work. A year and a half in one city, mostly teaching the same people, is not what a reader of Acts expects of Paul, and it is what produced the church that generated more New Testament correspondence than any other. The dramatic chapters get the attention. This verse is where the depth came from.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews made a united attack on Paul and brought him before the tribunal, saying, 'This man is persuading people to worship God contrary to the law.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews made a united attack on Paul and brought him before the tribunal.

Luke drops a Roman official's name and a date into the narrative, and in doing so hands historians the single most useful sentence in the New Testament for fixing chronology.

A stone found at Delphi carries a letter from the emperor Claudius which mentions Gallio as proconsul of Achaia, and it can be dated to within a few months. Proconsuls served, as a rule, for one year. So Paul was in Corinth in the early fifties, and every other date in his life — the conversion, the councils, the letters — is measured outward from this verse. The whole timeline of the apostolic age hangs on Luke having got one provincial governor's term right. The wider case for his care as a historian is set out at 5:37–38 and does not need repeating.

The man himself is not a stranger to Roman literature either. Gallio was the elder brother of Seneca, the Stoic philosopher and tutor to the young Nero, who dedicated books to him and described him as a man nobody could help liking. That is the temperament on the bench in this scene: cultivated, easy-going, and entirely uninterested in the matter in front of him.

The Jews made a united attack on Paul. United — after eighteen months in which the synagogue had lost its ruler and a good many of its members, the opposition finally coordinates. And they choose their moment: a new governor, freshly arrived, who might be expected to want a quiet province and to defer to established religious authority.

This man is persuading people to worship God contrary to the law.

That sentence is carefully built, and the ambiguity is the whole strategy. Contrary to which law? If Gallio hears Roman law, then Paul is promoting an unlicensed religion and can be shut down across the province by a single ruling. If he hears Jewish law, it is a synagogue quarrel and none of his business.

They are hoping he will not notice which. Everything depends on a bored proconsul hearing the word law and reaching for the wrong one.

A quick word on 'proconsul' (Greek anthypatos). Rome's provinces came in two kinds: the settled, peaceful ones governed on behalf of the Senate by a proconsul, and the frontier ones governed by the emperor's own appointees. Achaia (southern Greece, capital Corinth) was a senatorial province, so its governor was a proconsul — usually a senior senator sent out for about a year, holding supreme civil and judicial authority, which is why Paul is hauled before his 'tribunal' (the bēma, the judgment seat) for a ruling. In modern terms he was something like a centrally-appointed regional governor who was also the province's chief judge — combining in one man the executive and judicial powers our democracies usually keep apart, answerable not to local voters but to Rome. (Luke's precise title here is also a quiet mark of his accuracy: Achaia's status shifted over the years, and he names it correctly for this moment — the same Gallio whose term the Delphi inscription dates to c. AD 51–52.)

verseByVerse.quote: But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, "If it were a matter of wrongdoing or vicious crime, O Jews, I would have reason to accept your complaint. But since it is a matter of questions about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves. I refuse to be a judge of these things."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews...

Paul never gets to speak. He draws breath to make his defence and the governor cuts across him and decides the case. It is the only trial in Acts where Paul is not permitted to say a word, and it is the one that goes best for him.

If it were a matter of wrongdoing or vicious crime, O Jews, I would have reason to accept your complaint.

Gallio has seen straight through the ambiguity. He separates the two categories a Roman court existed for — an actual crime, or a serious fraud — and observes that this is neither.

But since it is a matter of questions about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves. I refuse to be a judge of these things.

Read the phrase words and names, because it is a small window into how the gospel looked from outside. Gallio has listened to the charge and concluded that the whole business is a dispute over terminology within a foreign religion — an argument about whether a particular Jewish title belongs to a particular dead Jew. He is not entirely wrong about the subject matter and he is completely wrong about its weight.

And that is worth sitting with, because it is the commonest reaction the gospel meets in a comfortable society. Not persecution, and not conversion. Classification. The thing is filed as a matter of words and names — a private religious preference, a vocabulary that some people find meaningful — and set aside without hostility by somebody who has other things to do. Athens laughed; Gallio simply did not think it was about anything.

Now the consequence, which is enormous and entirely unintended. By ruling that this is an internal Jewish question, the senior Roman official in Greece has placed the Christian movement under the legal shelter Judaism enjoyed as an ancient and licensed religion. A proconsul's ruling set a precedent, and every magistrate in Achaia would know of it. For years afterwards, Paul preaches across the empire with a decision on record that this is not a matter for the courts.

God gave his church a decade of legal cover through a man who could not have been less interested in it. Gallio was not being kind, or fair-minded about religion, or secretly sympathetic. He was declining to waste an afternoon. And the protection was real.

Which is a useful thing to know when you look at the people who currently hold power over the circumstances of your life. God's providence does not require their goodwill, or their understanding, or even their attention.

verseByVerse.quote: And he drove them from the tribunal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he drove them from the tribunal.

One short sentence, and the verb is not a polite one. He had them driven off — the court cleared, the case not merely dismissed but swept out.

Picture the reversal. These men had come with a coordinated complaint, timed for a new governor, framed in language designed to make a Roman act. They had brought their opponent under guard. And within about a minute they are being pushed away from the bench in the middle of the marketplace, in front of the whole city, having been told that their religion is not worth a magistrate's time.

The humiliation is public and it is total, and the next verse shows what a crowd does with a public humiliation.

It is worth pausing on what has actually happened here, because it is not what the opponents intended or what Paul could have arranged. The most effective protection the early church received in Greece came from contempt. Gallio did not defend Christianity; he refused to distinguish it from Judaism, and threw the whole quarrel out of court as beneath his notice.

God is quite willing to use a man's indifference. He used Pharaoh's hardness and Cyrus's ambition and Pilate's cowardice, and here he uses a cultivated Roman's boredom. None of these men were serving him and all of them were doing exactly what he intended.

There is comfort in that and there is also a warning, and both should be taken. The comfort is that the advance of the gospel has never depended on the sympathy of the people in charge. The warning is Gallio himself: he is on the right side of history in this chapter and there is no suggestion whatever that it did him any good. A man can render enormous service to the purposes of God and remain entirely outside them.

One last thing about the place itself. The tribunal Gallio cleared was the bema — the raised platform in the Corinthian marketplace from which a magistrate gave judgment. Its foundations are still there, and it is one of the very few spots on earth where a visitor can stand on the actual stones of a scene in the New Testament.

And Paul did not forget the word. Writing back to this church, to people who had watched him stand on that platform, he uses it twice for something else: we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Cor. 5:10), and we will all stand before the judgment seat of God (Rom. 14:10), written from this same city. The Corinthians knew exactly what a bema looked like, because there was one in their market square and their apostle had been dragged in front of it.

Set the two judgment seats side by side, which is surely what Paul intended. At the first, the judge would not hear the case, the accused was never allowed to speak, and the verdict came from a man who thought the whole matter beneath him. At the second, every case is heard, nothing is dismissed as a quarrel about words and names, and the Judge has taken the trouble to become one of the accused.

verseByVerse.quote: And they all seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the tribunal. But Gallio paid no attention to any of this. After this, Paul stayed many days longer and then took leave of the brothers and set sail for Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila. At Cenchreae he had cut his hair, for he was under a vow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they all seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the tribunal. But Gallio paid no attention to any of this.

A crowd has just watched a group of Jews thrown out of court by the governor, and it does what crowds do with people who have been publicly stripped of protection. They take the leader of the delegation and beat him where the proconsul can see.

Notice that this has nothing to do with Paul. Nobody here is defending him. The mob is not on the side of the gospel; it is on the side of whoever has just lost, and the undercurrent of feeling against Jews in a Roman colony has been given an opportunity.

But Gallio paid no attention to any of this.

That is the same indifference that had just protected the church, now watching a man beaten in front of the bench and declining to intervene. Luke sets the two effects of one man's temperament side by side without a word of comment, and the reader who was warming to Gallio in verse 15 is meant to feel the chill in verse 17. Detachment is not a virtue. It served the gospel in one verse and left a man bleeding in the next.

And who was Sosthenes? The ruler of the synagogue — which means the successor of Crispus, who had believed in verse 8. Then look at the first line of the letter Paul later wrote back to this city: Paul, called by the will of God to be an apostle of Christ Jesus, and our brother Sosthenes (1 Cor. 1:1).

It is not certain that they are the same man, and it should not be asserted. But it is a common enough coincidence to be worth noticing, and if it is the same man, then the beating in this verse is the last thing the New Testament records about him before he turns up as a Christian standing beside the apostle he had prosecuted.

After this, Paul stayed many days longer and then took leave of the brothers and set sail for Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila.

He does not leave in a hurry, which is itself a mark of how completely Gallio's ruling had changed the situation. And when he goes, the couple who took him in go with him, leaving the city and the business they had built after being deported from Rome. Luke names Priscilla first, as he does more often than not.

At Cenchreae he had cut his hair, for he was under a vow.

Cenchreae is Corinth's eastern harbour, and a church was planted there too — Paul later commends to the Romans our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae (Rom. 16:1), who very probably carried that letter to Rome.

And there, on his way to the boat, the apostle of justification by faith had his head shaved because of a vow. Luke tells us nothing else — not what the vow was for, not when he took it, not what he had asked. It has the shape of the Nazirite vow of Numbers 6, in which a man separated himself to the LORD for a period, drank no wine, let his hair grow, and cut it off at the end. Why he took it we are not told, and guesses about gratitude for Corinth or for safety are only guesses.

What cannot be avoided is the question it raises.

Paul's vow raises a real question: now that Christ has come, may a believer still keep the law, or parts of it? The Reformed answer distinguishes three strands in the law of Moses. The moral law (the Ten Commandments, summed up as loving God and neighbour) reflects God's unchanging character and abides always; we are not saved by it, but the believer gladly obeys it as the Spirit-enabled pattern of a thankful life. The ceremonial law (sacrifices, priesthood, temple, feasts, clean-and-unclean foods, circumcision as rite) was the shadow that pointed to Christ and is fulfilled in him (see on Col. 2:16–17) — no Christian is bound to keep it. The civil law that governed Israel as a nation expired with that nation, though its underlying justice still instructs. So: the moral law stands; the ceremonial and civil are not binding as obligations.

But notice the careful line Paul walks — here a Jewish vow, later a temple purification (21:23–26), and Timothy's circumcision (16:3), yet a flat refusal to circumcise Titus (Gal. 2:3–5) and thunder against anyone who made law-keeping a condition of salvation (Gal. 5:2–4). The difference is always why. Made a means of being right with God, or imposed on others as necessary, a practice denies the gospel and is forbidden. Kept freely — as heritage, devotion, conscience, or love that wins a hearing ('to the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might win Jews,' 1 Cor. 9:20) — it is Christian liberty. Paul kept his vow not to earn anything but as free devotion; that is the model.

So, the two cases. A Jewish believer may in liberty keep ancestral customs — feasts, food traditions, even a vow — as heritage, devotion, and witness among his people, as Paul did, provided he never makes them the ground of his standing nor binds them on others. A Gentile believer is under no obligation to the ceremonial law at all (the whole verdict of Acts 15); he may find devotional value in some Old Testament root — 'one esteems one day above another... let each be fully convinced in his own mind' (Rom. 14:5) — but must heed Galatians' warning never to put himself under the law as a system, which is to fall from grace (Gal. 4:10–11; 5:1). The test in every case: am I doing this to be saved or accepted, or imposing it as necessary? — then stop. Is it a free, loving, Christ-honouring practice that binds no one? — then you are free. Christ alone for salvation; liberty in the rest, governed by love. (Where the Lord's Day and Sabbath fit is one place Reformed and other believers differ — for another verse.)

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Ephesus, and he left them there, but he himself went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews. When they asked him to stay for a longer period, he declined.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they came to Ephesus, and he left them there.

That is a larger sentence than it looks. Ephesus was the greatest city in Asia, the place Paul would eventually spend three years and where the Spirit had refused to let him go at the start of this journey (16:6). He passes through it now for a few days, and what he leaves behind is a married couple with a trade.

Priscilla and Aquila are put down in Ephesus like a seed. Within a few verses they will take the most gifted preacher in the eastern Mediterranean aside and finish his education; by the time Paul writes to Corinth from this city, there is a church meeting in their house (1 Cor. 16:19). Paul's strategy for the greatest city in Asia was to leave two tentmakers in it.

But he himself went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews. Days off the boat, in a city he is only passing through, and he is in the synagogue arguing. There is no version of Paul that takes a week to look round a town.

When they asked him to stay for a longer period, he declined.

Now this is the remarkable thing, and it is almost never remarked on. For the first time in the book, a synagogue asks Paul to stay longer — and he says no.

Think of what he has been through to get a hearing like this. Thrown out of Pisidian Antioch, stoned at Lystra, run out of Thessalonica and Berea, mocked at Athens, hauled before a tribunal at Corinth. Here, at last, is a receptive synagogue in the most strategic city in the province, asking for more.

And he leaves.

Luke does not fully explain it; the next verses show a man determined to get to Jerusalem and Antioch, and there was a vow outstanding and a sending church to report to. What the passage plainly shows is that an open door is not the same thing as a summons. Paul had learned that in reverse at Troas, when every door was shut and it turned out to be direction; here every door is open and it is still not the instruction.

That is worth having, because we are generally taught to read opportunity as guidance — if it is possible, and it is good, and people want it, then surely. Paul had before him a genuine opportunity, in a strategic place, urged on him by people who wanted the gospel. He said no, and went home to report to his church.

Not every good thing you could do is a thing you are being asked to do. Some of them belong to somebody else, or to a later year — and Ephesus, in fact, was waiting for him. He would come back and give it three years, which is longer than he gave any other city in his life.

verseByVerse.quote: But on taking leave of them he said, "I will return to you if God wills," and he set sail from Ephesus. When he had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the church, and then went down to Antioch.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But on taking leave of them he said, I will return to you if God wills.

Four words that Paul evidently meant literally. He uses the same qualification writing to this region — I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills (1 Cor. 4:19) — and James turns it into a settled Christian habit: you ought to say, If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that (James 4:15).

It is easy to hear as a pious formula, and in our mouths it often is. In Paul's it had teeth, and this whole journey is the evidence. He had been forbidden by the Spirit to speak in Asia, forbidden to enter Bithynia, sent to Macedonia by a dream, and driven out of three cities in succession. A man whose plans had been overruled that often had stopped saying he would do things.

And he did return — for three years, the longest stay of his ministry. The qualification was not pessimism. It was accuracy about who was arranging the itinerary.

When he had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the church, and then went down to Antioch.

Luke's compression here is severe, and the two little direction words carry the meaning. You always go up to Jerusalem and down from it, whatever the map says, because it is the holy city. So went up and greeted the church, with no city named, means Jerusalem — several days' travel inland from the port, for a visit Luke covers in four words.

And then Antioch, which is where the whole thing started. The church that fasted and prayed and laid hands on Barnabas and Saul in 13:2 gets its men back for the second time. He has now been round the Aegean, planted churches in Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea, Corinth and Ephesus, and written the first of his letters, and he comes home and reports to the congregation that sent him.

That is worth noticing about a man with as much authority as any Christian has ever had. He had seen the risen Christ, he had been given the gospel by revelation, and he still travelled several hundred miles at the end of every journey to stand in front of an ordinary local church and tell them what had happened.

The second missionary journey ends here. It began with a quarrel about John Mark and it ends in the same room, with the mission enormously enlarged and neither Barnabas nor Mark anywhere in sight.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The third missionary journey opens in a single participle — Paul back on the roads of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples (v. 23) — and then Luke turns aside from him altogether for five verses to tell us about somebody else entirely.

A gifted man with a gap (vv. 24–25). Apollos arrives at Ephesus from Alexandria: a Jew, eloquent, powerful in the Scriptures, instructed in the way of the Lord, boiling over in spirit, and teaching accurately the things concerning Jesus. Everything in that list is a commendation. And then one clause undoes none of it and changes everything — though he knew only the baptism of John. His information stopped somewhere around the Jordan. He was preaching a true message with an end missing.

Two tentmakers take him aside (v. 26). Priscilla and Aquila hear him in the synagogue and do not correct him in it. They take him home and explain the way of God more accurately — the most gifted speaker in the eastern Mediterranean instructed privately by a couple who worked with their hands, and Luke names the wife first.

And then he is sent (vv. 27–28). When he wants to cross to Achaia the brothers write ahead to commend him, and in Corinth he is a considerable force: he greatly helped those who through grace had believed, and refuted the Jews in public, showing from the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus. The man Priscilla and Aquila finished off in a back room went on to water the field Paul had planted — and to become, without wanting to, the name of a faction in Corinth that Paul had to write a letter about.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Importance of Thorough Gospel Formation

Apollos's incomplete knowledge — accurate as far as it went but stopping before the resurrection — is the permanent challenge of theological formation. Every generation needs to receive not just the part of the gospel that resonates with its existing categories but the complete gospel that the Scriptures teach. Priscilla and Aquila model the ministry of theological completion: receiving those who are partially formed, honoring what is genuine, and filling in what is absent. This is the ministry of discipleship.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Apollos went to Achaia and was of great help to those who through grace had believed, for he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus. Now: The church continues to be built by ministers whose gifts complement each other — some plant (Paul in Corinth), some water (Apollos in Corinth, 1 Corinthians 3:6), and God gives the growth.

verseByVerse.quote: "After spending some time there, he departed and went from one place to the next through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After spending some time there, he departed and went from one place to the next through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples.

That is the whole of the beginning of the third missionary journey. One verse. No commissioning service, no vision, no laying on of hands — after the first journey Luke gave us a whole scene in the church at Antioch, and here Paul simply leaves and starts walking.

And where does he go? Back over the same ground. Galatia and Phrygia are the towns of the first journey — Derbe, Lystra, Iconium, Pisidian Antioch — the places where he was stoned and expelled, and which he had already revisited twice. This is the third time he has walked those roads.

Nothing about that is new territory or new converts. It is maintenance, and the verb Luke chooses says so: strengthening, making firm what is already standing. He used the same word when Paul went back through those towns the first time (14:22) and when he set out on the second journey (15:41). Three journeys, and every one of them begins the same way, with an apostle propping up small congregations he has already planted.

Notice too the word all. Not the promising ones, not the strategic ones. All the disciples, in one place after another, going from one place to the next — a phrase suggesting an unhurried, methodical circuit rather than a dash through.

There is a temptation, in Christian work as in anything else, to believe that the real thing is the founding and everything afterwards is administration. Luke does not present it that way. Paul spent an enormous proportion of his life going back — and the letters, which are the reason we know anything about him, are simply this same activity conducted by post when he could not go in person.

If your own service to God consists largely of turning up again for the same people, who are not obviously further on than they were last year, you are doing the thing this verse describes, and it is what the apostle to the Gentiles did with his time.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, competent in the Scriptures. He had been instructed in the way of the Lord. And being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus.

Alexandria is worth pausing on, because it explains the man. It was the second city of the empire, the intellectual capital of the Greek-speaking world, home of the great library, and it held the largest and most cultured Jewish community outside Judea. The Old Testament had been translated into Greek there. Philo, the most celebrated Jewish thinker of the age, was writing there in Apollos's own lifetime. A Jew educated in Alexandria was educated as well as anyone then living.

And Luke piles up the commendations, four of them, before he raises any difficulty.

An eloquent man — the word can mean learned or a fine speaker, and there is no reason to choose; he was evidently both.

Competent in the Scriptures — the word is dynatos, powerful. Not merely well-informed: strong in them, able to use them.

Being fervent in spirit — literally boiling. Paul uses the identical phrase when telling the Romans how a Christian ought to be (Rom. 12:11).

He spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus. Accurately. Luke is not damning him with faint praise and then correcting him; what Apollos said about Jesus was true.

So here is a man who is learned, powerful in the Bible, on fire, and doctrinally accurate — and Luke's next clause is though he knew only the baptism of John.

Hold those two things together, because the combination is the point of the whole paragraph and it is unusual in Scripture. There is nothing wrong with Apollos. He is not a false teacher, not a self-promoter, not lukewarm, not careless. He is excellent, and he is incomplete, and the two are not in tension. His problem is not his character, or his zeal, or his handling of the text. It is simply that the news had not all reached him yet.

That is a category we are not very good at. We tend to sort teachers into sound and unsound, and Apollos will not go in either box.

What does 'he knew only the baptism of John' mean? John the Baptist's baptism was a preparatory one — 'a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins' (Luke 3:3), in which people confessed their sins, turned to God, and got ready for the Messiah who was coming. John pointed beyond himself: 'I baptize you with water... but he who is coming after me... will baptize you with the Holy Spirit' (Matt. 3:11). So it looked forward to Jesus; it was the 'getting ready' baptism, not yet the full Christian one. To say Apollos 'knew only John's baptism,' then, is to say his grasp of the gospel reached accurately up to that preparatory point — he knew and proclaimed Jesus as the Messiah truly, as far as it went — but had not yet been brought up to the fuller apostolic message that followed: Pentecost, the outpouring and gift of the Holy Spirit, and baptism in the name of Jesus. His faith was real but incomplete, the fault of his teaching, not his heart — he taught what he had been taught, probably away from the centre in Alexandria before the fuller news reached him.

(He is the cousin of the Ephesian 'disciples' of 19:1–7, who also knew only John's baptism — though note the difference: Apollos, already fervent in the Spirit and teaching accurately, is simply taught 'more accurately' by Priscilla and Aquila (v. 26) and is never re-baptized, whereas those men, who had not even heard the Spirit was given, are baptized into Jesus and receive the Spirit; see on 19:1–2.) And the lovely lessons here: even a brilliant, eloquent, fervent Bible teacher still had more to learn — and humbly received it from a tentmaking couple (Priscilla named first). None of us has arrived; we keep growing. And the way to help someone whose understanding is incomplete is Priscilla and Aquila's way: not to attack him publicly, but to 'take him aside' and explain the way of God more accurately — gently, privately, helpfully.

verseByVerse.quote: "He began to speak boldly in the synagogue, but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He began to speak boldly in the synagogue, but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately.

Everything about that sentence repays slow reading.

They took him aside. Not up. Not out. Aside — privately, away from the congregation he had been addressing. They heard a brilliant man preaching something short of the truth in a public meeting, and they did not stand up.

Consider the alternatives they declined. They could have corrected him from the floor, which would have been humiliating and would probably have hardened him. They could have warned people about him afterwards, which is the modern method and requires no courage at all. They could have said nothing, on the grounds that he was clearly gifted and it was not their place — two tentmakers against an Alexandrian scholar.

Instead they took him home. Luke's word for what they did is not rebuked or refuted but explained — set it out for him — and the comparative is careful too: more accurately. Not accurately, as though he had been wrong. More accurately, because he had been right as far as he went.

That is the whole art of helping somebody whose understanding is incomplete, and there are two errors it avoids. One is the refusal to say anything, which leaves a man preaching half a gospel out of a misplaced deference. The other is public correction, which is far more satisfying and almost always makes the person defend the position he was about to abandon. If you have ever needed to say something difficult to a Christian you respect, this verse is the method: privately, personally, over a meal, beginning with what is right.

And notice who is doing it. A husband and wife, in partnership, teaching a man in their own home — and Luke names Priscilla first, as he does four times out of the six that the couple appear. In the ancient world that order is unusual enough to be deliberate, and the most natural explanation is that she took the lead in this.

It is fair to say plainly that Christians disagree about what follows from that for the question of women teaching, and that the disagreement is between people who take the whole Bible seriously. What the text itself gives is a private setting, a married couple acting together, and Luke's evident approval — and any position on the wider question has to be able to hold this verse comfortably and gladly, because Luke plainly regarded what Priscilla did as one of the most useful things anybody did in this chapter.

Consider, finally, what it cost Apollos. He was the most gifted speaker in the room, and he sat down in a tentmaker's house and let two manual workers teach him. Everything he became afterwards — the power in Corinth, the letter Paul wrote urging him to go back there — runs through that evening. The gifted man's greatest asset here is not his eloquence. It is that he could be taught.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he wished to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. When he arrived, he greatly helped those who through grace had believed, for he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he wished to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him.

A letter of commendation — the ordinary machinery by which the early church moved people around a hostile world where nobody could check anybody's credentials. A stranger arriving in a city with a letter from believers who knew him could be received at once. Paul refers to the practice repeatedly, and once, to this very church, with some feeling: are we beginning to commend ourselves again? Or do we need, as some do, letters of recommendation to you? (2 Cor. 3:1).

So the Ephesian church put its name behind a man who, weeks earlier, had been preaching an incomplete gospel in their synagogue. They did not send a warning ahead of him. They sent an endorsement.

When he arrived, he greatly helped those who through grace had believed.
