And here, years later, James quotes not his own speech but the letter — idols, blood, strangled, sexual immorality, in exactly that order. He is not reciting a memory of what he once said. He is citing a document that is still on file.

(On why these four things were asked of Gentile believers — not as law for salvation, but for the sake of love and table-fellowship between Jewish and Gentile Christians, and to keep new converts clear of pagan idolatry — see the full explanation at the Jerusalem Council, 15:19–20, which also shows how it harmonises with Paul's later teaching on food offered to idols in 1 Corinthians.)

Which is the point of the sentence. We have sent a letter with our judgment — sent, past tense, settled business, and still binding. That council was perhaps seven years earlier. In the intervening years the Gentile mission had exploded across three provinces, and nothing had been added to the terms. No one had crept up on the decision. No one had renegotiated it once the Gentiles were numerous enough to be inconvenient. The freedom granted to the nations at Jerusalem was not a temporary concession that quietly expired; it was a judgement that held.

And notice where James puts it. He builds the fence before anyone has had the chance to climb it. If Paul is about to be seen in the temple paying for sacrifices, some observer is bound to conclude that the Gentile churches must be next. James kills that inference in the same breath as he makes the request. Wise leadership says out loud what an action does not mean, in advance, while it can still be heard.

Then, verse 26, and Luke gives it no drama at all. Then Paul took the men, and the next day he purified himself along with them and went into the temple.

No argument is recorded. No delay, no conditions, no request for time to think it over. The next day. The man who wrote to the Galatians that if they accept circumcision Christ will be of no advantage to them, and to the Romans that a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law, takes four men to the temple, submits to the purification, and registers the completion date with the priests — giving notice when the days of purification would be fulfilled and the offering presented for each one of them. He puts his name on a list at the temple office and agrees to pay a bill for blood sacrifices.

He can do it precisely because he believes what he wrote. A ceremony that cannot save him also cannot endanger him. It is free. And because it is free, he can spend it on his brothers.

Now the hard question, and the chapter answers it within twenty-four hours. Did the plan work?

No. It failed completely. The vow put Paul in the temple, in public, at the one moment when Jews from Asia who knew him by sight were in the city for the feast — and being in the temple is what got him seen, seized and nearly killed. The advice of the wisest men in the Jerusalem church, offered in love and accepted in humility, is the immediate cause of his arrest.

Hold that steadily, because most of us have a private theology that says otherwise. We believe, somewhere below the waterline, that if we take the humble course, seek counsel, deny ourselves, and pay for it out of our own pocket, it ought to come out right. Here it does not. James was not foolish and Paul was not weak, and the thing blew up in their faces.

And yet. Two nights later, in a Roman barracks, the Lord stands by Paul and says, Take courage, for as you have testified to the facts about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome (23:11). The failed plan is the road. The arrest that the wise counsel produced is the passage to Caesar's household, and it is how Paul finally reaches the city he had been longing to preach in for years, at government expense, in chains. Wisdom is not a guarantee of outcomes; it never was. It is faithfulness in the choosing, and God takes responsibility for the rest.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the seven days were almost completed, the Jews from Asia, seeing him in the temple, stirred up the whole crowd and laid hands on him, crying out, 'Men of Israel, help! This is the man who is teaching everyone everywhere against the people and the law and this place. Moreover, he even brought Greeks into the temple and has defiled this holy place.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the seven days were almost completed, the Jews from Asia, seeing him in the temple, stirred up the whole crowd.

Almost completed. The plan was five or six days through a seven-day rite. Another day or two and Paul would have walked out of the temple with his name cleared in front of the whole city, and Acts would be a different book.

And notice who ends it. Not the Jerusalem Jews, who are the ones supposedly inflamed against him. The Jews from Asia — men from the province Paul had just spent three years working, in for the feast like everyone else. Ephesus is in Asia, and it was in Ephesus that some became stubborn and continued in unbelief, speaking evil of the Way before the congregation, so that Paul withdrew from the synagogue and took the disciples with him (19:9). Those men know his face. They know his companions' faces too, as the next verse will show. A three-year-old grievance from six hundred miles away bought a festival ticket, and it is standing in the court of the Gentiles when he walks past.

The verb Luke uses for what they do to the crowd (suncheo) is the one for throwing something into total confusion. They do not lodge a complaint with the temple authorities, who are standing right there. They work the crowd.

Then the charge, shouted: Men of Israel, help! This is the man who is teaching everyone everywhere against the people and the law and this place.

Now set that beside the charge sheet from earlier in this same book. False witnesses stood up against Stephen and said, This man never ceases to speak words against this holy place and the law... this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and will change the customs that Moses delivered to us (6:13–14). Against the people, the law, and this place. It is the same accusation, in the same city, in almost the same words.

And the young man standing at the edge of that first crowd, minding the coats of the men who threw the stones and approving of the execution, was Saul of Tarsus (7:58; 8:1).

He knows it, too. In three verses he will begin a speech from the barracks steps, and when he reaches the hardest part of it he will say to this crowd, when the blood of Stephen your witness was being shed, I myself was standing by and approving (22:20). The charge he once helped to prosecute is now the charge against him, brought by men doing exactly what he did, and he does not flinch from naming it. There is no revenge in this; God is not settling a score. It is something better — the persecutor has been so completely joined to the people he hunted that he now stands where they stood and hears his own words come back at him.

The last clause is the one that turns a shouting match into a death sentence. He even brought Greeks into the temple and has defiled this holy place.

The temple mount had an outer court that anyone could enter. Inside it, around the sacred precincts, ran a low stone barrier, and at each opening in it stood a notice in Greek and Latin. Two of those stones have been dug up — one complete, found in 1871 and now in Istanbul, and a fragment found in 1935. The wording is preserved: no foreigner is to pass within the barrier and enclosure around the sanctuary, and whoever is caught will have himself to blame for the death that follows. Josephus records that Rome, which reserved capital punishment jealously to itself, made this one exception and allowed the Jews to execute for it — even a Roman citizen.

So this is not an insult. It is a capital indictment, shouted in a crowded court, and every person who hears it knows that the law permits them to carry out the sentence on the spot. That is why the chapter goes from accusation to attempted murder inside two verses.

Hold on to that barrier, because of what happens next in Paul's own writing. The arrest that begins here becomes an imprisonment, and out of that imprisonment comes a letter to Ephesus — Trophimus's own city, the city these accusers came from — which says that Christ has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility, and that Gentiles who were once far off are now no longer strangers and aliens, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God (Eph. 2:14, 19). Whether or not Paul had this precise stone in mind when he wrote the words, he had stood in front of it, and he was arrested for allegedly breaching it. The wall the mob was defending had already been demolished by the cross; they simply had not been told. And the letter announcing the demolition was written from the chain their shouting produced.

And consider how that wall came down. Not by decree, not by a shift of policy in heaven, not by the slow erosion of an old rule that had outlived its usefulness. Christ broke it down in his flesh — Paul's phrase, and a violent one. The barrier that held the nations at a distance from the presence of God was not lifted off its footings and carried away. It was taken into a body and killed there, so that he might create in himself one new man in place of the two. Every Gentile who has ever drawn near to God has come in through a torn body and a poured-out life. And the stone with its warning notice sits in a museum in Istanbul under glass, an exhibit, out of work for two thousand years.

verseByVerse.quote: "For they had previously seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple. Then all the city was stirred up, and the people ran together. They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and at once the gates were shut."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They had previously seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple.

Luke stops the narrative to tell you that the charge is false and to show you, step by step, how it was manufactured. It is one of the most useful paragraphs in the New Testament for anybody who has ever been on either end of an accusation.

Take it apart. First, a true observation: they had seen Trophimus with Paul in the city. Perfectly accurate. Trophimus is a real man, an Ephesian, one of the seven delegates carrying the collection (20:4), and Paul really was walking around Jerusalem with him. These men were not hallucinating and they were not inventing.

Second, an inference: they supposed (enomizon) that Paul had taken him inside. Nobody saw it. No witness is produced then or at any of the four hearings that follow. The gap between what was seen in the street and what is alleged about the sanctuary is filled entirely by an assumption — a reasonable one, even, since a man who travels with Gentiles might well bring one to see the temple.

Third, certainty. By verse 28 the supposition has hardened into a shouted fact: he even brought Greeks into the temple. Note the plural. In the space of one verse, one man they think they saw has become Greeks.

Fourth, a crowd — and after that nothing can be undone, because a crowd cannot be shown evidence.

Here is the sobering thing, and it is the reason Luke bothers: not one of these men is lying. They believe it. They are sincerely defending the holiest place on earth from a defilement that never happened, and they will nearly kill an innocent man out of genuine reverence. Sincerity is not a safeguard. It never was.

So the test is a small one and it costs nothing. When you find yourself repeating something about somebody, stop and say out loud which part you saw and which part you supposed. Say the word supposed. It is astonishing how much of what we are certain about will not survive being spoken in that form.

Then verse 30, and the city goes up. Then all the city was stirred up, and the people ran together. The verb is the one for a physical shaking. People are running toward the noise from every direction, most of them with no idea what has happened — which is exactly the state the tribune will find them in at verse 34.

They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and at once the gates were shut.

The gate-shutting is the detail to sit with. The Levites on duty close the doors of the inner court, and they do it immediately. Part of the reason is crowd control. But part of it is this: a killing inside the sacred precincts would defile them, and so the man must be got outside before he is beaten to death. The doors are shut to keep the blood off the pavement. It is the same reflex as the men who would not enter the governor's headquarters lest they be defiled and unable to eat the Passover, on the morning they arranged a crucifixion (John 18:28) — meticulous about the floor, indifferent about the murder.

And there is a picture in it that Luke, who wrote a Gospel first, will not have missed. This is the last time Paul is ever recorded inside the temple. The final act of that building toward the apostle to the Gentiles is a door closing behind him. Within about a decade there will be no doors and no temple.

But those doors had already stopped being the way in. Luke had written, in his first volume, that as Jesus died the curtain of the temple was torn in two (Luke 23:45). While the priests were bolting the gates against one man, the way into the true holy place stood open — a new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh (Heb. 10:19–20). They shut Paul out of a building. They could not shut him out of the presence of God, and neither can anybody shut you out.

verseByVerse.quote: "And as they were seeking to kill him, word came to the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion. He at once took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. And when they saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as they were seeking to kill him, word came to the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion.

Not threatening to kill him. Seeking to. This is an execution in progress on the pavement of the outer court, being carried out by hand, and the only reason it does not finish is a piece of Roman administration.

The Antonia Fortress stood at the north-west corner of the temple platform, deliberately built to overlook it, with two flights of stairs running straight down into the outer court. Josephus records that at the great feasts a Roman guard was posted along the porticoes above the crowd, because Rome had learned that festivals and riots came as a pair. So there were soldiers already standing there, on duty, watching, for precisely this eventuality.

Which means that Paul is alive at the end of this verse because a pagan empire had a crowd-control policy and paid for the manpower to enforce it. God's rescues do not always come from the direction we are facing.

The tribune — chiliarchos, the commander of a cohort, something like a thousand men — is Claudius Lysias, though Luke will not give us his name until a letter reproduced in chapter 23 (23:26). We learn one other thing about him later: he had not been born a Roman citizen but had bought his citizenship for a large sum (22:28). He is a self-made provincial who purchased his way up, and God uses him to preserve the apostle to the nations.

He at once took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. Centurions, plural — at least two centuries, so two hundred men at the very least, probably more, and Luke says they ran. Down the stairs, into the court, at speed, in armour.

And when they saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.

Read that sentence slowly, because of what it does not say. They did not stop when someone's conscience woke up. They did not stop because a bystander appealed to the law, or because the temple authorities intervened, or because anyone remembered that no witness had been produced. They stopped when armed men appeared. That is the honest anthropology of Scripture about human beings in a mass: restraint arrives from outside, or it does not arrive.

Which is exactly why God gave the sword to the magistrate. Only a few months before this, wintering in Corinth, Paul had written a letter to Rome containing these words: he is God's servant for your good... he does not bear the sword in vain. For he is the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God's wrath on the wrongdoer (Rom. 13:4). The ink was barely dry. And now the doctrine comes down the fortress steps in hobnailed boots and saves the man who wrote it.

There is a quiet rebuke in the scene as well, and it should not be softened. Jerusalem contained tens of thousands of believers (v. 20). Not one of them appears in this paragraph. The church is nowhere; the pagan garrison is everything. Sometimes the help God sends is not the help we would have chosen, and it does not come from the people we would have expected, and it is still God who sent it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then the tribune came up and arrested him and ordered him to be bound with two chains. He inquired who he was and what he had done."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He ordered him to be bound with two chains.

Two chains means one wrist shackled to a soldier on either side. Luke has described that arrangement once before in this book: Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains (12:6). That night an angel came, the chains fell off Peter's hands, the iron gate opened by itself, and he walked out into the street.

Nothing of the kind happens here. Paul's chains stay on. He will wear them, in one custody or another, through the rest of Acts and to the end of the story.

Two men, the same words, the same God, opposite outcomes — and Luke reports both with the same steady voice, without a syllable of explanation or apology. That is one of the great honesties of Scripture. It refuses to teach us that faith produces release, and it equally refuses to teach us that suffering is the mark of the truly spiritual. It simply tells us that the Lord loosed one man's chains and left the other man's on, and that both of them were his.

Now follow one word backwards, because Luke has been laying a track. The verb here for binding is deo, and this is its fifth appearance in two chapters. At Miletus Paul said, I am going to Jerusalem, constrained by the Spirit — literally, bound in the Spirit (20:22). At Caesarea Agabus bound his own feet and hands, and said the Jews would bind the man who owned the belt (21:11). In the front room Paul said he was ready to be bound (21:13). And now the tribune orders him bound with two chains.

The Spirit's chain came first. By the time Rome puts iron on this man, he has been a bound man for months, and voluntarily. What Claudius Lysias does at the top of these steps does not make Paul a prisoner; it only ratifies, in metal, a captivity Paul had already accepted from God. That is why there is no panic in him, and no sense anywhere in the rest of the book that something has gone wrong.

It also explains the name he gives himself afterwards. Writing from custody he calls himself a prisoner of Christ Jesus (Eph. 3:1; Philem. 1, 9) and the prisoner of the Lord (Eph. 4:1). Not once, in any letter, does he describe himself as Caesar's prisoner. The chain changed owner the moment it was fastened.

The verse ends with the tribune's two questions: He inquired who he was and what he had done. Arrest first, investigate second — poor law, and here it saves a life. Those two questions open a legal process that will run through the Sanhedrin, two Roman governors, a Herodian king, an appeal to Caesar, a shipwreck and a rented house in Rome. Chapters 22 to 28 — a quarter of the book of Acts — are the answer to a soldier's routine enquiry at the top of a staircase.

And the belt is still lying somewhere back in Caesarea, in Philip's house, where a prophet used it a fortnight ago to show four young women and a doctor and a room full of weeping friends exactly what was going to happen.

verseByVerse.quote: "Some in the crowd were shouting one thing, some another. And as he could not learn the facts because of the uproar, he ordered him to be brought into the barracks. And when he came to the steps, he was actually carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some in the crowd were shouting one thing, some another.

Luke has written this sentence before. At Ephesus: Now some cried out one thing, some another, for the assembly was in confusion, and most of them did not know why they had come together (19:32). Two riots, two cities, two religions, one anatomy. A crowd can be entirely united in fury and completely unable to say what the charge is.

That is the standing signature of a mob, and it is worth knowing how to spot, because mobs have not gone out of fashion; they have only moved indoors and online. The test is not how many people are angry, or how certain they sound. The test is whether any two of them, asked separately, would give the same account of what the accused actually did.

And as he could not learn the facts because of the uproar. The tribune is trying to do his job. He wants a charge; he asks for one; and several thousand people cannot produce a single coherent answer between them. The first casualty of an outraged crowd is always the truth it believes itself to be defending.

So he gives up on the court and orders Paul into the barracks — into the fortress, out of reach.

Then verse 35, and it is the most physically humiliating sentence written about Paul anywhere in Scripture. When he came to the steps, he was actually carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd.

Carried is bastazo, the ordinary word for hefting a load. The press at the foot of the stairs is so violent that the soldiers cannot get their prisoner up the steps on his feet, so they lift him bodily — beaten, bleeding, clothes torn, hands chained — and haul him above the crowd like a piece of baggage. Luke's actually flags it as remarkable even to him. The greatest missionary in the history of the church goes up the last flight of stairs with his feet off the ground, held by four pagan soldiers, unable to help himself in any particular.

Some Christians will read that and recognise it immediately, because they are living in it. There are seasons in which you do not walk; you are carried — by other people's arms, in a direction you did not choose, to a place you would not have picked, with no say in any of it and no dignity left to protect. Luke does not treat that as a failure of faith. He treats it as a Tuesday afternoon in the life of a faithful man.

And notice whose arms they are. Not the church's. Roman soldiers, who thought they were suppressing a disturbance, were in fact carrying the word of God up a staircase — and in about thirty seconds their prisoner is going to ask them to stop at the top so that he can preach.

verseByVerse.quote: "for the mob of the people followed, crying out, 'Away with him!'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Away with him!

Two words in Greek: aire auton. Now open Luke's first volume, to the trial before Pilate: But they all cried out together, Away with this man! (Luke 23:18) — aire touton. Luke wrote both books for the same reader (1:1), and he knows perfectly well what he is doing. He has kept the cry until the last verse of the riot and then set it down without comment.

It is the fourth time in this chapter that he has laid the passion of Jesus underneath the arrest of Paul, and once you see the pattern you cannot unsee it. Agabus: the Jews will bind him and deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles (v. 11) — the exact phrase Jesus used of himself on the road to this city (Luke 18:32). The room at Caesarea: let the will of the Lord be done (v. 14) — Gethsemane (Luke 22:42). The charge in the temple: against the people, the law and this place (v. 28) — the accusation at the Lord's own trial and at Stephen's. And now the crowd's cry, word for word.

Be careful what we take from that, because a wrong step here would be serious. Paul is not a second saviour and Luke is not suggesting he is. Nothing Paul suffers atones for anybody. He is not carrying sin; he is carrying a message. The parallel is not redemptive but familial — it is the family likeness appearing in a son.

Jesus had said it plainly: A servant is not greater than his master. If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you (John 15:20). And he had said it about this man in particular, on the day he called him: I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name (9:16). That promise, made in a house in Damascus to a blind man nearly twenty-five years earlier, is being kept on this staircase.

Here is the part that searches us. Paul had asked for this. Writing later from prison, he set out what he wanted more than anything in the world: that I may know him and the power of his resurrection, and may share his sufferings, becoming like him in his death (Phil. 3:10). We are happy to pray the first half. The second half is being answered here, in the form of a mob screaming the same two words at him that they once screamed at his Lord.

We ask to be made like Jesus and are then surprised at the shape the answer takes. But there is only one Jesus to be made like, and he was despised and rejected, and the road he walked to glory went through a crowd exactly like this one. If we are given even a little of it, we are not being punished. We are being answered.

And when that cry was raised against him, he had the answer in his hand and would not use it. Twelve legions of angels were within call, and he said so, and then he let the sentence stand. Away with this man — and he went. Out of the city he had wept over, past the crowd he had come to save, carrying the beam of his own execution, and he did not open his mouth. The silence of the Lamb of God on that road was not weakness. It was the loudest thing that has ever happened in this world. Paul is walking a road his Master had already walked to the end, and the one difference is the one that matters: Paul was pulled out at the top of the stairs, and Christ was not, because there was nobody else who could go the whole way.

verseByVerse.quote: "As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks, he said to the tribune, 'May I say something to you?' And he said, 'Do you know Greek? Are you not the Egyptian, then, who recently stirred up a revolt and led the four thousand men of the Assassins out into the wilderness?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
May I say something to you?

Consider where that sentence is spoken. Paul is at the top of the barracks stairs, seconds from being swallowed by a Roman fortress. He has been beaten by a mob, chained between two soldiers, and carried up the last flight because he could not walk. And he turns to the officer and asks, in courteous, educated Greek, for permission to speak.

The tribune is astonished, and his astonishment is the whole comedy of the scene: Do you know Greek? He had assumed he was dragging an illiterate agitator out of a temple brawl. One well-formed sentence and his entire assessment of the man collapses.

Then he says what he had been assuming. Are you not the Egyptian, then, who recently stirred up a revolt and led the four thousand men of the Assassins out into the wilderness?

This is a real man and a recent manhunt. Josephus tells the story twice: a false prophet out of Egypt gathered a following in the wilderness, led them round to the Mount of Olives, and promised that at his command the walls of Jerusalem would collapse so that they could take the city. The governor Felix sent cavalry; the movement was cut to pieces; and the Egyptian himself escaped and was never caught. It had happened within the last two or three years, and the file was still open. So when an unidentified Greek-speaking man is pulled out of a temple riot, the tribune reaches for the obvious hypothesis.

Which tells you exactly what he thought he had in his hands, and explains the two chains. He believed he was holding a terrorist commander with four thousand armed men somewhere in the hills.

Now a word about Luke, because this verse is a small window onto whether his book can be trusted. Josephus gives two different accounts of the Egyptian's following: thirty thousand men in one work, and in the other a much smaller affair in which four hundred were killed and two hundred captured. Luke says four thousand, which is the sober figure, and he attaches to them the correct technical term — the sikarioi, the Assassins, named from the sica, the short curved dagger they carried under their cloaks, mingling with festival crowds to knife a man in the back and disappear into the throng before he fell. That is not a word a later writer, romancing about a period he never lived in, would happen to know. It is the vocabulary of somebody who was in Judea in those years and knew what the security services called the problem.

This is Luke's habit everywhere. He gets the ranks right — a proconsul on Cyprus, politarchs at Thessalonica, Asiarchs at Ephesus, a town clerk, and here a chiliarchos. He gets the harbours and the sailing seasons right. He records two other messianic risings without embroidering either of them, and puts the summary in Gamaliel's mouth rather than his own (5:36–37). The man who is this careful about the number of a rebel band is the same man who tells you that a tomb outside Jerusalem was empty on the third day, and he expects to be read the same way in both places.

And the mistaken identity is the opening God uses. Because the tribune has him wrong, he asks a question. Because he asks, Paul answers. Because Paul answers, the conversation begins that ends with permission to preach.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul replied, 'I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no obscure city. I beg you, permit me to speak to the people.' And when he had given him permission, Paul, standing on the steps, motioned with his hand to the people. And when there was a great hush, he addressed them in the Hebrew language, saying:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no obscure city.

That is a beautifully judged sentence. No obscure city is understatement of the kind an educated Greek speaker would recognise instantly as good manners and good breeding — and it happens to be true. Tarsus was a genuine university town; the geographer Strabo, writing a generation earlier, said its people so surpassed Athens and Alexandria in their zeal for learning that he scarcely knew how to describe it. In one clause Paul has told the tribune: I am not your Egyptian, I am a Jew, and I am a man of standing.

Far more striking is what he does not say. He does not say he is a Roman citizen.

He is. It is the single most powerful fact about him in that fortress, and it is worth a great deal — in the very next chapter, when the soldiers have stretched him out with the thongs for a flogging, he will produce it in one quiet question and the tribune will go pale (22:25–29). He is holding it. He is not asking to be rescued. He is asking for something else.

I beg you, permit me to speak to the people.

The people. Look at who that is. Ninety seconds ago they had him on the ground and were beating him to death. They are still packed at the foot of the stairs, still howling for his blood. A man with a legal trump card in his pocket, standing at the door of safety, uses his one request to ask if he can go back out and talk to them.

There is a test in that, and it is not a comfortable one. Name the people who have most recently hurt you. Then ask honestly what your instinct toward them is. A wall, or a hearing? Paul's whole life had been reorganised around one conviction — that his own people might yet be saved, and that he would take any beating and forgo any advantage to get one more sentence in front of them. I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers (Rom. 9:3). He meant it, and this staircase is the proof.

Permission is given. And then Luke slows everything down for the last picture of the chapter.

Paul, standing on the steps, motioned with his hand to the people. It is the orator's gesture, the one he had used in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch (13:16) and will use again in front of a king (26:1) — except that this hand is bruised and chained to a soldier.

And when there was a great hush. Thousands of people who were screaming for a lynching a moment before fall silent on a staircase because a beaten man lifted his hand. Luke lets the silence sit there in the sentence.

Then the last detail, and it is a courtesy: he addressed them in the Hebrew language. That is Aramaic, the language of the street and the kitchen and the bedtime story. He could have used Greek and been understood perfectly well. He chooses their mother tongue instead — and it lands, because chapter 22 opens by telling us that when they heard him speaking it, they became even more quiet (22:2). The last thing he does before he tells them about Jesus is honour them.

Now stand back and look at what the chapter has done. James's plan had failed. The vow had ended in a riot. The collection is not even mentioned. Paul is under arrest, in chains, beaten, and has just been carried up a flight of stairs like luggage. Every single thing he had arranged has come apart.

And by the last verse he is standing above the largest Jewish crowd he has addressed in years, in total silence, with official Roman permission, about to tell them how he met Jesus of Nazareth on the Damascus road.

He did not get the platform he asked God for. He got the barracks steps. Years later, from another cell, he wrote the sentence that explains this whole chapter: I want you to know, brothers, that what has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel (Phil. 1:12).

Luke ends the chapter with a colon. Nothing is finished; the page simply turns.

21.theology: The Will of God and the Path of Suffering. Acts 21 presents with unusual clarity the Reformed conviction that the will of God is not always comfortable, and that knowing it does not mean avoiding what it contains. Paul knows chains await. He goes anyway. His companions know Paul knows. They submit anyway. “Let the will of the Lord be done” is not fatalism — it is the active, willing submission of people who have learned that God’s purposes are worked out through suffering, not around it. This is the theology of Romans 8:28 embodied in a house in Caesarea: all things — including imprisonment, beatings, and the howling of a mob — work together for good for those who love God and are called according to his purpose. Paul’s chains will take him to Rome. God knew this. Paul submitted to it. Rome receives the gospel.
21.examples:
Then: A man walking knowingly toward chains, accompanied by weeping friends who have said everything they can say and now can only pray. A church in Jerusalem that receives the Gentile mission report with joy and then watches its guest arrested in the temple court. The will of the Lord, being done — at great cost, with great grief, toward a great purpose that none of them can yet see fully.

Now: The church in every age must learn the grammar of “let the will of the Lord be done.” It is learned most deeply in the moments when the will of the Lord leads into what we would not choose — illness, loss, rejection, persecution. Paul goes to Jerusalem not because it is easy or because he can see the outcome, but because the Spirit has said go and the Lord has said trust. This is the faith that follows a Lord who himself prayed “not my will, but yours.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A beaten man stands chained at the top of a Roman staircase, above the crowd that was killing him ten minutes ago, and asks for the floor. What he gives them is not a defence in any legal sense. It is his testimony — and it is aimed, sentence by sentence, at people who are exactly what he used to be.

The opening (vv. 1–2). He begins with Stephen's own opening line, brothers and fathers, and in Aramaic. The silence deepens: they had him down as a half-Greek from Tarsus, and the first three syllables kill the theory. That courtesy cost nothing and bought twenty verses of absolute quiet.

The credentials (vv. 3–5). Born in Tarsus, raised in this city, trained at the feet of Gamaliel — whose own advice to the council, that they might be found opposing God, his best student ignored. He grants the crowd their zeal as real, because it was his. Then the confession they will hear as a CV: he persecuted the Way to the death, men and women, with letters from the high priest and a plan to bring believers back in chains.

The road (vv. 6–11). At noon, when the Syrian sun is at its worst, a light that outshines it. The doubled name in Hebrew, and the question that founded half of Paul's theology — why are you persecuting me? Then the crux at v. 9: the men with him saw the light and did not understand the voice. They were inside the brightness and nothing happened to them. He who had always known what to do asks for orders, is given one step, and is led into Damascus by the hand — the man who came to lead others away in bonds.

Ananias (vv. 12–16). Introduced for this audience with Jewish credentials and, crucially, a good name among his unbelieving neighbours. He walks into the house where the man holding the warrants is sitting, and the first word the church ever says to Paul is brother. Then the commission from the God of our fathers, the title Paul first heard from Stephen — the Righteous One — and the call to be a witness to everyone, which slides past them unnoticed.

The temple and the sending (vv. 17–21). He tells a crowd that has accused him of defiling the temple that his commission was given him inside it, praying. He argues with the Lord and loses; he confesses that he held the coats at Stephen's execution; and the answer from heaven to that confession is not discipline but a commission — go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles.
verseByVerse.theology:
Sovereign Grace, and a Commission Older Than the Convert

Ananias's word for what God did to Saul is procheirizomai — appointed, designated beforehand — and Paul never forgot it, writing later that God had set me apart before I was born (Gal. 1:15). The light at noon was not God changing his mind about Saul of Tarsus. It was God keeping an appointment made before Saul existed. Nothing in the account belongs to the convert: Christ sought him, struck him down, named him in his mother tongue, blinded him, and told him what he would do. Paul did not find Jesus; Jesus took Paul.

Two guards keep this from being abstract. First, on the timing of the new birth Scripture is deliberately reticent, and we should be too — regeneration is the Spirit's secret work, known by its fruits and not by a stopwatch (see the note at vv. 9–10). Second, on wash away your sins (v. 16), the sign is spoken of in the language of the thing signified, as Scripture habitually does; the blood of Christ does the washing and baptism seals and publishes it, which is exactly how Paul afterwards handled circumcision as a seal of a righteousness already had by faith (Rom. 4:11).

And the chapter's summit is what grace does with a specific, named, unforgettable sin. The man who guarded the garments at Stephen's stoning is sent to the ends of the earth with Stephen's message. That is not grace overlooking a small thing. It is the blood of the Righteous One proving stronger than the blood that was shed.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A frightened disciple in Damascus was given the address of the man holding warrants for his arrest, and went. He knew his own name was probably on the list. He knocked, walked into the one house in the city where a Christian could be seized on the spot, and said two words before anything had been proved about the blind man sitting there: Brother Saul.

Now: Picture the person whose arrival in your church on Sunday would be hardest to absorb — not a stranger, but someone with a history, and a history with you. Somebody who did real damage and knew what they were doing. Now suppose the Lord has laid hold of them. How long, in practice, before anyone says brother, and means it, and stops watching the door? Ananias managed it in three days, before any evidence of change had been produced, because he understood that the church does not decide who its family is. It recognises whom the Lord has already taken in.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Brothers and fathers, hear the defense that I now make before you.' And when they heard that he was addressing them in the Hebrew language, they became even more quiet. And he said:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers and fathers, hear the defense that I now make before you.

Four words in, and he has already done something the crowd will not have expected. Brothers and fathers is not a formula Paul invented for the occasion. It is, word for word, how Stephen began his defence before the council (7:2) — and the young man holding the coats that day was Saul of Tarsus. He is opening his own trial with the dead man's opening line, and before he finishes he will say Stephen's name out loud (v. 20).

The word for defense is apologia, the term for a formal answer to a charge; it is the word behind our apologetics. And notice what Paul's apologia turns out to consist of. Not a rebuttal of the temple accusation. Not a legal argument, though he has a good one. Not a proof of the resurrection from Scripture, though he could give one. He tells them what happened to him. The most rigorously trained mind in the early church, given one chance to speak to the people who have just tried to kill him, gives his testimony.

Then verse 2, and Luke measures the room. When they heard that he was addressing them in the Hebrew language, they became even more quiet.

They were already quiet — chapter 21 ended with a great hush (21:40). Now the silence deepens. Luke's phrase is that they offered him still more quietness, as though the crowd were handing him something.

Why would the language do that? Because of what they had assumed about him. Paul was known as a Diaspora Jew, a man from Tarsus in Cilicia, and the standing suspicion about such men was that they had gone half Greek — that Jerusalem was a story to them rather than a home. Then he opens his mouth and out comes the Aramaic of the street and the kitchen, unaccented, fluent, native. Their whole theory about the man dies in the first three syllables. Whatever else he is, he is one of us, and he grew up here.

That courtesy cost Paul nothing and bought him twenty verses of absolute silence from a crowd that had been beating him to death ten minutes earlier. He could have insisted on Greek, which the tribune would have preferred and which every educated person present could follow. He chose the language they dream in.

There is a whole doctrine of communication in that choice, and it is not a technique. Paul is about to ask these people to hear the hardest thing they will ever hear. Before he does, he takes the trouble to speak to them as family, in their own tongue, on their own ground. The gospel does not need to be softened. But the man carrying it can decide whether he is going to make it as easy as possible to hear, or as hard.

verseByVerse.quote: "'I am a Jew, born in Tarsus in Cilicia, but brought up in this city, educated at the feet of Gamaliel according to the strict manner of the law of our fathers, being zealous for God as all of you are this day. I persecuted this Way to the death, binding and delivering to prison both men and women,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am a Jew, born in Tarsus in Cilicia, but brought up in this city, educated at the feet of Gamaliel.

Note the tense first. Not I was a Jew. I am. Twenty-five years after the Damascus road, in front of a crowd that has just accused him of apostasy, the first thing Paul says about himself is in the present tense. Nothing in what follows is a farewell to his people.

Then a standard rabbinic biography in three participles: born, brought up, educated. And the weight falls in the middle. Brought up in this city — this one, the one we are standing in. He is not answering the charge yet; he is dismantling the assumption underneath it, that he is an outsider legislating for Jerusalem from a distance.

At the feet of Gamaliel is literal. Pupils sat on the floor while the rabbi taught from a raised seat, and Paul is naming the most respected teacher of the age — Gamaliel the Elder, grandson of Hillel, a man this crowd revered.

And Luke has already introduced him to us. In chapter 5, when the council wanted the apostles dead, it was Gamaliel who stood up and said: leave them alone, for if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail; but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them. You might even be found opposing God (5:38–39).

Paul's own teacher had told the highest court in Israel to consider the possibility that this movement was from God. And his best student went out with warrants. It is possible to sit at the feet of a wise man for years, absorb his method, honour his name, and miss the one sentence he said that mattered.

According to the strict manner of the law of our fathers — the noun is akribeia, exactness, precision. This is the vocabulary he uses of himself in Philippians: as to the law, a Pharisee... as to righteousness under the law, blameless (Phil. 3:5–6). Whatever went wrong in Saul of Tarsus, it was not slackness.

Then the sentence that shows what kind of man is speaking: being zealous for God as all of you are this day.

He credits them. He does not say you think you are zealous, or your so-called zeal, or you are pretending. He looks at a mob that has just tried to lynch him and says, in effect: your zeal is real, and it is for God, and I know because it was mine. This is the same man who wrote of these same people, I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge (Rom. 10:2) — which is the kindest and the most devastating sentence ever written about religious sincerity, and he could write it because he had been the case study.

Here is a test worth running on your own arguments. Could you describe the people who are most wrong about Christ in words they would recognise and accept as fair? Paul can, and it is not a debating tactic. It is what a man sounds like when he remembers what he used to be.

And then, without a pause, verse 4: I persecuted this Way to the death, binding and delivering to prison both men and women.

To the death. Not to the courts, not to the point of inconvenience. And he adds a detail nobody asked for: men and women. He says it here, Luke said it of him at 8:3, and he said it himself again when he described dragging people off house by house. He keeps saying it because it is the detail that indicts him. A man making a real confession does not round the number down.

The dreadful thing about this paragraph is that his audience is hearing a curriculum vitae. He means it as a charge sheet. Both readings are accurate, and the gap between them is the whole speech.

verseByVerse.quote: "'as the high priest and the whole council of elders can bear witness. From them I received letters to the brothers, and I journeyed toward Damascus to take those also who were there and bring them in bonds to Jerusalem to be punished. As I was on my way and drew near to Damascus, about noon a great light from heaven suddenly shone around me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the high priest and the whole council of elders can bear witness.

Paul does something here that anyone inventing a story avoids: he names living witnesses who could contradict him. The high priest is in the city. The presbyterion — the whole body of elders — keeps records. He is telling a crowd that his account of his own past is checkable this afternoon, by men who have no reason to protect him.

From them I received letters to the brothers, and I journeyed toward Damascus.

Letters. That is the detail to sit with, because it is what makes Saul of Tarsus something worse than a hothead. Damascus lay outside Judea, well beyond the Sanhedrin's civil jurisdiction, and the only way to reach believers there was through the synagogues, by warrant and courtesy and correspondence. So Saul applied. Somebody drafted the documents. Somebody sealed them. A journey of a hundred and forty miles was funded and planned.

This was not a riot. It was a filing system. The worst things done to the church in this book are done on paper, in office hours, by men who believed they were serving God and kept proper records of it — which should make every religious institution, including ours, read this verse slowly.

And what were the letters for? To take those also who were there and bring them in bonds to Jerusalem to be punished. In bonds. Saul is travelling to Damascus in order to put chains on people. He is telling this story from inside a Roman chain, and one chapter ago Agabus tied his own hands with Paul's belt to show what was coming. Luke has been laying that thread since Miletus, and here is where it began: the man who set out to bind is bound.

Then verse 6, and everything stops. As I was on my way and drew near to Damascus, about noon a great light from heaven suddenly shone around me.

About noon. Chapter 9 does not mention the hour; Paul supplies it here, and again before Agrippa, where he adds that the light was brighter than the sun (26:13). He is not decorating. In Syria at midday in high summer the sun is directly overhead and merciless, and a traveller's eyes are already narrowed against it. Whatever it was that flashed around Saul on that road, it was not the low sun playing tricks at dawn, and it was not heat-shimmer, and it was not a dream — he was awake, on a road, at noon, on business. Paul names the hour because it closes every ordinary explanation before anyone can offer one.

There is a deeper thing in it too. God is light, and in him is no darkness at all (1 John 1:5). The man who believed he was defending the light of Israel against a blasphemous sect met the actual light on a public highway at the brightest hour of the day, and it put his eyes out.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?" And I answered, "Who are you, Lord?" And he said to me, "I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?

Take the doubled name first. When God says a name twice in Scripture it is never filler. Abraham, Abraham, with the knife raised (Gen. 22:11). Moses, Moses, at the bush (Ex. 3:4). Samuel, Samuel, in the dark (1 Sam. 3:10). Martha, Martha (Luke 10:41). Simon, Simon, Satan has demanded to have you (Luke 22:31). It is the address of someone who knows the person and means to stop them where they stand.

And it is the Hebrew form of the name — Saoul — spoken, as Paul tells Agrippa explicitly, in the Hebrew language (26:14). The risen and glorified Lord of heaven, speaking out of a light brighter than the noon sun, uses Aramaic. He addresses a man in his mother tongue.

Which is exactly what Paul is doing to this crowd as he tells them the story. He learned it from the Lord who did it to him.

Now the question itself, and it is one of the most theologically loaded sentences in the New Testament. Not why are you persecuting my people. Not why are you persecuting my church. Why are you persecuting me?

Jesus had been at the right hand of the Father for several years. Saul had never touched him, never met him, never been within a hundred miles of him in the flesh. And Jesus says: me. Every door Saul kicked in, every woman he dragged out, every prison sentence he arranged — those were laid on the body of the Lord of glory as personally as the nails.

This is the seed from which most of Paul's mature theology grows. He will spend his life writing that the church is the body of Christ, that we are members of one another, that no one ever hated his own flesh (1 Cor. 12:12–27; Eph. 5:29–30), that he fills up in his own flesh what is lacking in Christ's afflictions for the sake of the body (Col. 1:24). He did not construct that doctrine in a study. It was handed to him in one question on a road, and it cost him his sight.

Two things follow, and both are for us. If a believer in your congregation is being mistreated — overlooked, gossiped about, quietly frozen out — Christ takes it personally, and he does not grade the offence by how important the person is. And if you are the one suffering, note the comfort buried in the same sentence: you are not suffering alone, and you are not suffering unnoticed. Before Saul had finished the sentence, heaven had already registered every name.

Who are you, Lord? The word can mean no more than sir, and on Saul's lips at that instant it probably did. But you cannot ask that question of that light and keep the word small. The answer will fill it up.

I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting.

Now compare the tellings. In chapter 9 the answer is simply I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting (9:5), and before Agrippa it is the same (26:15). Only here, to a Jerusalem crowd, does Paul include the two extra words: of Nazareth.

He includes them because that is the name with the sneer in it. Nazareth was a nowhere village in the north, the place that prompted the question, can anything good come out of Nazareth? (John 1:46), and Nazarene was the label these very people used for the sect (24:5). The glorified Christ, blazing out of heaven, identifies himself to his persecutor by the name of his humiliation. He did not shed his humanity at the ascension and he is not embarrassed by the village. The man on the throne is the man from Nazareth, and he says so.

Consider him, then, on that road. He had every reason to announce himself by the titles that were now indisputably his — the Lord, the Son of God, the one seated at the right hand of the Majesty on high, before whom every knee will bow. He had been raised, and exalted, and glorified, and the light of him was too much for a man's eyes at noon. And out of that light he said: Jesus of Nazareth. The village name. The name that had been a joke. He kept it. He carries the marks of the nails still, and he answers to the name of the town they sneered at, and he will answer to it for ever. Heaven's glory has a carpenter's address, and the Lamb who was slain is not ashamed of a single scar.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Now those who were with me saw the light but did not understand the voice of the one who was speaking to me. And I said, "What shall I do, Lord?" And the Lord said to me, "Rise, and go into Damascus, and there you will be told all that is appointed for you to do."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now those who were with me saw the light but did not understand the voice of the one who was speaking to me.

This is the verse people bring to you as a contradiction, and it deserves a straight answer rather than a nervous one.

Set the two accounts side by side. Luke, narrating in chapter 9: the men who were travelling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one (9:7). Paul, testifying here: they saw the light but did not understand the voice. Hearing but not seeing; seeing but not understanding. Read carelessly, it looks like a straight collision.

Read carefully, it is two halves of one experience, and the older English versions obscured it. Take the seeing first: chapter 9 says they saw no one, and chapter 22 says they saw the light. Both are true at once, and neither is strained — there was a blaze of light that everyone on that road saw, and inside it a Person whom only Saul saw. Light yes; Person no.

Then the hearing, which is where the real work is. The Greek verb akouo can take its object in two different cases, and the distinction is a real one: at 9:7 it governs the sound as sound, while here it governs the voice as a message. That is why the ESV renders it did not understand — not a translator smoothing over an awkwardness, but the ordinary force of the words.

And you do not need any Greek at all to know the difference, because you have lived it. Stand next to somebody taking a phone call. You hear a voice perfectly well. You do not hear a single thing it says. Everyone on the Damascus road heard something. One man heard words.

Now stay with that, because the resolution is not the point. The point is the picture.

There were several men in that light. They all saw the same brightness. They all heard the same sound. They were close enough to catch Saul as he went down, and close enough afterwards to take him by the hand and walk him the rest of the way into Damascus. And nothing whatever happened to them. Not one of them is named. Not one of them is heard from again. They went to Damascus, delivered their blind chief to a lodging house, and presumably went home and told the story for the rest of their lives as the strangest thing they ever saw.

Proximity to revelation is not revelation. You can be inside the light and hear only weather. It is possible to sit in the same pew, under the same preaching, singing the same words, close enough to touch a man whom God is at that moment laying hold of, and hear a noise. He who has ears to hear, let him hear — and the reason that sentence is a warning rather than a truism is standing on the Damascus road holding Saul's arm.

Then verse 10, and Saul speaks a sentence he had never spoken before. What shall I do, Lord?

Here was a man who had known exactly what to do for years. He had a programme, a mandate, letters in his bag, a route, a list of names, and the full backing of the highest religious authority in the world. In one question all of it is handed over. He does not ask what has happened, or who else knows, or whether the letters are still valid. He asks for orders.

And look at the answer, because it is deliberately not enough. Rise, and go into Damascus, and there you will be told all that is appointed for you to do. Not the plan. Not the three missionary journeys, not the letters that will be read for twenty centuries, not Rome. Get up and walk into the city — the city he had come to raid — and wait to be told.

That is very nearly always the arrangement. God gives the next step and withholds the itinerary, and the withholding is not stinginess. If Saul had been handed his whole assignment on that road, including the shipwrecks and the beatings and the cell, he would have received it as information. Instead he received it as obedience, one instruction at a time, from a Lord he was learning to trust.

Was Paul already born again at this point? The honest answer is that we are not told, and we should not pretend to know what Scripture does not say. Luke narrates Paul's conversion as a connected whole — the blinding encounter on the road, three days of blindness and prayer (9:9, 11), then Ananias, the filling with the Spirit, and baptism (9:17–18; 22:16) — without putting a stopwatch on the exact instant of the new birth. That should not surprise us: regeneration is the Spirit's secret, invisible work, known with certainty only to God; we never observe the moment itself, only its fruits.

What we can observe is suggestive. By v. 10 Paul calls Jesus 'Lord,' surrenders his whole program, asks 'what shall I do?', obeys, and then spends three days in prayer (9:11, 'behold, he is praying') — all marks of a heart already being turned to Christ. And from a Reformed vantage, since the new birth is what produces faith and repentance, it is reasonable to think the Spirit's regenerating work was already underlying that genuine submission.

But we hold this loosely, because the same account locates the gift of the Spirit at Ananias's coming, and has Ananias say, 'rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name' (22:16) — language that warns us against fixing the moment too precisely. So: it is fair to say a converting work was plainly under way by v. 10; it is not fair to claim the text dates the new birth to this verse. We simply do not know the instant.

And here is the comfort in the honest uncertainty: what Scripture leaves unclear (the when) it more than makes up for in what it makes blazingly clear (the who). From first to last this is sovereign grace — Christ sought the persecutor, struck him down, named him, summoned him. Paul did not find Jesus; Jesus seized Paul. The exact timing of the new birth is God's secret; the source of it is no secret at all.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And since I could not see because of the brightness of that light, I was led by the hand by those who were with me, and came into Damascus. And one Ananias, a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since I could not see because of the brightness of that light, I was led by the hand by those who were with me, and came into Damascus.

Luke's word is cheiragogoumenos — led by the hand, the verb for guiding a small child or a blind beggar through a crowd.

Read that against the last thing Paul told us he was doing. He was on his way to Damascus to bring believers back in bonds, to lead men and women away helpless (v. 5). He arrives in Damascus led by the hand, helpless, unable to find a door. He had come to make people dependent and he entered the city more dependent than any of them.

And he stayed that way for three days. Chapter 9 fills in what these verses pass over: three days without sight, without food or drink, in a stranger's house, praying (9:9, 11). Everything Saul had ever relied on — his learning, his warrants, his standing, his certainty — was taken off him in an afternoon, and what was left sat in the dark and prayed.

Then a man arrives, and watch how Paul introduces him to this particular audience.

And one Ananias, a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there.

When Luke introduced the same man in chapter 9 he called him simply a disciple at Damascus (9:10). Paul, standing in front of a Jerusalem crowd that believes he abandoned Moses, gives a different set of credentials: devout, law-observant, and — this is the phrase that matters — well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there. Not well spoken of by the church. By the synagogue. By the neighbours who did not share his faith.

Paul is telling them that the man who received him into the Way was not some renegade on the fringe. If you had asked the Jewish community of Damascus about Ananias, they would have given him a good character.

Two things worth taking from that. The first is how carefully Paul is shaping his testimony for the room he is in. The story is the same story every time he tells it, but before a king in chapter 26 he leaves Ananias out altogether, because a provincial holy man means nothing to Agrippa; here he makes him the pivot, because to this crowd he means everything. Truthful preaching is not the same as identical preaching.

The second is the standard Paul reaches for. The qualification he cites is not Ananias's gifting or his courage or his visions, all of which he had. It is his reputation among people outside the church. Paul will later write that an overseer must be well thought of by outsiders (1 Tim. 3:7), and here is where he learned it: the first Christian ever to lay hands on him was a man whose unbelieving neighbours had nothing bad to say about him.

verseByVerse.quote: "'came to me, and standing by me said to me, "Brother Saul, receive your sight." And at that very hour I received my sight and saw him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brother Saul, receive your sight.

Two words. They are the first words the church of Jesus Christ ever addressed to the apostle Paul, and they are worth standing still for.

Consider what it took to say them. Chapter 9 records what Ananias said when the Lord first gave him the address: Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem. And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name (9:13–14). Ananias knew precisely who was sitting in that house. He knew about the letters. He knew his own name was very likely on them, along with every other name he could have given under questioning. To knock on that door was to walk into the one place in Damascus where a Christian could be arrested on the spot, and to identify himself as exactly the kind of man the warrants were drawn against.

He came anyway. And the first thing out of his mouth was not a caution, not a condition, not an interview, not a probationary period. Brother.

Think about the last Christian voice Saul had heard. On present evidence it was Stephen's, in a pit outside Jerusalem, praying for the men who were killing him while Saul stood at the edge of the coats and approved. That is the church's last word to him: a dying man asking God not to hold it against them. And the next word the church says to him, three days into his blindness, is brother.

Between those two words there is no negotiation, no restitution, no proving period. Ananias calls him brother because the risen Christ has claimed him, and that settles the matter. The church does not decide who its family is; it recognises who the Lord has already taken in.

Here is the test, and it is not a comfortable one. Picture the person whose arrival in your congregation on Sunday morning would be hardest to absorb — not a stranger, but someone with a history, and specifically a history with you. Somebody who did damage, and to your people, and knew what they were doing. Now imagine the Lord has laid hold of them. How long, in practice, before anyone in the room says brother, and means it, and stops watching the door?

Ananias did it in three days, to the man who had come to arrest him, and he did it first, before any evidence of change had been produced.

And at that very hour I received my sight and saw him.

The healing is instant, and Luke's detail is that the first thing Saul's restored eyes rest on is the face of a man he had come to Damascus to put in chains. He is looking at his intended victim, and his intended victim is calling him family.

He had been blind for three days. He had been blind for a good deal longer than that — a man of formidable learning who could not see the thing at the centre of his own Scriptures. Both blindnesses ended in the same room, and a devout, ordinary, frightened, obedient disciple was the instrument of it.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And he said, "The God of our fathers appointed you to know his will, to see the Righteous One and to hear a voice from his mouth; for you will be a witness for him to everyone of what you have seen and heard."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God of our fathers appointed you to know his will, to see the Righteous One and to hear a voice from his mouth.

The God of our fathers. Ananias's first phrase, and Paul repeats it to this crowd because it is the hinge of his whole defence. No new deity has entered the story. This is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob — the phrase Peter used at Solomon's Portico (3:13), the phrase Peter used before the council (5:30), the phrase Stephen used at the bush (7:32). The charge against Paul is apostasy. His answer is that the God who commissioned him is the one his accusers were named after.

Appointed you translates procheirizomai, to designate beforehand, to have chosen and set aside in advance. Ananias uses it of what happened before the road, not on it. Paul evidently never forgot the word; writing to Galatia he says God had set me apart before I was born, and who called me by his grace (Gal. 1:15). The light at noon was not God changing his mind about Saul of Tarsus. It was God keeping an appointment made before Saul existed — which is worth knowing if your own conversion looked, from the inside, like an accident.

Then three things he is appointed to: to know his will, to see the Righteous One, to hear a voice from his mouth.

The Righteous One is a title, and Paul had heard it before. Peter used it in the temple: you denied the Holy and Righteous One (3:14). And Stephen used it in the last speech of his life, in the sentence that got him killed: they killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, whom you have now betrayed and murdered (7:52).

Saul heard him say it. He was standing right there. That title went into his ears from a dying man he was helping to execute, and the next time he heard it, it was being applied to the person who had just spoken to him from heaven. Grace is not tidy about how it gets a word into a man.

To see and to hear — those two verbs are the foundation of everything Paul will later claim for himself. Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? (1 Cor. 9:1). Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me (1 Cor. 15:8). His authority does not rest on his intellect, his zeal, or his results. It rests on the fact that he saw the risen Christ with his own eyes and heard him speak, which is precisely what an apostle is.

Then the commission, verse 15: you will be a witness for him to everyone of what you have seen and heard.

A witness — martys, the word that will come to mean martyr, and will mean it partly because of the man Paul watched die. A witness in any court is not asked what he thinks, or what he finds meaningful, or what the evidence might suggest. He is asked what he saw and heard. That is the whole job, and it is why the least articulate Christian in your church can do it: nobody is going to cross-examine you on systematic theology, and if they do you may say you do not know. What you saw and heard is yours to give.

And now listen very carefully to one word, because Paul is being deliberate and the crowd has not noticed yet. A witness to everyone. To all men. Not a syllable about Gentiles — not yet. The scope is already total, and he has said it in the widest, softest, most unobjectionable form available, and they let it go by without a murmur.

He will say it once more, six verses from now, in the word they cannot bear. He is telling them the same thing twice: once so that they can hear it, and once so that they cannot.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now why do you wait? Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name.' When I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now why do you wait? Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name.

This is one of the sentences people are handed when someone wants to persuade them that the water itself does the saving, so it needs answering carefully — and Old Joe deserves the answer in plain words, not a shrug.

Start with what the sentence does not say. It does not say the water washes. It says four things at once, and they are bound together: get up, be baptized, wash away your sins, calling on his name. That last clause is not decoration; grammatically it is what the whole sentence hangs on. The washing happens in the calling.

Then let Scripture interpret Scripture, and notice that our best interpreter here is the man who obeyed this very command. If anybody ever had reason to believe that his sins went down a Damascus drain, it was Saul of Tarsus. What did he write afterwards?

He wrote that Abraham received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised (Rom. 4:11) — the sign stamps and certifies a righteousness the man already had; it does not manufacture it. He wrote, Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel (1 Cor. 1:17), which is an impossible sentence for a man who thought baptism washed sins away. And he told the Corinthians he could barely remember whom he had baptized (1 Cor. 1:14–16), which is not how anyone speaks about the thing that saves.

Luke's own book settles it too. In Cornelius's front room the Holy Spirit fell on a household of Gentiles while Peter was still talking, and only afterwards did anybody fetch water (10:44–48). The Spirit did not wait for the ceremony. And the dying thief, who could not have been baptized if he had wanted to be, was told today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43).

So what is Ananias actually saying? Scripture habitually speaks of the sign in the language of the thing signified, because God does not intend the two to be pulled apart. Baptism is the God-appointed sign and seal of a washing that only the blood of Christ performs — and to be baptized is to be publicly, visibly, irreversibly attached to the One who did the washing. Ananias is not telling Saul how to get clean. He is telling a man who has been made clean to go and say so, out loud, in water, in front of witnesses.

Which is where the urgency comes from, and it is pastoral rather than panicked. Why do you wait? is not a warning that Saul's soul is in danger for another hour. It is a man saying: you have sat in this dark room for three days. That is long enough. Stop being a secret.

And it was costly. For a Pharisee trained under Gamaliel, submitting to the rite that the Way used was the point of no return — the moment his old world could no longer pretend he was on loan to the other side.

Here is the test, and it is worth running honestly. Is there anything in your following of Christ that you have kept unofficial? Not unbelieved — unannounced. A faith that your colleagues have never had to notice, a repentance nobody has been told about, an obedience still pending because going public would cost something. Ananias's question is the whole of the application: why do you wait?

And look what is underneath the whole exchange. Saul's sins were not small ones and they were not vague. He had specific names in his memory, faces of specific people whose doors he had broken, and Stephen's blood, and now he is told the whole account can be washed. Not managed. Not offset by a life of service. Washed — the word for scrubbing a thing until the stain is gone and cannot be found.

That is what the blood of Jesus Christ does. It does not negotiate with sin, or reduce the sentence, or file it somewhere it will not be noticed. It removes it. The man who guarded the coats at a murder was made as clean as if he had never touched them, and he was made that clean in an afternoon, by the blood of the very Righteous One whose people he had been hunting. There is nothing in the universe like that blood. It has never yet met a stain it could not lift, and it never will.

Then verse 17, and Paul moves the story to a place his accusers will not expect. When I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance.

Read that in front of this particular crowd. He is on trial for defiling the temple. And he tells them that his commission — the one they are about to riot over — was given to him inside that building, on his knees, praying. Not in Damascus. Not among Gentiles. In the temple, in the middle of Jewish devotion, doing exactly what a devout Jew does.

It is the most disarming thing he could possibly have said, and it is also simply true. The God they think he has abandoned met him in their own house.

verseByVerse.quote: "'and saw him saying to me, "Make haste and get out of Jerusalem quickly, for they will not accept your testimony about me." And I said, "Lord, they themselves know that in one synagogue after another I imprisoned and beat those who believed in you."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Make haste and get out of Jerusalem quickly, for they will not accept your testimony about me.

The Lord's instruction is blunt, and it is negative: they will not have it, so go.

And Paul argues.

That is worth registering before anything else, because it is not what we expect from a man in a trance in the temple. He does not fall on his face and say yes. He puts a case: Lord, they themselves know that in one synagogue after another I imprisoned and beat those who believed in you.

And it is a good case. It may be the best case anyone could make. His argument is that his testimony is uniquely credible in this city and nowhere else — because in this city they know what he was. Anywhere in the empire, a preacher claiming that Jesus rose is a man making a claim. In Jerusalem, the man saying it is the man they hired to stop it. They have the paperwork. They know his teacher's name. They watched him leave for Damascus with warrants. If a change of that magnitude, in that man, in front of the people who commissioned him, will not persuade them, what possibly could?

The Lord says no.

Now hold on to that, because this is one of the great uncomfortable passages about guidance, and it does not resolve the way we would like. Paul's reasoning is not carnal. He is not asking to stay because Jerusalem is comfortable — it is the single most dangerous city on earth for him, and he knows it. He is not being lazy or cowardly or self-serving. He is offering the Lord the most strategically intelligent deployment of his own conversion, and the answer is get out, quickly.

So the no is not a verdict on the quality of the plan. Sometimes God's refusal has nothing to do with whether your reasoning was sound. It is simply that he has a different map, and it is a larger one, and you are not being shown it.

There is an ache in this that most Christians know and few say out loud: the ache of the good thing you were not permitted to do. The ministry you were plainly suited for and were not given. The person you were sure you could reach, whom God moved you away from. The place where your particular history would have counted for something, and where the door shut. Paul stood in the temple and made that argument to the face of the Lord Jesus Christ, and was told to leave.

And watch where the refusal took him. Out of Jerusalem, to Tarsus, to Antioch, to Cyprus, Galatia, Macedonia, Achaia, Asia — and eventually, with a chain on, to Rome. The whole Gentile mission is downstream of a no that Paul argued against.

One more thing to notice, and it makes this speech more remarkable than it first appears. What Paul is doing right now, on the barracks steps, is making that exact argument. He has told this crowd about Gamaliel, about the letters, about the imprisoning and the beating — his entire case is the one he put to the Lord in the trance, being tried out at last in front of the very audience the Lord said would not accept it. Twenty-five years later, the experiment is finally being run. Three verses from now we find out who was right.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And when the blood of Stephen your witness was being shed, I myself was standing by and approving and watching over the garments of those who killed him.' And he said to me, "Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the blood of Stephen your witness was being shed, I myself was standing by and approving and watching over the garments of those who killed him.

He is still arguing his case to the Lord — and this is the evidence he offers. Not his training. Not his zeal. The worst thing he ever did.

Luke gives three participles and Paul does not soften one of them. He was standing by: present, close enough to see it. He was approving: not swept along, not appalled and silent — in agreement.
