Nothing in this section is miraculous, and that is the theological point. The God who opened the Philippian jail with an earthquake here uses a boy's ears, an officer's fear of a court-martial, a standard troop deployment, and a piece of self-serving correspondence. Scripture is entirely comfortable with both, and Christians who will only recognise God's hand in the spectacular will miss most of what he does.

Two guards keep this from turning into fatalism. First, providence does not excuse the wickedness it employs: the chief priests who agreed to supply the pretext for a murder are guilty of it, and Lysias's falsified report is a lie, and Luke's silence is not approval. Second, providence does not promise comfort. This chapter's happy ending is a two-year detention under a governor angling for a bribe. God's certain purposes and a believer's real losses run down the same road, at the same time, and Scripture never asks anyone to pretend otherwise.

The pattern is Joseph's: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Gen. 50:20). The forty men were, without knowing it, working for the One they were trying to thwart — and so was the empire, which spent a great deal of money that night keeping alive a man it would one day execute.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The tribune's letter told the governor a true story arranged to flatter its author. He did not invent a single fact. He moved one clause — putting the discovery of Paul's citizenship before the rescue instead of after it — and let his superior draw a generous conclusion. Luke set the letter down beside the events of the previous chapter and left it there.

Now: Take the story you tell most often about a hard episode — why the job ended, why the friendship cooled, how the argument went. You have told it enough times that it runs smoothly now. Every detail in it probably happened. Then lay it beside a transcript, the way Luke lays this letter beside chapter 22, and ask the narrower question: is the sequence right, and is the motive you imply the motive you actually had? Most of us are not liars. Most of us are editors, and the edit is nearly always in our own favour.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then he called two of the centurions and said, 'Get ready two hundred soldiers, with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen to go as far as Caesarea at the third hour of the night. Also provide mounts for Paul to ride and bring him safely to Felix the governor.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Get ready two hundred soldiers, with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen to go as far as Caesarea at the third hour of the night.

Do the arithmetic, because Luke expects it. Two hundred legionaries, seventy cavalry, two hundred light troops: four hundred and seventy armed men, moving out at nine o'clock at night, to escort one prisoner sixty miles.

That is very close to half the entire Jerusalem garrison. A cohort was nominally a thousand men, and the tribune has just committed most of his infantry and all of his usable cavalry to a single overnight transfer, leaving the Antonia thin in a city that has rioted twice in three days. No commander does that lightly.

He does it for two reasons, and Luke lets both stand. The threat is real — forty men who have sworn to die trying. And the tribune's own neck is on the line, because he has already unlawfully chained a Roman citizen and a dead one in his custody would finish him.

The word for the third group, dexiolaboi, is so rare that its meaning is genuinely uncertain; it seems to mean something like right-hand-men, and it is usually taken as light-armed troops or spearmen. Luke reaches for an unusual military term because he is reporting an unusual deployment.

Now set the numbers against the promise, because this is the point of the passage.

Twenty-four hours ago the Lord said: you must testify also in Rome. Here is what that promise looked like when it started to be kept. No angel. No earthquake — the God who once opened the doors of a Philippian jail with one (16:26) does nothing of the kind here. No blinding of the enemy. Just a worried middle-ranking officer filling out a duty roster and detailing four hundred and seventy men who were on the payroll anyway.

God's protection of his servants almost never arrives in the form we would have designed. It comes as a rota, a phone call, a colleague who happens to owe someone a favour, a bureaucratic rule that turns out to work in your favour. The empire spent a very large amount of military resource that night keeping alive a man it would one day execute, and it did so because a nervous officer was covering himself.

Also provide mounts for Paul to ride and bring him safely to Felix the governor.

Mounts, plural — spare horses, so the pace never has to drop. And the verb translated bring him safely is diasozo, which means to bring through danger to safety; Luke will use it again of every soul reaching land from the wreck (27:44; 28:1).

The tribune wants his prisoner delivered alive to a governor. The Lord wants his witness delivered alive to Caesar. For one night those two intentions run on exactly the same road, and only one of them knows the destination.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he wrote a letter to this effect: 'Claudius Lysias, to his Excellency the governor Felix, greetings.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Claudius Lysias, to his Excellency the governor Felix, greetings.

The commander finally gets a name, and it is the name he bought. We learned in the previous chapter that he acquired his citizenship for a large sum (22:28); Lysias is the Greek name his parents gave him, and Claudius is the emperor's, taken when he was enrolled. His own signature is a receipt.

Luke reproduces the letter in proper form — sender, recipient, greeting — and it is worth pausing on the fact that he has it at all. A prisoner does not normally read his own escort's covering dispatch. Paul may have heard it read out at the hearing; the contents would have been disclosed at trial. Either way, Luke is doing what a careful historian does and giving his reader the document.

And a word about the man it is addressed to, because Felix will hold Paul for the next two years and Old Joe should know who he was.

Antonius Felix was a freed slave. His brother Pallas was the powerful freedman-secretary of the emperor Claudius, and it was that connection, not merit, that lifted Felix to the governorship of Judea — an almost unheard-of appointment for a former slave. He was cruel, corrupt and grasping, and he put down disturbances with a brutality that made things worse. The Roman historian Tacitus summed him up in a line that has never been bettered: he exercised the power of a king with the temperament of a slave.

He is also, at this moment, married to Drusilla — a Jewish princess, daughter of the Herod Agrippa who killed James, whom Felix had persuaded to leave her husband. She will appear in the next chapter, sitting beside him while Paul reasons about self-control and the judgment to come (24:24–25).

That is the man Paul is being sent to. Not a neutral magistrate — a bought official with a stolen wife and a bad record, who will keep an innocent man in custody for two years hoping for a bribe (24:26).

And it is into that man's jurisdiction that the Lord Jesus Christ is delivering his apostle, on purpose, under armed guard, at nine o'clock at night.

verseByVerse.quote: "'This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them when I came upon them with the soldiers and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman citizen.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them when I came upon them with the soldiers and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman citizen.

Every word of that is true, and the sentence as a whole is a lie.

It is worth laying the letter against the record, because Luke has just given us the record in detail and plainly intends us to check.

What the letter says: I discovered he was a Roman citizen, and so I intervened to rescue him.

What actually happened: he intervened because a riot was in progress and riots are a tribune's problem (21:31–32). He then arrested Paul, had him bound with two chains, and ordered him stretched out and interrogated under the scourge. He learned about the citizenship at the last possible second, from Paul himself, tied to the post — and his reaction was not satisfaction at having rescued a citizen but fear at having chained one (22:25–29).

The letter reverses the order of events, and in doing so it converts a near-catastrophe into a commendation. The tribune has written himself a promotion.

Notice how small the lie is, and how ordinary. He does not invent anything. He simply moves one clause and lets the reader assume a motive. It is exactly the kind of thing an anxious professional does with a report that will be read by his superior — a light touch on the sequence, nothing anyone could ever prove.

Two things follow, and they pull in opposite directions.

The first is about Luke. He includes it, and says nothing. No indignation, no aside about pagan dishonesty. He records the official document and trusts the reader who has just read chapter 22 to notice the seam. That is the behaviour of an honest historian, and it is one of the quiet reasons to trust him: a man inventing a case for Paul does not leave discrepancies lying about in his own evidence.

The second is a mirror, and it is not comfortable. The tribune's account of his week is accurate in every detail and false in its effect. He has arranged true facts so that they flatter him.

Most of us are fluent in this. It is the version of the argument you give to a friend, in which everything you report actually happened. It is the sentence about a colleague that is technically correct. It is the account of why the relationship ended, or why the job was left, in which nothing is fabricated and the shape is still wrong.

Here is the test. Take the story you have told most often about a difficult episode in your life — the one you have told enough times that it has smoothed out. Now imagine it laid beside a transcript, the way Luke has laid this letter beside chapter 22. Is the sequence right? Is the motive you have implied the motive you actually had? Or have you, like Claudius Lysias, moved one clause and let people draw the kind conclusion?

verseByVerse.quote: "'And desiring to know the charge for which they were accusing him, I brought him down to their council. I found that he was being accused about questions of their law, but charged with nothing deserving death or imprisonment.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I found that he was being accused about questions of their law, but charged with nothing deserving death or imprisonment.

That sentence is the reason Luke includes the letter, and it is the second of four Roman verdicts on Paul that run through the rest of Acts.

The tribune could not learn the facts because of the uproar (21:34); now, having tried, his official finding is that there is no crime here. Festus will tell Agrippa that the accusers brought no charge in his case of such evils as I supposed (25:18) and will admit it is unreasonable to send on a prisoner without indicating the charges (25:27). Agrippa's verdict is the plainest of all: this man could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar (26:32).

Four officials, four examinations, four times nothing. Luke is building a legal case in the pages of a history book, and he never once tells the reader what to conclude.

But look at the first half of the tribune's finding, because it is more revealing than the second: questions of their law.

That is what the empire saw. A Roman officer sat in that chamber, watched the supreme court of Israel tear itself in half, listened to a man on trial say that his whole case turned on the resurrection of the dead — and filed it as a technical dispute about Jewish religious regulations. Not dangerous. Not interesting. A local matter.

He was looking directly at the most important claim ever made in human history and could not see it. The empire that would eventually kill both Paul and Peter, that would burn Christians in gardens as lamps, began by finding the whole thing beneath its notice.

And that is worth holding still for a moment, because it is what the world has largely done ever since.

The resurrection of Jesus Christ is either the hinge on which everything turns or it is nothing at all, and the one thing it cannot be is a question of religious law. If a crucified Jew walked out of a tomb in Jerusalem, then death has been beaten on its own ground, and every grave in every churchyard is provisional, and the man on that throne holds the keys of Death and Hades. Claudius Lysias had that in front of him, in writing, in his own report, and he called it a local dispute — and the God who raised his Son from the dead used the report anyway, and sent it on, and got his witness one stage nearer Rome. He is not hurried by being underestimated. He has never needed the world's assessment of what he is doing in order to do it.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And when it was disclosed to me that there would be a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once, ordering his accusers also to state before you what they have against him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when it was disclosed to me that there would be a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once, ordering his accusers also to state before you what they have against him.

The last line of the letter does two things, and the second is the one that matters.

First, it puts the assassination plot on the official record. From this moment the conspiracy is not a rumour but a documented fact in the provincial archive, and Paul's accusers must proceed knowing that the governor has it in writing.

Second — and this is the hinge — it moves the venue. The tribune orders the accusers to state their case before you. With one administrative sentence, the trial of Paul is lifted out of Jerusalem and out of the Sanhedrin's reach, and placed in a Roman provincial court.

Follow what that unlocks. In Caesarea, Paul stands before Felix, then before Festus. Before Festus he does the thing no man could do in the Sanhedrin: I appeal to Caesar (25:11). And the appeal of a Roman citizen is not a request. It is a right, and it compels the state to transport him, at its own expense, under guard, to Rome.

Now put that beside the forty men.

They swore an oath to stop Paul, and they went to the chief priests, and the chief priests agreed to help, and the whole apparatus of the plot produced exactly one result: it frightened a Roman officer into transferring Paul to a jurisdiction from which he could appeal to the emperor.

The plot to prevent Paul reaching Rome is the mechanism by which Paul reaches Rome.

This is not a coincidence Luke stumbled on; it is his theology of history and he has shown it before. The scattering meant to destroy the church spread it (8:1–4). The stoning of Stephen produced Saul's conversion. The imprisonment at Philippi converted the jailer. Joseph said it first and said it best: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Gen. 50:20).

The comfort in that is not that opposition will fail to hurt. Paul spends two years in a cell as a direct result of this letter, and hurt is exactly what it is. The comfort is that opposition cannot get outside God's use of it. There is no hostile act available to your enemies that God has not already assigned a purpose to. The forty men were, without knowing it, working for him.

verseByVerse.quote: "So the soldiers, according to their instructions, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris. And on the next day they returned to the barracks, letting the horsemen go on with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the soldiers, according to their instructions, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris.

Look at the map for a moment, because the logistics are the point.

From Jerusalem the road drops out of the hill country through a series of narrow defiles and wadis — perfect ambush country, where forty men with knives could stop a column and where cavalry is close to useless. It then comes out onto the flat coastal plain at Antipatris, a town Herod the Great built and named for his father, roughly thirty-five miles from Jerusalem.

Thirty-five miles is a punishing forced march in the dark. They set out at nine at night and they do not stop, because the whole plan depends on being clear of the hills by daylight. Once on the plain, an ambush is no longer feasible: there is nowhere to hide, and seventy horsemen can outrun anything on foot.

Which is exactly why the next verse reads as it does. On the next day they returned to the barracks, letting the horsemen go on with him. The infantry turns round the moment the danger is behind them and marches back to a city that is short of troops. The cavalry takes Paul the remaining twenty-five miles to Caesarea at speed.

It is a professional, well-judged operation, and Luke describes it with the flat precision of a man reporting facts he has checked.

And that flatness is worth noticing, because of what it is describing. This is the night God kept his promise. The sentence spoken in a cell — you must testify also in Rome — is being carried out at this moment by four hundred and seventy men on a road in the dark, most of them tired, none of them praying, all of them simply doing their job.

There is no shining in this passage. No one senses anything. The Lord who stood beside Paul two nights ago is nowhere named in these verses, and he is doing everything in them.

That is worth keeping when you are in the middle of a stretch of life that feels entirely ordinary and entirely unaccompanied. The night march is not the gap between the promise and its fulfilment. The night march is the fulfilment, in progress, unfelt.

verseByVerse.quote: "When they had come to Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they presented Paul also before him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had come to Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they presented Paul also before him.

The order is correct and bureaucratic: paperwork first, then the man. Roman custody is a chain of documented handovers, and Luke, who has been recording this case like a court reporter, records the handover too.

Paul has been in Caesarea before. He passed through it on the way up, and stayed in the house of Philip the evangelist, whose four daughters prophesied, and it was there that Agabus took his belt and bound his own hands and feet (21:8–11). Everything Agabus said would happen has now happened. He has been bound by the Jews in Jerusalem and delivered into the hands of the Gentiles, and he is back in the same coastal city, in chains, precisely as predicted.

He will not leave it for two years.

Meanwhile, sixty miles away, forty men are still waiting. Somewhere on a Jerusalem street the ambush party is holding its position for a prisoner who has been gone since the previous night — hungry, under an oath they cannot keep, watching a road nobody is coming down.

Luke never tells us what became of them. He does not need to. He has simply placed the last sentence about the conspirators (they are ready, waiting for your consent) two dozen verses before this one, and left them there, waiting for a consent that never came.

The assassination plot has failed completely, and the men who swore it will never know why.

There is one more thing in this handover worth naming, and it is easy to miss because Luke states it so drily.

Paul is now, formally and finally, out of Jewish jurisdiction. From this verse to the end of the book he will be tried by Romans, guarded by Romans, transported by Romans, and shipwrecked with Romans. The men who wanted him dead will have to travel to Caesarea and argue their case in a Gentile court under Gentile rules, and they will lose.

The council that could not reach a verdict has permanently lost the power to reach one. The high priest who had him struck in the mouth will next appear as a plaintiff, having to come down from Jerusalem in person and hire a professional advocate to make his case (24:1) — and the advocate will lose too.

A week ago Paul walked into Jerusalem hoping to be welcomed by the church and heard by his own people. He leaves it under armed guard at night, having been rejected by both. It is a real loss and Luke does not dress it up.

But the door that shut behind him in the temple (21:30) has turned out to be a door he was meant to be on the other side of.

verseByVerse.quote: "On reading the letter, he asked what province he was from. And when he learned that he was from Cilicia, he said, 'I will give you a hearing when your accusers arrive.' And he commanded him to be guarded in Herod's praetorium."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On reading the letter, he asked what province he was from.

Felix's first question is not about God, or the resurrection, or even about the riot. It is a jurisdictional check: which province? He is establishing whether this case is legally his.

The answer — Cilicia — technically opens the possibility of transferring Paul to the governor of Syria, but Felix keeps the case, almost certainly because the accusers are Judeans and Judea is his patch. It is a small procedural moment, and it decides where Paul spends the next two years of his life.

I will give you a hearing when your accusers arrive. A reasonable ruling from an unreasonable man, and the last sensible thing Felix does. He will hold the hearing, find nothing, and then leave Paul in custody anyway — partly to please the Jewish leadership, partly in hope of a bribe (24:26–27).

And he commanded him to be guarded in Herod's praetorium.

The building matters. This is the seaside palace Herod the Great built at Caesarea, taken over as the Roman governor's residence. Paul is not thrown into a common cell; he is held in the guardroom of a palace, and later Felix gives orders that he should have some liberty and that his friends be allowed to see to his needs (24:23).

So look at where the chapter has arrived.

It opened with a man being punched in the mouth by order of the high priest, in the supreme court of his own nation, before he had finished a sentence. It ends with him under guard in a Herodian palace by the sea, alive, formally documented as charged with nothing, his accusers summoned to a Roman court, and the whole machinery of the empire slowly turning in the direction the Lord named in a barracks two nights ago.

And yet nothing is resolved. He is still a prisoner. He is fourteen hundred miles from Rome. Two years are about to disappear in this palace — two years of a mission-driven man's life, with no journeys, no new churches, no visible fruit, in the custody of a governor waiting for money that will never come.

Hold both halves together, because this is where most Christian lives are actually lived. The promise is certain and the waiting is long. The Lord said Rome, and he meant it, and the next thing on the schedule is twenty-four months of apparently wasted time in a nice room by the sea.

Paul does not know that Luke will be with him, or that the voyage is coming, or that he will preach unhindered in the capital of the world for two years at the end of it. He knows one sentence, spoken in the dark by someone who stood beside him: take courage. On some days that is the entire visible foundation of a Christian life, and it holds, because of who said it.

23.title: The Plot and the Providence
23.text: <sup>1</sup>And looking intently at the council, Paul said, “Brothers, I have lived my life before God in all good conscience up to this day.” <sup>2</sup>And the high priest Ananias commanded those who stood by him to strike him on the mouth. <sup>3</sup>Then Paul said to him, “God is going to strike you, you whitewashed wall! Are you sitting to judge me according to the law, and yet contrary to the law you order me to be struck?” <sup>4</sup>Those who stood by said, “Would you revile God’s high priest?” <sup>5</sup>And Paul said, “I did not know, brothers, that he was the high priest, for it is written, ‘You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.’” <sup>6</sup>Now when Paul perceived that one part were Sadducees and the other Pharisees, he cried out in the council, “Brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. It is with respect to the hope and the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial.” <sup>7</sup>And when he had said this, a dissension arose between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and the assembly was divided. <sup>8</sup>For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit, but the Pharisees acknowledge them all. <sup>9</sup>Then a great clamor arose, and some of the scribes of the Pharisees’ party stood up and contended sharply, “We find nothing wrong in this man. What if a spirit or an angel spoke to him?” <sup>10</sup>And when the dissension became violent, the tribune, afraid that Paul would be torn to pieces by them, commanded the soldiers to go down and take him away from among them by force and bring him into the barracks. <sup>11</sup>The following night the Lord stood by him and said, “Take courage, for as you have testified to the facts about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome.” <sup>12</sup>When it was day, the Jews made a plot and bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they had killed Paul. <sup>13</sup>There were more than forty who made this conspiracy. <sup>14</sup>They went to the chief priests and elders and said, “We have strictly bound ourselves by an oath to taste no food till we have killed Paul.” <sup>15</sup>Now therefore you, along with the council, give notice to the tribune to bring him down to you, as though you were going to determine his case more exactly. And we are ready to kill him before he comes near.” <sup>16</sup>Now the son of Paul’s sister heard of their ambush, so he went and entered the barracks and told Paul. <sup>17</sup>Paul called one of the centurions and said, “Take this young man to the tribune, for he has something to tell him.” <sup>18</sup>So he took him and brought him to the tribune and said, “Paul the prisoner called me and asked me to bring this young man to you, as he has something to say to you.” <sup>19</sup>The tribune took him by the hand, and going aside asked him privately, “What is it that you have to tell me?” <sup>20</sup>And he said, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though they were going to inquire somewhat more closely about him. <sup>21</sup>But do not be persuaded by them, for more than forty of their men are lying in ambush for him, who have bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they have killed him. And now they are ready, waiting for your consent.” <sup>22</sup>So the tribune dismissed the young man, charging him, “Tell no one that you have informed me of these things.” <sup>23</sup>Then he called two of the centurions and said, “Get ready two hundred soldiers, with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen to go as far as Caesarea at the third hour of the night. <sup>24</sup>Also provide mounts for Paul to ride and bring him safely to Felix the governor.” <sup>25</sup>And he wrote a letter to this effect: <sup>26</sup>“Claudius Lysias, to his Excellency the governor Felix, greetings. <sup>27</sup>This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them when I came upon them with the soldiers and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman citizen. <sup>28</sup>And desiring to know the charge for which they were accusing him, I brought him down to their council. <sup>29</sup>I found that he was being accused about questions of their law, but charged with nothing deserving death or imprisonment. <sup>30</sup>And when it was disclosed to me that there would be a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once, ordering his accusers also to state before you what they have against him.” <sup>31</sup>So the soldiers, according to their instructions, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris. <sup>32</sup>And on the next day they returned to the barracks, letting the horsemen go on with him. <sup>33</sup>When they had come to Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they presented Paul also before him. <sup>34</sup>On reading the letter, he asked what province he was from. And when he learned that he was from Cilicia, <sup>35</sup>he said, “I will give you a hearing when your accusers arrive.” And he commanded him to be guarded in Herod’s praetorium.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The forty assassins failed. The lawyers very nearly succeed. This chapter is the second attempt on Paul's life, and it is conducted entirely within the law, by respectable men, in courteous language.

The prosecution (vv. 1–9). The high priest travels sixty miles to a Gentile city and hires a professional advocate. Tertullus opens by thanking Felix for the peace of the province — a governor who had crucified insurgents in numbers and, Josephus says, arranged the murder of a former high priest. Then three charges: Paul is a plague; he stirs up riots throughout the world (sedition, the one charge Rome would kill for); he is front man of the sect of the Nazarenes; and he tried to profane the temple. The second charge is the dangerous one because it is built on a true fact with a false cause attached — riots really did follow Paul everywhere. Whether he lit them or simply turned the lights on is the question the accusation is designed to skip. The delegation then affirms it all, which is a chorus, not a witness list.

The missing verse (v. 8). Your ESV runs verse 6 straight to verse 8. That is not a misprint, and the explanation is worth having once: the verse numbers were added in 1551 to a text based on late manuscripts, older copies were found afterwards that lack this material, and translators follow the older evidence while keeping the old numbering so cross-references still work. The footnote at the foot of your page prints what is missing. Nothing of substance turns on it — and the fact that you can read the variant in your own Bible is a mark of honesty, not of weakness.

The defence (vv. 10–21). No advocate, no flattery — one true sentence of courtesy, and then arithmetic. Twelve days in the country, all of it checkable. No one found him disputing or gathering a crowd anywhere, and neither can they prove the charges. The eyewitnesses from Asia who started the riot have not travelled; the men who did travel saw nothing. Then he stops defending and starts confessing: he worships the God of the fathers, believes everything in the Law and the Prophets, and holds the hope of a resurrection of both the just and the unjust — a phrase nobody asked for, laid down in open court, which will go off eleven verses later in the governor's own conscience.

The adjournment (vv. 22–23). Felix knew more about the Way than anyone arguing in front of him, and could see there was no case. He neither convicts nor releases. He asks for more information — when Lysias comes down — and there is no record that Lysias was ever sent for. The custody is generous: friends may come and go freely.

The private hearing (vv. 24–25). Felix sends for Paul with Drusilla, a Jewish princess of twenty whom he had taken from her husband. They want to hear about faith in Christ Jesus. They get righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment — aimed, in that order, at a judge on the take, at the marriage in the room, and at a man who had never expected to be judged by anyone. Felix is terrified, and says later.

The two years (vv. 26–27). He hopes for a bribe, sends for Paul often, hears the gospel repeatedly, and is hardened by it. Then he is recalled, and leaves Paul in prison as a parting favour to men he had spent six years mistreating. It did not even buy him the goodwill he wanted.
verseByVerse.theology:
Almost Persuaded: the Sin of the Postponed Decision

Felix is the most quietly terrifying figure in Acts, because nothing about him is dramatic. He does not oppose the gospel. He is interested in it. He understands it accurately (v. 22), he sends for the preacher repeatedly (v. 26), and on the first hearing it frightens him badly enough to end the meeting. He is the nearest thing in this book to a man under conviction — and he dies outside of Christ, so far as Scripture records, with nothing standing between him and the kingdom except a word: later.

Scripture never treats delay as neutral ground. Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts (Heb. 3:15); behold, now is the day of salvation (2 Cor. 6:2). The reason is visible in this very chapter: Felix felt more at the first conversation than at any of the many that followed. Repeated exposure without submission does not keep the heart tender; it callouses it. The second hearing of a truth is always easier to survive than the first.

This is why the Reformed tradition has insisted that conviction is not conversion. Felix's fear was real and it was the Spirit's work on his conscience — and a frightened conscience saves nobody. What God requires is not to be moved but to be surrendered. Grace is sovereign and grace is free, and the same doctrine that says no one comes unless the Father draws him says also that whoever comes will never be cast out (John 6:37, 44). The only sane response to a conviction you can feel is to act on it while you can still feel it.

Alongside Felix stands Paul, and the contrast is the chapter's argument. One man is free and cannot decide; the other is in chains and settled to the point of cheerfulness (v. 10). One postpones; the other has already been told he must testify at Rome and simply waits. Circumstance is a poor guide to who in a room is actually at liberty.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul was asked, by the man who could have freed him with a sentence, to speak about faith in Christ Jesus. He was a prisoner, entirely in that man's power, and the governor's known weaknesses were a court that could be bought and a wife he had taken from another man. Paul chose righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment. He did not trim one of the three, and he stayed in prison for two more years.

Now: Most Christians will never address a governor, and nearly all of us will at some point have something true to say to somebody who holds an advantage over us — an employer, a relative whose goodwill we need, a friend whose reaction we fear. The pressure is not usually to lie. It is to select: to say the two things that will land well and leave out the third, and to call the omission tact. Ask what your version leaves out, and then ask why it is always the same one. Paul's three subjects took ten seconds to choose and cost him two years, and Luke thought them worth recording precisely because he did not shorten the list to two.

verseByVerse.quote: "And after five days the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a spokesman, one Tertullus. They laid before the governor their case against Paul. And when he had been called, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying: 'Since through you we enjoy much peace, and since by your foresight, most excellent Felix, reforms are being made for this nation,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And after five days the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a spokesman, one Tertullus.

Read that sentence as a measure of how badly they want this.

Ananias is the high priest of Israel. Caesarea is sixty miles from Jerusalem, two days on the road, and it is a Gentile city — Herod's showpiece, with a temple to Augustus on the hill and pagan statuary in the streets. He goes anyway. He takes a delegation of elders with him. And he hires a professional.

This is the same man who, five days ago, ordered Paul struck in the mouth before he had finished a sentence (23:2). He has had to come down from his own chamber, in his own city, where he was the law, to stand in a Roman audience hall as a plaintiff — and to pay an advocate to speak for him, because in this room his office means nothing at all.

Tertullus is a rhetor: a hired courtroom speaker, trained in the standard structure every advocate used. And he begins where every trained speaker began — with the exordium, the opening designed to secure the judge's goodwill before a single fact is mentioned.

Since through you we enjoy much peace, and since by your foresight, most excellent Felix, reforms are being made for this nation…

Now weigh that against the record, because it is not a small exaggeration. It is a lie told to a man who knew it was a lie.

Felix had governed Judea for around six years, and the province had rarely been less peaceful. He had put down the revolt of the Egyptian prophet — the man the tribune mistook Paul for on the barracks steps (21:38). He had crucified insurgents in numbers. Josephus records that he arranged the murder of the former high priest Jonathan, who had been pressing him to govern better, by hiring assassins who mingled with the crowd at a festival. Under Felix the sicarii — the dagger-men — became a permanent feature of Jerusalem life.

The Roman historian Tacitus summed his governorship up in a sentence that has outlived every speech Tertullus ever made: he wielded the power of a king with the instincts of a slave.

So the high priest of Israel sits and listens while his paid advocate thanks a murderer for the peace.

Luke writes the flattery out in full, and he does not add a word of comment. He does not need to. He simply lets the reader hear the opening of the case, and then, fourteen verses later, lets him hear Paul open his — and the difference between the two men is audible in their first sentence.

There is a quiet test in this for anyone who has ever been praised in terms he knew were not true. Flattery is not a compliment; it is a transaction. It is offered because the flatterer wants something and has judged that you will pay for it in goodwill. Felix took the payment. He sat there and let a delegation from a nation he had bled thank him for their tranquillity, and he did not correct them.

And the question that follows is not whether people flatter you — they will — but what it costs you to accept it. Every time a man swallows praise he knows to be false, he loses a little of his ability to hear the truth from anybody, including from God.

verseByVerse.quote: "'in every way and everywhere we accept this with all gratitude. But, to detain you no further, I beg you in your kindness to hear us briefly.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But, to detain you no further, I beg you in your kindness to hear us briefly.

The last note of the exordium, and a formula so standard it was almost furniture: the promise of brevity, the appeal to the great man's forbearance. The word rendered kindness is epieikeia — the quality of a judge who does not press the law to its harshest edge. It was a Roman virtue, and it flattered Felix by assuming he possessed it.

Two sentences of praise, and then Tertullus turns and asks the court to destroy a man.

What is worth noticing here is how ordinary all of this is. There is nothing lurid about the machinery being assembled against Paul. No conspiracy in a cellar, no forty men under an oath — that failed. This is the second attempt, and it is entirely respectable: a lawful summons, a professional advocate, a formal hearing, correct procedure, courteous language.

The forty assassins could not lay a finger on him. The lawyers very nearly did.

Persecution rarely arrives dressed as persecution. It arrives as a properly constituted committee, a correctly worded complaint, a hearing conducted in the appropriate register by people who are unfailingly polite. Everyone in the room is behaving well. That is precisely what makes it work.

And Luke gives Tertullus his full flattery, unedited, before he gives us a word of Paul's reply. He is confident enough in the truth to let the other side's best speaker go first and go uninterrupted. A book that is nervous about its case does not do that.

One more thing is worth noticing before the charges land, because it will matter when Paul stands up.

Tertullus says we throughout — we accept this, we beg you, we have found this man. He is a hired speaker from outside the community, quite possibly not a Jew at all, and he has been in the case a matter of days. The we is a professional's fiction, and everyone in the room knows it.

Paul, when his turn comes, will say I. I went up to worship. I take pains. This I confess. He has no delegation behind him, no advocate beside him, and nobody to share the sentence if it goes badly.

That is very often the shape of it. Opposition arrives as a body, with a spokesman and a collective voice and the comfort of numbers. Faithfulness usually has to be done in the first person singular, by somebody standing up alone and speaking for himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For we have found this man a plague, one who stirs up riots among all the Jews throughout the world and is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes. He even tried to profane the temple, but we seized him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we have found this man a plague, one who stirs up riots among all the Jews throughout the world and is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes. He even tried to profane the temple, but we seized him.

The flattery is over and the indictment lands. There are three charges, and it is worth taking them one at a time, because the construction is expert.

First, the man himself. The word is loimos — a plague, a pestilence. Not this man is troublesome, but this man is a disease. It is the language you use about something to be eradicated rather than answered, and it is always the first move: before you can do something terrible to a man, you have to stop describing him as one.

Second, sedition. Stirring up riots among all the Jews throughout the world. The Greek word behind riots is stasis — insurrection, civil disorder — and this is the charge that could actually kill Paul, because it is the one thing Rome genuinely cared about. Rome did not mind what you believed. Rome minded a province that would not stay quiet. Notice too the reach of it: throughout the world. Tertullus is not accusing Paul of a local disturbance; he is describing an empire-wide agitator, a travelling source of unrest in every city with a Jewish quarter.

And here is the thing that makes the charge so hard to answer: it is built on a true fact with a false cause attached. Riots really did follow Paul. There was one at Pisidian Antioch, one at Iconium, one at Lystra, one at Philippi, one at Thessalonica, one at Ephesus, and one in the temple ten days ago. Any Roman clerk could pull the file. What Tertullus does is take that undeniable pattern and reverse the arrow: the trouble happens where Paul goes, therefore Paul makes the trouble.

That is the oldest and most effective form of slander there is, and it is nearly unanswerable, because the facts underneath it are all correct. A quiet town gets loud when the gospel arrives. Whether the preacher is the arsonist or the man who turned the lights on is exactly the question the accusation is designed to skip.

Third, the sect. A ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes. The word for ringleader is protostates — literally the man who stands in the front rank of the line. And sect is hairesis, a party or faction; it is the same word used of the Sadducees and Pharisees, but in this mouth it means an unlicensed splinter group with no protection in law.

Nazarenes is the sting. It is the only time in the New Testament that Christians are called this, and it is not a compliment — it names them after a village so obscure and so disregarded that a man from the next region could ask, Can anything good come out of Nazareth? (John 1:46). They are being labelled the followers of a nobody from nowhere.

Which is the truth, and it is glorious, and neither Tertullus nor anyone else in that hall had the faintest idea. The carpenter's town is the address heaven answers to. The risen Lord had named himself by it from the middle of a light that outshone the noon sun — I am Jesus of Nazareth (22:8) — and he has not stopped. Men still use it as an insult. He wears it as a name.

Fourth, the temple. He even tried to profane the temple, but we seized him. This is the one charge with teeth in both legal systems: Rome had granted the Jews the right to execute even a Roman citizen who went past the barrier into the inner courts. It is also the charge that has quietly shrunk. In the temple it was a flat assertion that he had brought a Greek in and defiled the place (21:28). Here it is that he tried.

They have had five days to find a witness, and the charge has already begun to soften.

verseByVerse.quote: "'By examining him yourself you will be able to find out from him about everything of which we accuse him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Open an ESV at this page and something looks wrong. The text runs verse 6, and then verse 8. There is no verse 7. It is not a printing error, and Old Joe deserves a proper answer rather than a shrug, because a Bible that appears to have lost a verse is unsettling.

Here is what happened, and it is worth understanding once, because you will meet it again.

The chapter and verse numbers in your Bible are not part of Scripture. They were added centuries later — the verse divisions we use come from a Paris printer, Robert Estienne, in 1551 — and he numbered the Greek text that was available to him, which was based on a handful of late medieval manuscripts. Since then, far older manuscripts have been found: copies centuries closer to the apostles. In a number of places those older copies are shorter, because over the years a scribe here and there had added a clarifying line into the margin, and a later copyist had folded the margin into the text.

This is one of those places. The oldest and best manuscripts of Acts go straight from we seized him to by examining him yourself. Translators follow the older evidence — but they keep the old numbering, so that every commentary, concordance and cross-reference printed in the last four hundred years still works. The result is a number with nothing under it.

What does the missing material say? The ESV prints it in a footnote at the bottom of the page: and we would have judged him according to our law. But the chief captain Lysias came and with great violence took him out of our hands, commanding his accusers to come before you.

So it is Tertullus complaining that the Roman tribune snatched Paul away from a court that would have handled him properly. No doctrine hangs on it. Nothing in the Christian faith stands or falls with it. If it is original, it is one more piece of Tertullus's spin — describing a rescue from a lynch mob as an outrageous interference, which is exactly the kind of thing a hired advocate would say. If it is not original, some early reader thought the story needed the explanation and wrote it in the margin.

Now the important part, because the instinct at this point is to feel that the ground has moved: this is not evidence that the Bible is unreliable. It is evidence of the opposite.

We are able to see this variant precisely because we have so many manuscripts — thousands of them, from many centuries and many countries — that scholars can lay them side by side and watch exactly where and when a line entered the stream. No other document from the ancient world is attested anything like as richly. And notice what the translators do with it: they print it at the bottom of the page, in your own copy, where you can read it. A book with something to hide does not publish its own variant readings in a footnote for the ordinary reader to check.

You have met this twice already in Acts and will meet it once more. The most famous is 8:37 — the Ethiopian's confession, I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God — a lovely sentence, and a later addition. There is 15:34, about Silas remaining at Antioch. And 28:29 lies ahead. In every case the footnote is there, and in no case does anything of substance change.

By examining him yourself you will be able to find out from him about everything of which we accuse him.

That is the genuine verse 8, and it is the shrewdest sentence in the speech.

Tertullus has three charges and no witnesses. So he does what an advocate does when the evidence is thin: he hands the work to the judge. Examine him yourself — you will find it all out. It sounds like confidence. It is the opposite. Under Roman procedure the burden lay on the accuser to prove his charge, and Tertullus has just invited the governor to go and find the proof for him, because he has not got any.

And there is an irony here that Luke leaves lying in the open. Tertullus's advice was taken. Felix did examine Paul — repeatedly, over two years, sending for him often (v. 26). What he found out was not sedition. He got a sermon on righteousness, self-control, and the judgment to come, and it frightened him out of the room.

verseByVerse.quote: "The Jews also joined in the charge, affirming that all these things were so."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jews also joined in the charge, affirming that all these things were so.

The delegation adds its voice. Everyone agrees. And that is the whole of their contribution to the proceedings: agreement.

It is worth holding these two things apart, because a courtroom is one of the few places that insists on the distinction and ordinary life almost never does. Consensus is not evidence. Not one of the men affirming this was in the temple court when Paul was seized. The people who were there — the Jews from Asia who started the riot by pointing at him and shouting — are not in this room, and Paul is about to say so with some force (v. 19).

So what Felix is being offered is a chorus. A number of respectable men, including the high priest, all saying that yes, it is so. No one who saw anything. No one who can be questioned about what he saw.

Luke's word for what they do is a legal one — they joined in the attack, piling on to the accusation. It has the flavour of a crowd rather than a witness list.

Run the test on the way things actually reach you. Almost everything you believe about people you have not met arrived exactly like this: not from someone who saw it, but from several people who all say the same thing. And the fact that they say the same thing feels like corroboration, when very often it only means they all heard it from the same place.

The defining feature of gossip is not that it is false. Sometimes it is not. The defining feature is that the person who actually saw it is never in the room — and that nobody notices, because so many people are nodding.

And there is one more layer, which is the saddest in the verse. These men are not lying in the way a criminal lies. Most of them almost certainly believe every word. They have been told by people they trust that Paul is an apostate who defiles the temple, and they have arrived at a conclusion the way most of us arrive at most of ours — by inheriting it from a source we never audited.

Sincerity is not innocence. A man can be entirely honest and entirely wrong, and do enormous damage while behaving well throughout. Paul knew that better than anyone in the room: he had once held these exact convictions, with a clear conscience, on the way to Damascus with warrants in his bag.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when the governor had nodded to him to speak, Paul replied: 'Knowing that for many years you have been a judge over this nation, I cheerfully make my defense. You can verify that it is not more than twelve days since I went up to worship in Jerusalem,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the governor had nodded to him to speak…

No advocate stands up for Paul. He has no Tertullus. A nod from the bench, and a prisoner in chains begins to speak for himself.

Knowing that for many years you have been a judge over this nation, I cheerfully make my defense.

Set that beside the speech that has just finished, because the contrast is the point, and Paul has clearly made a decision about it.

He does not flatter. There is not one word here about peace, or foresight, or reforms, or Felix's benevolence. What he offers instead is a single sentence of genuine courtesy that happens to be entirely true: you have been judging this nation for a long time. That was a fact — six years or so, longer than most — and it was relevant, because it meant Felix could actually assess a Jewish religious dispute rather than being baffled by it.

So Paul is respectful and Paul is honest, and he shows that these are not in competition. He does not sneer at the court, and he does not buy it. There is a way to address a powerful and corrupt man that neither grovels nor postures, and it consists mostly of refusing to say anything untrue.

Then there is the word cheerfully — euthymos, in good spirits, with a settled heart. Consider who is saying it. This is his third hearing in under a fortnight. He has been beaten by a mob, chained, nearly flogged, ambushed by a murder plot, moved sixty miles under armed guard at night, and he is standing in a Gentile hall listening to the high priest of Israel pay a man to call him a plague. And he is in good spirits.

That is not temperament. Twelve days ago the Lord stood by him in the dark and said take courage, and told him he would testify at Rome (23:11). A man who knows the assignment holds can afford to be cheerful in a courtroom, because the courtroom is not the thing that decides.

You can verify that it is not more than twelve days since I went up to worship in Jerusalem.

And now the facts, and Paul starts with arithmetic, because arithmetic can be checked.

Twelve days. Count them off the record: the arrival and the welcome from the brothers, the meeting with James and the elders the following day, the four men and the purification rites, the arrest in the temple towards the end of the seven days, the night in the barracks, the council, the night march to Antipatris, the arrival at Caesarea, and five days waiting for the prosecution to arrive.

Now set that number against the charge. Tertullus has accused him of stirring up riots among all the Jews throughout the world. Paul's answer is that he has been in the country a week and a half, and that the governor's own staff can confirm every day of it.

Notice, too, the last three words: he went up to worship. Not to organise, not to agitate, not to lead a movement. He came to keep a feast and to bring money to the poor, and both of those are checkable as well.

verseByVerse.quote: "'and they did not find me disputing with anyone or stirring up a crowd, either in the temple or in the synagogues or in the city. Neither can they prove to you what they now bring up against me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they did not find me disputing with anyone or stirring up a crowd, either in the temple or in the synagogues or in the city. Neither can they prove to you what they now bring up against me.

Paul takes the charge apart with a list of places. Not in the temple. Not in the synagogues. Not anywhere in the city. He names every venue in which an agitator would have to have been seen agitating, and challenges them to produce one person who saw it.

Then the sentence that is the hinge of the whole defence: neither can they prove to you what they now bring up against me.

Under Roman procedure that was decisive. The burden lay on the accuser, and an accuser who brought a charge he could not sustain was not merely disbelieved; he could himself be liable for it. Paul is not asking for mercy or for the benefit of the doubt. He is pointing at an empty table and asking the court to notice that nothing has been put on it.

There is something bracing in the plainness of it. Paul does not begin with theology. He begins with: bring the evidence. Christianity has never asked to be exempted from that question, and it should never want to be. The faith is a set of claims about things that happened in public — a man executed under a named governor, a tomb found empty, witnesses who could be interrogated and were. Paul's own summary of the resurrection appearances says that most of the five hundred were still alive and could be asked (1 Cor. 15:6). That is not the language of a religion that wants to be taken on trust.

But the honest edge of this cuts both ways, and it is worth saying plainly. Paul can demand proof because there is nothing to find. A Christian accused of something he has actually done may not hide behind procedure — and the church has done exactly that, more than once, and brought the name of Christ into disrepute doing it. The right to say prove it belongs only to the man who could survive the investigation.

Which is why the small verse that comes a few lines later matters so much: I always take pains to have a clear conscience toward both God and man (v. 16). That is what makes verse 13 sayable. Paul's defence in this court rests on a life lived so that a subpoena would be boring.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But this I confess to you, that according to the Way, which they call a sect, I worship the God of our fathers, believing everything laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets, having a hope in God, which these men themselves accept, that there will be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But this I confess to you, that according to the Way, which they call a sect, I worship the God of our fathers…

Here the defence stops being legal and becomes testimony, and Paul signals the change with one deliberate word. I confess — homologo, the verb for openly acknowledging what you believe, the word the New Testament uses for confessing Christ before men. He has spent four verses saying you cannot prove that. Now he says: but here is what I will happily admit to, and I will say it louder than you did.

Watch what he concedes and what he refuses. The Way, which they call a sect. He will not accept their word — hairesis, a faction, a splinter group. He will not deny the reality behind it either. Yes, this is the Way, and yes, I belong to it, and no, it is not a breakaway.

Then the claim itself, and it is enormous: I worship the God of our fathers. The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Not a new god. Not an import from Greece. Not a revision. Paul is standing in a Roman court telling the high priest of Israel that the man in chains is the one worshipping Israel's God properly.

Believing everything laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets. Everything. Not the parts that suit him. This is a direct answer to the rumour that started all the trouble back in chapter 21 — that he taught Jews to forsake Moses. His answer is that he believes more of the book than his accusers do, not less, and that the difference between them is not that he has subtracted anything but that he has seen it arrive.

That is the sentence to hold on to whenever someone suggests Christianity is a departure from the Old Testament. Paul's position is not that the Law and the Prophets have been superseded. It is that they have been kept.

Having a hope in God, which these men themselves accept, that there will be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust.

And here Paul does something that ought to make the reader sit forward, because he is not only defending himself. He is laying a fuse.

Note first the generosity: which these men themselves accept. He grants his accusers their orthodoxy. The Pharisees in the delegation believe in the resurrection; so does he; on this they are together, and he says so in open court rather than scoring the point.

Then note what he adds, because it is the one phrase nobody asked for. Of both the just and the unjust.

This is the only place in Acts where Paul spells out that the resurrection is not only for the righteous. It is Daniel's vision — many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt (Dan. 12:2) — and it is the Lord's own teaching: an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, some to the resurrection of life and some to the resurrection of judgment (John 5:28–29).

Now ask why Paul says it here, in a defence speech, to a Roman governor who has asked him no question about eschatology.

Because Felix is listening. And eleven verses from now, when Felix sends for him privately and asks to hear about faith in Christ Jesus, Paul will reason with him about the coming judgment — and Felix will be terrified. The charge was laid in open court, in front of everyone, dressed as a point of Jewish doctrine. It goes off later, in a private room, in the governor's own conscience.

There is a test in that phrase for anybody, and it is not complicated. Most people, asked whether they believe in life after death, will say something warm. Very few have taken in the second half of the sentence. The resurrection is not a reward reserved for the deserving; it is universal. Everyone gets their body back. The question the Bible puts is never will you rise? but what will you rise to?

And consider the God whose hope this is. He has been the God of our fathers for two thousand years by the time Paul says it in that hall, and he has not changed his mind, or lost the thread, or grown tired of the promise. He spoke to Abraham about a family and to Daniel about the dust waking, and he kept every word of it, and the keeping of it was a grave outside Jerusalem that could not hold what was put in it. The God of the fathers is the God of the empty tomb. The hope of Israel and the risen Christ are not two things, and no court in the world had jurisdiction over either.

verseByVerse.quote: "'So I always take pains to have a clear conscience toward both God and man. Now after several years I came to bring alms to my nation and to present offerings,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I always take pains to have a clear conscience toward both God and man.

The word behind take pains is askeo. It is the athlete's word: to train, to work at something by discipline and repetition, the root that gives us ascetic. Paul is not describing a placid disposition. He is describing a practice.

That is worth pressing, because a clear conscience is usually imagined as something you either have or do not, like a good night's sleep. Paul treats it as something you build, daily, the way a runner builds a season — by keeping the accounts short. He does not let things accumulate. When something goes wrong with God he deals with it; when something goes wrong with a person he deals with that too, and he says toward both God and man because he knows perfectly well that people try to settle the first while leaving the second standing.

You met this claim eleven verses ago in a different room, and it got him hit in the mouth: Brothers, I have lived my life before God in all good conscience up to this day (23:1). He has not retreated from it. He says it again, in front of the men who were there.

And it is the quiet foundation under the whole defence. Paul can invite investigation, name every venue, and challenge the court to produce a witness, because he has spent thirty years making sure there would be nothing to find. A man who trains at this can afford to be examined.

Now after several years I came to bring alms to my nation and to present offerings.

This is a remarkable half-verse, and most readers go straight past it.

Paul is talking about the collection — the relief fund he had been gathering for years from the Gentile churches of Macedonia and Achaia and Galatia for the poor believers in Judea. It dominates his letters. He gives it two whole chapters in 2 Corinthians, organises it in 1 Corinthians 16, and tells the Romans that it is the reason he is going to Jerusalem at all (Rom. 15:25–28). It was the great project of his later ministry: hard currency carried across the empire by a committee of Gentile Christians, to prove that the church was one body and not two.

And in the whole book of Acts, this is the only time it is mentioned — in a single clause, in a courtroom, in a list of things Paul did in Jerusalem.

Luke's silence about it is its own lesson in how differently a thing can look from inside and outside. For Paul this was years of correspondence, delicate negotiation, and personal risk. For Luke it is a subordinate clause. Much of the work that costs a Christian most is recorded nowhere, summarised by somebody else in half a line, and known in full only to God.

There is a bitter irony in it too. He came to bring money to the poor, and it is the reason he is standing in the dock. And the mention of alms in open court may well have been the moment a thought entered Felix's head, because two verses from the end of the chapter we are told what the governor was really hoping for: that money would be given him by Paul (v. 26).

Paul's generosity toward the poor of Jerusalem bought him two years in a cell, because a corrupt man heard the word alms and concluded there must be a fund.

verseByVerse.quote: "'While I was doing this, they found me purified in the temple, without any crowd or tumult. But some Jews from Asia — they ought to be here before you and to make an accusation, should they have anything against me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
While I was doing this, they found me purified in the temple, without any crowd or tumult.

Every word of that is a charge being dismantled. They accused him of profaning the temple: he was purified, ritually clean, in the middle of the very rites that prove it. They accused him of stirring up riots: there was no crowd and no tumult until his accusers created one.

The prosecution's own picture of the scene has been quietly reversed. Paul was standing quietly in a holy place, having completed a purification he paid for out of his own pocket, when men who had come from Asia pointed at him and started shouting.

But some Jews from Asia—

And then the sentence breaks off. Luke leaves the dash in. Paul, mid-flow, stops and changes direction, and what he says next is the sharpest legal thrust of the whole speech.

They ought to be here before you and to make an accusation, should they have anything against me.

Here is the hole in the case, and Paul walks the governor straight to the edge of it. The men who actually saw the alleged offence — the Jews from Asia who recognised him, who assumed he had brought Trophimus past the barrier, who seized him and raised the shout (21:27–29) — are not in the room. They have not come the sixty miles. They are the only eyewitnesses in existence, and the prosecution has arrived without them.

Under Roman law that was not a small gap. An accuser was expected to appear and prosecute; abandoning a charge you had raised was itself an offence. Paul is saying, in effect: the people who made this accusation have dropped it, and the men standing here in their place did not see anything.

Notice the fairness in his phrasing, too — should they have anything against me. He does not claim they are lying. He says: if they have a case, let them come and make it. That is the confidence of a man who would rather be examined than excused.

And that is the test worth taking away. Almost every reputation ever damaged has been damaged by an accusation whose original source never appeared. Somebody said something to somebody, and it travelled, and by the time it reached you it had four confirmations and no author. Paul's question is the only one that matters and the one almost nobody asks: where is the person who actually saw it, and why are they not here?

verseByVerse.quote: "'Or else let these men themselves say what wrongdoing they found when I stood before the council, other than this one thing that I cried out while standing among them: "It is with respect to the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you this day."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or else let these men themselves say what wrongdoing they found when I stood before the council…

Having disposed of the absent witnesses, Paul turns to the men who are present. Very well — you were there at the Sanhedrin five days ago. You are the ones with first-hand knowledge of that hearing. Tell the governor what crime you established.

It is a dare, and it is safe, because he knows exactly what happened at that meeting: it collapsed into a brawl between Pharisees and Sadducees and never reached a finding at all. He is inviting them to describe their own most recent failure to the judge.

Other than this one thing that I cried out while standing among them: It is with respect to the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you this day.

And with that, Paul does something worth stopping over, because it settles a question the reader may still be carrying from the last chapter.

When he shouted that line in the council, it looked to many people like a manoeuvre — a clever man splitting his enemies by throwing a doctrinal bone between two factions who could be relied on to fight over it. Was it a trick?

Here is the answer. Five days later, under oath, in a Roman court, in front of a governor who cannot be split and a delegation who cannot be provoked, with nothing whatever to gain from repeating it — he repeats it. He not only stands by the sentence; he offers it to the court as the single accurate summary of the entire case.

A trick is something you use once and quietly drop. Paul will say this again to Festus, again to Agrippa, and finally to the Jewish leaders of Rome at the very end of the book: it is because of the hope of Israel that I am wearing this chain (28:20). It was never a tactic. It was the truth, and it happened to be a truth that broke the room.

And notice what he has now done to the charge sheet. Tertullus brought three counts: sedition, sect-leading, temple desecration. Paul has answered all three and reduced the case to one sentence about whether the dead are raised.

He has, in effect, told a Roman governor: the entire proceeding is a religious dispute about the resurrection, and you have no jurisdiction over that. He is right, and Felix knows he is right, which is exactly why the next thing that happens is not a verdict.

verseByVerse.quote: "But Felix, having a rather accurate knowledge of the Way, put them off, saying, 'When Lysias the tribune comes down, I will decide your case.' Then he gave orders to the centurion that he should be kept in custody but have some liberty, and that none of his friends should be prevented from attending to his needs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Felix, having a rather accurate knowledge of the Way, put them off.

Luke's aside is easy to skim and it is the key to the man. The phrase is a comparative — akribesteron, more accurately — and it means Felix understood the Christian movement better than the people arguing in front of him.

That is not a guess on Luke's part. Felix had governed Judea for years. The church had been in Caesarea since Cornelius, and Philip the evangelist lived there with his four daughters (21:8). His own wife was a Jewish princess. This governor knew who the Nazarenes were, knew they were not a band of insurrectionists, and could see that the prosecution had produced no evidence for anything.

So Felix knew. And Felix did nothing.

He does not convict Paul, because he cannot. He does not release Paul, because that would cost him with the Jewish leadership. He finds a third option, and it is one of the most recognisable moves in human affairs: he asks for more information.

When Lysias the tribune comes down, I will decide your case.

It sounds like diligence. It is a formula. There is no record that Lysias ever came down, no indication that Felix ever sent for him, and no sign in the following two years that the tribune's testimony was ever thought necessary again. The adjournment was not a step towards a verdict; it was a substitute for one.

This is the sin of this chapter, and it does not look like a sin at all. Felix is not cruel to Paul. He is scrupulously reasonable. He simply declines to act on what he already knows, and he dresses the refusal in procedure — and because the procedure is real, nobody can accuse him of anything.

Most of us are far more likely to fail this way than any other. Not by deciding against the truth, but by finding a legitimate reason to postpone deciding for it. There is always one more person to consult, one more consideration outstanding, one more sensible reason why now is not the moment. Felix invented nothing; he just never got round to it, on purpose, for two years.

Then he gave orders to the centurion that he should be kept in custody but have some liberty, and that none of his friends should be prevented from attending to his needs.

The terms are unusually generous. The word for liberty is anesis — a loosening, a relaxation of the conditions. Paul is not in a dungeon. He is in the governor's own palace complex under guard, permitted visitors, and his friends may come and go and bring him whatever he needs.

And it is worth pausing on what that arrangement made possible. For the next two years Paul is in one place, in a Roman provincial capital, with time and with free access to his companions. Luke is with him, and Luke has a Gospel to research and a second volume to write, in a country full of people who had been there — Philip, four doors away, who had known the church since chapter 6; Caesarea's own believers; anyone who could reach the coast.

Scripture does not tell us that this is where the research was done, and it would be wrong to state it as fact. But the two years are not blank, and the God who gave a discouraged prisoner a comfortable cell with an open door and a doctor for company was doing something, even while the governor was doing nothing at all.

verseByVerse.quote: "After some days Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish, and he sent for Paul and heard him speak about faith in Christ Jesus. And as he reasoned about righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment, Felix was alarmed and said, 'Go away for the present. When I get an opportunity I will summon you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
After some days Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish.

Luke names her, and the name carries a history that makes the next two verses almost unbearable.

Drusilla was the youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa I — the king who executed James with the sword and was struck down at Caesarea for accepting the shout that he was a god (12:1–23). It happened in this city. She was six. Her brother is Agrippa II and her sister Bernice, and both of them will walk into this same palace two chapters from now to hear this same prisoner. Her great-grandfather was Herod the Great, who ordered the children of Bethlehem killed.

She is about twenty years old, and she is a Jew, and she is on her second marriage. She had been given to King Azizus of Emesa. Josephus records that Felix, wanting her, employed a Cypriot magician named Atomos to work on her until she left her husband and married the governor instead.

So here they sit: a Roman official whose court was for sale, and a young Jewish princess living with him in a marriage her own law did not recognise. And they send for the prisoner, because they would like to hear him speak about faith in Christ Jesus.

It is a request for an interesting evening. What they get is verse 25.

And as he reasoned about righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment…

Three subjects. Look at who is in the room, and then look at them again, because this is the most precisely aimed sermon in the book of Acts.

Righteousness — dikaiosyne, which is both the character God requires and the justice a judge is supposed to dispense. Preached to a magistrate who was at that very moment hoping the defendant would offer him a bribe (v. 26).

Self-control — enkrateia, mastery of one's own appetites. Preached to a man with the woman he had taken from another man sitting at his side.

The coming judgment — krima to mellon. Preached to the most powerful man in the province, who had spent his life as the one who judges and had never seriously considered being judged.

Paul is a prisoner. Felix can hold him for two years without charge, and does. And Paul looks at the man who owns his freedom, and at the marriage everyone at court had agreed not to mention, and preaches righteousness, self-control, and the judgment to come.

He was asked to explain faith in Christ Jesus, and this is how he did it. That is worth noticing, because it is not how most of us would have gone about it with a governor. Paul did not begin with comfort or with benefits. He began where the New Testament habitually begins with the comfortable and the powerful: with the standard, the failure to meet it, and the day it will be assessed. There is no good news in a pardon until there is bad news in a verdict.

Felix was alarmed.

The Greek says he became emphobos — filled with fear. This is not irritation, and it is not intellectual disagreement. The governor of Judea, sitting in his own palace with his own soldiers outside the door, listening to a man in chains, became frightened.

Nothing in the room had changed. No sign was given, no miracle done. A prisoner talked, and the word of God found the conscience of a man who had buried it, and he could not sit still under it.

The most dangerous word in Felix's reply is 'later': 'Go away for the present. When I get an opportunity I will call for you.' He was alarmed — genuinely under conviction — yet he postponed, and so far as Scripture records, the convenient season never came (he left Paul in prison two years, still angling for a bribe, vv. 26–27). Here is a solemn lesson for every hearer: conviction delayed is conviction deadened, and the 'convenient season' for repentance almost never arrives on its own. The Bible's word is always now: 'Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts' (Heb. 3:15); 'now is the day of salvation' (2 Cor. 6:2). To say 'later' to Christ is the most natural thing in the world, and one of the most perilous.

verseByVerse.quote: "At the same time he hoped that money would be given him by Paul. So he sent for him often and conversed with him. When two years had elapsed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. And desiring to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the same time he hoped that money would be given him by Paul. So he sent for him often and conversed with him.

Luke gives the real reason, and it is squalid. The governor was angling for a bribe.

It was illegal, and it was routine, and Felix had reason to think it possible: he had heard Paul mention in open court that he had come to Jerusalem bringing alms for his nation (v. 17). A man who can carry a relief fund across the empire can presumably find a purse for a governor. Somewhere behind this is a calculation that Paul's friends would pay to end it.

They never did, and Paul never offered, and that silence is worth a moment. A payment would have been the easy and obvious thing — arguably even a reasonable thing, since the imprisonment was unjust and everyone knew it. Two years of a man's life and the whole Gentile mission were on the other side of the scale. He did not do it. There are things a servant of Christ cannot buy his way out of without ceasing to be one.

So he sent for him often and conversed with him.
